en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory" (Jaya). Om! Salutations to that Blessed One, Vyāsa, of immeasurable splendor.
By whose grace I shall recount the auspicious narrative of Nārāyaṇa. [Omnis] Then, what would be the condition of the world, blinded by the darkness of ignorance? Janamejaya said:
"O best of beings, I desire to hear the divine story of Maya,
as well as the assembly hall constructed by him for the wise Dharmarāja.
Janamejaya said:
Protected by Kṛṣṇa and by Agni himself, as well as by Pārtha of immeasurable splendor, the great Asura named Maya performed various deeds that served as a source of conviction for the Pāṇḍavas.
"Tell all that, O Blessed One, to the giver of life, Kirīṭin. Janamejaya said:
"Arjuna, the best among victors, having then liberated Maya,"
"O best of the twice-born, tell me what that one of great splendor did next.
Listen attentively, O King, to the account of your ancestor:
having liberated Maya there, Pārtha, the foremost of weapon-bearers,"
The Gāṇḍīva, the best of bows; two quivers with inexhaustible arrows;
divine weapons, O Indra among kings, which are difficult for rulers on earth to obtain;
and the chariot’s banner and flags—along with the white horses, the heroic one [remained].
Having obtained these from the Purifier (Agni), the immensely powerful Pārtha stood there filled with supreme joy along with Maya.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Maya, having been rescued by the Pāṇḍava, spoke to the son of Pṛthā in the presence of Vāsudeva; remembering what had been done for him,
he honored him again and again with folded hands and gentle words.
"O son of Kuntī, I have been saved by you from this enraged Kṛṣṇa and from the fire that desired to consume me. Tell me, what may I do for you?
For I am indeed Viśvakarman, O scorcher of foes, the architect of the Asuras."

"Therefore, I shall perform some feat that is very difficult for others to accomplish; you should not be amazed. Having been addressed thus, the highly heroic Pārtha, the son of Kuntī, reflected for a moment upon Maya, the master of illusions, and then spoke these words with a smile.
Arjuna said:
"Everything has already been accomplished by you; go in peace, O great asura!
May you always be well-disposed toward me, and may we also be well-disposed toward you."
"Indeed, it is my vow that I shall not take wealth from one who has already received assistance.
Maya said:
"O Lord, O bull among men, what you have said is entirely fitting for you."
"O Bhārata, out of affection, I desire to do something for you.
For I am indeed Viśvakarman, the great architect of the Dānavas;
as such, O Pāṇḍava, I wish to perform some service for your sake."
O Pārtha, in ancient times, I indeed constructed for the Dānavas thousands of palaces—
delightful, pleasant to behold, and rich in enjoyments— as well as beautiful gardens and various lakes.
And there were various weapons, as well as chariots that travel at will; vast cities with their palaces, ramparts, and gateways;
and thousands of diverse, preeminent vehicles.
"These caves are indeed delightful and exceedingly pleasant;
all of these have been prepared by me. Therefore, O Phalguna, I desire [to stay here].
Arjuna said:
"You consider yourself liberated from the peril to your life by me;
since things have come to this pass, I am unable to compel you to do anything.
Nor, O Dānava, do I wish for your resolve to be in vain."
"O Vāsudeva of auspicious countenance, let some service be done for Kṛṣṇa; what do you wish me to do for him in return?"
Vaiśampāyana said: O bull of the Bharatas, being thus urged by Maya, Vāsudeva reflected for a moment as to what he should be asked.
Having reflected upon the skillful artistry in heaven, Maya spoke;
then, having pondered with his mind, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World and Prajāpati, urged him, saying, "Let a hall indeed be constructed."
"O best among artisans, O son of Diti, if you wish to do what is pleasing to the King of Dharma,
then build such a hall as you deem fit here— one that cannot be attained by any human being."

Construct such an assembly hall that neither asuras, nor humans, nor gods, nor gandharvas, nor even rākṣasas could replicate it; indeed, let all men in this entire world of mortals stand amazed upon beholding it.
"O Maya, build that assembly hall where we may behold the divine designs ordained by you, as well as those of the Asuras and humans. Having accepted those words, Maya was then filled with great joy.
With joy, he fashioned the assembly hall of the Pāṇḍava so that it resembled a celestial chariot.
Then Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, having reported all this to the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira, showed him the work of Maya.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira offered him worship as was fitting;
the lord prepared a seat for him and honored him. Maya, having been honored in return, accepted that hospitality with due respect.
O lord of the people, O King, O Bhārata, that son of the Daityas, Maya, being greatly delighted, recounted there in detail the former deeds of the gods and of the Pāṇḍava among the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Having rested for a short while and reflected deeply, Viśvakarman set about constructing an assembly hall for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
in accordance with the intentions of the sons of Pṛthā and the great-souled Kṛṣṇa.
On an auspicious day, the highly effulgent and valiant one, having performed the rites of auspiciousness and having gratified thousands of the best of the twice-born with milk-rice (pāyasa),
bestowed upon them various kinds of wealth.
Having performed all the prescribed rites in this manner, he circumambulated [the city],
which was endowed with the excellences of all seasons, divine in form, and enchanting; indeed,
it was filled with throngs of people, multitudes of chariots, and various modes of transport and draft animals.
He measured it out on all sides as ten thousand *kiṣkus*.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having dwelt happily in Khāṇḍavaprastha, Janārdana—

Honored with worship by the sons of Pṛthā, who were filled with affection, he— worthy of veneration and longing to see his father— set his mind on departing. Then the large-eyed one took leave of Dharmarāja and Pṛthā.
He who is worshipped by the world bowed his head at the feet of his father’s sister;
and Keśava was smelled upon the crown of his head and embraced by her.
Immediately thereafter, the highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa beheld his own sister.
Approaching her, Hṛṣīkeśa, filled with joy and moved by tears,
spoke these words— meaningful, true, beneficial, concise, appropriate, and unsurpassed—
to the auspicious Subhadrā, who herself speaks auspiciously.
By her, he was made to hear words concerning his own kinsmen;
he was honored repeatedly and saluted with a bow of the head.
Having taken leave of that beautiful woman and having greeted her in return, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi departed.
Immediately thereafter, Janārdana saw Kṛṣṇā and Dhaumya as well;
that best of men paid homage to Dhaumya according to custom,
and after consoling Draupadī and taking his leave, Janārdana departed.
Accompanied by Pārtha, the wise and powerful one approached his brothers;
Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the five brothers like Śakra by the immortals,
performed the rites appropriate for the time of departure, he whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Desiring to depart, Kṛṣṇa— the best among those who stand— became pure, bathed, and well-adorned;
having taken leave of Pṛthā, Kṛṣṇā, and Dhaumya, that Supreme Person set forth.
That bull among the Yadus honored the gods and the twice-born with garlands,
prayers, prostrations, and various kinds of fragrances;
having performed all his duties, that best of those who stand firm set forth.
Having approached and emerged from the outer courtyard, that best of the Yadus caused the worthy brahmins to pronounce blessings, honoring them with vessels of curd, fruits, and unbroken grains;
and having bestowed wealth upon them, he then circumambulated them.
Then, having had auspicious rites performed by Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas,
he mounted a swift golden chariot bearing the emblem of Tārkṣya,
and equipped with weapons such as the mace, discus, sword, and Śārṅga bow.
Then, on a lunar day, under a constellation, and at a moment endowed with auspicious qualities,
the lotus-eyed one set forth, drawn by his chariot horses Sainya and Sugrīva; and King Yudhiṣṭhira also ascended after him out of affection.
Then the Lord of the Kurus himself took up the reins from Dāruka, the best of charioteers, whom he had set aside;
and Arjuna, having also ascended, took up a white yak-tail fan.
He brandished a large golden-handled [weapon] over his head, moving it clockwise;
likewise, the self-controlled and heroic Bhīmasena, accompanied by the twins,
mounted the chariot.
Bhīma swiftly held up for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow that parasol with its hundred ribs, adorned with celestial garlands, possessing a handle of lapis lazuli, and embellished with gold.
Having quickly ascended the chariot,
Nakula and Sahadeva fanned Janārdana with two white yak-tail whisks,
as did Bhīmasena and Arjuna.
Followed behind Kṛṣṇa, the officiating priest was surrounded by the citizens;
thus, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, shone as he was followed by his brothers,
like a preceptor by his beloved disciples.
Then Dhaumya, that bull among Brahmins, surrounded by the elders, placed Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā, upon his chariot and set out;
having traveled about a *krośa* beyond Indraprastha, the one of great luster—
Having addressed Pārtha and embraced him while he was overcome with emotion, Govinda honored Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and the twins as well;
he was in turn firmly embraced by those two and saluted by the twins.
Then, having made an agreement with them in the proper manner, Madhusūdana Kṛṣṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, traveled half a *yojana* and,
O Bhārata, addressed Yudhiṣṭhira, saying, "Please turn back."

Then Govinda, the knower of dharma, having offered his salutations, grasped the feet [of Yudhiṣṭhira]. But Dharmarāja, the Pāṇḍava, having raised Keśava up and smelled the crown of his head, [honored] Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed one, the best of the Yādavas.
Having obtained permission with the words "You may go," Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira then turned back the Pāṇḍavas along with their followers;
Kṛṣṇa then departed for his own city like a second Purandara.
Then the Pāṇḍavas followed that best of the Yādavas, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, with their eyes as long as he remained within the range of their vision;
and they followed Kṛṣṇa with their minds, filled with affection.
While their minds remained unsatiated with the sight of Keśava,
Śauri, whose appearance was so dear to behold, quickly vanished from their eyes.
Though they were unwilling to part, those Pārthas had their hearts entirely fixed upon Govinda.
Having returned, all those bulls among men went to their own city;
then Kṛṣṇa also, by means of his chariot, arrived at Dvārakā at the appointed time,
accompanied by the heroic Sātvata who followed behind him.
Accompanied by his charioteer Dāruka, the son of Devakī—
Vaiśampāyana said—
He, Viṣṇu, went to Dvārakā with the speed of Garuḍa.
Having returned with his brothers, the steadfast Dharmarāja,
the king surrounded by his friends, entered that best of cities;
then the Dharmarāja dismissed all his friends, brothers, and sons.
O King, that tiger among men rejoiced together with Draupadī; Keśava too, filled with joy, entered that best of cities while being honored by the foremost of the Yadus, headed by Ugrasena.
Having saluted his aged father Āhuka and his illustrious mother, as well as Balarāma, the lotus-eyed one stood there;
likewise, he greeted Pradyumna, Sāmba, Niśaṭha, Cārudeṣṇa, and Gada.
Having embraced both Aniruddha and Bhānu, Janārdana,
permitted by the elders, went to the palace of Rukmiṇī;
and that illustrious Maya also [prepared] a hall adorned with all kinds of jewels.
He duly prepared an assembly hall for the son of Dharma.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Maya spoke to Pārtha Arjuna, the best among victors.
"I take my leave of you; I shall depart, and I will return quickly.
I am going toward Mount Maināka, north of Kailāsa, at which time all the Dānavas are to perform sacrifices for me."

"O Bhārata, I shall go there and return having taken that beautiful vessel made of jewels which belonged to Vṛṣaparvan, who was true to his word, and which was kept in his assembly hall at Bindusaras, provided it still remains there."
O Pārtha, O Dhanañjaya, I shall construct for you a divine assembly hall, renowned throughout the three worlds,
which will cause wonder among all living beings and increase the joy of you and all the Pāṇḍavas.
"Therefore, I shall construct for the illustrious Pāṇḍava an assembly hall that gladdens the mind, wonderful, and adorned with every kind of jewel.
O best of the Kurus, there exists at Lake Bindu a preeminent mace."
This bow, which destroys enemies, was fashioned by King Yauvanāśva after he had slain his foes in battle;
it is variegated with golden spots, heavy, capable of bearing great weight, firm,
and constructed from a thousand *bhāra*s of gold.
That bow, equal to a hundred thousand [other bows], capable of destroying all enemies,
and worthy of Bhīma, is just as the Gāṇḍīva is yours;
and there is the great conch Devadatta, belonging to Varuṇa, which possesses a magnificent sound.
"I shall give all this to you; there is no doubt about this.
Having spoken thus, O Pārtha, that asura departed toward the north-eastern direction, heading northward from Kailāsa toward Mount Maināka.

The blessed mountain, with its golden peaks and composed of great jewels, is there; and there is the delightful lake named Bindusaras, where King Bhagīratha dwelt for many years after beholding the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Bhagīratha.
O best of the Bharatas, it was there that the high-souled Lord of all beings performed a hundred principal sacrifices;
there, the sacrificial posts were made of jewels and the altars were made of gold.
These were established there for the sake of beauty, and not created as mere illustrations;
it is there that the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī attained perfection after performing sacrifice,
and where the eternal Lord of Beings, having created all the worlds, [resides].
There, the one of fierce splendor is worshipped by thousands of beings,
where all the sages seeking liberation, beginning with Nārada, perform their sacrifices;
[there dwell] Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Yama, and Sthāṇu as the fifth.
Where, at the transition of a thousand yugas, they perform a sacrificial session (*sattra*),
and where Vāsudeva, ever full of faith for the sake of the instruction of the virtuous, performed sacrifices for thousands of years.
O Bhārata, having gone there, Keśava took up a mace and a conch shell— there where he had given thousands and millions of sacrificial posts adorned with golden garlands and extremely radiant altars.
From that mountain, he took beautiful and auspicious stones,
as well as all the crystal materials that had belonged to Vṛṣaparvan;
he took it all along with the *kiṃkara* demons.
Then the great asura Maya went there and took it all;
having brought that back, the asura constructed an incomparable assembly hall,
divine, made of jewels, auspicious, and renowned throughout the three worlds.
Then he gave an excellent mace to Bhīmasena,
and to Pārtha he gave the unsurpassed conch Devadatta,
by whose sound all living beings trembled.
O Great King, that assembly hall had trees made of gold;
it was ten thousand *kiṣkus* in extent on all sides,
and it was just like the abodes of Agni, Arka, and Soma.
Shining and divine, she bore a most excellent form;
as if striking down with her own radiance the brilliant light of the sun,
that celestial being gleamed as if ablaze with divine splendor.
Resembling a mountain cloud, it stands encompassing the sky—
long, vast, smooth, stainless, and free from fatigue;
endowed with the finest materials, it is garlanded by walls of jewels.
Abounding in jewels and great wealth, it was well-fashioned by Viśvakarman;
neither the Sudharmā hall of the Daśārhas nor even that of Brahmā was ever so endowed with beauty as this peerless structure which Maya fashioned.
Or from the high-souled Śambhu—
she who was exceedingly endowed with beauty;
there she was told by Maya, and they both guarded and carried her.
Eight thousand Rākṣasas named Kiṃkaras were in the assembly hall;
they moved through the air, were terrible, possessed massive bodies and great strength,
had red and tawny eyes, ears like shells, and were fierce strikers.
In that assembly hall, Maya fashioned a peerless lotus pond,
with leaves spread of lapis lazuli and lotuses made of jeweled stalks; it was filled with fragrant lotuses and frequented by flocks of various birds.
Variegated with blossoming lotuses and adorned with tortoises and fish, it possessed excellent landing-stairs, was free from turbidity, auspicious with waters flowing in all seasons,
and strewn with drops of pearl-like spray tossed up by the wind.
Some kings, having approached that [palace] which was encircled by a railing bound with slabs of great precious stones and strewn with jewels and gems,
did not recognize it even upon seeing it; through their ignorance, they fell down.
All around that assembly hall, there were always various kinds of great trees, blue-hued and beautiful, providing cool shade; and on every side there were fragrant groves and lotus ponds.
Filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and adorned by *cakravāka* birds,
the wind, taking up the fragrance of all kinds of aquatic and terrestrial flowers, attended upon the Pāṇḍavas.
Those eight thousand Rākṣasas named Kiṃkaras,
armed with iron weapons and holding spears and mallets in their hands,
surrounded them and danced, seeking to delight the Pāṇḍavas.
Having constructed such an assembly hall— encircled by a wall and adorned with a lattice of jewels— in fourteen months,
Maya announced its completion to King Dharmarāja.
Having constructed that most excellent assembly hall, Maya said to Arjuna:
"O you of great prowess, a host of servants shall be at the tip of your banner;
they will roar like a cloud at the sound of your stretching the bowstring."
For this is the supreme chariot of Jvalana, resembling the sun;
and these are the divine, white, and powerful best of horses.
Indeed, this banner bearing the mark of a monkey has been fashioned through illusion.
Unattached to the trees, rising high like a banner of smoke,
his many-colored standard bearing the emblem of a monkey will surely be seen;
for you shall behold that preeminent and unsurpassed banner firmly stationed in battle.
Having said this and embraced Bībhatsu, Maya took his leave and departed.
"O Savyasācin, this assembly hall shall be yours, and this banner shall be your foremost.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira,
the lord of men, caused her to enter [the city] and fed ten thousand Brāhmaṇas with ghee,
milk-rice, honey, various edibles, as well as roots and fruits.
With unwashed garments and various kinds of garlands,
the lord gave thousands of cows to each of them; O Bhārata, the sound of the proclamation of the auspicious day there seemed to touch the very heavens.
With various musical instruments and songs, with diverse perfumes,
as well as with foods, roots, fruits, and meats of boar and deer,
and furthermore with *kṛsara*, *jīvantī*, and all kinds of sacrificial oblations (*haviṣya*).

O King, having honored the deities by offering various kinds of meat, as well as diverse foods to be chewed, O King, and many varieties of things to be sucked and drunk in great abundance, that best of the Kurus established them there.
He gratified the foremost of Brahmins who had assembled from various directions.
There, wrestlers, actors, jhallas, bards,
and panegyrists waited upon the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira for seven nights.

Having thus performed that worship together with his brothers, the Pāṇḍava took delight in that beautiful assembly hall, just as Śakra does in heaven. In that assembly hall, the ṛṣis sat together with the Pāṇḍavas.
And the lords of men, gathered from various lands, performed these [rites]:
Asita, Devala, Satya, Sarpamālin, Mahāśiras,
Arvāvasu, Sumitra, Maitreya, Śunaka, and Bali.
Ātreya, Kaṇva, Jaṭhara, Maudgalya, Hastika, Kāśyapa, Baka Dālbhya, Sthūlaśiras, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Śuka,
Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and likewise we ourselves— the disciples of Vyāsa.
Tittiri, Yājñavalkya, Lomaharṣaṇa with his son,
Satyāṣāḍha, Durvāsas, as well as Bhāradvāja, Śunaḥśepha, Vasiṣṭha, Kaṇḍu, and likewise Uddālaka.
Śvetaketu, Saha, Kapardin, Āśvalāyana,
Bodhāyana, Bharadvāja, and likewise Āpastamba; Apsuhomya, Dhaumya, Āṇi, Māṇḍavya, and Kauśika.
Dāmoṣṇīṣa, Traivaṇi, Parṇāda, Ghaṭajānuka,
Mauñjāyana, Vāyubhakṣa, Pārāśarya, and the two Sārikas;
Balavāka, Śinīvāka, Sutyapāla, and Kṛtaśrama.
Jātūkarṇa, Śikhāvat, Subala, Pārijātaka, the highly blessed Parvata, as well as the sage Mārkaṇḍeya,
Pavitrapāṇi, Sāvarṇi, Bhālukī, and Gālava.
Jaṅghābandhu, Raibhya, Kopavegaśravas, Bhṛgu, Haribabhru, Kauṇḍinya, Babhrumālī, Sanātana,
Kakṣīvān Auśija, Nāciketa, and Gautama.
Paiṅga, Varāha, Śunaka, and the great ascetic Śāṇḍilya;
Karkara, Veṇujaṅgha, Kalāpa, and Kaṭha; as well as Śārṅgarava, Tailakūpya, and likewise Parṇavalka.
These sages, endowed with righteousness, self-controlled, and masters of their senses— these and many others who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
these best of ṛṣis wait upon that Great-Souled One in the assembly hall.
Engaging in meritorious discourse, pure, stainless, and knowledgeable in the Dharma,
the best of Kṣatriyas likewise wait upon Dharmarāja. So too does the illustrious, high-souled, and righteous Muñjaketu, the increaser of his lineage.
Saṃgrāmajit, Durmukha, and the heroic Ugrasena; Kakṣasena the lord of the earth, Kṣemaka the unconquered,
Kamala the king of the Kambojas, and the mighty Kampana.
He alone, endowed with strength and prowess, skilled in weapons and possessed of immeasurable energy, constantly caused the Yavanas to tremble—
just as the wielder of the thunderbolt, the god Indra, did to the Kālakeya Asuras.
Jaṭāsura and the king Madrakānta;
Kunti, Kuṇinda, and the king of the Kirātas; likewise Aṅga and Vaṅga together with Puṇḍraka.
The Pāṇḍya and Udra kings together with the Andhraka; Jaṭāsura and King Madraka; Kunti and Pulindaka;
the king of the Kirātas, as well as the lord of Vaṅga along with the Puṇḍra.
And the great king Pāṇḍya was [conquered] by the high-souled Andhraka;
as were Aṅga, Vaṅga, Sumitra, and Śaibya, the crusher of enemies;
as well as Sumanas, the king of the Kirātas, and the lord of the Yavanas.
Pāñcāla, Virāṭa, Drumashalya, Pṛthuśravas, Cāṇūra, Devarāta, Bhoja, Bhīmaratha,
Śrutāyudha the Kāliṅga, and Jayatsena the Māgadha.
Suśarman, Cekitāna, Suratha— the crusher of enemies— Ketumān, Vasudāna, Vaideha, Kṛtakṣaṇa,
Sudharmā, Aniruddha, and the mighty Śrutāyus.
The invincible Anūparāja, Kṣemajit, and Sudakṣiṇa; Śiśupāla with his sons, as well as the lord of Karūṣa;
and the two kings of Andhra together with Daṇḍadhāra—[these were] among the high-souled ones.
And the invincible youths of the Vṛṣṇis, possessing the forms of gods—
Āhuka, Vipṛthu, Gada, Sāraṇa,
Akrūra, Kṛtavarman, and Sātyaki, the son of Śini.
Then Bhīṣmaka, Āhṛti, and the heroic Dyumatsena;
the great archers of Kekaya, Yajñasena of the Somakas,
Ketumān, Vasumān, and the mighty Kṛtāstra, all skilled in weapons.
These and many other leading Kṣatriyas, highly esteemed,
used to wait upon Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, in the assembly hall;
and mighty princes also took refuge with Arjuna.
Clad in the skins of the ruru deer,
they trained in the science of archery; there, O King, the princes who were the delights of the Vṛṣṇis—
Raukmiṇeya, Sāmba, and Yuyudhāna Sātyaki— were likewise instructed.
Sudharmā, Aniruddha, and Śaibya, that bull among men—
these and many other kings, O lord of the earth,
waited upon Dhanañjaya, desiring to master the science of archery.
And Tumburu, the friend of Dhanañjaya, was always present there;
twenty-seven [Gandharvas] waited upon that high-souled one as he sat,
as did Citrasena with his ministers, along with the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
In that assembly hall he sat, surrounded by many attendants;
there were *kiṃnaras* who were skilled in song and instrumental music, experts in the rhythm of the *śamyā* and the *tāla*, and who had mastered the correct proportions and the placement of tempo.
Urged by Tumburu, the Gandharvas sang together;
those wise ones sang with divine melodies according to the proper method,
pleasing the deities, the sages, and the kings.
Skilled in the *śamyā* and *tāla* rhythms, and proficient in singing and instrumental music,
they attend upon and delight the sons of Pāṇḍu and the sages.
Hāhā, Hūhū, Parvata, Nārada, and Pṛthuśravas [are among them].
In that assembly hall, the hosts of Apsarases, led by Urvaśī, sing and dance; seated there, those of excellent vows who are true to their word attend upon Yudhiṣṭhira,
just as the gods in heaven attend upon Brahmā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, while those high-souled Pāṇḍavas were thus seated there, as were the great Gandharvas, [the following occurred].
He was a seer who knew the Vedas and Upanishads, honored by the hosts of gods;
he was a knower of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and one who understood the specific details of ancient kalpas.
He was a master of logic, a knower of the true essence of dharma, and unsurpassed in his knowledge of the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga).
He was an expert in unity, conjunction, diversity, and inherence; he was a bold speaker, wise, intelligent, possessed of a retentive memory, skilled in policy, a poet,
a knower of the distinction between the higher and the lower, and one who had reached certainty through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He was one who discerned the merits and defects of a five-membered syllogism, a superior debater even against Bṛhaspati himself as he spoke, and one who had attained correct certainty regarding virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
Likewise, the Great-minded One, who perceives directly this entire universe— the world horizontally, above,
and below— and who understands the distinctions of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, desired to instruct the gods and asuras.

He was one who knew the true principles of peace and war, understood the distinctions of inference, was skilled in the application of the sixfold policy, and was proficient in all the sciences; he was devoted to both warfare and the arts of music, and was likewise unimpeded in every respect.
Endowed with these and many other multitudes of virtues, the sage,
the seer Nārada of great splendor, then arrived at that assembly hall while wandering through all the worlds, accompanied by other rishis.
O king of kings, the celestial sage of immeasurable luster, accompanied by Parijāta, the wise Raivata, Sumukha, and Saumya,
traveled with the speed of thought, full of joy, to see the Pāṇḍavas seated in their assembly hall.

Having praised him with blessings of victory, the Brahmin honored Dharmarāja. Seeing that the sage Nārada had arrived, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, who knew all duties, suddenly rose up along with his younger brothers.
Then, bowing low with humility, he greeted him with affection; having offered him a seat worthy of him according to the prescribed rite,
he presented him with a cow, the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the water for honoring (*arghya*).
The knower of dharma honored him with jewels and all objects of desire;
and having received that worship from Yudhiṣṭhira, he was satisfied according to tradition.
Thus honored by all the Pāṇḍavas, that great seer had mastered the Vedas.
Nārada asked Yudhiṣṭhira this question, which was connected with dharma, kāma, and artha: Nārada said: "Is wealth being acquired appropriately, and does your mind delight in dharma?"

Pleasures are experienced and the mind is not distressed. O god among men, do you follow that undecaying way of life, consistent with dharma and artha toward people, which was practiced by your ancestors and grandfathers?
I hope that you do not obstruct Dharma with Artha, nor Artha with Dharma, nor both of them with mere pleasure, but rather with the essence of joy;
and I hope, O best among victors, that you pursue Artha, Dharma, and Kāma in harmony.

O knower of time, O giver of boons, do you always attend to [your duties] by dividing them according to the proper time? O sinless one, do you thoroughly examine the six royal qualities, the seven expedients, as well as strength and weakness— these fourteen factors?

O best among victors, O Bhārata, having examined both yourself and others, do you perform the eight duties after establishing [the proper] alliances? O bull of the Bharatas, are your six constituent elements not neglected?
Are they wealthy, free from vices, and entirely devoted to you? Is your secret counsel ever leaked by spies, by envoys, or even by those who are unsuspected—
whether by you, by your ministers, or by others?

Do you know what your friends, neutrals, and enemies intend to do? Do you employ peace and war at the appropriate times? And do you maintain proper conduct toward both the neutral and the intermediate powers?
O hero, have you appointed as ministers those who are pure, capable of enduring hardships, of noble birth, devoted to you, and equal to yourself in wisdom? For,
O Bhārata, the victory of kings is rooted in secret counsel.

Well-restrained by ministers who are experts in the treatises and rich in the wealth of counsel, O dear one, the kingdom is well-protected and is not plundered by enemies. Do you not fall under the power of sleep? Do you wake up at the proper time?
Do you, as one who knows what is meaningful, reflect upon your affairs during the latter part of the night?
Do you deliberate alone, or do you not deliberate with many? And does the counsel you have deliberated not leak out throughout the kingdom?
I trust that, having determined those matters which require little effort but yield great results,
you begin to carry them out quickly and do not allow such tasks to be obstructed.
I trust that none of your undertakings are conducted behind your back or cause you suspicion.
"Or perhaps, O Great King, it is out of your sight; for in this matter, moderation is praised.
Are those [officials] who are trustworthy, free from greed, and orderly being appointed by you?
Or have they all been dismissed? For in this matter, the cause is a matter of close connection."

O King, O hero, I trust that your deeds are already accomplished or nearly completed, and that there are none among them that remain unachieved? I trust that all your officials are experts in every branch of learning?
Do they cause the princes and the chief warriors to be trained in every respect?
Do you perhaps purchase a single wise man for a thousand fools?
For a wise man can bring about the highest good in times of financial crisis.
I trust that all your fortresses are fully supplied with wealth, grain, weapons, water, and machines, as well as with artisans and archers;
and that you have at least one minister who is intelligent, brave, self-controlled, and discerning?

It will bring great prosperity to a king or a prince. Do you keep watch over the eighteen [offices] among your enemies, and over the fifteen among your own side, through three secret spies for each of these, as you would at sacred fords?
O destroyer of enemies, I hope you remain unperceived by your foes, ever prepared, and constantly vigilant as you observe all your adversaries.
I hope that a son of noble family, endowed with discipline and great learning, [stands at your side].
Is your domestic priest free from malice, inquisitive, and honored by you?

Is he diligent regarding the sacred fires, knowledgeable in the ritual procedures, wise, and upright; and does he always inform you at the proper time regarding what has been offered and what is yet to be offered?

Is there an astrologer skilled in your service, one who is proficient in the limbs of the science and capable of explaining the movements of the luminaries, as well as all portents? Are the foremost men appointed to the greatest tasks, and those of middling rank to the middling ones?

Do you employ inferior servants in inferior tasks? And do you appoint ministers who have passed the tests of integrity, who are pure, and whose lineage extends back through father and grandfather— appointing the most excellent among them to the most important duties?

O bull of the Bharatas, do your ministers govern the kingdom without excessively agitating the subjects with harsh punishment? Do the officiating priests not despise you as they would one who has fallen from his status?

Is there no one in your kingdom who destroys your fame— such as one who accepts gifts with arrogance, like a woman lusting after a lover? Is there anyone who is bold, heroic, wise, steadfast, and pure?
Is your general of noble birth, devoted, and capable? Are all the leaders of your army skilled in warfare,
men of proven valor who have been honored and respected by you?

Do you provide the food and wages for your army as is appropriate when the time for them has arrived, rather than withholding them? For these retainers, through the delay of their food and wages, [become disaffected].
Out of misfortune, they become angry with their husband; that is remembered as a very great calamity.
I trust all the rulers of the earth bear your command upon their heads, and I trust all your friends honor you for your sake.
I trust that the women of the inner apartments have been attended to by you at the proper times; I trust that the queens of the royal palace give birth to sons worthy of their lineage—
princes who are righteous, heroic, and proficient in the duties of kingship.
Do you arrange the marriages of those sons for the sake of the continuity of your great lineage? O King, do you offer consolation to those who have come to you for refuge?

Do all the sons of noble family, preeminent among them, remain deeply devoted to you with minds free from stinginess, even when gods and others are utterly terrified? And do they always sacrifice their very lives for your sake in battle?
I hope that you, being self-centered and transgressing the teachings, do not instruct many people in all matters concerning the future life according to your own whims;
and I hope that as a man, you adorn your actions with human effort.

Do you grant them greater honor, or even more food and wages? And do you support with gifts those men who are disciplined by learning and proficient in knowledge, according to their merit and their qualities?
O bull among the Bharatas, do you support the wives of men who have met their death for your sake, or those who have fallen into calamity?
Do you support one who has surrendered out of fear, or a weak enemy who has come to you?
O Pārtha, you protect like a son that which has been won in battle; O lord of the earth, are you indeed impartial toward the whole world,
free from suspicion, and like a mother and like a father?

O bull of the Bharatas, having learned that your enemy is in distress, do you advance with speed after carefully assessing the threefold force? O subduer of foes, by good fortune you have begun your expedition at the opportune time.

O Great King, having ascertained the rear-guard, the resolve, and the potential for defeat, and having paid the wages to the army in advance, do you [inquire] among the leaders of the forces in the enemy kingdom, O scorcher of foes?
Do you bestow concealed treasures upon those worthy of them? Having first conquered yourself,
O Pārtha, do you— with senses mastered— seek to conquer others who are heedless and have not mastered their senses?

I trust that as you advance against your enemies, the four expedients— conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force— are being properly applied beforehand. O Lord of the People, I trust you set out on your expedition having first made your foundation firm.

You exert your prowess to conquer them, and having conquered, you protect them. Is your fourfold army, endowed with its eight constituent parts and well-led by the chief commanders, capable of repelling your enemies?
O scorcher of foes, O great king, do you strike down your enemies in battle without sparing even a blade of grass or a handful of grain belonging to another kingdom?
And are there many officials appointed by you throughout both your own and other kingdoms?
Do they carry out their duties and protect one another? O Great King, do they, with your permission, guard the foods to be consumed, the objects of bodily contact, and the things to be smelled?
I trust that your treasury, granary, mounts, gates, and weapons,
as well as your revenue, are being managed by devoted servants who have performed auspicious rites.
And I trust, O lord of people, that you are protected from both internal and external threats.
O protector, do they first guard themselves, and then those [others], both from their own kin and from one another?
Do they not, in the forenoon, acknowledge expenditures arising from vices— whether in drinking, gambling, sports, or with women— as being caused by addiction?
Is your expenditure being balanced by half of your income, or perhaps by a fourth part,
or even by three-quarters?
Do you [support] your kinsmen, elders, the aged, merchants, artisans, and those who depend upon you?

Do you constantly favor the destitute with wealth and grain? Are all your accountants and scribes diligent regarding income and expenditure, and do they always attend to your accounts in the forenoon?

I trust that you do not remove from their duties those who are experienced in affairs, who desire your welfare, and who are devoted to you, before they have incurred any fault. I trust that you recognize men as superior, inferior, or middling.
O Bhārata, you assign them to duties according to their respective capacities. O Lord of the People, I trust that those who are greedy, thieves, or enemies,
or those who have not yet attained legal majority, are not employed in your administrative tasks.
I hope the kingdom is not oppressed by greedy men, or by thieves, or by princes, or by the power of women, nor by yourself; and I hope the farmers are well-nourished.
And I hope the great reservoirs in the kingdom are full.
Are they distributed in their respective portions? Is agriculture not dependent solely upon the gods? Does the seed and the food of the cultivators suffer from want?
And do you grant loans at a rate of one percent interest as a favor?

"Are all those who depend on agriculture and cattle-rearing dear to you? O dear one, is the livelihood (*vārttā*) properly maintained by virtuous people? For this world prospers in happiness when it is supported by a sound livelihood."

O King, do the five wise [officials], having been purified and well-established in their duties, work together to ensure the security of your realm? And for the sake of protecting the city, have the villages been made like fortified towns?
Is protection provided for [your villages] as if they were single villages, and are all those people entrusted to them?
Do old thieves, accompanied by forces and supervised by officials, roam through your territory across both level and uneven ground?

Do you console the women, and are they well-protected? Do you not place undue trust in them, and do you not disclose secrets to them? Having heard reports from your spies at night and having reflected upon what must be done, [do you act accordingly]?

Experiencing pleasant things, you lie down knowing your people to be well-disposed; O lord of the people, having slept during the first two watches of the night, do you indeed rise during the final watch and reflect upon dharma and artha?
Do you constantly show yourself to men well-adorned,
rising at the proper time, O knower of the right moment, together with your ministers, O Pāṇḍava? Do [your guards] wear red garments, carry swords in their hands, and remain well-decorated?

O subduer of enemies, they wait upon you from all sides for the sake of protection. O lord of the people, do you conduct yourself with justice toward those deserving of punishment and those worthy of honor— whether they be unpleasant or pleasant— after having duly examined each case?

I trust you always dispel physical ailments through medicines or disciplined regimens, and mental afflictions by serving the elderly; and I trust that physicians skilled in the eightfold medical science attend to your treatment.
Your friends are devoted and always intent on your welfare;
O Lord of the People, do you not, out of pride, delusion, or even desire,
ever turn away those petitioners who have approached you as plaintiffs or defendants?
I trust that you do not, out of greed, delusion, misplaced confidence, or affection,
obstruct the livelihood of those people who have sought refuge with you. And I trust that you [employ] those who are mature in worldly affairs and skilled in the management of wealth.

Do you not withdraw those citizens and those inhabitants of the realm who are engaged in their duties, thinking "they are useful," lest they should somehow be bought over by enemies and turn against you?
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, is it that your weak enemy has been crushed by force, or some powerful one by counsel, or perhaps both?
And are all the rulers of the earth, especially the foremost ones, devoted to you?"
Do they sacrifice their lives for your sake, drawn by you?
Does your worship proceed according to merit in all branches of knowledge,
and does it bring auspicious welfare to the Brahmins and the virtuous?
"You constantly bestow sacrificial fees upon these [priests], which grant both heaven and liberation.
Are you, while abiding in the Dharma rooted in the Three Vedas as practiced by people of old,
likewise engaged in performing that very same duty?"

Do the twice-born, endowed with virtues, eat delicious and excellent food in your house under your supervision, accompanied by ritual fees? Are you single-mindedly performing all the Vājapeya sacrifices and other rites?
Do you, being self-possessed, strive to perform all the *puṇḍarīka* sacrifices in their entirety? Do you pay homage to your kinsmen, elders, the aged, the deities, ascetics,
sacred trees, and the auspicious Brahmins?
O sinless one, I hope that neither grief nor anger is being provoked by you; I hope that people with auspicious offerings in their hands attend upon you at your side.
O sinless one, I hope that this is your way of thinking and this is your mode of conduct.
This intelligence promotes longevity and renown, and it perceives dharma, pleasure, and wealth;
for one who conducts himself with this wisdom, the kingdom does not perish,
and having conquered the earth, that king prospers in ultimate happiness.
I hope that the noble one, pure of soul and innocent, is not being executed out of greed by those unskilled in the treatises, having been accused of the crime of theft;
for he was apprehended while questioned, found by experts to be the perpetrator, and seen with the evidence of the act.

O bull among men, I hope that a thief is not released due to greed for wealth. O Bhārata, I hope that your ministers, having been corrupted by riches, do not view the assets of the wealthy and the poor with partiality when they are being distributed.
Atheism, falsehood, anger, negligence, procrastination, not seeing those who possess knowledge, laziness, a distracted mind,
thinking about matters alone, and deliberating on goals with those who do not understand what is beneficial.

Do you avoid these fourteen faults of a king: failing to initiate decisive actions, failing to protect one's counsel, failing to employ auspicious rites, and excessive addiction to the objects of the senses?
By what means are kings generally destroyed, even when they have established firm roots?
Are your Vedas fruitful? Is your wealth fruitful? Are your wives fruitful? Is your sacred learning fruitful?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How indeed do the Vedas become fruitful? How indeed does wealth become fruitful? How indeed do wives become fruitful? And how indeed does sacred learning become fruitful?
Thus addressed by the king, Nārada, who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, spoke again in accordance with reality to the high-souled Dharmarāja. Nārada said:

"The fruit of the Vedas is the Agnihotra sacrifice; the fruit of wealth is giving and enjoying it; the fruit of a wife is pleasure and sons; the fruit of sacred learning is good character and conduct.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having related this, the sage Nārada, of great ascetic merit and righteous soul, immediately asked this of Yudhiṣṭhira. Nārada said:
I trust that merchants who have arrived from afar for the sake of profit are made to pay the toll exactly as prescribed by those who live off the tolls. I trust,
O King, that those men are honored in your city and throughout your kingdom.
Do they bring forth their wares without being deceived by fraudulent means?
And do you, my dear son, constantly listen to the words of the elders— who are experts in worldly affairs and who perceive the true nature of dharma— in accordance with both dharma and artha?

I trust that those appointed to oversee your agricultural operations, cattle, flowers, and fruits are skilled in those matters, knowledgeable in their distribution, and worthy of your family; and that honey and clarified butter are given to the twice-born for the sake of dharma?
Do you always provide the necessary materials and tools properly and regularly to all craftsmen at least once every four months?
Do you acknowledge their work and praise the artisan?
O Great King, you show honor and pay respect among the virtuous;
O bull of the Bharatas, do you master all the *sūtras*— the *sūtras* on elephants, the *sūtras* on horses, and the *sūtras* on chariots, O Lord?
O bull among the Bharatas, is the manual of archery (*dhanurveda-sūtra*), the manual of mechanical engines (*yantra-sūtra*), and that of the city (*nāgara*) constantly practiced in your home?
O sinless one, are all the divine weapons (*astras*) and the Brahma-staff (*brahmadaṇḍa*) mastered by you?
All those methods for the removal of poison, which destroy enemies, are known to you.
Do you protect your own kingdom from the fear of fire, as well as from the fear of snakes and predatory beasts, and from the fear of disease and malevolent spirits?
O knower of dharma, do you protect the blind, the mute, the lame, the deformed, and those without kin, as well as those who have gone forth into the religious life, like a father?
O Great King, I trust that the six adversities have been cast behind you.
Sleepiness, laziness, fear, anger, softness, and procrastination.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The high-souled bull among the Kurus [spoke these words]..."
Having heard the words of that best of Brahmins,
the king, joyful, bowed at his feet and saluted him, and spoke to Nārada, who possessed a divine form.
"I shall do exactly as you have said;
for my wisdom has indeed increased all the more.
Having spoken thus, the king acted accordingly.
And he obtained the earth girt by the oceans.
Nārada said:
"A king who conducts himself in this manner for the protection of the four social orders [attains such results]."
Having dwelt here in great happiness, he goes to the same world as Śakra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having been honored and permitted by the words of the great seer, he departed.
The Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira replied in due order:
"O Blessed One, you have spoken this determination of dharma correctly and justly;
according to my ability and in accordance with what is right, this ritual is performed by me."

Whatever was to be done by kings in the past, that remains exactly so, without doubt; it was performed with reason and purpose, according to the principles of justice. But we, O Lord, desire to follow the path of those who tread the way of truth.

"But it is not possible to go in the same manner as those of self-restraint have done. Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled one honored those words and [addressed] the celestial seer of immeasurable luster as he sat there at rest.

After a moment, seeing that the time was right and that the world-wandering sage Nārada was seated at ease, the high-minded Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira approached him and questioned him there in the midst of the kings.
"You constantly travel through many diverse worlds created by Brahmā in the past, observing them with the speed of thought.
Have you ever before seen such an assembly hall anywhere?"
"O Brahmin, tell me who am asking you whether there is anything superior to this.
Having heard those words spoken by the King of Dharma, Nārada replied to the Pāṇḍava with a smile and in a sweet voice:

"O dear one, among humans, neither have I ever seen nor heard of a council hall made of jewels such as this, O King, descendant of Bharata, which you possess. But [I have heard of] the halls of the King of the Ancestors and of the wise Varuṇa."
I shall describe the assembly hall of Indra, whose abode is Kailāsa,
and I shall describe the divine assembly hall of Brahmā, which dispels all fatigue—
divine, endowed with celestial designs, and possessing manifold forms.

O bull among the Bharatas, if your mind is inclined toward hearing it, [then listen to this land] which is frequented by gods, the hosts of ancestors, the Sādhyas, and sacrificers of self-restrained soul; and by peaceful throngs of sages, and by Vedic sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees.
Thus addressed by Nārada, the high-minded Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, with palms joined in reverence, surrounded by his brothers and all those kings,
replied to Nārada as follows.
"Tell us of all those assembly halls; we wish to hear of them.
O Brahmin, what materials are they made of, what is their width, and what is their length?
And who are those who sit in attendance upon the Grandfather in that assembly hall?"
Who are those who wait upon Vāsava, the king of the gods, and Yama Vaivasvata,
as well as Varuṇa and Kubera, in their assembly hall?
All this, O celestial sage, I wish to hear from you exactly as it is.
"We all desire to hear this, for our curiosity is great.
Thus addressed by the Pāṇḍava, Nārada replied to him:
"O King, let those divine assemblies be heard by us here in due order."
Nārada said:
"O Kauravya, the divine assembly hall of Śakra is radiant, won by his own deeds;
it was fashioned by Śakra himself and possesses a splendor equal to the sun."

It was a hundred yojanas wide and one hundred and fifty yojanas long; it moved through the air at will and rose five yojanas high. It was free from old age, sorrow, and fatigue, and was secure, auspicious, and beautiful.

O Pārtha, descendant of Bharata, in that assembly hall— which possesses rooms and seats, is delightful, and is adorned with celestial trees— the Lord of the Gods sits upon a supreme throne together with Śacī, the consort of Mahendra, as well as Śrī and Lakṣmī.
Wearing an indescribable form, crowned and with red armlets,
clad in spotless garments and adorned with variegated garlands, he dwells there together with modesty, fame, and splendor;
in that city, they constantly wait upon the high-souled Śatakratu.
O King, the Maruts from all sides, as well as all the householders,
the Siddhas, the celestial rishis, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of gods,
together with the Marutvats— resplendent and wearing golden garlands— were present there.
All these, together with their followers, possessing divine forms and well-adorned, wait upon the high-souled king of the gods, the subduer of enemies.
Likewise, O Pārtha, all the celestial sages wait upon Śakra.
Stainless, with their sins shaken off, they blazed like fires; full of splendor, joined with Soma, they were free from evil and devoid of weariness—
Parāśara, Parvata, as well as Sāvarṇi and Gālava.
The great sage Ekata, Dvita, and Trita; Śaṅkha, Likhita, and likewise the sage Gauraśiras;
Durvāsas, Dīrghatapas, Yājñavalkya, and Bhāluki.
Likewise, the sage Dīrghatamas,
Pavitrapāṇi, Sāvarṇi,
Uddālaka, Śvetaketu, and the lord Śāṭyāyana.
Haviṣmān, Gaviṣṭha, and the king Hariścandra; Hṛdya, Udarasāṇḍilya, Pārāśarya, and Kṛṣīvala;
Jābāli, Vāmadeva, Śakti, Gārgya, and Suvāmana.
Vātaskandha, Viśākha, Vidhātṛ, and Kāla; Anantadanta, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśvakarman, and Tumburu—
some born from a womb and some not born from a womb, subsisting on air and consuming the sacrificial oblations.
Sahadeva, Sunītha, and Vālmīki of great asceticism, as well as Samīka, Satyavān, and Pracetas who is true to his promise— all worship the wielder of the thunderbolt, the Lord of all the worlds.
Medhātithi, Vāmadeva, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marutta, Marīci, Sthāṇu, Atri of great asceticism,
Kakṣīvān, Gautama, Tārkṣya, and likewise the sage Vaiśvānara.
Ṣaḍartu, Kavaṣa, Dhūmra, Raibhya, Nala and Parāvasu, Svastyātreyi, Jaratkāru, Kahoḷa, as well as Kāśyapa,
Vibhaṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Unmukha, and Vimukha.
The sage Kālakavṛkṣīya, Āśrāvya, Hiraṇyada,
Saṃvarta, Devahavya, and the heroic Viṣvaksena;
Kaṇva, Kātyāyana, O King, Gārgya, and Kauśika as well.
The divine waters, as well as the medicinal herbs, faith, intelligence, and Sarasvatī; purpose, righteousness, desire, and the lightning flashes too, O Pāṇḍava;
the water-bearing clouds, the winds, and the thunders.
The eastern quarter, the sacrificial carriers, and the twenty-seven purifiers;
Agni and Soma, as well as Indra and Agni, Mitra, Savitṛ, Aryaman, Bhaga, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, Śukra, and Manthin, O Bhārata.
Śukra is likewise the venerable preceptor of all the Maruts;
so too are Viśvāvasu, Citrasena, Sumanas, and Taruṇa.
Furthermore, there are the sacrifices, the sacrificial fees, the planets, and the chanted hymns in their entirety.
And all those mantras that carry the sacrifice reside there;
likewise, O King, are the Apsarases and the charming Gandharvas— Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Menakā.
Ghṛtācī and Pañcacūḍā, led by Vipracitti; Viśvāvasu, Citrasena, Parvata, and Tumburu— these,
O king of kings, are the Vidyādharas.
With dance, instrumental music, song, and various kinds of laughter,
O King, they delighted Śatakratu, the king of the gods;
likewise, they praised him with hymns, auspicious rites, and ritual acts.
And all the Brahman-sages, royal sages, and celestial sages, by means of their heroic deeds, [honored] that high-souled slayer of Bala and Vṛtra,
arriving in various divine celestial chariots that shone like fires.
Some went wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments, while others arrived and departed;
Bṛhaspati and Śukra both came together to that assembly,
along with these and many others who were self-controlled and firm in their vows.

O King, by the word of Brahmā, Bhr̥gu and likewise the Seven Sages, possessing forms as pleasing to behold as the moon, travel in celestial chariots resembling the moon. O King, this assembly hall named Puṣkaramālinī was seen by me.
O great king, O sinless one, hear from me concerning the southern region of Śatakratu.
Nārada said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe that divine assembly hall; listen to it."
O King, Pāṇḍava, for the sake of Vaivasvata, Viśvakarman constructed that assembly hall made of refined gold; it was a hundred yojanas in extent, both in width and length, and even greater than that.
Radiant like the light of the sun, brilliant, and able to travel everywhere at will,
it was neither too cold nor too hot, but gladdened the mind. In it there was no sorrow, no old age, no hunger or thirst, and nothing unpleasant.
There was neither dejection nor fatigue, nor anything disagreeable;
all desires, both divine and human, were present there,
O subduer of enemies, along with abundant and flavorful food and drink.
There are foods to be licked, sucked, and drunk— heart-pleasing, sweet, and captivating.
There are garlands of holy fragrance, trees that bear flowers and fruit perpetually,
and waters both cool and warm, all full of flavor.
And there were various trees, ever-flowering and delightful; they were cool, beautiful, and pleasantly warm, O Bhārata. In that place dwelt meritorious royal sages as well as stainless Brahman-sages.
"O dear one,
Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Pūru, Māndhātṛ, Somaka,
Nṛga, Trasadasyu, Turaya, Kṛtavīrya, and Śrutaśravas— these rejoice as they sit in attendance upon Yama, the son of Vivasvat."
Aripraṇut, Susiṃha, Kṛtavega, Kṛti, Nimi, Pratardana, Śibi, Matsya, Pṛthvakṣa, and Bṛhadratha;
Aiḍa, Marutta, Kuśika, Sāṃkāśya, Sāṃkṛti, and Bhava.
Caturaśva, the king Kārtavīrya who was like a wave of excellent horses,
Bharata, Suratha, Sunītha, and Nala the king of Niṣadha;
likewise Bharata, Suratha, and King Taporatha.
Sunītha, Niśaṭha, King Nala the lord of Niṣadha,
Divodāsa, Sumanas, Ambarīṣa, Bhagīratha,
Lomapāda, Anaraṇya, Lohita, Pūru, and Udvaha.
Vyaśva, Sadaśva, Vadhryaśva, Pañcahasta, Pṛthuśravas,
Ruṣadgu, Vṛṣasena, and the exceedingly powerful Kṣupa; Ruṣadaśva, Vasumanas, Purukutsa, Dhvajin, and Rathin.
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Dilīpa, and the high-souled Uśīnara;
Auśīnara, Puṇḍarīka, Śaryāti, Śarabha, Śuci,
Aṅga, Ariṣṭa, Vena, Duḥṣanta, Saṃjaya, and Jaya.
Bhāṅgāsvari, Sunītha, Niṣadha, Tviṣīratha,
Karaṃdhama, Bāhlika, Sudyumna, the mighty Madhu,
Aila, and likewise Marutta, the powerful lord of the earth.
Kapotaroman, Tṛṇaka, Sahadeva, and Arjuna; likewise Vyaśva, Sāśva, Kṛśāśva, and King Śaśabindu;
as well as King Daśaratha, Kakutstha, and Pravardhana.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, as well as Lakṣmaṇa and Pratardana;
Alarka, Kakṣasena, Gaya, and Gaurāśva;
then Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, as well as Nābhāga and Sagara.
Bhuridyumna, Mahāśva, Pṛthvaśva, Janaka, as well as King Vainya, Vāriṣeṇa, Puruja, Janamejaya,
Brahmadatta, Trigarta, and likewise King Uparicara.
Indradyumna, Bhīmajānu, Gaya, Pṛṣṭha, Naya, Anagha,
Padma, Mucukunda, Bhūridyumna, Prasenajit,
Ariṣṭanemi, Pradyumna, Pṛthag-aśva, and likewise Aja.
There were one hundred Matsya kings, one hundred Nīpas, and one hundred Hayas;
there were one hundred and one Dhṛtarāṣṭras and eighty Janamejayas.
There were one hundred Brahmadattas and one hundred Īriṇas and Vairiṇas.

In this [list], there are two hundred Bhīṣmas and likewise one hundred Bhīmas; one hundred Prativindhyas, one hundred elephants, and one hundred horses. One hundred Palāśas should be known, as well as one hundred Kāśas, Kuśas, and so forth.
The royal seer Śantanu, your father Pāṇḍu, Uśadgu, Śataratha, Devarāja, Jayadratha,
and the royal seer Vṛṣādarbhi together with his counselor Dhāman.
Furthermore, there were thousands of others who followed Śaśabindu;
having performed many great horse-sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees,
these royal sages were meritorious, renowned, and deeply learned in the scriptures.
In that assembly hall, O royal sage, they wait upon the son of Vivasvat:
Agastya, Mataṅga, Kāla, and likewise Mṛtyu;
as well as those who have performed sacrifices, the Siddhas, and those whose bodies are composed of yoga.
The Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, those who drink foam, those who drink heat, the Svadhāvants, the Barhiṣads, and others who possess physical forms;
as well as the Wheel of Time and the Lord Havyavāhana himself.
Men who have performed evil deeds and die during the sun’s southern course are led away by the messengers of Time and those servants of Yama;
there, trees such as the *śiṃśapa*, *pālāśa*, as well as *kāśa* and *kuśa* grow.
These and many others, embodied and free from affliction, wait upon Dharmarāja; these members of the assembly of the King of the Ancestors are impossible to enumerate by name or by deed.
"For that assembly hall, O Pārtha, is unobstructed, delightful, and moves at will;
it was constructed by Viśvakarman after he had performed austerities for a long time.
It shines and blazes, O Bhārata, with its own splendor."
To that [world] go those of fierce asceticism, who are firm in their vows, speakers of truth,
peaceful, renunciants, perfected ones, and purified by meritorious deeds;
all of them possessing radiant bodies and all wearing stainless garments.
Adorned with variegated armlets and wonderful garlands, all of them wearing blazing earrings,
they were embellished by the excellent retinues resulting from their well-performed and meritorious deeds;
so too were the high-souled Gandharvas and hundreds of hosts of Apsarases.
Musical instruments, dance, song, laughter, and the *lāsya* dance were present there in every way;
and holy fragrances and sounds, O Pārtha,
as well as divine garlands, attended upon her from all sides.

A hundred times a hundred thousand righteous beings— endowed with beauty and possessed of great intelligence— wait upon that high-souled lord of creatures. Such, O King, is the assembly hall of the high-souled king of the ancestors.
I shall also describe the assembly hall of Varuṇa, adorned with lotus garlands;
O King, O ruler of the earth, listen with a one-pointed mind.
Nārada said:

O Yudhiṣṭhira, the divine assembly hall of Varuṇa possesses a white radiance; in its dimensions it is equal to that of Yama’s, with beautiful walls and gateways. Situated within the waters, it was constructed by Viśvakarman.
It was filled with celestial trees made of jewels that bestowed fruits and flowers,
and with creepers and shrubs bearing clusters of blossoms, which were blue, yellow, black, dark green, white, and even red.

Likewise, there were birds of various forms and soft voices, indescribable and beautiful, by the hundreds and thousands, in that assembly hall. That hall was pleasant to the touch, being neither cold nor hot.
It is a beautiful, white city, provided with houses and seats, protected by Varuṇa;
there Varuṇa dwells together with Vāruṇī, O Bhārata,
wearing divine jewels and garments, adorned with ornaments.
By his second name, she who is renowned on earth as Gaurī,
that god Varuṇa rejoices happily with his wife in great bliss;
wearing celestial garlands and garments, and adorned with divine ornaments.
Wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments, trailing celestial wreaths,
the Ādityas there wait upon Varuṇa, the lord of the waters;
as do Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the serpent Airāvata.
Kṛṣṇa, Lohita, Padma, and the heroic Citra;
the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Balāhaka; Maṇi, Maṇināga, and likewise the Nāga Śaṅkhanakha.
Kauravya, Svastika, Elāputra, Suvāmana, Aparājita, Doṣa, Nandaka, and likewise Pūraṇa;
Abhīka, Śibhika, Śveta, Bhadra, and Bhadreśvara.
Maṇimān, Kuṇḍaladhara, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya,
Pāṇimān, Kuṇḍadhāra, and the powerful [Nahuṣa], O lord of the earth; as well as Prahlāda, Mūṣikāda, and likewise Janamejaya.
02,009.010c Bearing banners, possessing circular hoods, and having hoods on all sides; 02,009.010d Artha, Dharma, Kāma, Vasu, and Kapila,
as well as the great nāga Ananta— seeing whom the Lord of Waters [is subdued].
He honored that Lord with respectful offerings and a seat;
and all those led by Vāsuki stood with palms joined in reverence. Having been permitted by Śeṣa, they sat down according to their rank.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, these and many other serpents,
as well as Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, and others who are his attendants,
wait upon the high-souled Varuṇa, free from all fatigue.
King Bali Vairocana, Naraka the conqueror of the earth,
Prahlāda, Vipracitti, and all the Kālakhañjas; Suhanu, Durmukha, Śaṅkha, Sumanas, Sumati, and Svana.
Ghaṭodara, Mahāpārśva, Krathana, and Piṭhara;
Viśvarūpa, Surūpa, Virūpa, and Mahāśiras; Daśagrīva, Vālin, Meghavāsas, and Daśāvara.
Kaiṭabha, Viṭaṭūta, Saṃhrāda, and Indratāpana—
all these hosts of Daityas and Dānavas wore beautiful earrings;
they were all adorned with garlands and crowns, and likewise possessed divine attire.

All of them have obtained boons, all are heroes, and all are free from death; standing ever within the noose of dharma, they all, having well-performed their vows, wait upon the high-souled god Varuṇa there.
Likewise, there are the four oceans, as well as the river Bhāgīrathī, the Kālindī, the Vidiśā, the Veṇṇā, the swift-flowing Narmadā,
the Vipāśā, the Śatadrū, the Candrabhāgā, and the Sarasvatī.
The Irāvatī, the Vitastā, the Sindhu, and likewise the Devanada;
the Godāvarī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā, and the Kāverī, the best of rivers—
these and other rivers, sacred fords, and lakes.
Furthermore, there is the Viśalyā and likewise the Vaitaraṇī river;
the third is the Jyeṣṭhilā, as well as the great river Śoṇa;
and also the Carmaṇvatī and the great river Parṇāśā.
The Sarayū, the Vāravatī, and the Lāṅgalī, the best of rivers;
likewise the Karatoyā, the Ātreyī, and the great river Lauhitya; as well as the Laṅghanī, the Gomatī, the Saṃdhyā, and the Trisrotas.
The Kambudā, the Viśalyā, the Kauśikī, and likewise the Gomatī;
the Devikā, the Vipaṅkā, and the river Vaitaraṇī;
the third is the Jyeṣṭhilā, and the great river Śoṇa as well.
The Carmaṇvatī, the Śvetanadī, the great river Phalguṇā,
the Sarayū, the Cīravalkelā, and likewise the Kuliśā— these rivers are renowned throughout the world as having excellent bathing places.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, all other rivers and lakes,
as well as wells and springs, appear in embodied forms and wait upon the god Varuṇa in his assembly hall.
O Bhārata, ponds and lakes then took on bodily forms;
likewise the quarters, the earth, and all the mountains,
as well as all aquatic creatures, waited upon that Great-Souled One.

And hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, accompanied by song and instrumental music, all sit together in that assembly praising Varuṇa. Therein are the jewel-bearing mountains upon which the waters (rasas) are established.
All of them, possessing physical forms, worship that Lord;
speaking very sweet words, they sit there together.
And likewise, the minister Vāruṇa and Sunābha attend upon him.
Surrounded by his sons and grandsons, along with the one named Go and Puṣkara—
O bull of the Bharatas, while traveling through the air, I previously beheld this beautiful assembly hall of Varuṇa; now hear about the assembly hall of Kubera.
Nārada said:
"O King, the assembly hall of Vaiśravaṇa is a hundred yojanas in length and seventy yojanas in width, possessing a white radiance."
O King, that city was fashioned by Vaiśravaṇa himself through ascetic power;
it possesses the luster of the moon, is like a peak of Kailāsa, and belongs to the sky-dwellers.
Carried by Guhyakas, it appears as if suspended in the air.
Divine, adorned with lofty trees made of gold,
radiant and shining like the sun, possessing celestial fragrance and enchanting to the mind,
it has the form of the peak of a white cloud and appears as if it were floating.
Divine, with limbs made of gold, variegated like flashes of lightning—
therein sits the glorious King Vaiśravaṇa, adorned with diverse ornaments and garments, surrounded by thousands of women, his earrings blazing.
O Great King, together with his wife Puṣpavatī, who was adorned with every ornament, the Lord of Wealth shone forth through his supernatural power; he sat upon a holy,
celestial carpet that resembled the sun.
Seated upon a supreme throne with a divine footstool,
the pure wind-god, bearing the fragrances of vast and sweet-smelling groves of celestial *mandāra* flowers and *saugandhika* blossoms, approached.
A breeze, gladdening the mind and heart, waits upon him from the Nalinī lake known as Alakā and from the grove of sandalwood trees.
There, the gods, together with the Gandharvas, are surrounded by hosts of Apsarases.
O Bhārata, they sing divine songs with celestial voices;
Miśrakeśī, Rambhā, Citrasenā of the pure smile,
Cārunetrā, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and Puñjikasthalā [are there].
Viśvācī, Sahajanyā, Pramlocā, Urvaśī, and Irā; Pramlocā, Urvaśī, Iḍā, Citrā, Vibhāvarī,
Vargā, Saurabheyī, Samīcī, Budbudā, and Latā.
The goddess Rambhā, Manoramā, Gopālī, Pañcacūḍā, Vidyudvarṇā, Sulocanā,
Citradevī, and Nīlā.
Thousands of others, skilled in dance and song—
hosts of Apsarases belonging to the Pāṇḍavas— wait upon the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) in that assembly hall with divine musical instruments, dances, and songs, without ceasing.
It shines, beautiful and not empty, with hosts of *gandharvas* and *apsarases*.
There are *gandharvas* named *kiṃnaras*, and others likewise named *nara*;
these sing, dance, and gladden the Giver of Wealth (*Dhanada*).
Then Maṇibhadra, Dhanada, Śvetabhadra the Guhyaka, Sthūṇa,
Sūryabhānu, as well as Śoṇaka and Tiṇḍuka,
Kaśeraka, Gaṇḍakaṇḍu, and the very powerful Pradyota.
Kustumburu, Piśāca, Gajakarṇa, Viśālaka,
Varāhakarṇa, Sāndroṣṭha, Phalabhakṣa, Phalodaka, Mudga, Camūhila, Puṣpa, Hemanetra, and Praṇāluka.
Aṅgacūḍa, Śikhāvarta, Hemanetra, Vibhīṣaṇa, Puṣpānana, Piṅgalaka, Śoṇitoda, Pravālaka,
Vṛkṣavāsyaniketa, and Cīravāsas, O Bhārata.
These and many other yakṣas by the hundreds of thousands,
as well as the Blessed Goddess Śrī and likewise Nalakūbara,
and I myself, and others like me, frequently dwell there.
There were teachers there, as well as other celestial sages; likewise,
there were flesh-eaters and other Gandharvas of great strength who waited upon that high-souled lord, the Giver of Wealth.
The Blessed One, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of hosts of spirits—
the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Creatures, the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes,
the three-eyed one— appeared, O tiger among kings, along with the goddess who was free from fatigue.
Some were dwarfish, some were misshapen, and some were hunchbacked; they had bloodshot eyes and were as swift as thought.
Feeding on flesh, fat, and marrow, their ears and appearance were fierce, and they bore various terrible weapons, possessing great speed like the winds.
O King, surrounded [by them], he always attends upon his friend, the Giver of Wealth;
and hundreds of others, joyful and accompanied by their retinues,
as well as the lords of the Gandharvas— Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū— are present.
Tumburu, Parvata, Śailūṣa, and Nārada; Citrasena, who is skilled in song, as well as Citraratha—
these and other Gandharvas wait upon the Lord of Wealth.
And Candrāpīḍa, the lord of the Vidyādharas, together with his younger brothers,
worships the high-souled Lord, the master of riches;
and there, hundreds of Kinnaras [worship] the Lord, the master of riches.
The kings led by Bhagadatta are also seated there; Druma, the lord of the Kimpuruṣas, waits upon the Lord of Wealth (Kubera),
as does Mahendra Gandhamādana, the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Together with the yakṣas, the gandharvas, and all the night-stalkers,
and the most righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, waits upon his lord, his brother;
as do Himavat, Pāriyātra, Vindhya, Kailāsa, and Mandara.
Malaya, Dardura, Mahendra, Gandhamādana,
Indranīla, Sunābha, and likewise the two divine mountains—
these and many others, all of whom have Meru as their foremost.
They worship the Great-Souled One, the Lord and Master of riches;
and the blessed Nandīśvara, as well as Mahākāla,
and all the divine attendants with Śaṅkukarṇa at their head likewise wait upon him.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa, Somanandin, Vijaya, Tapodhika,
Śveta, and Vṛṣabha bellowed there with a most mighty roar;
other Rākṣasas and Gandharvas sat beside Dhanada.

Seeing Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods, who brings prosperity to the three worlds, approaching surrounded by hosts of attendants— the multiformed Śiva, the Lord of Umā— the descendant of Pulastya bowed his head in salutation.
Then, having obtained permission from Mahādeva, the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneśvara) remained there.
At times, the Blessed Lord Bhava would stay as a friend to the Lord of Wealth;
meanwhile, Śaṅkha and Padma, the two foremost and preeminent among treasures, were the Lords of Wealth.
Having taken all the treasures, they indeed waited upon the Lord of Wealth. O King, such was that assembly hall seen by me in the sky;
now, O King, I shall describe the assembly hall of the Grandfather, which is free from all fatigue.
Nārada said:
O King, in former times, during the age of the gods, the blessed Āditya descended from heaven to the world of men, free from fatigue and desiring to behold it.
"O dear one, listen to me as I describe the assembly hall of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
O Bhārata, which cannot be described as being of such-and-such a form.
While wandering in human guise, I beheld that assembly hall of the Self-born One."
O Pāṇḍava, O bull of the Bharatas, they described to me in truth that divine assembly hall of Brahmā— immeasurable in its splendor, mental in nature,
indescribable by its power, and enchanting to all beings.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having heard of the virtues of that assembly hall,
O King, I likewise spoke to the Sun, desiring to see it:
"O Blessed One, I wish to behold the assembly hall of the Grandfather."
"O Lord of the Earth, tell me by what austerity,
or by what ritual action, or by appropriate medicinal herbs, or even by means of *māyā*, she might be made possible;
O Blessed One, explain that to me so that I may see that assembly hall."
Having heard those words of mine, O best of the Bharatas, the thousand-rayed maker of day spoke: "Observe the Brahma-vow for a thousand years with a restrained inner self."
Then, on the ridge of the Himalayas, I undertook a great vow.
Thereupon, the powerful Lord Sūrya took me with him and went to that assembly hall of Brahmā, which is free from sin and devoid of fatigue.

"O lord of men, it is impossible to describe her form as being of such a kind; for in an instant she assumes another indescribable body. O Bhārata, one cannot know its measure or even its configuration."
"And never before have I seen such a form as that.
O King, that assembly hall is most pleasant; it is neither cold nor does it give heat. Having reached it, they experience neither hunger, nor thirst, nor exhaustion."
It appears as if constructed from various forms, most diverse and brilliantly radiant;
yet it is not supported by pillars, for it is eternal and not subject to decay.
It is adorned with divine objects of many kinds, shining with immeasurable splendor.
Surpassing the moon, the sun, and the fire, she shines by her own radiance,
stationed upon the vault of heaven as if illuminating the sun itself;
there the Blessed One dwells, manifesting through divine illusion.
O King, the Grandfather of the worlds himself remains there alone and unceasingly; and the lords of creatures approach that Lord—
Dakṣa, Pracetas, Pulaha, Marīci, and Kaśyapa as well.
O King, the Ādityas, as well as the Rudras, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins; Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Aṅgiras;
Pulastya, Kratu, Prahrāda, and Kardama.
Then the Atharvāṅgirases, the Vālakhilyas, and the Marīcipas,
as well as the highly fortunate sages, attend upon the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Mind, the intermediate space, the sciences, wind, fire, water, and earth [are also there].
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, O Bhārata,
as well as primordial nature (prakṛti), its transformations (vikāra), and whatever other cause there is for the earth—
patience, fortitude, purity, wisdom, intellect, memory, and fame.
O Bhārata, there were commentaries endowed with logic and embodied forms;
and Agastya of great splendor, the heroic Mārkaṇḍeya,
Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Saṃvarta, and likewise Cyavana.
The highly fortunate Durvāsas, the righteous Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
the blessed Sanatkumāra, the master of yoga and great ascetic,
as well as Asita Devala and Jaigīṣavya, the knower of reality.
Ṛṣabha, Jitaśatru, and likewise Mahāvīrya and Maṇi; and Āyurveda with its eight branches, embodied, was there, O Bhārata;
as was the great sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana together with his disciples.
The Moon together with the constellations, the Sun with its rays,
the winds, the sacrificial rites, as well as volition and the vital breath— these high-souled beings, who are devoted to great vows, have taken on embodied forms.
These and many others have approached the Self-Existent One:
Purpose, Virtue, Desire, Joy, Hatred, Austerity, and Self-Control;
likewise, the Gandharvas and Apsarases arrive there together.
The goddesses Kālikā, Surabhī, Saramā, Gautamī,
Prapā, and Kadrū— these goddesses and their sons, the gods, as well as twenty-seven other world-protectors from every quarter, were all present there.
Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Budha, Aṅgāraka,
Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and all the other planets likewise;
as well as the mantra, the Rathantara, Harimān, and Vasumān.
The Ādityas, with Sādhirāja at their head, are mentioned in various pairs;
as are the Maruts, Viśvakarman, and the Vasus, O Bhārata—
all of whom are ever-present in that assembly hall, abounding in the fulfillment of every desire.
Likewise, O Pāṇḍava, lord of the people, all the hosts of ancestors, as well as all the sacrificial oblations, the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda,
Atharvaveda, and the Parvas [appeared].
The Itihāsas and Upavedas, and all the Vedāṅgas;
the planets, the sacrifices, Soma, and all the deities;
as well as the Sāvitrī, the Durgataraṇī, and the sevenfold Vāṇī.
O lord of the people, intelligence, fortitude, sacred learning, wisdom, intellect, fame, and forbearance;
as well as the Sāman chants, hymns for praise, various Gāthā verses,
and commentaries joined with logic— all these existed in embodied form.
Various dramas, poems, stories, legends, and verses—
therein abide those meritorious ones and others who honor their gurus;
as well as moments, instants, hours, days, and nights.
O Bhārata, there are half-months, months, and the six seasons;
years, the five-fold cycle (yuga), and the four kinds of days and nights. And there is the divine wheel of time, which is eternal, imperishable, and undecaying.
Likewise, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Wheel of Dharma remains eternally established. Aditi, Diti, Danu, Surasā, Vinatā, Irā,
Kālakā, the goddess Surabhi, Saramā, and Gautamī;
Prādhā and Kadrū were indeed goddesses, mothers of the deities;
so too were Rudrāṇī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, and another, Ṣaṣṭhī;
as well as the goddess Pṛthivī who has entered the earth, Hrī, Svāhā, and Kīrti.
The goddess Surā, Śacī, as well as Puṣṭi, Arundhatī,
Saṃvṛtti, Āśā, Niyati, the goddess Sṛṣṭi, and likewise Rati—
these and other goddesses indeed waited upon Prajāpati.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and also the two Aśvins;
the Viśvedevas, Sādhyas, and Pitṛs who are as swift as thought—
know, O bull among men, that there are exactly seven such hosts of Pitṛs.
Four indeed possess physical forms, while three are bodiless; the highly fortunate Vairājas and the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, O Bhārata,
as well as the Gārhapatyas who dwell in heaven, are the world-renowned ancestors.
The Somapas, the Ekaśṛṅgas, the Caturvedas, and likewise the Kalās—
these, O King, are the ancestors who are honored among the four castes.
When these have first been gratified, Soma is then gratified in turn.
All these Pitṛs have approached Prajāpati,
and they wait upon Brahmā of immeasurable splendor with great joy;
likewise, the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Dānavas, and Guhyakas are present.
The Suparṇas, Nāgas, and animals wait upon the Grandfather (Pitāmaha),
as do stationary beings, moving beings, and other great elements;
likewise Purandara, the lord of the gods, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Yama.
Mahādeva, accompanied by Umā, always comes there from all sides;
and Mahāsena, O king of kings, constantly worships the Grandfather (Brahmā). Likewise, the god Nārāyaṇa and the divine sages are present there.
The Vālakhilya sages, both those born from a womb and those not so born,
and whatever else is seen in these three worlds, whether stationary or moving—
know, O lord of men, that all of it was seen by me within her.
O Pāṇḍava, eighty-eight thousand ascetics with vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), as well as fifty rishis who possessed offspring,
