were there; and all those dwellers of heaven, having seen them there according to their desire, [honored them].
Having bowed their heads to him, they depart as they came—
whether they be guest-gods, Daityas, Nāgas, or sages,
as well as Yakṣas, Suparṇas, Kāleyas, Gandharvas, or Apsarases.
The highly fortunate Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, possessed of immeasurable intellect and compassionate toward all beings, conducts himself toward them according to their merit;
and having accepted [the offerings], the self-existent one, the soul of the universe, of infinite splendor, [proceeds].
The Blessed One always receives them with sweet and gentle words;
O lord of men, he unites them with consolation, honor, wealth, and enjoyment.
Likewise, O Bhārata, he attends to those who come to him and those who depart.
O dear one, that assembly hall, though crowded, became a bestower of happiness;
divine and composed of all splendors, it was frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages and shone, free from fatigue, blazing with the glory of Brahmā.

Such an assembly hall as that has been seen by me, rare to find in all the worlds; O tiger among kings, it is just like this one of yours among men. These other assembly halls among the gods have also been seen by me before, O Pāṇḍava.
"In this world of men, this assembly hall of yours is the most excellent of all.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of speakers, you have described for us almost the entire world of kings."
O Lord, just as you have described it in the assembly hall of Vaivasvata, so too,
O All-pervading One, have you spoken of the Nāgas in the assembly hall of Varuṇa,
as well as the lords of the Daityas in great numbers, the rivers, and the oceans.
Likewise, the Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Rākṣasas of Dhanapati,
as well as the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and the Blessed One whose banner is the bull (Śiva),
and those great Ṛṣis, have been described to you in the assembly hall of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
O Sage, all the hosts of gods, as well as all the scriptures,
were indeed proclaimed in the assembly of Śatakratu; and the Gandharvas and various great ṛṣis were mentioned there by way of summary.
But, O great sage, you have mentioned that the royal seer Hariścandra alone was a constant member of the assembly of the high-souled Lord of the Gods.
By what ripening of karma, O bull among the twice-born, did Hariścandra attain this?
Among those thousands of kings, he shone forth even with his splendor.
What deed did he perform, or what austerity with fixed vows?
What was given by him, or what oblation offered, or what sacrifice performed, O great sage?
"O Brahmin, how was it that you saw my father Pāṇḍu, the highly illustrious one who, while in the world of the ancestors, vied even with Śakra? And how did you come to meet him?"
"O Blessed One, what did he say? I wish to know this:
the future and the past—all that is established in you.
I desire to hear it all from you, for my curiosity is great."
Nārada said:
O Indra among kings, O Lord, regarding that which you ask me concerning Hariścandra,
I shall fully relate to you the greatness of that wise man.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus was a king named Triśaṅku, a hero who ruled Ayodhyā and was closely associated with Viśvāmitra. His wife, born of the Kekaya dynasty, was named Satyavatī.
O descendant of Kuru, a fetus was conceived in her according to the natural law;
and in due time, that highly fortunate woman, having entered the month of childbirth,
gave birth to the stainless prince Hariścandra.
That King Hariścandra was indeed known as Traiśaṅkava.
That king was powerful, a sovereign over all the rulers of the earth;
all the protectors of the world remained bowed before his command.

Mounting a single victorious chariot adorned with gold, O lord of men, he conquered the seven continents by the prowess of his weapons. Having thus subdued the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, he [ruled].
O great king, he performed the great sacrifice, the Rājasūya.
At his command, all the rulers of the earth brought wealth,
and they served as the attendants for the twice-born at that sacrifice.
And the lord of men, out of affection, bestowed wealth upon the officiating priests—
more than five times as much as they had requested there—
and likewise gratified the Brahmins with various riches.

When the time for the wandering [of the sacrificial fires] had arrived, the twice-born who had gathered from various directions— satisfied by heaps of jewels and gratified by various kinds of foods and delicacies served according to their desires— proclaimed:
He became more radiant and more illustrious than all other kings;
for this reason, O Pārtha, Hariścandra shines forth—
know that, O bull of the Bharatas, he excelled those thousands of kings.
And having completed the great sacrifice, the majestic Hariścandra,
consecrated as a sovereign, shone with imperial power, O lord of men;
for he had been anointed in the Rājasūya, once the excellent sacrificial fees had been distributed.
And those other rulers of the earth who perform the great Rājasūya sacrifice,
O Bhārata, they rejoice together with Mahendra;
as do those who have met their end in battle without fleeing.
O bull of the Bharatas, having reached that assembly hall, they rejoice;
and those who cast off their bodies here through intense austerity,
having also reached that place, shine there eternally in splendor.
And your father Pāṇḍu, O son of Kuntī, the joy of the Kurus,
having seen the splendor of King Hariścandra and being filled with wonder,
recognized me as I was coming to the world of men, O lord of men.
Bowing down, he said: "O Bhārata, you should say to Yudhiṣṭhira:
'You are capable of conquering the earth; your brothers remain under your command;
perform the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices.'"

"When you have become my desired son, I shall indeed rejoice like Hariścandra for many and eternal years in the assembly of Śakra. "So be it," [the father replied], "I shall speak thus to your son, the lord of men."
"I said to Pāṇḍu, 'If I am to go to the world of Bhūrloka,
then you, O tiger among men, O Pāṇḍava, must fulfill that resolve.
All your ancestors have gone before you to the abode of Mahendra."

O King, you shall attain the same world as Mahendra, the lord of the three worlds and sovereign of the gods; you shall share that same world with your ancestors. Yet, O King, this great sacrifice is known to be beset by many obstacles.
For here, the Brahmarākṣasas who destroy sacrifices seek out vulnerabilities;
there is war and retreating from the field, which causes the destruction of the earth,
and even a slight pretext here brings about ruin.

All this has been told to you; what more may I do for you? Reflecting upon this, O Indra among kings, perform whatever is appropriate, remaining ever vigilant and alert in the protection of the four social orders.
Prosper, flourish, and rejoice; satisfy the twice-born with gifts.
This which you asked me has been told to you in detail. I take my leave of you; I shall go toward the city of the Daśārhas.
02,011.072 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus spoken to the sons of Pṛthā, O Janamejaya, Nārada departed,
O King, surrounded by those same sages with whom he had met.
When Nārada had departed, O Kaurava descendant of Bharata, Pārtha, together with his brothers,
began to contemplate the Rājasūya, the most excellent of sacrifices.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of the seer, Yudhiṣṭhira sighed;
reflecting upon the attainment of the Rājasūya sacrifice, O Bhārata, he found no peace.
For he had heard of the greatness of those high-souled royal sages.

Having observed that those who perform sacrifices attain the celestial worlds through their meritorious deeds— and specifically having considered the royal sage Hariścandra, who was preeminently radiant—
he, being himself a performer of sacrifices, desired to undertake the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having honored all the members of the assembly and being honored by them in turn, O king of kings, set his mind upon the sacrifice itself—
the Rājasūya, that ritual of the Kurus, performed by that bull among men.
Having reflected repeatedly, he inclined his mind toward bringing [the girl] back;
and once more, that one of wondrous heroism and vigor, upholding dharma alone,
set his heart upon what would be for the welfare of all the worlds.
Favoring all his subjects, Yudhiṣṭhira— the best among those who know all dharmas— acted for the welfare of everyone without distinction,
depriving both anger and pride of their power while ensuring that what was to be given was bestowed upon all.
"Excellent! Dharma! Dharma!"—nothing else was heard being spoken.
When he had departed in this manner, the people felt as secure as if with a father; because no one hated him, he was known as Ajātaśatru (the one whose enemy is unborn).
Through the protection of the kingdom by King Bhīma,
through the destruction of enemies by Bībhatsu Savyasācin,
and through the wise Sahadeva’s instruction in the duties of righteousness.

Free from conflict and devoid of fear, the people were always devoted to their own duties; likewise, the provinces were prosperous and received rain according to their desire. Moneylending, sacrifices, animal husbandry, agriculture, and trade [flourished].
Through the king’s governance, all this arose by way of excellence:
drawing in and driving out, as well as disease, fire, and fainting;
yet none of these existed while Yudhiṣṭhira remained constant in righteousness.
Neither from robbers nor from deceivers, nor from one king toward another,
nor even from the king’s favorites, was any falsehood ever heard;
for all were intent on doing what was pleasing, attending upon him, and offering the tribute of their own labor.
While Yudhiṣṭhira remained ever devoted to righteousness, the realm increased there as kings brought tribute from the six directions,
along with various classes of merchants and people born of greed who utilized resources even for their own desires.
He is all-pervading, possessed of all virtues, all-enduring, and the sovereign of all;
he under whom the illustrious universal emperor rules with splendor,
O King, throughout the ten directions, both by his father’s line and his mother’s.
The subjects, including even the cowherds and the twice-born, were devoted to him. Then that best of speakers, having summoned his ministers and brothers,
questioned them again and again regarding the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Then those ministers, being questioned together,
spoke these meaningful words to the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, who was desirous of performing the sacrifice:
"By means of which [consecration] a king, once anointed, attains the quality of Varuṇa."
Therefore, although you are already a king, you desire the full status of a universal sovereign (*samrāj*).
O joy of the Kurus, your friends consider this to be the proper time for you— who are worthy of the qualities of a universal sovereign— to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
The time for that sacrifice was entirely at his own disposal due to his kṣatriya excellence; it was a sacrifice in which six fires were piled with chants by those of firm vows,
and which, by means of ladle-offerings, attained all ritual sacrifices.
"And because he performed the consecration at the end of the sacrifice, he is called Sarvajit (the All-Conqueror). O mighty-armed one, you are capable; we are all under your command.
Before long, O Great King, you shall attain the Rājasūya."
"O Great King, without further hesitation, set your mind upon the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Thus did all his friends speak, both individually and together.
O Lord of the People, the son of Pāṇḍu heard those words of theirs, which were consistent with righteousness.
The slayer of enemies, having heard those words of his friend and knowing them to be suitable for himself, resolved in his mind upon that bold, desired, and most excellent course. Vaiśampāyana said:
Highly commended, he began the examination with the four brothers, Bhīmasena and the others, who were intent on what was beneficial. Thus addressed,
Pārtha then fixed his mind upon dharma alone.
Yudhiṣṭhira, that lord of kings and bull among the Kurus, immediately set his mind upon performing the Rājasūya sacrifice; yet,
possessing extraordinary heroism and vigor, he continued to strictly observe the path of dharma.

O Bhārata, he set his mind again and again upon the Rājasūya sacrifice. That wise Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by his brothers, the high-souled officiating priests, and his ministers, [prepared for the rite].
He consulted with his ministers, including Dhaumya, Dvaipāyana, and others,
as well as with Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins, the wise son of Pṛṣata,
Virāṭa, Drupada, and the sagacious Sātyaki.
Surrounded by Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, by the wise son of Subhadrā, and by the sons of Draupadī— all supreme heroes— he held counsel.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How might this desire of mine come to pass— that which belongs to the Rājasūya sacrifice, worthy of a sovereign, performed by one of noble rites, full of faith, and speaking [of it]?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lotus-eyed one, having been thus addressed by that king,
they spoke these words at the proper time to the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O knower of dharma, you are worthy of the great Rājasūya sacrifice."
When the king had spoken thus, the officiating priests and the sages,
as well as his ministers and brothers, honored those words. Then that highly wise king, self-possessed, once again [reflected] within himself.
Pārtha reflected further, desiring the welfare of the worlds;

having carefully considered the application of his capability, as well as the place and time, and the expenditure and income, the wise man who acts after such thorough deliberation with his intellect does not come to grief.
O Bhārata, having reached a firm conclusion with all of them that it was indeed the right time,
and understanding that the undertaking of a sacrifice does not lead solely to one's own ruin, he diligently bore the burden of the task.
To ascertain the outcome of his undertaking, he considered Janārdana Kṛṣṇa to be superior to all the worlds; thus, in his mind, he went to Hari—
the immeasurable, mighty-armed, unborn one who had taken birth among men by his own will.
The Pāṇḍava reflected upon him through his deeds, which were equal to those of the gods:
"There is nothing unknown to him, and there is nothing that is not born of his own action;
there is nothing he would not endure"—thus he regarded Kṛṣṇa.
Having formed that final resolution, Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira immediately dispatched a messenger to the Teacher of Beings as if he were his own guru.
Reaching the Yādavas swiftly on a fast-moving chariot, that messenger arrived at once.
The messenger approached Kṛṣṇa, who was residing in Dvārakā at Dvāravatī;
bowing low with palms joined in reverence, he made his request to Mādhava.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, that Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, together with Dhaumya, Vyāsa, and others,
along with all his brothers including those from Pañcāla and Matsya,
longs for a vision of you, O mighty-armed one.

Having heard the words of Indrasena, the mighty and infallible Mādhava, the foremost of the Yādavas, took leave of Vasudeva and Baladeva, and with a desire to see Pārtha— who likewise longed for his sight— set out.
Accompanied by Indrasena, Janārdana then departed for Indraprastha;
passing through various regions with swift conveyances and great haste,
he approached Pārtha who was staying in Indraprastha.
Honored like a brother by his brother Dharmarāja in the palace, and likewise by Bhīma, he then beheld his father’s sister with joy; delighted,
he then took his pleasure together with that dear friend.
He was attended upon like a preceptor by Arjuna and the twins;
when he had rested in a pleasant place, refreshed and fit for action, Dharmarāja approached him and made known his purpose.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have sought the Rājasūya sacrifice, yet it is not attained through mere desire alone;
how that may be obtained, O Kṛṣṇa, is known to you in every respect."
"He in whom everything is possible, who is honored everywhere,
and who is the sovereign lord of all— that king obtains the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having come together, my friends said to me that this Rājasūya was what ought to be performed.
In this matter, O Kṛṣṇa, my conviction shall rest upon your word;
for some, out of mere friendship, do not point out a fault,
while others speak only what is pleasing for the sake of their own interests.
Some desire only that which is dear to them, provided it is beneficial to themselves;
such are generally the popular sayings observed regarding worldly affairs.
But you, having transcended these motives and having passed beyond both desire and anger—
"It is most fitting for us in this world that you should speak to us as is appropriate.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O great king, you are worthy of the Rājasūya sacrifice by virtue of all your excellent qualities."
O Bhārata, although you already know all this, I shall say something further to you:
that which remains of the kṣatriya order after it was decimated by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni,
is this present class known as the kṣatriyas in the world.

"O lord of the earth, O bull of the Bharatas, this resolve regarding the lineage was made by the Kṣatriyas through their words of command; that is indeed known to you. They declare this to be the traditional nature of the dynasties of Aila and Ikṣvāku."
There were kings organized into guilds and other Kṣatriyas on earth; O King,
know that those belonging to the lineage of Aila and likewise the royal Ikṣvākus constitute one hundred and one families, O bull of the Bharatas.
The lineage of the Bhojas, descended from Yayāti, is exceedingly virtuous and vast;
O great king, that lineage extends in all four directions,
and all the kṣatriyas likewise revere their prosperity.
"O King, it was only this very moment that Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of the earth,
having overcome the prosperity of those royal lineages, was consecrated;
he now stands at the head of all monarchs, having completely surpassed them in his prowess."
Having enjoyed the central region of the earth, he set his mind upon creating dissensions among them.
Then there was another king, Caturyu, in whose reign one hundred and one kings existed;
from that lineage, Jarāsaṃdha obtained universal sovereignty.
O King, having relied upon him in every way, that highly wise and powerful Śiśupāla became his general; and he,
O great king, attended upon him like a disciple.
Vakra, the lord of Karūṣa, a mighty warrior of great strength who fights with illusions,
and two other high-souled men of great heroism—
both Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka— have sought refuge with the immensely powerful Jarāsaṃdha.
Dantavakra, Karūṣa, Kalabha, and Meghavāhana;
he who bears upon his head a divine gem which they know as the *bhūtamaṇi*; and he who rules over Mura and Naraka, the two lords of the Yavanas.
O Great King, Bhagadatta, who possesses boundless strength like Varuṇa in the western quarter,
was an aged friend of your father; O Bhārata, he was devoted to him both in word and in deed.

But he who is bound by affection for you, like a father, and who with a devoted mind protects the western and southern ends of the earth— that high-souled king, though afflicted by fear, has also bowed down before him.
Your maternal uncle Śūra, the conqueror of many and the enhancer of the Kunti lineage, is alone among those who bow before you out of affection, O scorcher of enemies;
he is the very one who previously went to Jarāsaṃdha and was not slain by me.
That evil-minded man among the Cedis, who is known as Puruṣottama,
claims for himself in this world the title of Puruṣottama; out of delusion, he constantly assumes my very insignia.
O great king, there is a powerful king among the Vaṅgas,
Puṇḍras, and Kirātas, known throughout the worlds as Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva;
he is a mighty Bhoja, a friend of Indra, who possesses four horses.
He who by the power of his learning conquered the Pāṇḍya, Kratha, and Kaiśika kings;
whose brother was the heroic Āhṛti, equal to the son of Jamadagni in battle— that devoted King Bhīṣmaka, the slayer of enemy heroes, [is here].

"O King, he who was always devoted to us— acting kindly, humble, and ever a true kinsman— now dwells in enmity and does not favor us. He takes no account of our lineage, nor his own strength, O King."
Beholding his blazing glory, [the kings] took refuge with Jarāsaṃdha; likewise, O Lord,
the eighteen royal clans of the Udīcyas and Bhojas fled toward the western direction out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha alone.
The Śūrasenas, Bhadrakāras, Bodhas, Śālvas, Paṭaccaras, Sustharas, Sukuṭṭas, and Kuṇindas together with the Kuntis,
as well as the kings of the Śālveyas along with their brothers and followers.
The Pāñcālas of the south, the eastern Kośalas among the Kuntis, as well as those of the northern region, being afflicted by fear, have abandoned their lands; likewise,
the Matsyas and the Saṃnyastapādas have taken refuge in the southern direction.
In the same way, all the Pāñcālas, afflicted by the fear of Jarāsaṃdha,
completely abandoned their own kingdom and fled in every direction;
for the Pāñcālas were at the front of that army of the high-souled one.
While the strength of the Sārasvata army had not yet departed from Girivraja among the Māgadhas, after some time, Kaṃsa, the son of Bṛhadratha, having oppressed his kinsmen,
approached the two queens with a perverted mind.
O weak one, those two younger sisters of Sahadeva were named Asti and Prāpti.
By that strength, he of vain intellect overcame his kinsmen and attained preeminence; that was a truly great transgression on his part.
Oppressed by the wicked Bhoja king and his elders,
and desiring the protection of their kinsmen, they placed their trust in us;
for they had then given that slender-waisted daughter of Āhuka to Akrūra.
With Saṃkarṣaṇa as my second, I have performed this duty toward my kinsmen;
both Kaṃsa and Sunāman were slain by me and by Rāma as well. Having likewise killed Kaṃsa in battle, I was filled with fear of Jarāsaṃdha.
"By me and by Rāma, our kinsmen were protected elsewhere; but when danger had approached and Jarāsaṃdha had risen up, O King,
this counsel was deliberated upon by eighteen principal clans."
Even if we were to strike him incessantly with great weapons and *śataghnīs*,
we could not destroy his strength even in three hundred years;
for he possesses two [sons] who resemble the immortals and are the foremost among the strong in their power.
Those two best of warriors were known by the names Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka;
together with the heroic Jarāsaṃdha,
those three were, in my opinion, a match for the three worlds.
O best among the wise, it was not only for us, but for all other kings as well, that such was their thought;
eighteen hair-raising battles were fought by me against him.
O King, Jarāsaṃdha of great strength was neither slain nor given away.
Now, O King, there was once a certain great monarch known as Haṃsa;
he, together with others numbering eighteen at least, engaged in battle.
"O Bhārata, then someone cried out, 'The swan has been killed!
Upon hearing that, O King, Ḍibhaka plunged into the waters of the Yamunā,
thinking, 'I cannot bear to live in this world without the swan.'"
Having adopted this resolve, Ḍibhaka met his death. Hearing that Ḍibhaka had perished, Haṃsa, the conqueror of enemy cities,
went to the Yamunā and plunged into its waters.
O bull of the Bharata race, having heard that those two had met their death in the waters, King Jarāsaṃdha departed for his own city of Śūrasena.
O slayer of enemies, after that king had thus departed, we...
"Then, all of us shall dwell again in Mathurā with renewed joy.
For when that lotus-eyed daughter of Jarāsaṃdha, the king of Magadha, comes to her father Kaṃsa as his wife..."
"O Indra among kings, afflicted by the grief of her husband's death, she indeed urged him again and again, O subduer of enemies, saying, 'Kill my husband-killer!
Then, O great king, we [acted upon] that counsel previously deliberated."
Remembering [this], O lord of men, they departed with dejected minds; O King,
having hastily withdrawn their great wealth,
they fled in various directions out of fear of him, along with their riches, kinsmen, and relatives.
Having reflected thus, O King, we all took refuge in the western direction;
we established our residence once more in that beautiful city of Kuśasthalī, which was adorned by Mount Raivata.

In that very same way, we dwell without fear from any quarter in that city, which has been so well-fortified that it is difficult even for the gods to assail; therein, even women could fight, let alone the bulls among the Vṛṣṇis, O slayer of enemies.
Beholding that preeminent mountain and the Mādhavī-tīrtha as well,
O tiger among the Kurus, the Mādhavas attained supreme joy.
Thus, from the very beginning, we have been rendered guilty by Jarāsaṃdha.
Possessing great power, they have come to rely upon you through their connection [to you].

Your abode extends three *yojanas* in length; it has three sections, each rising one *yojana* high, and at the end of each *yojana* there is a gateway with a hundred doors, featuring triumphal arches that mark the progress of your strides.
Bound together by eighteen kṣatriyas who are fierce in battle,
there are eighteen thousand clans in our family;
Āhuka has one hundred sons, each of whom has at least three hundred followers.
Cārudeṣṇa with his brother Cakradeva, Sātyaki,
myself, the son of Rohiṇī, and Sāmba, who is equal to Śauri in battle—
these, O King, are the seven chariot-warriors; now learn from me of others as well.
Kṛtavarman, Anādhṛṣṭi, Samīka, Samitiñjaya,
Kahva, Śaṅku, and Nidānta— these seven alone are great chariot-warriors (mahāratha).
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Bhānu, Akrūra, and Sāraṇa...
Niśaṭha and Gada— these seven were great chariot-warriors (mahārathas); Vitadru, Jhalli, Babhru, Uddhava, Vidūratha,
Vasudeva, and Ugrasena— these seven were the preeminent among ministers.
Prasenajit and Yamala, endowed with the virtues of a king of kings; the Syamantaka jewel from which much gold flows forth;
and the two sons of Andhakabhoja—these ten, along with the aged king, [are the protectors].
The heroes, who were the pillars of the world, possessed of vigor and great strength, remembered the Middle Country while standing among the Vṛṣṇis, free from all distress. The Blessed Lord.
O King, we have always had you as our protector along with the Pāṇḍavas.
O best of the Bharatas, you who are ever endowed with the qualities of a sovereign, it behooves you,
O Bhārata, to establish yourself as the emperor over the Kṣatriyas.
Duryodhana, the son of Śantanu (Bhīṣma), Droṇa, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), Kṛpa, Karṇa, Śiśupāla, the archer Rukmin,
Ekalavya, Druma, Śveta, Śalya, and Śakuni.

Without having conquered these in battle, how can you perform that sacrifice? Or perhaps these lords of men will not fight out of sheer respect; for there is only one there, Karṇa Vaikartana, the bull-like hero, who is intoxicated with his own strength.

He, full of strength and indignation, will fight, proud of the power of his celestial weapons. But as long as the mighty Jarāsaṃdha remains alive, it is not possible for you to achieve the Rājasūya sacrifice; this, O King, is my opinion.
For by him all the kings were imprisoned after being conquered at Girivraja,
like great elephants trapped in a mountain cave by a lion.
That King Jarāsaṃdha, too, was desirous of sacrificing those lords of the earth.
O subduer of enemies, having propitiated Mahādeva, the high-souled lord of Umā,
by means of eight thousand consecrated kṣatriyas,
he thereby conquered the kings of the earth.
That bull among Kṣatriyas has reached the further shore of his vow;
for having repeatedly conquered the kings who came with their armies,
he brought them to his city, bound them, and made a herd of men.

O Great King, out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha, we too at that time completely abandoned Mathurā and went to the city of Dvāravatī; there we still dwell today, together with our wealth, kinsmen, and relatives.
"For the sake of Kaṃsa, there was indeed enmity between the King of Magadha and me;
having reached the end of that [enmity] in battle, he now desires to sacrifice to the Supreme Deity.
O Great King, if you wish to attend this sacrifice here,"

"Exert yourself for their liberation and for the slaying of Jarāsandha. For this undertaking is possible only through such effort, O joy of the Kurus, and not otherwise; it is possible for you to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice in its entirety, O best among the wise."
"O bull of the Bharatas, let a means for the slaying of Jarāsaṃdha be devised;
when he is conquered, the entire force of all the kings will be conquered.
This, O King, is my opinion, or however you may think it, O sinless one."
"Since this is the case, tell me yourself, having determined it through your own reasoning.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"That which has been spoken by you, the wise one, is such that no other is capable of saying it."
Indeed, there is no one else on earth besides you who can dispel the doubts of those in uncertainty.

For in every house there are kings who do what is pleasing to their own respective subjects, yet they have not attained universal sovereignty; for the title of *samrāj* belongs only to one who possesses the whole.
How can one who knows the power of others deign to praise himself?
Only he who is praised when compared with another is truly honored.
Vast and extensive is the earth, filled with many jewels.
"O scion of the Vṛṣṇi clan, having gone far, one recognizes that peace (*śama*) alone is supreme;
yet I do not believe that peace can exist apart from liberation (*mokṣa*). It is my conviction that the state of the Supreme Lord (*pārameṣṭhya*) cannot be attained through mere worldly exertion."

In this very way, those born of noble lineage and possessed of wisdom understand, O Janārdana: "At some time or another, one among these might become the best. And we ourselves, O highly fortunate one, were then [driven away] out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha.

O illustrious and sinless one, we were filled with apprehension because of his wickedness. For I, O invincible Lord, rely upon the strength of your arms; therefore, I did not consider myself strong while you were full of doubt.
O Mādhava, O mighty-armed one, knowing whether he can indeed be slain by you, by Rāma, by Bhīmasena, or by Arjuna,
I reflect upon this again and again, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis.
"O Keśava, you are my authority in all matters.
Having heard this, Bhīma, who was skilled in speech, spoke these words.
Bhīma said:
A king who is intent on non-action perishes like an anthill;
so too does a weak man who, lacking skillful means, opposes one who is strong.
However, a weak man who remains vigilant generally [overcomes] a powerful enemy.
"O King, let right policy conquer our own beneficial goals through statesmanship.
In Kṛṣṇa is policy, in me is strength, and in Pārtha Dhanañjaya is victory. Together we three shall overcome the King of Magadha, like the three sacrificial fires."
"Relying on the power of your intellect, the King of Dharma shall obtain everything. Victory is indeed ours, O Govinda, for those who always have you as their protector.
Kṛṣṇa said:

The fool, intent on his own interests, takes what he desires without considering the consequences; therefore, those who are devoted to their own welfare do not tolerate an enemy who is likewise solely focused on his own gain,
even if it means disregarding all his kinsmen for the sake of a single moment with the virtuous.

We have heard that Yauvanāśva became a sovereign by renouncing taxes, Bhagīratha through his protection of the people, Kārtavīrya through the power of his asceticism, the lord Bharata through his strength, and Marutta through his prosperity— these five were universal emperors.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for you who desire universal sovereignty in every respect, consider all lineages: such men do not exist in every age;
one who possesses the characteristics of being restrained by the principles of dharma, artha, and policy is rare.
O bull of the Bharatas, know that Jarāsandha is the son of Bṛhadratha;
and although one hundred and one royal lineages do not obey him,
he nevertheless exercises this imperial sovereignty today solely by means of force.

For kings who possess jewels wait upon Jarāsaṃdha; yet he is not satisfied even with that, having resorted to such misconduct since his youth by forcibly seizing an anointed monarch, a preeminent man.
He takes [tribute], yet no one has ever been seen to be without a share from him;
thus Jarāsaṃdha has brought all those numbering more than a hundred under his control.
How, O Pārtha, will a king who is weaker than he approach him?
In a vessel of rice, the king worshipped Kapardin. [The gods asked:
"How will you return to us after having conquered [us]? [They replied:
"Of kings who have been consecrated and purified in the abode of Paśupati..."
O bull of the Bharatas, what joy can there be in life for living beings, like that of cattle?
Since a Kṣatriya is honored when he dies by the sword,
why indeed did we all not resist the King of Magadha?
"O King, eighty-six kings have been brought together; fourteen remain. Jarāsaṃdha will then treat them cruelly.
He who would cause him hindrance therein shall attain radiant glory."
"And whoever shall conquer Jarāsaṃdha will certainly become the sovereign emperor.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Desiring indeed the qualities of an emperor, and intent upon my own welfare, [I seek you]."
"How could I slay Bhīma through mere force and sheer audacity?
I consider Bhīma and Arjuna to be my two eyes, and Janārdana to be my mind.
What kind of life would there be for one deprived of both mind and sight?"

Having encountered the army of Jarāsaṃdha, which is difficult to cross and possesses terrible prowess, fatigue alone would surely cause you defeat; what then could be achieved by further exertion? In this particular situation, an undertaking that was appropriate turns into a disaster.
"Listen then to me as I reflect upon this alone:
therefore, in my view, it is not proper to act;
O Janārdana, I favor the renunciation of this undertaking."
"The Rājasūya sacrifice strikes my mind today, though it is difficult to attain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Pārtha, having obtained the best of bows and two inexhaustible great quivers..."
He spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira regarding the chariot, the banner, and the assembly hall:
"O King, I have obtained this bow, these weapons, these arrows, heroism, allies, territory, fame, and strength— all that was desired and difficult to attain."
"Learned men who are well-established in their knowledge praise birth in a noble family;
however, there is nothing equal to strength, and it is heroism that I prefer. What can one born in the lineage of Kṛtavīrya achieve if he is devoid of valor?"
But one born into a family lacking in vigor who is himself vigorous is distinguished above all,
O King— especially a Kṣatriya whose very livelihood depends on victory. For even if he is deficient in all other qualities, a man of vigor shall indeed overcome his enemies.
Even if one is endowed with all virtues, what can one who lacks prowess accomplish?
For all virtues exist as mere substances within valor;
indeed, the cause of victory depends upon accomplishment, human effort, and destiny.
For even one who is joined with forces may, through negligence, fail to employ them;
by that very means, the enemy, though possessing strength, is destroyed by his foes. Just as there is dejection in one who is weak, so too is there delusion in one who possesses power.

Both of those causes for destruction must be abandoned by a king who desires victory. If we could achieve the destruction of Jarāsaṃdha and the liberation of the kings for the sake of the sacrifice, what could be more supreme than that?
But in the absence of undertaking [virtuous action], there would necessarily be a certainty of being devoid of qualities.
O King, how can you consider yourself to be without qualities when your virtues are beyond doubt?
Furthermore, the saffron robe is easily obtained later on for sages who desire tranquility.
"Desiring imperial sovereignty for you, we shall fight against the enemies.
Vāsudeva said:
"For one born into the Bhārata lineage, and likewise for a son of Kuntī,"
"Indeed, this very resolve has been demonstrated by Arjuna:
'We do not know the time of death, whether it be by night or by day;
nor have we ever heard of anyone who became immortal even without engaging in battle.'"
This alone is what must be done by men to satisfy the heart:
that one should advance against enemies through policy prescribed by the sacred law. This is the supreme course of action in battle for one whose policy is sound and free from error.
Doubt arises when there is equality, and equality cannot exist between two [opposing sides]. Therefore,
having adopted this policy and approaching the enemy's person,
how might we not bring about his end, just as the currents of a river destroy a tree?

Those who exert their prowess against the vulnerabilities of others while remaining steadfast in guarding their own weaknesses, and who do not advance against a stronger foe with poorly arrayed forces or insufficient reinforcements—
this is the policy of the wise, and it is pleasing to me as well.
For those blameless ones have entered that enemy's abode unperceived;
having approached the body of the enemy, we shall obtain that desire.
For he alone, O bull among men, constantly upholds royal fortune.
Like the inner self of all beings, when that [body] perishes, strength indeed perishes.
[He is] four-kneecapped,
four-fanged, twice-tusked, and possessing ten lotuses.
A king is pervaded by six protrusions and ten large parts;
if, having slain him in battle, we remain together with the survivors, then, devoted to the protection of our kinsmen, we shall attain heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, who is this Jarāsaṃdha? What is his strength and what is his prowess, that he was not consumed like a moth upon touching you, who are like fire?"
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, hear of Jarāsaṃdha’s strength and prowess, and how he,
despite having repeatedly committed offenses against us, was overlooked by us."
There was a king named Bṛhadratha, the lord and ruler of Magadha, who was proud in battle; he possessed three akṣauhiṇīs,
was handsome, endowed with heroism, illustrious, and of incomparable prowess.
He ruled his own kingdom in Girivraja among the Magadhas,
his body perpetually emaciated by consecration rites like another Śatakratu;
he was equal to the sun in brilliance and equal to the earth in forbearance.
In wrath he was like Yama, the Ender; in splendor he was indeed like Vaiśravaṇa.
O best of the Bharatas, this entire earth was pervaded by his qualities, which were consistent with his noble lineage, just as it is by the rays of the sun.

O bull of the Bharatas, that hero of great prowess married the twin daughters of the King of Kāśī, who were highly esteemed for their beauty and wealth. That best of men established a mutual agreement between the two of them.
"I shall not go beyond [this]," he said thus in the presence of his two wives.
Then that king, O lord of men, shone with those two beloved and worthy wives,
like an elephant with two female elephants.
Standing between those two, the lord of the earth shone like the personified ocean situated between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. As he remained immersed in sensual pleasures, his youth passed away.
Yet no son was born to him who could perpetuate his lineage;
despite many auspicious rites, burnt offerings, and sacrifices performed with the desire for a son,
that best of kings did not obtain a son to increase his family.
At that time, together with his two wives, he experienced profound world-weariness;
having renounced even his kingdom, O Lord of the People, though restrained by his subjects out of devotion to the king, he then took refuge in a forest of asceticism.
Then he heard of the noble Caṇḍakauśika, the son of the great-souled Gautama and Kakṣīvat, who was weary from his ascetic penances;
he had arrived by chance and was taking rest at the foot of a tree.

Accompanied by his two wives, the king gratified him with all kinds of jewels; and that seer greeted Bṛhadratha in accordance with tradition. Then, having sat down, he was permitted by that high-souled one.
Then the brahmin asked him, "What is the reason for your coming? To which the king, accompanied by his citizens and his two wives, replied to the sage: "O Blessed One, I have no son."
"The best of sages say that the birth of one without a son is in vain;
for what purpose is sovereignty to such a person in old age?
Therefore, I shall practice asceticism in the forest together with my two wives."
"O Sage, for one who has no offspring, there can be neither fame nor eternal heaven.
When the king had spoken thus, compassion arose within the sage;
that best of seers, firm in truth and truthful in speech, addressed him:

"I am well-pleased with you, O King; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. Then Bṛhadratha, together with his wife, bowed down and spoke to him in a voice faltering with tears due to his despair of ever seeing a son.
Bṛhadratha said:

"O Blessed One, for one like me who has abandoned his kingdom and set out for the forest of asceticism— what use is a boon to one of such little fortune, and what use is a kingdom to one who is childless?"
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard this, the sage, his senses agitated,
entered into meditation and sat down in the shade of that very mango tree.
As that sage sat there, a single mango fruit— unblown by the wind and untouched by parrots— fell indeed into his lap. Taking it, the best of sages consecrated it with a mantra from his heart.
The great sage gave the king that incomparable [remedy] which brings about the attainment of a son, and the highly wise one said to that king:
"Go, O King, you have achieved your purpose; return, O lord of men."
"O King, this is your son; do not distress yourself with asceticism in the forest. Protect your subjects according to dharma, for this is the duty of those who rule the earth.
Perform various sacrifices and gratify Indra with the soma juice."
"Having established your son in the kingdom, you may then return to the hermitage. O King, I grant eight boons to your son:
devotion to the Brahmins, invincibility, and likewise a love for battle."
Furthermore, Kauśika bestowed upon him hospitality toward loved ones, compassion for the distressed, as well as great strength, eternal fame in the world, and the affection of the subjects.

"Go, O King; you have achieved your purpose. Return, O lord of men! Having been thus permitted by the seer, the king, accompanied by his two wives and followed by the citizens, entered his own city once again.
Having heard these words of the sage and bowing his head in prostration, that highly wise king went to his own home; then,
having recognized the proper time, that best of kings [proceeded].

O bull of the Bharatas, out of great respect for the sage and because of the reversal of time, he gave that single fruit to his two wives. Having divided that mango into two parts, those two auspicious women ate it.
Because of the power of their cultivated merit and because of the sage’s truthful word,
a conception occurred for the two of them, resulting from the consumption of the fruit.
And seeing this, the lord of men attained supreme joy.
Then, O wise king, when the time had arrived according to the season,
both of them gave birth to two fragments of a body,
each having one eye, one arm, one foot, half a belly, half a face, and half a hip.

Seeing the two fragments of bodies, both of them trembled violently. Distressed, those two weak sisters then consulted together and, being deeply grieved, abandoned the two lifeless fragments of living beings.
Having wrapped those two infants in their wombs with two well-folded white silk cloths,
the two nurses went out from the gate of the inner apartments, cast them away, and quickly departed. At that time, both were thoroughly covered by the two pale silk garments.
When they were not recognized by anyone, the two of them abandoned the child at a crossroads;
then the two nurses entered the inner apartments once more and each reported the matter separately to the two queens.
Then, O tiger among men, a Rākṣasī named Jarā, who feeds on flesh and blood, seized those two pieces cast aside at the crossroads;
for that Rākṣasī desired to join them together so they might be easily carried.
Then, impelled by the power of destiny, she joined them together.
O bull among men, as soon as those two fragments were brought together and formed into a single body, a heroic boy was produced.
Then, O King, that Rākṣasī, her eyes wide with amazement,
was unable to lift up the infant who was as hard as adamant.
The child, having formed a fist with his copper-palmed hands, placed it in his mouth.

In great agitation, he cried out like a rain-cloud filled with water. Startled by that sound, O tiger among men, the people in the inner apartments suddenly rushed out along with the king, O scorcher of foes.
Those two women, weak and exhausted, their breasts full of milk and now hopeless of obtaining a son, suddenly approached him.
Then, seeing them in such a state and the king’s continuous exertion, [they spoke].
And the Rākṣasī thought of that very strong boy:
"While dwelling within the domain of this righteous and high-souled king who is so fond of his son, it is not right for me to kill this young child."
Like a streak of cloud taking up the sun, she assumed a human form and said to the lord of men:
"O Bṛhadratha, here is your son; he was given by me, please accept him."
"Born of your two wives by the command of the best of the twice-born,
this child was abandoned by the nurses and protected by me. Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, [I have brought] those two auspicious daughters of the King of Kāśī."
They quickly flew toward that child and drenched him with their milk.
Then the king, filled with joy upon perceiving all of this, questioned that Rākṣasī— who, though appearing like fresh gold, was no Rākṣasī at all.
"Who are you, O lady with the luster of the interior of a lotus, who have granted me a son? Tell me out of affection, O auspicious one; you appear to me to be a goddess.
The Rākṣasī said:
"O auspicious one, my name is Jarā; I am a Rākṣasī who can assume any form at will. O Indra among kings, I have lived happily, honored in your palace.
This Rākṣasī dwells constantly in every house of men."

In ancient times, she was indeed created by the Self-Existent One under the name Gṛhadevī; possessing a divine form, she was established for the destruction of the Dānavas. Whoever should paint me on a wall with devotion, together with my son and endowed with youth—
In his house there shall be prosperity; otherwise, he would meet with ruin. O Lord, while staying in your house, I am always honored, and I am depicted on the walls, surrounded by many sons.
O King, having been well honored with perfumes, flowers, incense, and various kinds of food and edibles, I, thinking constantly of how to repay your kindness,
O righteous one, beheld these two fragments of your son.

"By chance, O Great King, while I was embracing [the child], a boy was produced; this was through your own merits, and I here was merely the instrumental cause. I am capable of devouring even Mount Meru, how much more so your infant?"
Out of satisfaction with the worship of my household, I have returned this to you;
O lord of men, perform whatever rites are required for that child,
and he shall indeed become famous in this world by my name.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having spoken thus, O King, she vanished right there;
and taking that boy with him, the monarch entered his own home.
Then the king performed whatever rites were required for that child and commanded a great festival for the Rākṣasīs among the Māgadhas.
There, his father, who was equal to Prajāpati, bestowed a name upon him.

Because he was joined together by Jarā, he therefore became known as Jarāsaṃdha. That son of the lord of Magadha, endowed with great splendor, grew up possessed of stature and strength like a fire fed by oblations.
Endowed with strength like a Magadhan king, like fire fed by oblations,
bringing joy to his mother and father like the moon in the bright fortnight—
thus did that lotus-eyed prince grow, O King.
After a long time, he indeed reached the prime of youth. Then, after some time had passed, the venerable Caṇḍakauśika, a man of great asceticism, once again set out for the Magadha country.
Delighted by his arrival, Bṛhadratha, together with his ministers, his attendants, his wife, and his son, went out to meet him.
O Bhārata, he honored him with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for rinsing the mouth.
That king offered him his son along with the kingdom.
Having accepted that honor from the monarch,
the blessed seer spoke to the King of Magadha with a joyful heart:
"O King, all of this has been known by me through the eye of wisdom. But hear, O Indra among kings, what kind of son this shall be— his form, his character, and his exceedingly great strength."
This son of yours, endowed with glory, will undoubtedly attain all that through his prowess;
the kings of the earth shall not be able to equal the valor of this heroic one.
Just as other birds cannot match the flight of Vainateya as he swoops down,
so shall those who stand as his adversaries meet their destruction;
even weapons hurled by the gods, O lord of the earth, shall be powerless against him.
They shall not cause him pain, any more than the currents of rivers can affect a mountain;
he shall blaze upon the heads of all consecrated kings,
depriving them of their luster, just as the sun does to all other luminaries.
Having encountered him, kings with abundant forces and vehicles will meet their destruction like moths in a fire;
he shall seize the accumulated prosperity of all monarchs.
As the lord of rivers and streams holds the rivers whose waters have risen during the rains,
so this one of great strength shall properly sustain the four castes;
as the vast earth supports all crops, it supports both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
All those kings shall attain great prosperity;
all those kings shall become subject to his command,
just as all embodied beings are subject to the wind, which has become the self of all beings.

"This Magadha king, possessed of supreme strength, shall himself behold Rudra, Mahādeva, Hara, the destroyer of Tripura, throughout all the worlds. While speaking thus, the sage reflected upon his own purpose.
Then the slayer of enemies dismissed King Bṛhadratha;
having entered the city surrounded by his kinsmen and relatives,
Jarāsaṃdha was then consecrated as the lord of Magadha.
King Bṛhadratha attained supreme peace.
When Jarāsaṃdha had been consecrated, King Bṛhadratha,
followed by his two wives, became devoted to the forest of asceticism.
O Bhārata, while his father was staying in the penance grove with his two mothers,
Jarāsaṃdha brought the kings under his control by means of his own prowess. Then, after a long period of time had passed, the king [returned] to the penance grove.
Having performed austerities, Bṛhadratha went to heaven together with his wife. King Jarāsaṃdha also, having obtained the entirety of that boon as it was spoken by Kauśika, protected his kingdom.
When King Kaṃsa had been slain by Vāsudeva,
a persistent enmity indeed arose between him and Kṛṣṇa,
O Bhārata, because [Kṛṣṇa] had whirled him around ninety-nine times.
The mace, hurled with great force by the King of Magadha from Girivraja,
fell ninety-nine yojanas away upon the auspicious Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds as he stood in Mathurā.
Having seen [the scene], the citizens then correctly reported the matter regarding the mace;
that spot near Mathurā became famous as Gadāvasāna (the End of the Mace). Both Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka met their deaths there without weapons.
The two best among the wise, experts in the science of war, [spoke thus].
When Kaṃsa had been slain by me, along with Saṃha and Ḍibhaka,
Jarāsaṃdha’s daughter was weeping at her father’s side.
Then, O Bhārata, enmity was established between him and me;
those two of great strength whom I previously mentioned to you—
I consider that three of us together would be a match for the three worlds.
Thus, O great king, that hero was at that time overlooked by the powerful Kukuras, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis for the sake of political expediency. Vāsudeva said:
The two ministers of Kaṃsa, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, have fallen; they have been struck down.
The time has now arrived for the destruction of Jarāsaṃdha;
he cannot be conquered in battle even by all the gods and asuras combined.
"We understand that he must be conquered through a battle of life-and-death.
Strategy resides in me, strength in Bhīma, and Arjuna is the protector of us both.
O King, we three shall overcome him, like the three sacrificial fires."

That lord of men has been encountered by us three in a secluded place; there is no doubt that he will engage in battle with one of us alone. This is because he has been humiliated by the world and provoked by our great physical prowess.
He will certainly come forward to fight with Bhīmasena;
the mighty-armed and immensely powerful Bhīmasena is a match for him,
just as Antaka is for the world when it has reached its zenith.
"If your heart knows [this] and if you have confidence in me,
then quickly give me Bhīmasena and Arjuna as a trust.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Yudhiṣṭhira replied,
looking at Bhīma and Pārtha, who stood there with joyful faces:
"O Acyuta, O Acyuta, do not speak thus, O crusher of enemies!"
"You are the protector of the Pāṇḍavas, and we have taken refuge in you.
O Govinda, everything that you say is entirely appropriate;
for you do not stand at the head of those from whom fortune has turned its back."
O Kṛṣṇa, for those before whom prosperity stands face-to-face, you are at their very forefront.
Jarāsandha has been slain and the kings have been liberated;
and while remaining under your command, I have obtained the Rājasūya sacrifice.
"O best of men, act swiftly so that this task may be accomplished; perform my work as well as the work of the world. Indeed, without you three, I have no desire to live."
Deprived of virtue, pleasure, and wealth, like one who is impoverished and afflicted by disease—without Śauri, Pārtha is nothing; and without the son of Pāṇḍu, Śauri is nothing.
It is my conviction that there is nothing in this world unconquerable for these two Kṛṣṇas.
Moreover, this Vṛkodara, the best among the strong,
endowed with splendor and great fame, what could he not accomplish when joined by you two?
For a force well-led indeed achieves the highest purpose.
They say that an army is blind and inert; it must be led by those who possess insight.
For just as water flows here toward whatever is low-lying, so do those whose wealth is wisdom direct the army wherever there is an opening.
Therefore, relying upon Govinda, who is world-renowned and knows the methods of policy, let us strive for the accomplishment of our purpose—
one who possesses the power of wisdom and insight, and is endowed with the means of action.

One should place Kṛṣṇa at the forefront in all undertakings for the sake of accomplishing one's goals. In this very same way, O best of the Yadus, let Arjuna follow Kṛṣṇa for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, and let Bhīma follow Dhananjaya.
"Through this method, victory, and indeed strength, he shall attain success in his prowess.
Having been addressed thus, all those brothers of immense energy—
the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and the two sons of Pāṇḍu— then set out toward Māgadha.
Having clothed the radiant Brāhmaṇas who were Snātakas in their garments, and being cheered by the pleasing words of their friends,
Mādhava and the two sons of Pāṇḍu set forth, observing their vows.

The bodies of those foremost warriors, who were tormented by indignation for the sake of their kinsman and possessed forms like the sun, moon, and fire, then became terrifying to behold. Seeing Bhīma at their head, they considered Jarāsaṃdha already slain.
Engaged in a single purpose, the two Kṛṣṇas are undefeated in battle;
for those two high-souled ones are masters in the initiation of all undertakings,
as well as in the restraint of actions pertaining to dharma, artha, and kāma.
Having set out from the Kurus, they traveled through the center of Kurujāṅgala;
having reached the beautiful Padmasaras lake and passed beyond Kālakūṭa,
they likewise crossed the Gaṇḍakī, the Śoṇa, and the Sadānīrā.
Crossing the rivers in succession on Mount Ekaparvataka, they proceeded; having crossed the lovely Sarayū and beheld the eastern Kosalas,
they passed beyond them and went to Mithilā, crossing the Mālā and the river Carmaṇvatī.

Having crossed the Gaṅgā and the Śoṇa, all three of those infallible ones proceeded eastward toward the Magadha region, which is covered with *kurava* and *uraśchada* trees. They [saw] that land, which was perpetually crowded with herds of cattle, abundant in water, and filled with beautiful trees.
Having reached Mount Goratha, they beheld the city of Magadha.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Pārtha, this great mountain is delicious, rich in cattle, and always abundant in water."
The auspicious settlement of Māgadha is free from disease, rich in fine dwellings,
endowed with flowers, medicinal herbs, and fruits, and abounding in wealth and grain; likewise,
there are the Vaihāra, Vipula, Śaila, Varāha, and Vṛṣabha mountains.
Likewise, O dear one, there are Ṛṣigiri and the auspicious Caityaka as the fifth;
these five mountains with their great peaks and cool trees stand together with joined limbs, as if guarding Girivraja.
Where, as if hidden by forests of *lodhra* trees— delightful with fragrant scents and their tips entwined with flowers, beloved by those filled with desire—
the seer named Dīrghatamas dwelt, most strictly self-restrained.
Where the high-souled Gautama, firm in his vows,
begot upon an Auśīnarī Śūdra woman sons such as Kākṣīvat and others; from that very dwelling of Gautama, he [the child] was born in that house.
Through the favor of those kings, he enjoyed the Māgadha lineage;
and the exceedingly powerful kings of Aṅga, Vaṅga, and others,
having approached the inexhaustible hermitage of Gautama, used to take their pleasure there in former times, O Arjuna.
Behold, O lotus-eyed King, these delightful rows of *priyāla* trees and the beautiful *lodhra* groves growing near the hermitage of Gautama,
O Pārtha.
There are the arbuda and śakravāpī nāgas, who scorch their enemies, among the pumnāga trees; and here is the abode of Svastika and the supreme Maṇināga.
The power of the clouds cannot be warded off for the sake of the Māgadha jewel;
indeed, both Kauśika and the possessor of the jewel increased their favor.
Thus, having reached that delightful city, which was unassailable from every side...
On Pāṇḍara and Vipula, as well as on Vārāhaka,
on Caityaka the best of mountains, and on Mātaṅga the mountain peak—
on these lords of mountains are the abodes of all supernatural powers.
And also the hermitages of ascetics and high-souled sages, as well as the dwellings of the immensely powerful Vṛṣabha and Tamāla,
and likewise the abodes of the Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas.
02,019.010d Through the power of Kakṣīvat’s asceticism, they became renowned as "Givers of Penance" (Tapodās).
02,019.010d All of them are celebrated as sacred pilgrimage sites (puṇyatīrtha) and as the abodes of the Siddhas.
02,019.010d Indeed, by the mere sight of Maṇi, one shall obtain auspiciousness and well-being.
"Jarāsaṃdha, however, considers his own success in achieving his goals to be unshakable;
yet today, upon encountering him, we shall surely destroy his pride.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, all those brothers of immense prowess—
the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and the two sons of Pāṇḍu— set out for the city of Magadha,
which was filled with contented and well-fed people and crowded with members of the four social orders.
They reached Girivraja, which was full of festivities and unassailable.
Having bypassed the city gate and entered through a non-gate,
they then failed to find the entrance to the city and [climbed] the lofty mountain.
He was being honored by the descendants of Bṛhadratha as well as by the city-dwellers;
there, Bṛhadratha encountered the bull Māṣādman,
and having slain him, he had three kettledrums made from his marrow and stalks.
Having fastened it with that hide, he established it in his own city,
where those drums resounded, strewn with celestial flowers;
and having shattered those three drums, they rushed toward the enclosure of the shrine.
Then, facing toward the gate, they all went forth with various weapons;
these [beings] always let out a terrible roar upon the approach of a hostile army.
Hearing that most dreadful sound, the inhabitants of Girivraja [were struck with fear].
Desirous of slaying Jarāsaṃdha, they rushed toward the most beautiful and lovely shrine of the Magadhas, as if wishing to strike him on the head;
it was a firm, vast, and very great ancient peak.
Constantly honored with garlands of flowers and firmly established,
those heroes struck it down with their massive arms and cast it away;
then, having seen the city of Māgadha, they entered it.
Having seen that ill omen, the Brahmins, who had mastered the Vedas,
then propitiated the gods with rites for peace, gifts, recitations, and burnt offerings.
At that very time, they were honoring Jarāsaṃdha.
While the domestic priests were performing the fire-circumambulation (*paryagni*) of the king as he sat upon his elephant,
the powerful King Jarāsaṃdha, for the sake of that propitiation,
underwent initiation, remained observant of his vows, and became intent on fasting.
They performed the lustration ceremony for him with lamps and with recitations that ward off untimely death.
At that very time, however, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Dhanañjaya—
observing the vows of a *snātaka*, armed only by their arms and bearing no weapons— [approached].
Beholding the prosperity of the city and its magnificent splendor,
O Bhārata, they entered it eager for battle with Jarāsandha.
They beheld the supreme beauty of the shops filled with food and garlands.
He saw a marketplace for jewels and garments,
with various divine stalls,
flourishing, endowed with every excellence, and abounding in all desired objects.
Seeing that prosperity in that street as they proceeded along the royal road, those best of men— Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Dhanañjaya—
forcibly took garlands from the florists, for they were possessed of great strength.

Having forcibly taken camphor, saffron, and fine fruits from the market stalls from the Vaiśyas, those great chariot-warriors, all dressed in discolored garments yet adorned with garlands and polished earrings, wandered about.
Then they arrived at the residence of the wise Jarāsandha, looking upon it as lions from the Himalayas might look upon a cow-pen. Their pillars,
resembling mountains, were adorned with sandalwood and aloe-wood.
O Great King, the arms of those mighty-armed men shone resplendently;
seeing them, who resembled elephants and rose up like the trunks of *śāla* trees,
with broad chests, the people of Magadha were filled with wonder.
Leaping over the gate, they entered the palace of the Magadhan king;
having passed through three courtyards crowded with people, those bulls among men of great strength approached the king with pride.
Those great chariot-warriors addressed the king simply with the word "Bhoḥ.
One should say, "May you live long, O gentle one," when greeting a Brahmin; one should say "Victory! to a Kṣatriya, and to a Vaiśya, one should say "Prosperity."
One should utter the word "health" regarding the enemy's feet, but one should not pronounce the sound "no.
Even upon those priceless seats bestowed by the king, they did not sit;
instead, having dragged a seat with their foot, the enemy sat down upon it.
Whether on the bare ground or even in the house of an enemy, this was the course of action:
Jarāsandha rose up and approached those who were worthy of water for the feet and the honey-mixture, who deserved honor, and who had received his hospitality, according to the prescribed rite.
Then that lordly king said to them, "Welcome to you.
At that time, O Janamejaya, the two sons of Pṛthā, Bhīma and Arjuna, remained silent;
however, in their midst, the highly intelligent Kṛṣṇa spoke these words.

"O Indra among kings, it is not possible for these two, who abide in their vows, to speak until midnight; after that time, they will converse with you. Having placed them in the sacrificial hall, the king went to his royal palace.
Then, when midnight had arrived, he went to where the twice-born were staying;
for this was his vow, O King, which was renowned throughout the earth:
"The lord of kings, Bārhadratha, possessed of great strength and prowess..."
O Bhārata, upon hearing that *snātaka* Brahmins had arrived, that king, victorious in assembly, would go out to meet them even at midnight, O Bhārata,
whether he was in the midst of a group of women or not.
Having heard that the brahmins had assembled,
and seeing them in their unprecedented attire, Jarāsaṃdha, the best of kings, approached them and was then filled with wonder.

O best of the Bharatas, as soon as those bulls among men beheld King Jarāsandha— who was like truth, splendor, strength, fortitude, and profundity incarnate— all those slayers of enemies spoke these words.
"O King, know us to be guests who have come from afar seeking your favor;
grant us that which we desire—blessings be upon you!
What is unbearable for those who practice endurance? What is an unworthy act for the virtuous?"
What is there that cannot be given by the generous? Who is a stranger to those who see with equanimity?
He who, though capable, does not himself acquire enduring fame to be sung by the virtuous through this impermanent body—he alone is to be censured; he alone is truly pitiable.
Hariścandra, Rantideva, Uñchavṛtti, Śibi, Bali, the hunter, and the pigeon—many indeed have attained the eternal through the impermanent.
"May it be well with you; may you be prosperous, O King," thus they all remained established.

O tiger among kings, those Brahmins gazed at one another as they looked upon that monarch. Then, O Indra among kings, Jarāsandha spoke to those Yādavas and Pāṇḍavas who were disguised as Brahmins, saying, "Be seated."
Then all three of those bulls among men sat down together,
blazing with splendor like the three fires at a great sacrifice; they were distinguished by their voices, their physical forms, and even by their forearms scarred by the bowstring.
Recognizing them as kinsmen of royalty whom he had seen before, he reflected:
"These are indeed kinsmen of royalty who bear the marks of Brahmins;
I shall give to them even my own self, though it is so difficult to abandon."
His fame was not heard proclaimed in all directions; moreover,
he was deprived of his sovereignty by Viṣṇu under the guise of a brahmin,
as Viṣṇu, in the form of a twice-born, desired to seize the fortune of Indra.
Even though he knew [the danger], the king of the Daityas gave away the earth even while being restrained;
for what purpose is there for a mere kinsman of the Kṣatriyas who has been conquered for the sake of Brahmins? What great fame would one not seek with this body that is subject to suffering?
Thus the noble-minded one spoke to Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, and Vṛkodara:
"O brahmins, let your desire be chosen; I shall give even my own self and my head.
To them, King Jarāsaṃdha, who was true to his promise, replied.

O descendant of Kuru, he censured Hari, Indra, and Samīra, who had assumed human forms for sport, on account of their taking on such attire; for Brahmins observing the *snātaka* vows do not wear garlands or ointments externally.
"It is known to me in every way that such beings exist here in the world of men; you are they— possessing flowers, with arms marked by the scars of bowstrings,
with bearded faces, red in hue, and with sharp, crimson sprout-like nails."
Wearing red turbans and adorned with rows of red teeth,
you possess the vigor of the Kṣatriyas while professing the status of Brāhmaṇas;
thus, though clothed in dyed garments, you wear garlands and ointments on the outside.
"In this world, I have come to know all those who are truly Kṣatriyas.
Speak the truth: who are you? Truth shines among kings.
O rulers of the earth, this very earth is truth; she is the embodiment of truth."

"Abiding in truth, one should speak the truth; otherwise, one will perish. Why have you broken through the peak of this mountain-caitya like our own dwelling, and entered by a non-doorway, fearless of the king’s wrath?"
One must enter the house of an enemy;
yet I am not your enemy, O Brahmins, for you are my deities. Why then have you beaten the kettledrums that signal the mobilization for battle?
"You must not fight with me; this is the work of one who has cast off his marks. What is being observed by you today? Speak, for the power of speech is especially the strength of a Brahmin."
"Having thus attended upon me, why do you not accept our refined hospitality according to the prescribed rite? What purpose do you have for coming to us?
Thus addressed, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa then replied:
O King, the one skilled in speech addressed these words in a smooth and profound voice:
"Regarding those who observe the vows of a *snātaka*, there are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
among them, there are both specific and general rules."
"O King, O lord of men, know us to be *snātaka* Brahmins.
A Kṣatriya who is always distinguished attains prosperity;
prosperity is certain among those who possess flowers, and therefore we are flower-bearers."

The Kṣatriya possesses the strength of his arms, but not so much the strength of his speech; therefore, the speech of one born of Bṛhadratha’s lineage is remembered as lacking boldness. The Creator has placed the inherent power of the Kṣatriyas in their arms.

O King, if you wish to see it, you shall see it today without a doubt. The virtuous always enter the house of an enemy through a non-gate, but they enter the house of a friend through the gate; therefore, we have avoided that [non-gate].
"Know this to be our eternal vow: having gone to the houses of those with business, we do not accept hospitality from an enemy.
Jarāsandha said:
"I do not recall ever having committed an act of enmity toward you; even upon reflection, I see no cause for hostility on your part.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, O best of kings, the mighty son of Bṛhadratha, perceiving his own agitation, spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"Since there is no transformation [of my nature], how can you consider me, who am sinless?"
"O wise ones, declare the enemy; for this is indeed the compact of the virtuous.
For the mind is surely tormented by the violation of righteousness—there is no doubt that even a Kṣatriya who releases [an arrow] at one who is innocent suffers."
"It is known to me in every respect that in this world only Kṣatriyas [may do so].
Therefore, one who acts otherwise in the world— even if he is a knower of dharma and observes great vows—
attains the state of the wicked and destroys his own welfare."

For those people who know the Dharma praise no other duty in the three worlds as superior to the duty of the Kṣatriyas for those who walk the path of the righteous; and so, today, I remain here established in my own duty, with my self restrained.
"Knowing him to be innocent, you speak as if out of negligence.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Great King, for the sake of the family's welfare, some single upholder of the lineage [must act]."
"Indeed, it is by his command that we three have arisen;
and by you, O King, the Kṣatriyas dwelling in the world were brought here. Having committed such a cruel offense, why do you consider us to be innocent?"
"O best of kings, how could a king harm other virtuous kings?
You wish to seize that king and offer him up to Rudra;
may that sin committed by you against the son of Bṛhadratha fall upon us."
"For we, who practice righteousness, are indeed capable of protecting the Dharma;
therefore, today we shall approach you, O descendant of Bṛhadratha.
Indeed, the seizing of human beings has never been seen before."
"How can you, O King, desire to sacrifice the god Śaṅkara with human beings?
For one who is of the same class as others will surely designate them as sacrificial animals;
who else, indeed, is such as you, Jarāsaṃdha, of vain intellect?"
In whatever state one performs whatever action,
in that very state one shall obtain its fruit.
We, however, being afflicted and following after you, [shall suffer] because you are the cause of the destruction of our kin.
"We have come here for the purpose of increasing our kinsmen;
and as for your thought, O King, that 'there is no other man among the Kṣatriyas,' that too is a very great delusion of your intellect."
For what Kṣatriya king, O monarch, knowing his own noble lineage, would not enter that incomparable and imperishable heaven immediately after battle? Indeed,
having set their hearts solely upon heaven, those consecrated by the sacrifice of war [enter it].
Know this, O Lord of Magadha: Kṣatriyas sacrifice for the sake of the worlds.
Victory, O King, is the source of heaven; great fame is the source of heaven;
austerity is the source of heaven; that path in battle is unfailing.
For this is the eternal, concentrated attribute of Indra, known as Vaijayanta,
by which the performer of a hundred sacrifices, having utterly defeated the Asuras, protects the world;
by which, having conquered all, victory was indeed achieved.

"O King, having ascended to heaven, who would dare to challenge you in battle as you do, with your vast Magadhan armies, arrogant in their great numbers and strength? Do not despise your enemies; there is no man who lacks valor."
O lord of men, your splendor is indeed equal to mine alone;
as long as it has not been fully realized, it shall remain so for you.
This is endurable for us; therefore, O King, I speak thus to you.
"O King of Magadha, abandon pride and arrogance toward those who are your equals;
do not go to the abode of Yama along with your sons, ministers, and army.
[Such were the words spoken to] Dambhodbhava, Kārtavīrya, Uttara, and Bṛhadratha."
"For indeed, kings who were powerful have perished in this world by disregarding what is superior.
Yet we, who seek liberation from you, are not merely those who call themselves Brahmins;
I am Śauri Hṛṣīkeśa, and these two are the Pāṇḍava heroes."

"Know that this maternal cousin of yours, Kṛṣṇa, is your enemy. O King, O ruler of Magadha, we challenge you; stand firm and fight, or else release all these monarchs so that you do not go to the abode of Yama."
Having heard this, Jarāsaṃdha became enraged and spoke these words.
I am neither Kaṃsa nor Pralamba, nor Bāṇa nor Muṣṭika; I am not Naraka, nor Indratāpana, nor Keśin, nor Pūtanā;
nor even Kālayavana—those who were slain by you in battle.
But you, born into a family of cowherds, remember indeed your former birth— you who, out of fear of us, fled and took refuge on the coastal marshlands of the ocean,
abandoning your native land of Mathurā like a commoner.
O Śauri, you now roar like a cloud in autumn;
today, O Mādhava, having slain you, I shall discharge my debt to the wise King of the Bhojas,
the son-in-law of Ugrasena.
For a long time I have desired this battle to slay you along with your circle of friends.
By good fortune, my effort has been made fruitful through the gods, including Indra.
And both these [sons], Bhīmasena and Arjuna, O Govinda, are but eunuchs.
"I shall strike him down in battle with valor, like a lion attacking small deer," said Vaiśampāyana as Jarāsaṃdha, overcome by rage, roared.
The illustrious Blessed One said:
"All the beings who were assembled there were struck with terror.
O Jarāsaṃdha, why do you roar? Perform those deeds through action."
O lowest of kings, today in battle I shall cause you, along with your ministers and your sons— the two Pāṇḍavas who gave me my instructions— to be slain;
you shall certainly not enter that best of cities alive by any means whatsoever.
Jarāsaṃdha said:
"I do not seize any kings who have not been conquered. Who has been conquered that remains standing? Who is there here who has not been defeated by me?"
They say that for a Kṣatriya, this very livelihood through agriculture is righteous, O Kṛṣṇa,

provided he acts according to his will after exerting prowess and bringing [the land] under his control. But having dedicated it for the sake of the gods, how could a king, out of fear, [abandon it], O Kṛṣṇa?
"Today, mindful of my kṣatriya vow, I shall release it: I will fight the army with my own arrayed army, or one by one;
or again, I will fight with two or three, either simultaneously or individually."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, King Jarāsaṃdha, desiring to fight those of terrible deeds, then gave orders for the consecration of Sahadeva.
But that king, the commander-in-chief, O bull of the Bharatas,
called to mind Kauśika and Citrasena when that battle was at hand—
those two whose names in the world are Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka.
When this had been previously discussed by men in the world of mortals, which is honored by the world,
Jarāsaṃdha then sighed, reflecting upon his fate.
But then, O King, the powerful Śauri [addressed] that king, the best among the strong.
O tiger among men, remembering Jarāsaṃdha— who possessed the prowess of a tiger, was true to his word, and was of terrible valor on earth—
the steadfast king designated him as the portion of another, destined for slaughter.

Madhusūdana, the younger brother of Haladhara, did not wish to kill the foremost of those who possess the self by means of his own self; rather, he placed the command of Brahmā before him. Janamejaya.

For what reason were those two, Kṛṣṇa and the Māgadha, enemies? And how was Mādhava defeated in battle by Jarāsaṃdha? Who was Kaṃsa, and for whose sake did he harbor enmity toward the King of Magadha?
"O Vaiśampāyana, tell me all of this in its true essence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"In the lineage of the Yādavas, there was the high-minded Vasudeva."
The Vārṣṇeya [Ugrasena] was born as the counselor of Ugrasena;
and Kamsa became the powerful son of Ugrasena,
O Kauravya, the eldest of many and skilled in all weapons.
The daughter of Jarāsaṃdha was his highly renowned wife;
she had been given as a bride-price for the kingdom by the wise Jarāsaṃdha. For her sake, a son was then born to Ugrasena in Mathurā.
Then, having been consecrated by his ministers, he of fierce prowess—
intoxicated by the power of sovereignty and deluded by that strength— seized his father and enjoyed the kingdom together with the ministers.
That dull-witted one did not hear of that duty of Vasudeva;
nevertheless, he protected that kingdom together with him according to dharma.
And that lord of the Daityas was well-disposed toward Vasudeva’s Devakī.
At that time, he married her who was the daughter of Devaka.
O Janamejaya, while she was being led away in a chariot,
Kaṃsa, the lord of the earth, then mounted after the descendant of Vṛṣṇi.
Then, from the sky, there arose the voice of a certain divine messenger;
Vasudeva heard that voice, as did that king [Kaṃsa]:
