"O Kaṃsa, the Devakī whom you are carrying away today is she whom I am carrying."

"Whichever of her eight pregnancies is the eighth, that shall be your death. Having descended from there, the king, possessed of an exceedingly wicked mind, drew forth his stainless sword and desired to cut off her head.
Then, consoling Kaṃsa while smiling at him as he was under the sway of anger,
the high-minded Vasudeva spoke these words of persuasion, O King:
"In all matters of dharma, O Ruler of the Earth, they say that a woman must not be harmed."
"O King, you would be slaying this innocent, helpless woman all of a sudden; furthermore, whatever fear you have in this matter can be dispelled by you,
for she can be protected and the agreement itself can be preserved."
"O Lord of the Earth, when her eighth child is born, destroy it immediately; in this way, what has been foretold will be averted. Thus was the king addressed by Vasudeva, O Bhārata.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the lord of the Śūrasenas acted upon those words of his,
and from her were born princes who possessed the splendor of the sun.
Madhureśvara slew every one of them as soon as they were born.
Then, O lord of the people, Baladeva was born as the seventh [son] from her;
however, King Yama, by means of his power of illusion (*māyā*), [seized him].
He transferred Devakī’s incomparable embryo into the womb of Rohiṇī;
because he was drawn out (*ākṛṣya*) by pulling (*karṣaṇāt*), he is remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Due to his preeminence in strength, he is remembered as Baladeva.
Furthermore, Madhusūdana was born as the eighth child in that same [family]. O King, he (Vasudeva) provided exceptional protection for that embryo.
Then, at the proper time, for the sake of protecting Vasudeva, the Sātvata...
The fierce minister of Kaṃsa, a performer of cruel deeds, having been dispatched,
arrived there by the power of his deluding influence over those who were bewildered;
then, having approached the cowherd settlement, he of great splendor departed.
O King, as soon as Vāsudeva was born, his father then drew him away and offered him to the son of a certain cowherd who had been purchased,
desiring to escape that voice of the divine messenger.
Kaṃsa struck that maiden, but she went away laughing;
crying out the sound "Ārye!", she was therefore celebrated as Āryā. Having thus deceived the king, that highly intelligent one—
He caused the high-souled Vāsudeva to grow up in Gokula;
and Vāsudeva, too, grew among the cowherds like a lotus in the water,
unknown to Kaṃsa, hidden like fire within wood.
Then Madhureśvara, the mighty-armed Vardhamāna, endowed with splendor and strength, overpowered all those cowherds. Thereupon,
being thus oppressed, they [sought refuge] with the lotus-eyed Acyuta.
Out of fear, others surrounded him in groups out of desire;
but having obtained the support of Ugrasena, O King,
that son of Vasudeva, highly esteemed by all his brothers, [again set forth].

Having conquered the lord of the Bhojas in battle and slain Kaṃsa, the one of great strength then consecrated Ugrasena in the kingdom, O lord of the people. Then, having heard that Jarāsaṃdha had been killed in battle by Mādhava...
O King Janamejaya, he then made the son of Kaṃsa the ruler of Śūrasena. Having mustered a great army, he forcibly approached Vāsudeva and there consecrated his own son as king over his daughter.
O descendant of Kuru, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, endowed with great strength, oppresses Ugrasena and the Vṛṣṇis there;
this is the enmity between Jarāsaṃdha and Mādhava.
O Indra among kings, having achieved his desired object and having conquered his enemies, that prosperous monarch, intending to perform a sacrifice, besieged those other kings—
the supreme deity Mahādeva, the three-eyed one clad in animal hide.
O bull of the Bharatas, all this has been related to you exactly as it occurred;
now hear how that king was slain by Bhīmasena.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Adhokṣaja, the eloquent descendant of Yadu, spoke to King Jarāsaṃdha, who was resolved upon battle:
"O King, with which of the three of us does your mind desire to fight?"
"Let one of us here prepare for battle;
who will fight? O Kṛṣṇa, I shall never fight with you, a master of illusions, while the Yadus are fleeing out of fear instilled in them by me."
"Arjuna would not be a warrior equal to my strength;
as for Bhīma, he might be capable for a moment or even half a moment—such was my thought beforehand.
Having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, that one of great splendor chose battle.
Then, O King, Jarāsaṃdha of Magadha said to Bhīmasena:
"I will not fight with you, a coward whose mind falters in battle;
having abandoned my own city of Mathurā, I have sought refuge in the ocean."
"But this one is equal to me in age, yet he is neither of great strength nor my equal;
let Arjuna be our warrior, for Bhīma is equal to me in strength.
Having said this, he gave the great mace to Bhīmasena.
Taking the second [lute] himself, he went out from the city; taking yellow pigment, garlands, and other auspicious items,
and carrying the foremost medicines, restoratives, and pain-relievers.
The family priest approached Jarāsaṃdha, who was eager for battle; the King of Magadha avoided both Arjuna and Vāsudeva,
thinking that Arjuna was merely a young cowherd and considering him to be a god.
Having had the rites for success performed by a learned and illustrious Brahmin,
Jarāsaṃdha, devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, put on his armor;
then, having removed his crown and smoothed his hair, he prepared himself.
Jarāsaṃdha rose up like an ocean that has overstepped its shores.
The wise king spoke to Bhīma of terrible prowess:
"Bhīma, I shall fight with you; it is better to be conquered by one such as you."
"O Kṛṣṇa, this Arjuna is but a child, born later than he.
Having spoken thus to Bhīmasena, Jarāsaṃdha,
the subduer of enemies and possessor of great splendor, advanced against him like the Asura Bali against Śakra.
Then, having consulted with Kṛṣṇa and having had the rites for success performed,
the powerful Bhīmasena approached Jarāsaṃdha with a desire to fight.
Then those two tigers among men, whose weapons were their arms, encountered one another.

The two heroes, exceedingly thrilled and each desiring victory over the other, first grasped each other’s hands and performed salutations at the feet; then, shaking one another’s armpits with their own, they made a slapping sound there.
Striking him on the shoulders with both arms and repeatedly knocking him down,
they locked limb with limb; O Lord, they then performed the slapping of the body,
various hand-movements, and the seizing of the armpits.
Having struck them with a thunderbolt accompanied by sparks and a blow to the throat-tumor,
and having employed the noose-of-arms and other weapons, he struck both on the head with his feet;
then, employing those two as full jars, he performed the chest-slap.
Pressing their palms together like two roaring elephants,
both resembling clouds, they roared with their arms as their only weapons;
striking one another with their palms, they glared at each other.
Like two lions highly enraged, they fought by repeatedly seizing one another;
pressing limb against limb with both their arms,
they also encircled each other’s waists with their arms.
Both Supārśva and Takṣavan were skilled and well-trained;
they placed their lower hands upon their own necks, bellies, and chests,
and they performed a backbend that transcended all limits of physical possibility.
With their arms, they performed the *saṃpūrṇamūrchā* and the *pūrṇakumbha*;
likewise, the *tṛṇapīḍa*, the *yathākāma*, the *pūrṇayoga*, and the *samuṣṭika*.
Thus did they engage in various such combats with one another.
Then, O tiger among men, the city-dwellers gathered to witness their combat:
thousands of brahmins and merchants, kṣatriyas,
śūdras, women, and the elderly from all sides.
There, the place became completely filled with a continuous flood of people. Then,
from the blows of their arms and from their seizing and grappling one another,
there arose a most terrifying roar, like that of a thunderbolt striking a mountain.
Both were exceedingly joyful, and both were exceedingly powerful in strength; they fought each other fiercely with their palms,
seeking one another's weak points and desiring victory over each other.
Like two rams with their heads, like two night-stalkers with trees,
like two auspicious horses with their hooves, or like two partridges with their beaks—
having cleared away that terrifying crowd of people, the battle took place in the vicinity.
O King, like the two powerful Vṛtra and Vāsava in combat, they dragged each other forward and backward, pulled one another near and pushed away,
and likewise struck each other with their knees.
Then, threatening one another with a great roar,
they struck each other with blows resembling the clashing of masses of stone.
Then Jarāsaṃdha struck Bhīma on the chest with his fist.
Bhīma also struck Jarāsaṃdha on the chest;
both broad-chested, long-armed, and skilled in wrestling,
they locked together with their arms like iron clubs.
On the first day of the month of Kārttika,
that battle then commenced; it continued for fifteen days,
proceeding incessantly day and night without respite.
On the fifteenth day, a terrible and astonishing event occurred;
however, that which had transpired on the thirteenth day was the meeting of those two great-souled ones, who,
pressing limb against limb, found rest.
For Vṛkodara was restored by the wind from his immortal breath.
On the night of the fourteenth day, however, the King of Magadha turned back due to exhaustion.
O King, seeing the monarch thus fatigued, Janārdana—
He spoke to Bhīma of terrible deeds, as if awakening him,
while cutting through the midst of men in battle as if awakening them;
he who knew the birth and death of the enemy, and life brought about by old age.
Strengthening Pārtha with his own splendor,
Hari reflected; having considered the means for slaying the enemy, he whose vision is infallible revealed [himself] to Bhīma by means of a sign, as if splitting open a tree branch.
O son of Kuntī, an exhausted enemy cannot be further oppressed in battle;
for if he is completely overwhelmed, he may even lose his own life.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, this lord of men must not be oppressed by you.
"Fight him on equal terms with your two arms alone, O bull among the Bharatas.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, that Pāṇḍava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
perceiving Jarāsaṃdha’s vulnerability, set his mind upon killing him.
Then Vṛkodara, the joy of the Kurus and foremost among the strong, becoming enraged, seized Jarāsaṃdha in order to conquer that unconquerable one.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Bhīmasena, having formed a vast resolve with the intent to slay Jarāsaṃdha, spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of the Yadus:
"O Kṛṣṇa, this wicked man does not deserve to be conciliated by me."
"O tiger among the Yadus, with my life-breath and my loincloth tied together,"—
having been addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa, that tiger among men, desiring the slaughter of Jarāsaṃdha, then replied to Vṛkodara, urging him on.
"O Bhīma, show us today that supreme divine essence of yours, as well as the power you possess from Mātariśvan, within Jarāsaṃdha. O mighty-armed Balarāma, slay this king of Magadha."
"This evil-minded Jarāsaṃdha, a great chariot-warrior, was to be slain by you"—
this I heard in the sky when the wind had subsided,
on the Gomanta, the best of mountains, where he was liberated.

"O mighty-armed one, having encountered the arm of Baladeva, who else could survive from the Magadha king? Therefore, O one of great strength, death has been ordained for him by you alone; thinking of Vāyu, do you slay the lord of Magadha."
Thus addressed, Bhīma then mentally invoked Māruta;
having paid homage to Janārdana and embraced Phalguna,
Bhīma, the subduer of enemies, spoke thus to Jarāsaṃdha.
O King, the immensely powerful one lifted up the strong man and whirled him around;
having whirled him a hundred times with his two arms, O bull of the Bharatas,
he bent his back, crushed him, and let out a roar.
Seizing his foot with his hand, the one of great strength tore him in two.
As that Pāṇḍava was being crushed and was roaring,
there arose a tumultuous sound that struck fear into all living beings.
Drawing back his left foot and seizing him with his right hand,
Pārtha tore the mighty Jarāsaṃdha in two.
All the people of Magadha were terrified, and even the fetuses of women miscarried.
From the roar of Bhīmasena and that of Jarāsaṃdha, the people of Magadha thought:
"Has the Himavat mountain been split asunder, or is the earth itself being torn apart? Such was their perception from the sound of Bhīmasena.
Seizing the enemy by the feet, he threw him down upon the ground;
treading on one foot with his own foot and grasping the other with both arms,
he tore him apart from the anus like a great elephant tearing at a branch.
The people saw [the body] divided into two halves, each possessing one foot, thigh, testicle, hip, heart, back, and nose; one arm, eye, eyebrow, and ear.
Then, beholding that terrifying sight, Kṛṣṇa seized Nala with his hand.
He split that [spear] in two, aiming for the slaying of Jarāsaṃdha.
Then, having understood her [intent],
he cast the weapon aside and let out a roar.
Then the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, having once again resolved himself, encountered Bhīma and engaged him in a wrestling match. A tumultuous battle ensued between the two, causing the hair to stand on end.
Desiring the slaughter of Jarāsandha, Mādhava overturned and threw down that [weapon], which causes the destruction of the entire world.
Then Bhīmasena, having recognized him, pierced the Māgadha;
having split him in two with his foot, he hurled him away and roared aloud,
while the mass of his head was shattered, along with its dry flesh, bones, fat, and blood.
Then, O King, having become like a corpse, he appeared as if rolled into a ball.
Then, at night, having abandoned that king— who was lying there at the gate of the royal palace as if fast asleep and deprived of life— the subduers of enemies departed.
Having yoked Jarāsaṃdha’s chariot, which was adorned with banners, and having caused his two brothers to mount it, Kṛṣṇa liberated his kinsmen.
Then those lords of the earth [honored] Kṛṣṇa, who is worthy of jewels, by offering him jewels.
Having been delivered from great danger, the kings approached him;
uninjured, fully equipped with weapons, and having conquered his enemies, he mounted that divine chariot and went forth from Girivraja along with the kings.
Having transported a great deal of wealth— consisting of hundreds of thousands of camels,
highly precious gems, silver, and likewise gold—
he established Sahadeva in Girivraja as one who was independent and under his own command.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, he set out from Girivraja.
He was known as Sodaryavān, a dual-fighter with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer; a striker who could be seen in close combat, he was invincible to all kings.
Mounted by the two warriors Bhīma and Arjuna and with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer,
that excellent chariot— invincible to all archers— shone resplendently;
for it was like Śakra and Viṣṇu moving together in battle during the Tārakāmaya war.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having mounted that chariot, departed.
Thus, these two mighty-armed ones, performers of difficult deeds, were led by Kṛṣṇa; who in this world would be able to look upon them on the chariot?
Thus spoke those residing in the city of Jarāsaṃdha to Vāsudeva, the best of men, as he was departing yoked to horses possessing the speed of the wind,
[driven by a chariot] shining like molten gold and garlanded with networks of small bells.
With that victorious chariot, which roared like the thunder of clouds and was the slayer of enemies—
with it Śakra had slain ninety-nine of the Dānavas—
those bulls among men rejoiced upon obtaining it.

Then, seeing the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa standing upon his chariot accompanied by his two brothers, the people of Magadha were filled with wonder. His chariot was yoked to celestial horses and was equal to the wind in speed.
O Bhārata, presided over by Kṛṣṇa, that chariot shone exceedingly;
upon that best of chariots stood the divine, unattached banner,
beautiful and radiant like Indra’s bow, visible from a distance of a yojana.
Then Kṛṣṇa thought of Garuḍa, and he arrived;
in that very instant, he stood with him like a towering sacrificial pillar.
Together with spirits who made great roars with gaping mouths, he became the abode of banners.
The bird Garuḍa, the devourer of serpents, stood upon that excellent chariot; indeed,
difficult for all beings to behold, he shone with exceeding splendor like the sun at midday surrounded by its thousand rays.
It does not get caught in trees, nor is it harmed by weapons;
O King, this supreme divine banner is seen by both gods and men.
Having mounted that divine chariot, which resounds like a rain-cloud, [he set forth].
That tiger among men, Acyuta, set forth together with the two Pāṇḍavas.
The king Vasu had obtained [the bow] from Vāsava, and from him Bṛhadratha received it;
through this very succession from Bṛhadratha, it reached the king who was the son of Bṛhadratha.
Then the mighty-armed, lotus-eyed one of great renown departed from Girivraja and stood upon level ground outside. There,
all the citizens then approached him with due honor.
O King, headed by the Brahmins, the kings— released from their bonds through rites prescribed by the sacred law— worshipped Madhusūdana and spoke these words with conciliatory intent:
"O mighty-armed son of Devakī, it is no wonder that the protection of dharma rests with you, who are endowed with the strength of Bhīma and Arjuna—
especially for those sinking into the terrible lake of Jarāsaṃdha, which is a mire of suffering."

O Viṣṇu, O Supreme Person, by good fortune you have attained radiant glory through the liberation of these kings who were perishing in this most dreadful mountain fortress; for today you have performed this rescue of those fallen into distress.
"What shall we do, O tiger among men? Speak, O bull among men!
Let it be known that it is already accomplished by the kings, even if it be difficult to achieve.
Having thus consoled them, the high-minded Hṛṣīkeśa spoke to them.
"Yudhiṣṭhira desires to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice. To him, who is devoted to righteousness and seeks to attain the status of a sovereign monarch,
you all must provide assistance for the sake of the sacrifice."
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, those kings, with hearts full of confidence,
all said, "So be it," and they pledged themselves to those words.
And those lords of the earth made the descendant of Daśārha the recipient of the jewels.
Out of compassion for them, Govinda accepted [the challenge] with great difficulty. Then Sahadeva, the son of Jarāsaṃdha and a great chariot-warrior,
went forth accompanied by his kinsmen and ministers, placing the family priest at the head.
Having become humble and deferential, with many jewels before him,
Sahadeva approached Vāsudeva, the god among men.
Sahadeva.
O Janārdana, O tiger among men, that which was done for me by my father—O mighty-armed Puruṣottama, you should not take that to heart.
I have sought refuge in you, O Govinda; grant me your grace, O Lord.
"O son of Devakī, having obtained permission from you, as well as from Bhīmasena and Arjuna, I wish to perform the funeral rites for my father. —
Vaiśampāyana.
"I shall wander about fearless, according to my desire and at my ease.
O noble one, when Sahadeva had thus made his request,
the son of Devakī and the two Pāṇḍava great-chariot warriors were filled with joy.
"O King, let the funeral rites for your father be performed," they said.
Having heard those words of Vāsudeva and the two sons of Pṛthā, the King of Magadha,
together with his ministers, quickly entered the city.
With sandalwood logs, as well as kāleya and sarala wood, with fragrant black aloe-wood and various oils,
with streams of clarified butter, unbroken grains of rice, and *sumana* flowers, [they prepared] the funeral pyre for Māgadha.
They were scattered all around and burned the lord of Magadha;
then Sahadeva, together with his younger brother, provided water for him.
Having performed the rites for his father’s journey to heaven, he departed for the place where Keśava was.
And having become humble with palms joined in reverence, he addressed Mādhava on behalf of both the illustrious Pāṇḍavas, Bhīmasena and Arjuna:
"These are abundant jewels, as well as cattle, goats, sheep, buffaloes, and so forth."
"O Govinda, let elephants, horses, and various garments be given to the King of Dharma, or whatever you deem appropriate. Then,
having granted him freedom from fear, Kṛṣṇa gave it to him who was afflicted by terror."
The Supreme Person, Janārdana, took for himself the highly precious jewels from Sahadeva,
the protector of the Magadhas.
Right there, he then consecrated the son of Jarāsaṃdha;
having attained unity with Kṛṣṇa and being honored by the two sons of Pṛthā,
the wise king re-entered the city of Bārhadratha.
The mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the son of Jarāsaṃdha, having been consecrated by the high-souled ones, met with the two Pārthas and all the lords of the earth according to their age,
and then dismissed the kings.

"Having dismissed all the kings at the Rājasūya sacrifice, you great-souled ones must come here, desiring to do what is pleasing to the King of Dharma. Having been addressed thus by Mādhava, all those lords of the earth—
Having said, "So be it," Bhīma, Arjuna, and Hṛṣīkeśa, filled with supreme joy and delight, set out together,
those slayers of enemies blazing as they took up abundant jewels.
But Kṛṣṇa, blazing with supreme splendor together with the two sons of Pṛthā,
took vast quantities of jewels and departed; the lotus-eyed Acyuta,
having arrived at Indraprastha along with the two Pāṇḍavas, [remained there].
Having approached the King of Dharma, he spoke with joy:
"By good fortune, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha has been struck down by Bhīma;
and these kings have been liberated from their bonds, O best of monarchs."
"By good fortune, O Bhārata, both Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya have returned safely to their own city unharmed. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having honored Kṛṣṇa as was his due, [spoke].
He joyfully embraced both Bhīmasena and Arjuna. Then,
Jarāsaṃdha having been slain,
Ajātaśatru, having attained the victory achieved by his two brothers, rejoiced together with them.
And the King of Dharma, filled with joy, addressed these words to Janārdana:
"O tiger among men, having obtained you as his protector, Bhīmasena has struck down that powerful Jarāsaṃdha of Magadha, who was intoxicated by his own strength."
"Free from all feverish anxiety, I shall attain the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices;
relying on the power of your intellect, O Janārdana, I am worthy of performing the sacrifice. Your fame has been drunk up by the enraged Earth, O Supreme Person."
"By the very slaying of Jarāsaṃdha, you have obtained vast riches.
Having spoken thus, O Lord, the son of Kuntī presented that excellent chariot;
and Govinda, having accepted that chariot of Jarāsaṃdha, [departed].
Delighted by that feat of Phalguna, Janārdana rejoiced;
O King, he was filled with joy, being honored by Dharmarāja.
And the Pāṇḍava, having met with those kings according to their seniority, [was likewise honored].
Having honored and worshipped them, he dismissed the lords of men;
then, permitted by Yudhiṣṭhira, those kings, with joyful hearts,
departed quickly for their own countries in various kinds of vehicles.
Thus did Janārdana, that tiger among men and possessor of great intelligence,
cause his enemy Jarāsaṃdha to be slain by the Pāṇḍavas at that time;
having thus caused Jarāsaṃdha to be killed through his strategic wisdom, the subduer of foes [departed].
O Bhārata, having obtained the permission of Dharmarāja, as well as Pṛthā, Kṛṣṇā,
Subhadrā, Bhīmasena, Phalguna, and the twins,
and having taken leave of Dhaumya, he set out toward his own city.
Followed by the Pāṇḍavas with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, Kṛṣṇa—
filled with great joy and having attained unsurpassed fame—
returned delighted to the city of Dvāravatī.
With that very preeminent chariot, which possessed the splendor of the rising sun and had been dispatched by Dharmarāja, it made the quarters of the sky resound.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira—
They performed circumambulations of Kṛṣṇa, the doer of effortless deeds.
Then, when the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, had departed,
those who grant fearlessness to kings obtained a very great victory.

O descendant of Bharata, O King, by that deed their vigor was further increased, and the Pāṇḍavas brought supreme joy to Draupadī. At that time, they performed whatever was appropriate and consistent with virtue, pleasure, and worldly prosperity.
The king, possessing the fame of protecting his kingdom, governed according to righteousness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having obtained the best of bows and the two inexhaustible great quivers, Pārtha—
He spoke of the chariot, the banner, and the assembly hall to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Reflecting upon those words of the ṛṣi, Yudhiṣṭhira sighed;
that scorcher of foes, the best among the upholders of dharma, desired to act in accordance with righteousness.
Bībhatsu, the best among all wielders of weapons and son of Indra, perceiving his intention,
desired to turn back from the fire;
for he possessed the bow, missiles, arrows, valor, allies, territory, fame, and strength.
"O King, that which was desired and difficult to attain has been obtained by me.
Having heard this, the best of the Kurus, Dharmarāja, together with his younger brothers and his ministers, including Vyāsa, Dhaumya, and the others, was filled with joy.
Then Vyāsa, possessed of great intelligence, spoke these words to Arjuna:
"Excellent, excellent, O son of Kuntī! By good fortune you possess such an intellect;
you alone are resolved to conquer the entire earth."
Blessed is King Pāṇḍu, who has such a son as you!
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and lord of kings, shall obtain everything; through your prowess, that righteous soul shall attain the status of a sovereign emperor.
Relying on the strength of your arms,
and through the wise policy of Vāsudeva, the power of Bhīma and Arjuna,
and the valor of the twins, the King of Dharma shall attain everything, including the Rājasūya sacrifice.
"Therefore, O Phalguna, go toward the northern quarter protected by the gods;
you are capable of conquering the deities and bringing back jewels by your own prowess.
Let Bhima, who boasts of his strength, proceed toward the eastern quarter, O bull of the Bharatas."
Let the great chariot-warrior Sahadeva go there toward the southern direction;
Nakula shall go toward the western quarter protected by Varuṇa.
O bulls among the Bharatas, let this be my final resolve; act accordingly.
Having heard the words of Vyāsa, the sons of Pāṇḍu were delighted and said to him:
"So be it, O best of sages; as you command us, O Lord. Having taken leave of the king, they departed surrounded by a vast army.

"In this matter, O best of kings, I consider the task to be the increase of this treasury; I shall cause all the kings to pay tribute. For the sake of victory, I shall set out toward the quarter protected by the Giver of Wealth."
All were impelled by the force of the wind and adorned with every ornament. Then,
on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, and under a propitious constellation,
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira heard the words of Dhanañjaya.
With a voice that was smooth, deep, and resonant, he replied to him:
"O bull among the Bharatas, go forth after having offered words of blessing to the worthy brahmins,
for the lack of joy to the ill-disposed and for the delight of your friends."
"Victory is surely yours, O Pārtha; may you attain your desired wish.
Having been addressed thus, Pārtha set forth, surrounded by a great army and mounted upon the divine chariot of wondrous deeds given by Agni.
In the same manner, Bhīmasena and the twins, those bulls among men,
all set forth with their armies, honored by Dharmarāja.
The son of Pākaśāsana conquered the quarter favored by the Lord of Wealth.
Bhīmasena likewise conquered the eastern quarter, Sahadeva the southern,
and Nakula, O King, skilled in weapons, conquered the western direction;
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira dwells in Khāṇḍavaprastha.
The Lord was surrounded by a circle of friends and possessed supreme splendor.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, recount in detail the conquest of the quarters."
"I am not yet satiated by hearing the great deeds of my ancestors.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I shall first relate to you the victory of Dhanañjaya."
For this earth was conquered by the sons of Pṛthā simultaneously;
having obtained half of the kingdom, the high-minded King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī,
set his mind upon the greatness of the title "King."
Then, having learned of his conquest of the earth,
those lords of the earth, out of indignation and desiring to fight, assembled against him;
and that host of the world's warriors, consisting of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry, gathered together.

O lord of men, he advanced against the victorious king in order to frustrate him; then the mighty-armed son of Indra, Pārtha, desiring to fight that royal warrior in the great battle, rushed forward with speed.

That royal host was shattered by Pārtha of unwearied deeds; like a mass of clouds dispersed by the wind, it fled in all directions, rendered futile. Having conquered that royal army in battle, the slayer of enemy heroes—

Then the son of Pāṇḍu set out to bring the northern region under his control. First, in the kingdom of Kuṇinda, the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya brought the lords of the earth under his sway without employing excessively harsh means.

Accompanied by him alone, the victorious one set out toward the city of the Sālvas. Having reached the city of the Sālvas, the high-minded Dhanañjaya brought the king of the Sālvas— the fierce archer— under his control through his prowess.
Having swiftly conquered Dyumatsena, the lord of wealth, Pārtha,
the subduer of enemies, set out for the region of Kaṭa with his entire army;
there, Jiṣṇu encountered Sunābha, the king of the earth, who had conquered evil.
Having brought them under his control by his prowess, he made them follow the Anusainika;
having conquered the Ānartas, the Kālakūṭas, and the Kuṇindas,
he made the Pāpajitas follow Sumaṇḍala.
Accompanied by him, O King, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
conquered the entire continent as well as King Prativindhya and all the inhabitants of the continents,
including those kings who dwell within the seven continents.
Pārtha conquered them all out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Dharmarāja;
a tumultuous conflict then broke out between Arjuna and the enemy forces.
Having defeated them as well, O bull of the Bharatas, that great archer—
Accompanied by all of them, he rushed toward Prāgjyotiṣa.
There, O lord of the people, was the great king Bhagadatta;
with him, a truly massive battle took place against the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Surrounded by Kirātas, Cīnas, and many other warriors dwelling on the coastal regions of the sea, that ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa took his stand.
Then, having fought Dhananjaya for eight days, he...
Bhagadatta, along with his fourfold army, was defeated;
struck by the arrows of Pārtha, his limbs reeling and deeply distressed,
the king, free from fatigue in the midst of battle, spoke while laughing.
"O mighty-armed one, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas, this is fitting for you— this prowess in battle, O heir of Indra who shines in combat!
I am the friend of the Lord of the Gods, and I am not inferior to Śakra himself in war."
"O father, I am not able to stand before you in battle.
O son of Pāṇḍu, tell me what you desire; what may I do for you? Whatever you say, O mighty-armed one, that I shall do, my dear son."
Arjuna said:
"The bull among the Kurus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
is a knower of dharma, true to his promise, a performer of sacrifices, and a giver of abundant sacrificial fees."
"I desire his status as a sovereign; let tribute be paid to him. You are both a friend of my father and one who is dear to me;
therefore, I do not command you, but let it be given out of affection."
Bhagadatta said:
"O son of Kuntī, as you are to me, so is King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having been thus honored there by him, Dhanañjaya stayed for one month.
Having conquered [the region] toward the east of the waters, he set out toward Rāmagiri;
then, having subdued Rāmagiri as well as Bhuvanaparvata,
the son of Indra brought others too under his control by force.
"I shall do all this; what else may I do for you?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having conquered him, the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, [proceeded].
From there, he set out toward the northern direction protected by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Thus addressed, Dhanañjaya replied to Bhagadatta:
"By your very acquiescence, everything will be accomplished."
The son of Kuntī, that bull among men, likewise conquered the region within the mountains, as well as the region outside the mountains,
and the region upon the mountains. Having subdued all the mountains and the lords of men who dwelt there, he prevailed.
Having brought them under his control and taken all their jewels from every side,
he— accompanied by all of them and having won the affection of those kings—
approached Bṛhanta, the king dwelling in Kulūta, O monarch.
With the excellent sound of kettledrums, the rattling of chariot wheels,
and the trumpeting of elephants, he caused this earth to tremble;
then Bṛhanta, young and accompanied by a fourfold army, [advanced].
Having emerged from that city, he fought the son of Pāṇḍu;
there occurred a truly great encounter between Dhananjaya and Bṛhanta,
yet Bṛhanta was unable to withstand the prowess of the Pāṇḍava.
Realizing that the son of Kuntī was utterly invincible, the dull-witted lord of the mountains retreated, taking with him all kinds of jewels;
under the pretext of hospitality, he presented those accumulated riches.
There were twenty thousand elephants and likewise one hundred million horses.
Then Dhanañjaya, accompanied by that Kaulūta,
established himself in that kingdom and departed together with the Kulūta.
Then, O King, he swiftly deposed Senābindu from his kingdom;
he brought under his power Modāpura, Vāmadeva, Sudāmāna, Susaṃkula,
the Kulūtas, and those of the north— all those kings.

Stationed there, O King, by the command of Dharmarāja, Dhanañjaya conquered five regions according to their extent through his own men alone. Having reached Divaḥprastha, he arrived at the great city of Senābindu.
The lord established his camp with his fourfold army. Surrounded by all of them, that man of great splendor and bull among men approached Viṣvagaśva, the king of the Pauravas.
Having conquered in battle the heroic mountain-dwellers, those great chariot-warriors, he then, O King, with his army, overcame the city protected by the Pauravas;
there, the joy of the Kurus crushed them with his vast host.
In battle, he cast down both Urasāvalina and Romāṇa;
having utterly defeated Paurava, he subdued the Dasyus dwelling in the mountains and Senābindu in his city.
The immeasurable-souled one caused [the drums] to be placed;
the Pāṇḍava conquered the seven festive hosts (gaṇas).
Then, that bull among kṣatriyas [conquered] the heroic kṣatriyas of Kaśmīra.
He conquered Lohita along with ten mandalas;
then, O King, the son of Kuntī subdued the Trigartas, the Dārvās, and the Kokanadas,
as well as many other Kṣatriyas from all directions.

Then the joy of the Kurus conquered the delightful Abhisārī, and he defeated Rocamāna, who dwelt in Uraśā, in battle. After that, he took the beautiful Siṃhapura, which was well-guarded by Citrāyudha.
Relying on his strength,
the son of Indra crushed them in battle; then Kiritin, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas and joy of the Kurus, together with his entire army, crushed the Suhmas and the Colas.
Then, supremely valiant, the joy of the Kurus brought the Bāhlīkas—
who were difficult to subdue— under his control through a great slaughter.
Having seized their elite forces and abandoned the weak, the Pāṇḍava [proceeded].
The son of Indra conquered the Daradas along with the Kambojas;
O great king, he also defeated the Yavanas and the Śakas in battle.
He subdued the Kirātas, the Sabhayas, the Kharvas, the Khalas, the Kācas, and the Bahuvṛtas.
He conquered the Nīras, the Utpāsikas, and thousands of other Mlecchas;
Pārtha defeated them all out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Dharmarāja. Furthermore, he subdued those bandits who dwell in the northeastern quarter.
The lord conquered all those who dwell in the forest,
as well as the Lohas, the supreme Kambojas, and the northern Rishikas;
O great king, the son of Pakaśāsana defeated them all together.
A most terrifying battle took place among the Ṛṣikas,
resembling the conflict between Tāraka and Maya, between the supreme Ṛṣika and the son of Pṛthā. Having then conquered the Ṛṣikas at the forefront of the battle, O King—
He brought forth eight horses with a luster like the belly of a parrot;
others resembling peacocks, and yet others of both types—
swift and fleet-footed— for the sake of the king's hand.
Then, O Janamejaya, having conquered that land of Bhārata-varṣa,
Bībhatsu also defeated other divine regions and the principal mountain ranges.
"How did that son of Pṛthā conquer the celestial regions along with the mountains?
O twice-born one, tell me in due order, together with their names.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having conquered the land of Bhārata by force, King Dhanañjaya also subdued all the Dasyus in the region within the Himalayas by his might. Having completely defeated Himavat along with Niṣkuṭa in battle, he—
Having reached the White Mountain, that bull among men took up residence there.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, having traversed the White Mountain, that hero—
The best of the Pāṇḍavas conquered the region inhabited by Kimpuruṣas,
which was protected by Drumaputra, through a great encounter that brought an end to the Kṣatriyas, and he established a tribute upon them.
Having conquered that country named Hāṭaka, which was protected by Guhyakas,
the son of Pākaśāsana (Indra), unperturbed, approached it together with his army.
Having subdued them through conciliation, he reached the supreme Lake Mānasa.
The joy of the Kurus beheld all those rivers flowing from the sages; having reached Lake Mānasa, the lord,
the Pāṇḍava, then conquered the region protected by the Gandharvas, which was surrounded by the Hāṭakas.
There, he received as tribute from the city of the Gandharvas excellent horses, brindled like partridges and with eyes like frogs;
then Phalguna, having reached Hemakūṭa, took up residence there.
O Indra among kings, having crossed over that Hemakūṭa mountain, the Pāṇḍava,
surrounded by a vast army, then entered Harivarṣa. There, the son of Pṛthā beheld many delightful sights.
Having seen there the cities and forests, the rivers of pure water,
the men who were like gods, and the women of lovely appearance,
Dhanañjaya was filled with joy.
He brought the treasures under his control and obtained very many of them;
then, having reached Niṣadha, the lord conquered those situated on the mountain. Then, O King, having crossed the long Niṣadha mountain...
Pārtha entered the central, divine region of Ilāvṛta.
There, Dhanañjaya beheld godlike, celestial men of auspicious appearance, whom he had never seen before and who resembled the gods themselves.
Having seen those radiant dwellings and women resembling celestial nymphs (apsaras),
he conquered those delightful places and was then beheld by them;
and having defeated those illustrious beings, he placed them under his authority.
Taking divine jewels along with ornaments and garments,
O Indra among kings, Pārtha then departed for the north, filled with joy;
he then beheld Meru, the great lord of mountain peaks.
That divine mountain Meru, made of gold, possessing four colors, difficult to approach,
extending for a hundred thousand yojanas and firmly established,
blazing, immovable, and an unsurpassed mass of splendor.
It eclipsed the radiance of the sun with its own peaks, which were brilliant with gold;
it was adorned with divine golden ornaments, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
and always endowed with flowers and fruits, served by siddhas and cāraṇas.
Immeasurable and unassailable by people abounding in unrighteousness,
frequented by fierce beasts of prey and illuminated by divine medicinal herbs,
that great mountain stands encompassing heaven in its height.
Inaccessible even to the minds of others, endowed with rivers and trees,
and made resonant by flocks of various most enchanting birds—
seeing that Mount Meru, Phalguna then became filled with joy.
The region of Ilāvṛta surrounds Mount Meru on all sides in a circular form. On the southern side of Meru, however, stands a great tree named Jambū,
which is endowed with eternal flowers and fruits and is frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
O King, the branches of that lord of the forest rose high toward heaven;
it was after his name that this continent became known as Jambūdvīpa.
Then Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, beheld that Jambū tree.
Seeing those two, who were peerless in the world, standing like Mount Jambū and Mount Meru,
O King, he became filled with joy as he gazed upon them from all sides;
thereupon Jiṣṇu received [homage] from the Siddhas and the divine Cāraṇas.
Having then obtained many thousands of jewels, garments, ornaments,
and other highly precious things there, Arjuna took leave of them all for the sake of his preceptor’s sacrifice.
Then, taking many jewels, the Lord prepared to depart;
having circumambulated Meru, the preeminent mountain,
he went along the bank of the Jambū river, gazing upon that most excellent of streams.
He beheld that delightful, divine river, which brought forth the sweet juice of the jambu fruit; it was frequented by flocks of golden birds, filled with golden lotuses,
possessed of golden mud and golden waters, auspicious, and strewn with golden sands.
In some places it was crowded with golden lotuses and golden flowers;
in other places it was strewn with well-blossomed golden water-lilies and blue lotuses;
and in some places it was covered with golden trees growing on the banks, all in full bloom.
It was auspicious, crowded on all sides with bathing-ghats featuring golden staircases,
endowed with networks of spotless jewels and the sounds of dancing and singing,
and beautified everywhere by radiant canopies of gold.

Seeing such a river, Pārtha praised it; O Indra among kings, having seen that which he had never seen before, he was filled with joy. He beheld men on the riverbank who were handsome and exceedingly charming.
From those who subsisted on the water of the river, who were accompanied by their wives and resembled immortals,
who were constantly endowed with happiness and joy, and adorned with every ornament,
Dhanañjaya then obtained many jewels and wealth.
Having obtained divine ornaments made of Jāmbūnada gold and exquisite golden trinkets— those things so difficult to acquire— Pārtha set out toward the western direction;
thereafter, Arjuna conquered the region guarded by the Nāgas.
Then, O great king, having gone to Vāruṇī,
the lordly son of Indra reached Gandhamādana and conquered those stationed there.
O King, Arjuna then proceeded beyond that Gandhamādana.
Then he entered the region of Ketumāla, which is endowed with jewels and inhabited by women as beautiful as gods;
having conquered it, O King, Arjuna established it under tribute.

Having gathered there such jewels as are difficult to obtain, O King, Arjuna Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, then turned back and went from Ilāvṛta in the Middle Country toward the eastern direction.
Between Mount Meru and Mount Mandara, on both sides of the river Śailodā, those Khashas, Jhashas, Nadyotas, Praghasas, and Dirghavenikas dwell, enjoying the delightful shade of the kīcaka bamboos.
Having conquered the Paśus, Kuṇindas, Ṭaṅkaṇas, and Paraṭaṅkaṇas— all these together— and having established them under tribute,
he took jewels from all of them and then proceeded toward Mālyavat.
Having crossed that Mālyavat, the lord of mountains, the son of Pāṇḍu then entered the auspicious region of Bhadrāśva, which was like heaven;
there he saw men resembling gods, beautiful and endowed with happiness.
Having conquered them, brought them under his own control, and placed them in his power,
the Lord gathered innumerable jewels from here and there; then,
having gone to the mountain named Nīla, he defeated those stationed there.
Then Jishnu, having traversed the long Blue Mountain (Nīla),
entered the delightful region of Ramyaka, which was filled with auspicious pairs of beings.
Having conquered that land, he then established it under his tribute.
And Bibhatsu also conquered that region protected by the Guhyakas;
there, O king of kings, he obtained golden deer and birds,
beautiful and enchanting, which he took for the sake of the success of his sacrifice.
Then, having obtained other jewels, the mighty Pāṇḍava conquered that region protected by the Gandharvas along with its hosts; there,
O King, Arjuna then acquired divine treasures.
Having reached Mount Śveta and conquered those who dwell upon the mountain,
that Pāṇḍava, O King, having crossed over Mount Śveta,
then entered the region named Hiraṇyaka, O lord of the earth.
O Indra among kings, as Arjuna proceeded along the great highways in every direction, he set out for those delightful regions like the moon moving amidst clusters of palaces and the stars.
Standing upon the pinnacle of that excellent palace, all those women, endowed with supreme splendor of valor, beheld Pārtha, who enhances his own fame—
the heroic lord, equipped with his quiver, together with his chariot and his followers.
Clad in armor, wearing a diadem, fully equipped with his accoutrements— tender yet a being of great strength, an unsurpassed mass of splendor,
equal to Śakra, a slayer of enemies, and a restrainer of opposing forces.
Beholding him there with a spear in hand, the throngs of women thought:
"This is that tiger among men, possessed of wondrous prowess in battle;
having encountered the strength of his arms, hosts of enemies cease to exist."
Speaking thus with words of love, those women praised Dhanañjaya and showered a rain of flowers upon his head;
seeing this, they were filled with joy and overcome with curiosity.
They rained down jewels and ornaments upon the Pāṇḍava.
Then, having conquered them all and having placed them under tribute,
[he took] gems, gold, corals, garments, and ornaments.
Having obtained these, Pārtha also went to Mount Śṛṅgavant;
and having passed beyond Mount Śṛṅgavant, Phalguna, the son of Kuntī, [proceeded].
Having reached the northern region of Harivarṣa, that son of Pāṇḍu conquered the hosts of Vidyādharas and the lords of the Yakṣas; there,
the high-souled one indeed obtained a supreme and divine dwelling.
There, Dhanañjaya obtained many divine black antelope skins and leaves from the *kiṃnara* trees, as well as those fit for sacrifice;
then the son of Indra desired to conquer that region.
Then the gatekeepers— of massive body, great heroism, and immense strength— approached him and, being delighted, spoke these words:
"O Pārtha, it is not possible for you to conquer this city by any means whatsoever."
"Turn back, O auspicious one; this is enough, O Acyuta. Any man who enters this city will surely cease to exist.
We are pleased with you, O hero; your victory is sufficient."
"Furthermore, O Arjuna, nothing at all remains here to be conquered;
for these are the Northern Kurus, and no battle takes place here.
Even if you enter, O son of Kuntī, you will see nothing more here."
"For it is not possible to behold this with a human body.
Now, O tiger among men, if you desire to do anything else here, speak it; we shall do it at your word, O Bhārata."
Then, O King, Arjuna, the son of Indra, spoke to them:
"I desire to perform the royal consecration for the wise Dharmarāja;
indeed, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, he himself desires to perform the royal consecration."
"I shall not enter your territory if it is subject to oppression by humans;
let whatever tribute be due to Yudhiṣṭhira be given to us.
Otherwise, O protectors, I shall fight you accompanied by Kṛṣṇa."
Then they presented him with divine garments, divine ornaments,
and divine deer-skins as tribute.
Thus did that tiger among men conquer the northern quarter.
O bull of the Bharatas, having fought many battles with both Kṣatriyas and Dasyus, that best of men completely conquered this island of Sudarśana and brought those kings under tribute.
Having taken wealth and various kinds of jewels from all of them,
he also took horses— some speckled like partridges, some resembling the wings of parrots,
others like peacocks— all possessing the speed of the wind.
O King, surrounded by a very great fourfold army,
the hero returned once more to Śakraprastha, that most excellent of cities; thereupon,
Pārtha presented all that wealth, together with the vehicles, to Dharmarāja.
Having been granted permission by that king, he announced his departure and went home.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, the heroic Bhīmasena also—

Having obtained the permission of Dharmarāja, the majestic one set out toward the eastern direction with a great circle of forces that crushes enemy kingdoms— a host filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, all clad in armor.
Surrounded by his followers, that tiger among the Bharatas, who increases the grief of his enemies,
went to the great city of the Pañcālas; having arrived there, that tiger among kings,
the Pāṇḍava, conciliated the Pañcālas with various means.
Taking a small tribute, he went to the city of the Videhas;
then that hero, that bull among men, having conquered the Gaṇḍakī and the Videhas in a short time, the lord proceeded to the Daśārṇas.
There, King Sudharmā of Daśārṇa performed a hair-raising feat,
engaging in a great unarmed combat with Bhīma.
But Bhīmasena, the scorcher of foes, beheld that deed of his.
Exerting all his strength, he traversed the circle;
having crushed the entire city, he then conquered Sudharman.
He appointed the mighty Sudharman as his supreme commander.
Then, O King, Bhīma of terrible prowess marched toward the eastern direction with a vast army, as if making the earth tremble.
He [conquered] Rocamāna, the lord of Aśvamedha, along with his younger brother, O King.
The hero, the best among the strong, conquered him in battle by means of his own strength.
Having defeated him with effort that was not excessively harsh, the son of Kuntī,
the joy of the Kurus and possessor of great valor, conquered the eastern region.
Then, having arrived at the great city of Pulinda in the south,
he brought Sukumāra and the king Sumitra under his control.
Then, O bull of the Bharata race, by the command of the King of Dharma, he [proceeded further].
O Janamejaya, he marched against the highly heroic Śiśupāla;
and the King of Cedi, that scorcher of foes, having heard of the Pāṇḍava’s intention, went out from the city and received him.

O great king, having met then, those two bulls of the Kuru and Cedi lineages inquired after the welfare of each other’s families. Then, O lord of the people, the king of the Cedis reported that kingdom [to him].
Laughing, he said to Bhīma, "O sinless one, what is this that you are doing?
Bhīma then explained to him what the King of Dharma intended to do;
and having accepted that proposal, the lord of men acted accordingly.
Then, O King, Bhīma, having stayed there for thirty nights and being honored by Śiśupāla, departed with his army and vehicles.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, that subduer of enemies conquered Śreṇimanta in the kingdom of Kumāra, as well as Bṛhadbala, the lord of Kosala;
and in Ayodhyā, he [conquered] the knower of dharma, Dīrghaprajña, who possessed great strength.
The best of the Pāṇḍavas conquered them without excessively harsh deeds. Then the lord subdued Gopālakaccha, as well as the Uttaras,
and also the king who was the ruler of the Mallas.
Then, having approached Jaradgava on the slopes of the Himavat,
the powerful one brought that entire region under his control in a short time. Thus,
that bull among men conquered various lands in this manner.
The Pāṇḍava, of immense heroism and the foremost among the strong by virtue of his strength, conquered in battle Unnāṭa, Abhitojigya, and the mountainous Kukṣimant;
he then encountered Subandhu, the King of Kāśi, who never retreated from the fray.

The mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess brought them under his control. Then that bull among the Pāṇḍavas, by force, conquered Supārśva and likewise Kratha, the lord of kings, as they fought in the battle.

Then the one of great splendor [conquered] the Matsyas and the mighty Malayas; likewise the irreproachable Gayas and the entire region of Paśubhūmi. Having turned back, the mighty-armed one [reached] Mount Madarvīka.
Having conquered Sopadeśa, the son of Kuntī, the powerful one, set out facing north; he then forcibly subdued Vatsabhūmi,
as well as the lord of the Bhargas and the king of the Niṣādas.
He conquered many rulers of the earth, headed by Maṇimat;
then Bhīma, the Pāṇḍava, swiftly defeated the Dakṣiṇamallas and Bhogavat with no great exertion of effort.
The Lord conquered the Śarmakas and Varmakas through conciliation alone;
and that tiger among men defeated Janaka, the King of Videha and lord of the earth, by means of no excessive exertion.
He conquered the Śakas and the Barbaras by means of stratagem. While stationed in Videha, O son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava defeated the seven lords of the Kirātas in the vicinity of Mount Indraparvata.
Then the heroic and powerful son of Kuntī, having conquered the Suhmas, the Eastern Suhmas, and the Samakshas in battle, proceeded toward the Magadhas;
and having defeated the two lords of the earth, Daṇḍa and Daṇḍadhāra.
Accompanied by all of them, he rushed toward Girivraja;
having conciliated the son of Jarāsaṃdha and having made him pay tribute,
O King, that powerful one, together with those very men, charged against Karṇa.
Making the earth tremble, as it were, with his fourfold army,
that best of the Pāṇḍavas fought with Karṇa, the slayer of enemies;
accompanied by all those very warriors, the lord even defeated Karṇa.
Having defeated him along with Śiśupāla, that son of Pāṇḍu,
O Bhārata, having conquered Karṇa in battle and brought him under his control,
the powerful hero then subdued the kings dwelling in the mountains.
Then,
in that great battle, the Pāṇḍava, by the strength of his arms, slew King Modāgiri,
who was exceedingly powerful; thereafter, he [slew] the heroic and mighty Vāsudeva, the lord of Pauṇḍra.

"Now, out of fear for Kṛṣṇa’s arms, King Pauṇḍraka will not fight by the prowess of Vṛṣṇi," [he thought]. Then, the king of great majesty, who dwelt in the marshlands of the Kauśikī river, quickly paid tribute.
Both heroes, endowed with strength and both possessed of fierce prowess,
having conquered [their foes] in battle, O Great King, rushed against the king of Vaṅga;
and having defeated Samudrasena and King Candrasena, they proceeded further.
[He subdued] King Tāmralipta, as well as Kāca, the lord of Vaṅga,
the sovereign of the Aṅgas, and the ruler of the Kaliṅgas,
along with the lord of the Suhmas and those who dwell by the ocean.
The bull among the Bharatas conquered all the tribes of Mlecchas,
as well as the Kirātas, the man-eaters, and even those adorned with ear-rings; and those who are known as Kākamukhas, born of the lineage of both men and Rākṣasas.
Having conquered the Kirātas, the Tṛṇamūlas, the Kirātas, and the Oṣṭhakarnikas—
thus subduing many kinds of regions and taking wealth from them, the powerful son of the Wind-god went to Lauhitya.
He caused all the Mleccha kings dwelling on the islands of the ocean to pay tribute and various kinds of jewels,
as well as sandalwood, aloe-wood, garments, and unsurpassed gems and pearls.
Then that one of immeasurable soul, with a vast wealth consisting of gold, silver, diamonds, and coral numbering hundreds of millions,
rained down a shower of riches upon the Pāṇḍava.
Then, having arrived at Indraprastha, Bhima of terrible prowess presented that wealth to Dharmarāja. Vaiśampāyana said:
In the same manner, Sahadeva also, honored by the King of Dharma,
set out toward the southern direction together with a vast army.
That lord first conquered the Śūrasenas in their entirety.
The powerful Kauravya brought the King of Matsya under his control by force; likewise, in a great battle, he conquered Dantavakra, the sovereign of Adhiraja,
and established him as a tribute-payer within his own kingdom.
He brought Sukumāra and the king Sumitra under his control;
likewise, he conquered the other Matsyas and the Paṭaccaras. Having then defeated the Śreṇimantas, he subsequently subdued the Paṭaccaras at Gośṛṅga.
The wise one swiftly conquered Niṣādabhūmi, as well as Gośṛṅga, the preeminent mountain, and King Śreṇimant;
having completely defeated Navarāṣṭra, he marched against Kuntibhoja.
And with a heart full of joy, he accepted his instruction. Then,
on the banks of the Carmaṇvatī, he beheld the king who was the son of Jambhaka, who had been spared by Vāsudeva because of their former enmity.
O Bhārata, he waged battle there with Bhoja;
having utterly defeated him in combat, the mighty-armed one proceeded toward the south,
[encountering] Bhagadatta, the Kṣatriya son of Naraka.
Having heard that tribute had been given there to Arjuna, he turned back;
the exceedingly powerful one then conquered Sekas and Aparasekas,
taking from them tributes and various kinds of jewels.
Then, accompanied by those very men, he went toward the Narmadā. There,
the powerful son of the Aśvins defeated in battle the two heroic princes of Avanti, Vinda and Anuvinda, who were surrounded by a vast army.
Then, taking the jewels, he went to the city of Bhojakata.
There, O King, O Acyuta, a battle took place for two days.
Having conquered the invincible Bhīṣmaka, that son of Madri—
He likewise [defeated] the lord of Kośala and the lord of the banks of the Veṇā,
as well as the Kāntārakas in battle, and the kings of the Prākoṭakas;
and in battle the Nāṭakeyas, and the Herambakas in combat.
Having conquered Māruḍha and Ramyagrāma by force,
as well as the Nācīnas, the Arbukas, and thousands of kings,
the son of Pāṇḍu defeated all those various forest-dwellers.
The one of great strength brought King Vātādhipa under his control;
having defeated the Pulindas in battle, he proceeded once more toward the south.
There, Nakula’s younger brother fought with the Pāṇḍya king for an entire day.
Having conquered him, that mighty-armed one set out for the southern region;
he reached the world-renowned cave-city of Kiṣkindhā,
where he encountered the two monkey kings, Mainda and Dvivida.
They fought for seven days, yet neither of them underwent any change of state.
Then those two high-souled monkeys, being satisfied, spoke these words with joy and affection to Sahadeva:
"Go, O tiger among the Pāṇḍavas, taking all kinds of jewels;
may there be no obstacle to the mission for the wise Dharmarāja.
Then, having taken the jewels, he went to the city of Māhiṣmatī.

There, O bull among men, that Pāṇḍava Sahadeva, the slayer of enemy heroes and possessor of great majesty, engaged in battle with King Nīla. Then a truly great battle took place between them, striking fear into the hearts of the timid.
Causing the destruction of the army and leading to the peril of lives,
the blessed Lord Havyavāhana indeed rendered him assistance;
O tiger among the Bharatas, he assumed many forms to provide that aid.
Then, at that time, the horses, chariots, elephants, men, and armor in Sahadeva’s army were seen to be ablaze. Thereupon,
the joy of the Kurus became deeply agitated in mind.
And Janamejaya was unable to offer a reply.
Janamejaya said:
"For what reason did the blessed Agni become an adversary in battle?"
"O twice-born one, while Sahadeva was indeed striving for the sake of his sacrifice," Vaiśampāyana said,
"the blessed Havyavāhana (the Fire-god) dwelt there in Māhiṣmatī."
It is heard that in former times a man was indeed apprehended for adultery.
King Nīla had a daughter who was exceedingly beautiful;
she would always attend upon the *agnihotra* fire to awaken her father.
Even though he was being fanned with fans, that fire did not blaze up as long as it was not fanned by the wind from her lovely lips; then the Blessed One Agni desired that Sudarśanā.
He had previously been brought as a bridegroom to King Nīla;
at that time, wandering at will in the guise of a Brahmin,
he fell in love with that beautiful, lotus-eyed maiden.
Then the righteous king instructed him according to the scriptures;
thereupon, the blessed carrier of oblations blazed up in anger.
Seeing this, the king was struck with wonder and bowed his head before the sage.
Then, in due course, the king likewise gave that maiden to Agni, who was in the form of a brahmin, bowing his head in reverence;
and he then accepted that fair-browed daughter of King Nīla.
Then Vibhāvasu,
the most excellent performer of sacrifices, showed favor to that king and invited him to choose a boon.
And the lord of the earth chose the gift of fearlessness for his own army.
From that time forward, O King, whatever monarchs out of ignorance sought to conquer that city by force were consumed here by fire.
And it was thus, O best of the Kurus, in that city of Māhiṣmatī at that time.
Women indeed became unseizable at their own will;
thus did Agni grant a boon regarding the lack of restraint for women,
for the women there acted according to their desire as independent agents.
And from that time forth, O great king, the kings have always avoided that kingdom out of fear of the fire, O best of men. But the righteous Sahadeva, seeing his army afflicted by fear, [acted].
O King, enveloped by the fire, he trembled like a mountain. Having touched water and become pure, he then spoke to the purifier:
"This undertaking is for your sake; O you whose path is black, salutations be unto you."
"You are the mouth of the gods; you are the sacrifice, O Purifier.
You are called *Pāvaka* because of your purifying nature, and *Havyavāhana* because of your carrying of the oblations. The Vedas were born for your sake, and therefore you are *Jātavedas*."
You are Citrabhānu, Sureśa, Anala, Vibhāvasu,
Agni, Duḥsparśana, Hutāśa, Jvalana, Śikhin,
Vaiśvānara, Piṅgeśa, Bhūritejas, and Plavaṃgama.
You are the Lord Kumārasūnu, Rukmagarbha, and Hiraṇyakṛt;
you are Citrabhānu, Sureśa, and Anala, O Vibhāvasu. You are the one who touches the gate of heaven, the consumer of oblations, the blazing fire, and the crested one.
You are Vaiśvānara, Piṅgeśa, the monkey of vast splendor;
you are the blessed Kumārasū, Rudradharma, and the maker of gold. May Agni grant me brilliance, and may Vāyu grant me vital breath.
May the Earth bestow strength upon me, and may the Waters grant me auspiciousness.
O Womb of the Waters, Great Being, Jātavedas,
Lord of the Gods, Agni, you who are the mouth of the deities— purify me through truth.

By the ṛṣis, the brahmins, the deities, and even the asuras who have constantly offered oblations in sacrifices, purify me through truth. You are the smoke-bannered one, the crested one, born from the destruction and removal of sin.
"Ever-present among all living beings, purify me with truth! Thus have you been praised by me, O Blessed One, with a joyful and pure heart.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Agni, grant me contentment, nourishment, mindfulness, and joy.
Reciting this mantra dedicated to Agni while offering oblations to the Lord,
one becomes prosperous, ever self-controlled, and is liberated from all sins.
"O Bearer of Oblations, you ought not to create this obstacle to the sacrifice.
Having spoken thus, the son of Mādrī, that tiger among men, spread kusha grass upon the earth and sat down before the fire according to the prescribed rites.
O Bhārata, while he stood at the head of his entire army, which was terrified and agitated,
the fire did not overstep him, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.
Approaching him slowly, the Fire spoke to that descendant of Kuru.
He spoke these words, preceded by a conciliatory tone, to Sahadeva, that god among men:
"Arise, arise, O Kauravya! This was merely a test conducted by me regarding the God of gods, Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor."

O Sahadeva, I know that you desire to perform that sacrifice by relying on the arm of the son of Pāṇḍu; I know your intention and that of the son of Dharma. You have achieved your purpose; depart now.
"O best of the Bharatas, I must protect this city as long as there are those who carry on the lineage of King Nīla;
however, O Pāṇḍava, I shall fulfill the desire of your heart."
Then, rising up with a joyful soul, his hands joined in reverence and his head bowed low,
that bull among men, the son of Mādrī, paid homage to the Purifier (Agni). When the Purifier had withdrawn, King Nīla then approached.
By the command of Pāvaka,
the king honored Sahadeva, that tiger among men and lord of warriors,
with due hospitality; and having accepted that worship, he subjected him to tribute.
Then the victorious son of Mādrī set out toward the southern direction; having brought the king of Tripura, who possessed immeasurable splendor, under his control,
the mighty-armed hero swiftly subdued the lord of Potana.
Then, with great effort, the mighty-armed one brought Āhṛti, the teacher of the Kauśikas, as well as the lord of Surāṣṭra under his control;
and while staying in the territory of Surāṣṭra, he sent word to Rukmin.
To the wise king Bhīṣmaka, the high minister residing in Bhojakaṭa— who was indeed a righteous soul and a direct friend of Indra— he, O King,
delivered that command, which the king accepted along with his son.
Then the mighty-armed lord of warriors, looking upon Vāsudeva with affection, took the jewels and set out once more. Thereafter,
he visited Śūrpāraka and the group known as Upakṛta.
The one of great splendor and immense strength brought under his control the Daṇḍakas,
as well as the kings dwelling on the islands of the ocean who were born of Mleccha stock, the Niṣādas,
the man-eaters, and even the Karṇaprāvaraṇas.
There he conquered the Niṣādas, those born from the womb of the Sāgara-mlecchas,
and those men of Rākṣasa origin known as the Kālamukhas,
as well as the one-legged humans who dwell within the hollows of trees.
The high-minded one brought under his control the entire Kollagiri as well as Muracīpattana,
the island called Tāmra, Mount Rāmaka,
and King Timiṅgila.
He brought under his control by means of messengers alone the one-legged men who dwell solely in the forests,
as well as the cities of Sañjayantī, Picchaṇḍa, and Karahāṭaka,
and he compelled them to pay tribute.

The wise subduer of enemies went to Bhṛgukaccha with his army; having brought the Barbaras, the Pāraśas, and other island-dwellers under his control, he likewise subdued the Tūlakas, the Daradas, the Sindhus, and those who dwell in the forests.
By means of envoys alone, he brought the immensely powerful Aśmakas, Mūlakas, and Vidarbhas under his control and established them in tribute. Then,
[he subdued] those inhabitants of the southern region who were devoid of wisdom regarding crooked paths.
There, the Pāṇḍava conquered them in battle according to the path of righteousness—
the Pāṇḍyas and the Draviḍas together with the Coḍras and Keralas— and by force brought through messengers under his control the people of Siṃhaladvīpa and others.
"Come," he said by the command of Dharmarāja, addressing the mighty-armed Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, who was terrible to behold;
and the king, taking all their wealth as tribute, set out together with them.
Having reached the northern shore of the ocean garlanded with waves, he,
surrounded by his retinue of *rākṣasas*, quickly paid homage to him and stood there;
[he traversed] Andhra, Talavana, Kaliṅga, and Oṣṭrakarṇika.
By means of messengers alone, he brought Antākhi, Romā, and the city of the Yavanas under his control and compelled them to pay tribute; likewise,
having swiftly overcome the Kānanadvīpakas in battle, he subdued them.
Then, O King, having gone to the Tāmraparṇī and passed beyond Kanyātīrtha,
Sahadeva, the joy of the Kurus, conquered the entire southern region together with his ministers.
Having deliberated with his most intelligent ministers, the mighty-armed Kaurava thought of his brother’s son, Ghaṭotkaca. Then,
as soon as he was thought of, the Rākṣasa appeared.
Extremely tall and long-armed, adorned with all ornaments,
Ghaṭotkaca then saluted Sahadeva, O King; standing bowed with palms joined in reverence, he said, "What is to be done?"

O Indra among kings, when that one who resembled the peak of Mount Meru arrived at Bharukaccha, the wise son of Pāṇḍu and son of Mādravatī dispatched messengers to the high-souled descendant of Pulastya.
The righteous subduer of enemies affectionately granted [the kingdom] to Vibhīṣaṇa;
and he, in turn, accepted his command with affection. That wise lord also acquiesced to that which was ordained by time.
"O great-souled one, I shall do whatever you desire.
Then he dispatched various jewels,
including the finest sandalwood and aloe, as well as divine ornaments.
Seeing those costly garments and highly precious jewels,
as well as that flood of gems, the Pāṇḍava Janamejaya was filled with joy.
"O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear about the arrival of the son of Hiḍimbā;
O Brahmin, [I wish to hear] of his journey to Laṅkā and his meeting with the descendant of Pulastya,
as well as his sight of the Kāverī and all those kings."
"And tell me everything in due order, O bull among Brahmins.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen, O King, to the ancient account of Sahadeva’s heroic deed."
Having swiftly conquered the Kānanadvīpakas in battle and having subdued the southern region, he proceeded to the territory of Cola;
there he beheld the Kāverī, the best of rivers, with its sacred waters.
It was frequented by flocks of various birds and graced by ascetics;
it was surrounded by *sāla*, *lodhra*, and *arjuna* trees, as well as *bilva*, *jambu*, *śālmali*, and *kiṃśuka* trees,
and by *kadamba*, *saptaparṇa*, *kāśmarya*, and *āmalaka* trees.
It was surrounded by banyan trees with massive branches, as well as *plakṣa*, *audumbara*,
*śamī*, *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and *khadira* trees; it was abundant with *badarī* trees and adorned with *aśvakarṇa* trees.
It was adorned with clusters of *karañja*, *tintriṇī*, and *tāla* trees,
and surrounded on all sides by *śirīṣa*, *kuṭaja*, *nimba*, *madhūka*, and *kṣīraka* trees, as well as *puṃnāga*, *bakula*, *kunda*, and *campaka*.
It was beautified by *priyaṅgu*, *aśoka*, and *tilaka* trees, and by *atimuktas*; it was adorned with *asanas*, *karṇikāras*, *nāga* trees,
*ketakīs*, *kurabakas*, *jātis*, *yūthikās*, and *kundalas*.
It was surrounded by *aṅkola*, *karavīra*, *puṃnāga*, and *pāṭala* trees;
it was adorned with *kramuka*, coconut palms, jackfruit, and mangoes;
and it was covered with mangoes, *puṇḍraka* leaves, plantains, and *āḍhaka* trees.
It was strewn with *nīpa* and *vetasa* trees, and covered with *nāla*, *kunda*, and *kuśa* grass;
thus it was adorned with many kinds of divine trees and others as well,
and filled with *haṃsa*, *kāraṇḍava*, *kurara*, *sārasa*, and *śuka* birds.
It was frequented by flocks of *cakravāka* birds, water-fowl,
and sea-crows; it resounded with the cries of *krauñca* cranes and water-hens,
and was thus filled with the calls of many such aquatic birds.
It was endowed with many hermitages and adorned with sacred *caitya* trees; it was frequented by radiant Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and in some places it was graced by trees growing on the banks that resembled garlands.
It was like a woman adorned with ornaments consisting of flowering shrubs and creepers;
in some places it was graced by lotuses covered in leaves, in others by fragrant *saugandhika* and blue lotuses, and in others by blossoming *kahlāra*, water-lilies, and lotuses.
Covered with the pollen of various flowers like an adorned woman,
it was delightful and charming, frequented by hosts of *apsarases*;
with its clear bathing-places, it was stainless, auspicious, and the very life-sustainer of living beings.
Seeing the Kāverī— boundless, with sweet water, and adorned with sandbanks and islands— the Pāṇḍava was filled with joy and said:
"Just as the Gaṅgā is in our kingdom, so is this Kāverī here."
Sahadeva, however, having crossed that river with his followers and reached the southern bank, prepared to depart.
Hearing that the Pāṇḍava had arrived there, the inhabitants of the region [came forth].
Filled with curiosity,
O King, those Draviḍa men and women of lovely appearance went there for the sake of a sight; having arrived, they beheld the son of Pāṇḍu there, filled with joy.

Those Draviḍas, with focused minds, beheld him as he walked— tender-limbed, large-eyed, resembling a god of the thirty, most beautiful to behold in the world, and a source of wonder— as if with unblinking eyes.
Beholding him who resembled Mahāsena, they indeed performed worship for him with various precious gems, desired enjoyments, and other esteemed offerings,
praising the younger brother of Nakula with songs accompanied by auspicious hymns.
But Sahadeva, O great king, having seen those Dramilas who had arrived,
dismissed them and set out toward the southern direction;
having swiftly conquered the Cola king, the lord of the Dramilas, by means of an envoy.
Then, having taken the jewels, he went to the territory of Pāṇḍya;
the people there were not satiated by the sight of Sahadeva,
and they followed him as he departed, filled with affection and curiosity.
Then, O King, the son of Mādrī beheld herds of deer;
he saw wild elephants, other forest-dwelling beasts, tigers, and many black antelopes;
and having seen parrots, peacocks, vultures, and wild jungle fowl.
Then, having reached the territory of his father-in-law, the lord of the earth,
the son of Mādrī dispatched messengers to the Pāṇḍya king;
Malayadhvaja received his command with great affection.
The beautiful and auspicious wife of Jiṣṇu was the daughter of Pāṇḍya,
renowned as Citrāṅgadā, the most excellent among the women of Dramiḷa.
Having heard that Sahadeva had arrived in her father’s inner apartments, she [went forth].
With great affection, he sent many offerings and jewels; Pāṇḍya also dispatched numerous gems along with messengers,
including many jewels, pearls, corals, and conch shells together with mother-of-pearl.
O King, seeing that worship, the Pāṇḍava was filled with joy; then, with delight,
he bestowed many jewels upon his brother’s son, Babhruvāhana,
as well as upon his father-in-law, Malayadhvaja, the Pāṇḍya king of the Dramiḷas.
Having brought that lord of Maṇalūra under his control by means of messengers,
he then took precious gems and, surrounded by the Dramiḷas,
departed for the divine mountain, the abode of Agastya, which is equal to the world of the gods.
O bull of the Bharata race, having circumambulated that Malaya mountain,
the son of Mādrī crossed the auspicious Tāmraparṇī river—
a divine stream of clear water, pleasantly cool, and carrying sandalwood.
Having reached the shore of the ocean, the son of Pāṇḍu encamped there;
thus spoke Vaiśampāyana.
Then, O King, descendant of Bharata, Sahadeva, together with his ministers, [did the same].
Having deliberated with his most wise ministers and having obtained their approval, O King, the mighty-armed Sahadeva, acting with haste,
thought, O Indra among kings, of his brother’s son, Ghaṭotkaca.
Then, as soon as he had thought of him, the Rākṣasa appeared—
exceedingly tall, possessed of a massive body, adorned with all kinds of ornaments,
resembling a dark blue cloud, and wearing earrings of refined gold.
Adorned with variegated necklaces and armlets, decorated with tinkling bells and jewels, wearing a golden garland, possessing great tusks, crowned with a diadem, and girded at the waist;
with copper-colored hair, a tawny beard, terrifying eyes, and golden armlets.
With his limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, wearing fine garments, and full of strength,
he went there with such speed that he seemed to make the earth tremble.
Then, O King, the people saw him approaching like a mountain.
Indeed, they all fled out of fear, like small animals before a lion;
and he approached the son of Mādrī as Rāvaṇa once approached Pulastya.
Then, O King, Ghaṭotkaca saluted Sahadeva.
Bowing low with palms joined in reverence, he stood there and asked, "What shall I do?
Then the son of Pāṇḍu embraced him, who resembled the peak of Mount Meru,
with both arms and smelled his head again and again.
Having honored him, Sahadeva, together with his ministers, spoke these words with joy:
"Go to the city of Laṅkā, my child, at my command for the sake of tribute."
There, having seen the high-souled Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
[he saw] many various kinds of jewels for the purpose of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O you of great strength, having taken all these [beings], return!
Thus addressed by the Pāṇḍava, Ghaṭotkaca, filled with joy,
said "So be it," O Great King, and set out toward the southern direction.
Having circumambulated Sahadeva, Ghaṭotkaca,
O King, set out toward Laṅkā and gazed upon the ocean,
which was teeming with tortoises, crocodiles, and large fish, and crowded with smaller fish and sea-monsters.
Covered with heaps of shells and strewn with clusters of mother-of-pearl,
he beheld the Rāmasetu and reflected upon the prowess of Rāma;
having bowed to it and passed beyond, he gazed toward the southern shore.
Having reached the southern shore of the ocean,
O king of kings, that Ghaṭotkaca beheld the auspicious Laṅkā, which resembled the surface of heaven, beautiful,
enclosed by a wall, and adorned with splendid gates.
It was crowded with many thousands of palaces, white and red,
adorned with golden latticed windows,
networks of pearls, and beautiful screens of gold, silver, and ivory.
It was crowded with palaces and gate-towers, filled with golden archways, resounding with the sounds of divine drums, adorned with pleasure gardens and groves,
and graced by flowering trees that bear fruit in all seasons.
He entered the city of Laṅkā, inhabited by Rākṣasas— a city filled with flowers and perfumes, possessing delightful main roads, and replete with various jewels like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
He beheld many throngs of Rākṣasas bearing spears and pikes,
as well as skillful women of pleasing appearance, wearing various garments,
adorned with divine garlands and celestial ornaments.
With eyes reddened by intoxication and full hips and breasts,
they were filled with joy and wonder upon seeing the son of Bhīmasena;
he then reached the palace of the king, which resembled the abode of Indra.
Ghaṭotkaca,
having approached the gatekeeper, spoke these words:
"The king of the Kurus, a bull among men named Pāṇḍu, who is possessed of great strength— "
His younger son is known as Sahadeva, the heir. Now, for the sake of the Rājasūya sacrifice, I have been sent by my teacher Kṛṣṇamitra as an envoy to the Kaurava king in order to collect tribute.
"I wish to see the king of kings; announce me to him quickly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
