Having heard those words of his, the gatekeeper [approached] the lord of the earth.
Having said, "So be it," that messenger then entered the palace;
with palms joined in reverence, he then related the entire message of the envoy.
Upon hearing the words of the gatekeeper, Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, [acted accordingly].
The righteous-souled one spoke these words: "Let him be brought into my presence.
Thus addressed, O king of kings, by that high-souled knower of dharma, the gatekeeper then went out in haste and spoke to the son of Hiḍimbā.
"Come, messenger, go to see the king; enter yourself quickly! Hearing the words of the gatekeeper, Ghaṭotkaca entered.
Having entered, he then beheld the palace of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Then [he saw] that city, resembling Mount Kailāsa, with archways of refined gold,
surrounded by a wall and adorned with gate-towers;
it was densely packed with mansions and palaces, and endowed with various kinds of jewels.
With pillars made of gold, refined gold, crystal, and silver, and even those containing diamonds and lapis lazuli— pillars that captivate the eye—
it was adorned with various banners and flags and variegated with jewels.
Seeing all those delightful objects there— charming with various garlands and featuring altars of refined gold— the son of Bhīmasena,
the son of Hiḍimbā, as he was entering, heard the sound of drums.
Resounding with the songs of lutes, with syllables measured by equal rhythm, filled with the roar of divine drums and crowded with hundreds of musical instruments—
he, hearing that sweet sound, then became full of joy.
Then, O Bhārata, having plunged through many delightful courtyards, the son of Hiḍimbā beheld the high-souled one together with the gatekeeper,
Vibhīṣaṇa, seated upon a supreme golden throne.
[He saw] the Lord, who was divine and resplendent like the sun, adorned with pearls and gems; whose limbs were variegated with celestial ornaments, who bore a divine form,
who wore celestial garlands and garments, and who was auspiciously anointed with divine perfumes.
Resplendent in body with the brilliance of the sun and Vaiśvānara,
he was seated with his ministers like Śatakratu with the gods,
surrounded by divine yakṣas, great chariot-warriors, and women of lovely appearance.
He was being honored according to the prescribed rites with auspicious hymns, while two excellent women held over his head two costly fly-whisks with golden handles,
fanning him.

O King, seeing the lord of the Rākṣasas— who was radiant, endowed with splendor, comparable to Kubera and Varuṇa, eternally established in righteousness, and truly wonderful— Ghaṭotkaca paid him homage with palms joined in reverence.
The immensely powerful one stood bowed down like Śakra with his variegated chariot.
Seeing that messenger arrived, Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
Vibhīṣaṇa— [acted].
Having honored him according to custom, he spoke these words preceded by conciliation:
"In whose lineage was this lord of the earth born, desiring tribute? [Tell me] of all his younger brothers, as well as his city and his country."
"I wish to hear from you, in accordance with the truth, all of this—both yourself and that which must be done.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Tell me all of these things in detail, one by one."
Thus addressed by the high-souled descendant of Pulastya,
Ghaṭotkaca,
the son of Hiḍimbā, then spoke with joined palms, consoling the lord of the Rākṣasas.
In the lineage of Soma, there was a king named Pāṇḍu, possessed of great strength. Pāṇḍu had five sons whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra;
the eldest among them was known by the name Dharmaputra.
The righteous Ajātaśatru was like Dharma personified;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having obtained the kingdom,
ruled from the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having given that to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he then went from there to Śakraprastha;
together with his brothers, O king of kings, he took delight in Śakraprastha.
Both those excellent cities were situated between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
While the king, ever established in righteousness, was ruling from Śakraprastha,
his younger brother, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena— possessed of great strength,
great splendor, and great heroism— that Pāṇḍava was like a lion.
That son of Pāṇḍu is equal in strength to ten thousand elephants;
his younger brother, named Arjuna, possesses great heroism and prowess,
is delicate yet of great being, and is renowned in the world for his valor.
Arjuna is equal to Kārtavīrya in heroism, equal to the ocean in strength,
equal to the son of Jamadagni in weaponry, and equal to Rāma in battle;
Pārtha is equal to Śakra in beauty and comparable to the sun in splendor.
Phalguna is invincible in battle by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, rākṣasas, and all human beings combined; by him,
that Khāṇḍava forest was offered as a libation to Jātavedas (the Fire-god).
Having swiftly gratified Śakra along with the hosts of gods,
and having gratified the sacrificial fire after obtaining the divine weapons— those weapons,
O Great King, which are difficult even for the deities to attain— were obtained by him.
The sister of Vāsudeva, renowned by the name Subhadrā,
and the younger brother of Arjuna, O King, known as Nakula,
were most beautiful in the world, like the god of love incarnate.
His younger brother, of great splendor, is known as Sahadeva.
O King, O noble one, I have been sent by that Sahadeva;
I am the mighty Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīmasena.
"My mother is the highly fortunate Rākṣasī named Hiḍimbā; for the sake of assisting the sons of Pṛthā, I wander this earth. Yudhiṣṭhira was the protector of the entire world."
He began to perform the Rājasūya, the most excellent of sacrifices,
and dispatched his brothers to all directions to collect tribute.
Arjuna quickly set out toward the north for the sake of tribute.
Having traveled hundreds of thousands of yojanas, the one of great strength,
having conquered all kings in battle and slain them by his might,
that self-controlled one approached the gateway to heaven, taking with him a vast abundance of jewels.
Taking all kinds of divine horses and various forms of wealth, O King, Phalguna indeed gave them to the son of Dharma.
For Bhimasena, O Indra among kings, having conquered the eastern quarter by force, [gave it to him].
Having brought the rulers of the earth under his control, he gave wealth to the Pāṇḍava;
likewise, Nakula set out toward the western quarter to collect tribute.
Sahadeva, having conquered all the lords of the earth, went toward the southern quarter.
O Indra among kings, having been honored here, he sent me to you for the sake of tribute;
thus has the conduct of the sons of Pṛthā been related to you in brief. O great king, look upon that Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira.
Pāvaka, Rājasūya, and the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign—having considered these, O knower of dharma, you ought to grant me your hand.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O knower of dharma, having taken account of these, you ought to give me your hand."
Having heard those words spoken by him, O King, the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, together with his ministers, became filled with joy;
and he accepted his command with affection.
The wise Lord considered that [the world] was created by Time;
then he gave away various woolen blankets and rugs,
as well as couches made of ivory and gold, adorned with jewels and gold.
Many various ornaments, highly precious and numerous;
bright corals and many diverse jewels;
and golden vessels, jars, and pots.
He gave fourteen palm-tree pillars joined to the gateway of the sacrifice, consisting of many variegated silver vessels, weapons adorned with gold, and decorated with jewels and pearls.
Golden lotus flowers, palanquins adorned with jewels,
highly precious crowns, golden-colored earrings,
various golden blossoms, and other golden garlands.
Conchs resembling the moon, marked with a hundred whorls and variegated; the finest sandalwood; numerous gold and jewels;
and many costly garments as well as numerous woolen blankets.
O King, at that time, King Vibhīṣaṇa gave various other things and many jewels to Sahadeva;
then, having saluted King Vibhīṣaṇa with palms joined in reverence, [Sahadeva departed].
Having circumambulated him clockwise, Ghaṭotkaca departed;
O King, all those eighty-eight thousand Rākṣasas then brought back all those jewels together with the son of Hiḍimbā.
Taking all those jewels, Ghaṭotkaca set forth;
then, having taken the jewels along with the Rākṣasas,
the son of Hiḍimbā went swiftly from Laṅkā toward the abode of Sahadeva.
Having crossed the great ocean, they all approached the son of Pāṇḍu.
Then Sahadeva beheld those night-rangers who had come to collect jewels, appearing as formidable as Bhīma, as well as the son of Hiḍimbā, O King.
Seeing the Nairṛtas, the Dramilas fled, afflicted by fear. Then the son of Bhīmasena approached the son of Mādrī and stood with palms joined in reverence;
and seeing that flood of jewels, the Pāṇḍava was filled with joy.
Having dismissed all the Dramilas, he prepared to depart.
Then the wise and powerful Sahadeva turned back.
Thus, having conquered them by force, by conciliation, and by victory, he proceeded.
Having made the kings pay tribute, the subduer of enemies returned;
taking with him the essence of jewels, he departed along with the night-stalkers and entered Indraprastha, as if making the earth tremble.

O King, having seen Yudhiṣṭhira, Sahadeva stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing low and offering his salutations; he was indeed honored by him. Having seen those vast heaps of wealth, so difficult to obtain, which had been brought from Laṅkā, [he was filled with wonder].
The king became filled with joy and attained the highest wonder; O bull of the Bharatas, having reported all that to Dharmarāja,
he gave to the high-souled one more than a thousand crores of gold.
Having performed his duties, O King Janamejaya, he dwelt in happiness among various kinds of gems and jewels, as well as cattle, goats, sheep,
and buffaloes. Vaiśampāyana said:
I shall now describe the deeds and the victory of Nakula,
and how that lord conquered the quarter already subdued by Vāsudeva;
having set out from Khāṇḍavaprastha toward the western direction.
With this in mind, the wise king set out with a vast army,
making this very earth tremble with the great lion-roars of his warriors, their shouting, and the clatter of chariot wheels.
Then he rushed toward Rohītaka, a delightful city rich in wealth, cattle, horses, and grain, which was dear to Kārttikeya.
There, a great battle took place with the heroic Mattamayūrakas.
The one of great splendor brought Marubhūmi in its entirety, as well as Bahudhānyaka, Śairīṣaka, and Maheccha, under his control;
he also subdued the royal sage Ākrośa, with whom he engaged in a great battle.
Having conquered those Daśārṇas, the son of Pāṇḍu set forth;
he subdued the Liliṭas and the Pāṭanas by means of messengers alone.
He [conquered] the Śibis, Trigartas, Ambaṣṭhas, Mālavas, and Pañcakarpaṭas.
Likewise, that bull among men conquered the Madhyamikas, the Vāṭadhāna Brahmins, and furthermore, turning back again, he defeated the hosts of Puṣkara forest-dwellers known as the Utsavasamketas.

And those village chiefs of great strength who dwell on the banks of the Indus, the hosts of Śūdras and Ābhīras who live along the Sarasvatī, those who subsist by fishing, and those who are mountain-dwellers.
The entire Pañcanada region, as well as Aparaparyata;
Ratnākara, Amitraghna, and again Vellātaṭa; likewise Siṃhanada and other cities as well.
By means of messengers alone, Nakula, the joy of his lineage,
brought [the king] under his control; likewise, the immensely radiant one swiftly brought Uttarajyotika and the city of Vṛndāṭaka, as well as Dvārapāla, under his sway.
The son of Pāṇḍu brought under his control the Ramaṭhas, the Hārahūṇas, and all those kings who dwell in the western regions, simply by means of his command;
as well as Araṇa, Roma, and the cities of the Yavanas.

O best of men, while stationed there, the conqueror brought under his control even those born in Lambānudeśa and the Bandhakas by means of messengers alone, and he compelled them to pay tribute. Furthermore, remaining there, the lord sent word to Vāsudeva.
O Bhārata, he then appointed a messenger who was a knower of dharma, tranquil, eloquent, pure, and most excellent; and he, in turn, accepted his command from the ten kings along with Vāsudeva.
Then, having arrived at Śākala, the capital city of the Madras,
the powerful hero brought Śalya, his maternal uncle, under his control with affection.
O lord of the people, being worthy of honor, he was received with great hospitality by the king.
Taking abundant jewels, the lord of warriors set forth;
then he brought under his control all those most fierce Mlecchas dwelling within the belly of the ocean— the Pahlavas and the Barbaras alike.
Then, having taken the jewels and brought the kings under his control,
Nakula, the best of men and skilled in various paths, returned;
thousands of young camels [filled] the treasury of that high-souled one.
O Great King, they carried him, like a great treasure with difficulty, for ten days.
Then, having approached the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira who was staying at Indraprastha,
the illustrious son of Mādrī presented that wealth to him.

In this manner, O bull of the Bharatas, Nakula, the best of the Kurus, conquered the western quarter protected by Varuṇa, which had already been subdued by Vāsudeva. Having thus conquered the earth, the brothers, O joy of the Kurus—
Abiding by their own dharma, they governed this earth;
the king, together with his four brothers beginning with Bhīmasena,
having shown favor to all subjects, protected all the social orders.
Yudhiṣṭhira acted for the welfare of all without causing offense.
"Let it be bought; let everything be given—casting aside anger and without force"—this was the only speech heard from the son of Pṛthā, who spoke thus of the dharma of the virtuous.
When the world had thus come into being, he was beloved by all as if by a father;
no one hated him, and for that reason he was known as Ajātaśatru (He Whose Enemy Was Unborn).
Vaiśampāyana said:
Because he protects the King of Dharma, because he upholds truth,

and because he destroys his enemies, the subjects remain devoted to their own duties; likewise, through the proper collection of taxes and through governance according to dharma, they abide in their respective roles.
Parjanya poured down rain according to desire, and the country became prosperous.
All undertakings—pastoralism, agriculture, and trade—proceeded successfully;
[the people] were free from disease and free from calamities.
The earth produced sweet crops and was filled with trees bearing abundant flowers and fruits;
the Brahmins maintained the continuity of sacrifices— all this arose specifically from the king's righteous governance.
O King, among robbers or deceivers, or even toward one another,
or from those favored by the king, false words were never heard.
Nor did there occur drought, excessive rain, disease, fire, or fainting spells.
All this did not exist at that time while Yudhiṣṭhira was constant in righteousness;
thinking, "How might men attain satisfaction of mind? those people, with such thoughts, began with all their soul to perform only what is pleasing.
To do what was pleasing, to attend upon him, and to bring offerings born of their own nature,
the kings came individually with various tasks;
through righteous acquisitions of wealth, his great store increased.
He was the most excellent of all kings and a lord of the earth, whose depletion could not be effected even in hundreds of years;
that lord of the earth [knew] the measure of his own treasury and granary.
Having understood this, the son of Kuntī, the king, set his mind upon the sacrifice alone.
And all his friends, both individually and together, said to him:
"O Lord, the time for your sacrifice has arrived; let it be performed now."
Even as they were speaking thus, Hari approached—
the ancient seer whose essence is the Veda, visible to those who possess true knowledge,
the supreme among all things moving and stationary, and both the source and the dissolution of the world.
The lord of the past, future, and present; Keśava, the slayer of Keśin; the primordial source of all worlds; the leader of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas;
the rampart for all the Vṛṣṇis; the bestower of fearlessness in times of distress; the destroyer of enemies.
Entrusting the administration of power to Balarāma and uniting with Ānakadundubhi,
Mādhava— that tiger among men— surrounded by a great force, brought a vast flood of wealth of various kinds to Dharmarāja.
Making that boundless flood of wealth— an inexhaustible ocean of jewels—
resound with the roar of his chariot, he entered the supreme city;
filling it to its full capacity, he brought grief to his enemies.
Like the sunless region by the sun, or a windless place by the wind, so it was;
then they all rose up and brought forth golden seats. With Kṛṣṇa having arrived, the city of the Bharatas rejoiced.
Having approached him with joy and honored him according to the prescribed rites,
and having inquired after his welfare once he was comfortably seated, Yudhiṣṭhira—
that bull among men— stood together with his officiating priests, headed by Dhaumya and Dvaipāyana.
Accompanied by Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Kṛṣṇa, it is because of you that the entire earth remains under my control;
and O Vārṣṇeya, great wealth has been acquired through your grace."
Therefore, O son of Devakī, O Mādhava, I desire to employ all of that according to the prescribed rites among the foremost of the twice-born and in the sacrificial fire; thus,
O scion of the Daśārhas, I wish to perform the sacrifice together with you.
"O mighty-armed one, along with my younger brothers, you ought to grant me permission for this.
O Govinda, O great-armed one, do you yourself undergo the initiation;
for when you have performed the sacrifice, O descendant of Daśārha, I shall indeed be cleansed of all sin."
"O Lord, grant me permission as well, along with these younger brothers;
permitted by you, O Kṛṣṇa, may I attain this supreme sacrifice.
To him, Kṛṣṇa replied thus after speaking at length on the manifold virtues [of the undertaking].
"O tiger among kings, you alone are worthy to perform this great sacrifice as a sovereign emperor;
once it has been accomplished by you, we shall have achieved our purpose. Perform the sacrifice you desire while I remain here for your welfare."
"And appoint me also to a task; I shall carry out every word of yours.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, my resolve has borne fruit, and my success is certain."
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, since you have presented yourself to me according to my desire," Yudhiṣṭhira said, looking upon the assembled rulers of the earth,
toward Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals and who accomplishes every task in every way.
"In the great Rājasūya sacrifice, water for washing the feet should be offered;
such [water] has not been seen by me, nor has it been brought together by kings.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O mighty-armed one, from where could the acquisition of such wealth be obtained?
Do not despair, O Indra among kings, for the sake of wealth in any way whatsoever.
I shall dispatch the son of Hiḍimbā, the terrifying subduer of enemies."
In order to bring the lord of the *rākṣasas* to fulfill the abundance of wealth,
Mādhava then summoned the son of Hiḍimbā with great respect and spoke to him in gentle words, as if honoring him.

"Go, O son of Hiḍimbā, may you be blessed; report to the lord of the Rākṣasas in Laṅkā, in my name, that which was said regarding the Rākṣasa. Remembering that, return here and keep my favor in mind."
Then the son of Bhīma, having prostrated at the feet of Kṛṣṇa,
went swiftly and directly to see the worlds of Paulastya;
then he reached the ocean, which had been bound by Rāma like a tree.
Having then duly worshipped the god Rāmeśvara there,
the son of Hiḍimbā, acting swiftly by the king’s command, entered the worlds;
having traveled with the speed of the wind, he arrived at the gate of Laṅkā.
Questioned by the gatekeepers, "Who are you, you who have the form of a eunuch, and from where do you come? he then laughed at some of those standing at the gate with his ears.
For it is said that demons difficult to behold are born there in Kurujāṅgala.

Then the son of Bhīmasena, filled with wrath, spoke to those standing at the gate: "O best of Rākṣasas, inform Vibhīṣaṇa immediately that I have arrived by the command of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of business."
Having heard what was said, they reported it to the descendant of Pulastya;
having summoned him, he spoke these words: "Listen to what must be done.
He then related everything that had been spoken by Kṛṣṇa in his presence.
And the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, bearing Kṛṣṇa’s command upon his head,
recalled Rāma’s words and then fulfilled Kṛṣṇa’s order; having informed Mandodarī of that which was born from the grace of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
"I shall go to see Kṛṣṇa; give me leave, O princess!
Having conquered the gods and others, Daśagrīva brought back that abundant collection of jewels, the very essence of the world, which he had guarded."
O princess, for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa, I shall send all of that;
while he looks on from both sides with wealth filled with jewels,
the highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa has gone to Indraprastha.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lords of the Yādavas, let us go without delay to see that Rākṣasa.
Having heard these words of his, she spoke this speech in astonishment.
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"O King, tell me, why do you pay tribute to human beings?
I give it for a virtuous reason; of what am I afraid?"
O daughter of Māyana, in the past, when the Dvāpara age had arrived, Rāma spoke before me: "My birth shall be in the lineage of the Yādavas;
at that time, I will provide assistance for the sake of the Pāṇḍava. Therefore, go."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O mighty-armed one, I shall grant you my presence at Indraprastha.
Having spoken thus, he went to where Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, was staying.
Having honored the perfectly pure Kṛṣṇa, the great and supreme descendant of Pulastya, Viṣṇu, having likewise honored the Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa, spoke thus to him. Vibhīṣaṇa said:
Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one; may all be well with you at all times. By the sight of you, O Viṣṇu, no inauspiciousness remains for me anywhere.
Today my birth is truly blessed, and my life is well-lived.
"O delight of the Yadus, this gold has been brought by me in tens of millions for the sake of the sacrifice of Dharmarāja; I have boldly accepted your command through your word.
Having heard these words of his, his eyes then began to quiver with emotion.
He gave the command to the high-souled descendant of Pulastya to go to Laṅkā:
"Go to Laṅkā, O great hero; here, O Asura, you are equal in strength to Bali.
Having heard this, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa then departed for Laṅkā.
O bull of the Bharatas, while being honored by the great heroes, the Rākṣasa [spoke].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been granted permission by Kṛṣṇa, the Pāṇḍava, together with his brothers, [departed].

He began to prepare the means for the performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice. Then the Pāṇḍava, the destroyer of his enemies, issued commands to Sahadeva— the best among warriors— and to all his ministers.
In this sacrifice, all the sacrificial components as prescribed by the twice-born,
as well as all the implements and auspicious items in their entirety,
and the materials for the sacrifice mentioned by Dhaumya, were indeed quickly prepared.
"Let the men assemble according to their fitness and in due order:
Indrasena, Viśoka, and Pūru, Arjuna’s charioteer;
and let all the charioteers come together, pure and wearing polished earrings."

Samīka and Dhvajāsena— let these five preeminent charioteers be intent on bringing food and provisions out of a desire to do what is pleasing to me. May all desired objects, radiant with fragrant gold, be presented [to us].
"O best of the Kurus, let all desirable things be prepared, endowed with flavor and fragrance— things that are captivating and pleasing to the twice-born.
At the very moment those words were spoken, he informed him that everything had been accomplished.
Sahadeva, the best among warriors, [was appointed] to the high-souled Dharmarāja.
Then, O King, Dvaipāyana brought forward the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
those highly fortunate twice-born ones who were like the Vedas themselves, appearing in embodied form.
The son of Satyavatī himself performed the office of the *brahmán*;
he was the Sāmaveda incarnate, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*).
That bull among the Dhananjayas, Susāman, became the chanter of the Sāmans.
Then Yājñavalkya became the most excellent Adhvaryu priest, most devoted to Brahman;
Paila, the son of Vasu, became the Hotṛ priest, accompanied by Dhaumya.
O bull of the Bharatas, their groups of disciples and sons were likewise present.
All those who served as *hotṛ* priests were masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*).
And there, O King, the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana himself, honored by all his disciples, acted as the presiding member of the assembly (*sadasya*).
Having had the day declared auspicious and having performed that ritual according to the injunctions of the scriptures, they prepared that great sacrificial ground for the gods.
There, being duly authorized, the artisans constructed the shelters.
[They were] like the vast, jewel-adorned palaces of the dwellers of heaven. Then that king, the best of monarchs and the foremost of the Kurus, immediately commanded his minister Sahadeva.
Then Vaiśampāyana said:
The best of the Kurus, King Kaunteya, spoke these words worthy of being spoken to his minister Sahadeva.
"Dispatch swift messengers immediately for the purpose of summoning them.
Having heard the king's words, he then sent forth messengers [with the command]:
"Go and invite the brahmins and the rulers of the land throughout the kingdoms."
"Bring all the Vaiśyas, the Mānyas, and the Śūdras as well! At the command of the son of Pāṇḍu, they summoned all those rulers of the earth and dispatched others.

Likewise, those messengers, traveling swiftly on their mounts, went to many other kingdoms and to other men who were as quick-moving as themselves. Then, at the appropriate time, they [reached] Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
O Bhārata, on the new moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūla, surrounded by a great multitude of people, the Brahmins initiated him into the Rājasūya sacrifice;
he was clothed in the skin of the Ruru deer and his body was anointed with fresh butter.
Then that righteous-souled Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, having been initiated,
proceeded to the sacrificial ground surrounded by thousands of Brahmins,
as well as his brothers, kinsmen, friends, and ministers.
O lord of men, together with Kṣatriyas gathered from various lands and with ministers, that best of kings appeared like Dharma incarnate;
and Brāhmaṇas arrived there from their respective territories from every direction.
Expert in all branches of knowledge and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
they constructed dwellings for them by the command of Dharmarāja—
each with abundant food and provided with beds, for the various groups separately.
O King, thousands of artisans, endowed with the excellence of all seasons,
dwelt there; and among them lived Brāhmaṇas who were highly honored,
as they told many stories and watched actors and dancers.
And as the brahmins ate and spoke with great voices, the sound of those joyful, high-souled men was heard there incessantly:
"Give! Give! Eat! Eat!"
Such conversations were heard there constantly:
"O Bhārata, Dharmarāja gave away hundreds of thousands of cows, couches, gold, and women, each separately."
Thus did that sacrifice of the high-souled Pāṇḍava proceed—
of that sole hero upon earth, like Śakra’s sacrifice in Triviṣṭapa.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched the Pāṇḍava.
O bull of the Bharatas, [he sent] Nakula to Hastinapura for Bhīṣma,
for Bāhlīka and his sons, for Bhūriśravas and Bhīṣma,
for Droṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vidura, and Kṛpa.
And all those brothers who were devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira [were likewise honored].
Then, O King, having been invited and duly honored,
those kings departed for their own cities like immortals ascending from their celestial chariots.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to Hāstinapura, Nakula, the victor in assemblies, then,
with self-restraint and palms joined in reverence, brought the Bharatas together.
The son of Pāṇḍu took leave of Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
then, having heard of the sacrifice of the King of Dharma, those who were experts in sacrificial rites set out for the sacrifice with joyful minds, preceded by the Brahmins.
And hundreds of others, O bull among men, with contented minds,
departed after taking vast wealth; various kings went forth desiring to see the assembly hall and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja.
O Bhārata, kings from all directions gathered there,
bringing with them various and great treasures;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, and the high-minded Vidura were also present.
And all those brothers, headed by Duryodhana,
as well as all the kings led by the Preceptor, along with Subala, the king of Gandhāra, and the mighty Śakuni, were all honored and invited.
Acala and Vṛṣaka, and Karṇa, the best of chariot-warriors; Śalya, the King of Madra, who is righteous, and the great car-warrior Bāhlika;
then Somadatta of the Kuru lineage, Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Droṇa, and Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus;
Yajñasena with his son, and Śālva the lord of the earth;
and the highly illustrious Bhagadatta, the king of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Together with all the Mlecchas dwelling along the coastal regions of the ocean,
as well as the mountain kings and King Bṛhadbala, Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, Vaṅga, and likewise the king of Kaliṅga.
Ākarṣa, Kuntala, as well as the Vānavāsya and Āndhraka peoples; the Draviḍas and Siṃhalas, and likewise the king of Kaśmīra;
the highly resplendent Kuntibhoja, and the exceedingly powerful Suhma.
And other heroic kings, all Bāhlikas; Virāṭa with his sons, and the great car-warrior Mācella;
these kings and princes, lords of various realms.
O Bhārata, the immensely powerful Śiśupāla, intoxicated by the pride of battle, came with his son to the sacrifice of the Pāṇḍava’s son.
Also present were Rāma, Aniruddha, Babhru, and Sāraṇa.
Gada, Pradyumna, Sāmba, and the heroic Cārudeṣṇa;
Ulmuka, Niśaṭha, and the valiant son of Pradyumna—
these and all the other Vṛṣṇis, great chariot-warriors, arrived in their entirety.
These and many other kings born in the Middle Country came to the great Rājasūya sacrifice of the son of Pāṇḍu;
by the command of the King of Dharma, lodgings were provided for them.
O King, those palaces possessed many courtyards and were adorned with ponds and trees; the son of Dharma offered them unsurpassed honor,
and the kings, having been thus honored, departed for their assigned lodgings.
Resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, they were charming and adorned with precious materials;
on all sides they were enclosed by high, well-constructed white walls,
covered with golden lattices, and beautified with floors inlaid with jewels.
With stairways easy to ascend, furnished with great seats and coverings, draped with garlands of flowers, scented with the finest aloe-wood,
resembling the color of swans or rays of light, and beautiful to behold for a league around.

Then those lords of the earth, having rested, beheld the one who bestows abundant sacrificial fees— a place unobstructed, with symmetrical gates, endowed with various excellences, its parts adorned with many minerals, like the peaks of the Himavat.
Surrounded by many members of the assembly, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, sat there; that assembly hall, crowded with kings and high-souled Brāhmaṇas,
then shone, O King, like the vault of heaven filled with immortals.
Then the Pāṇḍava, the destroyer of enemies,
gave orders to Sahadeva, the best of the Kurus, and to all his ministers regarding the sacrificial requirements for this rite as prescribed by the twice-born.

"O bull of the Bharatas, O Sahadeva, quickly bring us all the sacrificial materials and requisites mentioned by Dhaumya exactly as they are. Let Indrasena, Viśoka, and Rukma, the charioteer of Arjuna, [also come]."
O Sahadeva, by your command, let them be occupied with food and drink— providing all desired objects acquired through effort, mixed with fragrant flavors,
captivating, delightful, and well-prepared for the purpose of nourishment.
Samīka and Dhvajāsena, along with those five bulls among charioteers—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, having gone out to meet his grandfather and his preceptor, [spoke].
Then, O King, having offered salutations,
he spoke these words to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Duryodhana, and Vivimśati:
"In this sacrifice, may you all favor me in every way."
"Both this property of yours and whatever wealth of mine is here—
may you all satisfy yourselves with it as you wish, without restraint.
Having spoken thus to them all, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, being consecrated for the sacrifice, [proceeded].
Immediately thereafter, he assigned them to their respective offices according to their fitness:
he appointed Duḥśāsana to the offices of food and edibles,
and he appointed Yuyutsu [to the office of the scribes].
Regarding the task of arranging the rows, the removal of leftovers,
the supervision of the meal,
and the reception of the Brahmins, he spoke of Aśvatthāman.
To honor the kings, however, he appointed Saṃjaya;
as for the discernment of what had been done and left undone, the two high-minded elders, Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
remained there under the king’s command, being highly esteemed by him.
The king appointed Kṛpa to the supervision of gold, fine gold, and precious gems, as well as to the distribution of sacrificial gifts; likewise,
he appointed other tigers among men to their respective duties.
Bāhlīka, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Somadatta, and Jayadratha,
brought there by Nakula, enjoyed themselves like lords;
Vidura, the steward, was the manager of expenditures, for he knew all the laws of dharma.
Duryodhana, however, accepted all the offerings in their entirety.
"Let Kuntī, Mādrī, and Gāndhārī perform the honoring of the women;
let all the other daughters-in-law carry out their instructions without delay."
This Arjuna shall remain in the presence of Kṛṣṇa for the accomplishment of our purpose;
for Kṛṣṇa himself has become the one who washes the feet of the Brahmins,
while Karṇa is the superintendent of the treasury and the overseer of income and expenditure.
The entire world had gathered there, desiring to obtain the highest fruit,
wishing to behold both the assembly hall and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja;
no one brought there a gift of honor less than a thousand.
And there they honored the King of Dharma with many jewels.
"How indeed may the descendant of Kuru complete my sacrifice through gifts of jewels?"— thinking thus, the kings, vying with one another, bestowed wealth.
With palaces topped by excellent celestial mansions, surrounded by armies and accompanied by the palaces of world-rulers as well as the dwellings of brahmins,
and with divine residences constructed that were like unto celestial chariots.

O King, the assembly hall of the high-souled son of Kuntī shone with kings who were endowed with supreme supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), possessed of various jewels, and were exceedingly rich in glory and prosperity.
Competing with the god Varuṇa through his supernatural power, Yudhiṣṭhira then performed a sacrifice with six fires accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
he satisfied all people with every object of their desires.
Abounding in food and many delicacies, with people gathered after they had eaten,
that assembly became worthy of offerings of jewels;
it was graced by oblations of clarified butter and *iḍā*-offerings accompanied by the mastery of mantras.
For in that sacrifice performed by the great seers, the gods were gratified;
as were the brahmins with sacrificial fees, food, and great wealth. And all the social orders, filled with joy, were gratified in that sacrifice, just as the gods were.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
on the day of the consecration, the great ṛṣis and the Brahmins, together with the kings, entered the inner sacrificial enclosure for the sake of honoring [the king].
Seated there within the inner altar of that high-souled one, those headed by Nārada shone together with the royal sages,
like the gods and celestial seers assembled in the abode of Brahmā.
Engaged in various activities, those of immeasurable luster conversed;
many there spoke to one another in debate, saying, "It is thus," "It is not thus," "It is exactly so," and "It is not otherwise."
Some there made meager points appear substantial, while others,
by means of arguments established in the scriptures, made what was substantial appear meager.
Among them, some wise men [refuted] a point that had been fully elaborated by others.
They scattered [the arrows] like hawks scattering meat in the sky;
some there, observers of great vows and the best among those who know all the Vedas, took delight in recounting stories connected with dharma and artha.

That sacrificial altar, crowded with gods, twice-born men, and great seers endowed with Vedic knowledge, shone like the stainless sky filled with stars. No Śūdra was present in its vicinity, nor anyone who had not observed his vows.
Then, O King, within the sacrificial enclosure at Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence,
Nārada beheld that splendor born of the performance of the sacrifice belonging to the wise Dharmarāja, and he was filled with joy.
Then, O lord of men, seeing that assembly of all the Kṣatriyas, the sage Nārada fell into reflection;
and he recalled that story of ancient times, O bull of the Bharatas.
O descendant of Kuru, having learned of that assembly of the gods which took place in the abode of Brahmā during the partial incarnation (aṃśāvataraṇa),
Nārada mentally called to mind the lotus-eyed Hari.

In person, that all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, has been born among the Kṣatriyas as a wise conqueror of enemy cities, fulfilling his vow. He is the very same creator of beings who, in the past, personally commanded the gods.
"By slaying one another, you shall regain the worlds," so commanded Nārāyaṇa Śambhu, the Blessed Lord and Master of the universe,
all the gods, and he was born in the house of Yadu.
On earth, in the lineage of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis,
that best of lineage-bearers shone with supreme splendor like the moon, the lord of the stars.
All the gods, including Indra, relied upon the strength of his arms.
This very Hari, the crusher of enemies, dwells here in the guise of a human.
Oh, how wonderful! That the Self-Existent One himself shall once again take up the kṣatriya order, endowed with such power—this is indeed a great marvel.
Thus did Nārada, the knower of dharma, reflect upon this thought;
for he knew Hari Nārāyaṇa, that Lord who is to be praised with sacrifices. In him, the best among those who know dharma, [the son] of the wise Dharmarāja [was born].
At that great sacrifice, the one of great intelligence stood with profound respect.
Then, those foremost among the virtuous, endowed with all preeminent qualities, gathered together.
Many self-disciplined subduers of enemies,
the Pāñcālas from all sides, and the Vṛṣṇis, who were capable of leading the van of the army, having recognized that it was their own duty, assembled there.
Accompanied by their wives, kinsmen, and ministers, and carrying heaps of jewels,
they traveled joyfully behind the kings, for they could not keep pace with them due to the distance of the land and the weight of their burdens.
Having gathered from all sides the remaining forces that had assembled,
Śauri— the wielder of the discus-weapon, the crusher of hosts of enemies— honored Ānakadundubhi, who had been appointed to the command of the army by the kings.

When Yudhiṣṭhira was performing the sacrifice, Mādhava, the best of the Yādavas, having taken various kinds of wealth and placed a vast flood of riches before the King of Dharma, returned to Khāṇḍavaprastha.
There, [he addressed] all the hosts of kings who had come to the sacrifice, led by the crooked Caidya—
hosts who were like radiant clouds,
like leaders of herds sighing amidst their flocks.

Then Madhusūdana approached, making the ocean-like assembly of kings— which was crowded with throngs of people and filled with powerful men resembling lions standing over the earth— resound with the roar of his chariot.
Like the sunless world when the sun appears, or like a windless place when a breeze blows,
the city of the Bharatas rejoiced at the arrival of Kṛṣṇa;
for he was a knower of all duties who came for the sake of honoring the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.

Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, became the one specialized in discerning [the qualities of the sacrificial animals]. Then the powerful and all-pervading younger brother of Śveta entered the sacrificial ground, radiant with splendor like the sun.
To those who did not perceive or recognize the seer, the Brahmin Tejorāśi— who was invisible and remained established within himself as the path for the aged and those advanced in years,
and who is the infallible source and dissolution of all that moves and stands— [they were lost].
The infinite end of his enemies, the crusher of hostile hosts, the source of all beings, the fearless and infallible one in times of distress,
the future, the creator, the past, and the subduer of foes at Dvāravatī.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa approaching, the Pāṇḍava honored that one of immeasurable splendor and conducted himself toward Keśava with due propriety,
having carefully considered their relative seniority and the merits and demerits of their respective qualities.
Desiring to honor the Dharma, he first paid homage to the best of the twice-born; then,
having prepared a great seat resembling the sun, which had never been attained by anyone before, he sat down upon it, O Lord of the World.
Then, O King, Bhīṣma said to the Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O Bhārata, let the honoring of these kings be performed according to their merit—
honoring the teacher, the officiating priest, and those who are closely associated with them, O Yudhiṣṭhira."

They say that a Snātaka, a beloved friend, and likewise a king—these six are worthy of the Arghya offering. They say that these worthy persons, when they have arrived as guests, are considered to have resided for a full year;
and so it is with these who have come to us after a vast interval of time.
"O King, let the guest-offering (arghya) be brought for each of these one by one;
rather, let it be presented to the most excellent among them, the one who is most capable.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"To whom do you consider the guest-offering (*argha*) due, O joy of the Kurus? Tell me, Grandfather, to which single one it is fitting that it be presented.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O Bhārata, Bhīṣma the son of Śantanu, having deliberated with his intellect,
considered Kṛṣṇa of the Vṛṣṇi clan to be the most worthy of honor on earth; for he,
among all those assembled there, excels in energy, strength, and prowess.
Shining in our midst like the sun among the stars,
this assembly hall of ours has indeed been illuminated and gladdened by Kṛṣṇa, as a sunless place is by the sun and a windless place is by the wind.
Then, authorized by Bhīṣma, the powerful Sahadeva offered the highest *arghya* according to the prescribed rites to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi;
having brought a cow, the *arghya*, and the *madhuparka*, he presented them at that time.
O lord of the people, Sahadeva touched the feet of Śauri,
and Keśava, the best among weapon-bearers, having smelled the head of Sahadeva,
then spoke to him: "Is all well with you at home?"
He too said to him, "So be it; indeed, everything shall be according to your command. In the meantime, O King, this wonder occurred:
seeing her, all the Kṣatriyas offered even greater honor to Kṛṣṇa.
Gazing at one another as they sat, they held her in their hearts.
Kṛṣṇa accepted that offering according to the rites prescribed by the scriptures;
however, Śiśupāla could not endure that worship being offered to Vāsudeva.
Having reproached Bhīṣma and Dharmarāja in that assembly,
the mighty King of Cedi insulted Vāsudeva;
Sahadeva, who understood their facial expressions and inner dispositions, could not tolerate this.
When his path was revealed before the proud and powerful kings,
a great rain of flowers fell upon the head of Sahadeva.
From his very birth, Sunītha had been an enemy of the Vṛṣṇis.
The questioner is a king born of a low womb; the respondent is the son of a river. The recipient is a cowherd, and the giver is likewise born of a low womb.
All the members of the assembly sit here like the mute—what more can be said?
Having said this, he laughed and quickly spoke again to the Pāṇḍava:
"O Pāṇḍava, do you overlook everyone else, or do you not see them at all? While other venerable men were present, you have honored a cowherd."
"O dear one, both of these—excessive vision and lack of vision—are destroyers of one's purpose; which of these two have you adopted? Śiśupāla said:

"O Kauravya, while these high-souled lords of the earth are present here, this descendant of Vṛṣṇi does not deserve royal worship as if he were a king. This conduct is not appropriate toward the high-souled Pāṇḍavas."

"O Pāṇḍavas, because you worshipped the lotus-eyed one out of desire, you children do not understand; for dharma is subtle, O Pāṇḍavas. In this matter, the son of the River (Bhīṣma), being of limited vision, has transgressed."
For one like you, endowed with righteousness, acting out of a desire to do what is pleasing,
becomes exceedingly despised among the virtuous in the worlds— just as Bhīṣma [is].
For how can the Daśārha, being no king, [speak thus] in the midst of all the lords of the earth?
He deserves honor in such a manner as you have already paid him.
Or, O bull of the Bharatas, if you consider Kṛṣṇa to be the elder,
how can his son deserve it while the aged Vasudeva is still present?
"Or rather, even Vāsudeva acted out of a desire to please [Drupada]; while Drupada is present, how can Mādhava deserve worship? Or do you consider Kṛṣṇa to be the preceptor, O bull among the Kurus?"
"While Droṇa is present, O Vārṣṇeya, why have you honored him?
Do you consider Kṛṣṇa to be the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), O joy of the Kurus? While the brahmin Dvaipāyana is standing here, how is it that Kṛṣṇa has been honored by you?"
O King, while Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, that best of men who possesses the power of death at his own will, is present— O King, how is it that you have honored Kṛṣṇa?
And while the heroic Aśvatthāman, skilled in all the scriptures, stands here.

O King, descendant of Kuru, how was Kṛṣṇa honored by you while Duryodhana, that best of men and lord of kings, was present, as well as Kṛpa, the preceptor of the Bharatas? How was Kṛṣṇa honored by you?
Having passed by Druma, the preceptor of the Kiṃpuruṣas, he was likewise honored;
and by Bhīṣmaka, who is invincible, by Pāṇḍya, who is marked with auspicious signs,
by the eminent King Rukmin, and likewise by Ekalavya.
And how was Kṛṣṇa honored by you in the presence of Śalya, the lord of the Madras?
For he is the one among all kings who boasts of his strength, a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha),
and the beloved disciple of the Brahmin son of Jamadagni, O Bhārata.
How is it that you have honored Kṛṣṇa while bypassing Karṇa, by relying on whose own strength kings were defeated in battle? O King,
while Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu and the best of men, was still present?
While he, whose death was subject to his own will, was still alive, how could Kṛṣṇa have been worshipped by you?

And while Kṛpa, the preceptor of the Bharatas, was present, how could Kṛṣṇa have been worshipped by you? While the heroic Aśvatthāman, skilled in all weapons, remained [alive], how could Kṛṣṇa have been worshipped by you?
"O King, how was Kṛṣṇa, the joy of the Yadus, honored by you? How was Kṛṣṇa honored by you in the presence of Druma, the preceptor of the Kiṃpuruṣas—
he who is not inferior to Pārtha in the science of archery and in prowess?"
O King, while Ekalavya was present, how could Kṛṣṇa have been honored by you? O King,
while the immensely powerful Bhagadatta and Jayatsena of Magadha,
as well as the king of Kaliṅga, were present, how could Kṛṣṇa have been honored by you?
While the heroic lord of the eastern region, the mighty Kausalya,
and the brave Virāṭa remain present, as well as the invincible Bhīṣmaka and Pāṇḍya, the master of the bow— how is it that Kṛṣṇa has been honored by you?
While King Nṛpa, the eminent Rukmiṇi, and King Dantavakra were present,
as well as Śalya, the lord of the Madras, and while the heroic king of Surāṣṭra and the king of Mālava remained there— how was Kṛṣṇa worshipped by you?
And when you had found leisure, O Vaideha, how was Kṛṣṇa honored by you?
He who is the great chariot-warrior (mahāratha) among all kings, boasting of his strength,
the beloved disciple of the Brahmin son of Jamadagni, O Bhārata.

How is it that you have honored Kṛṣṇa while bypassing Karṇa, by relying on whose own strength Jarāsaṃdha was defeated in battle? [And how is it you have bypassed] Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja?
While the lord of kings, Śālva, was present, how was Kṛṣṇa honored by you? O King,
while this friend of Pārtha, the heroic Citraratha, the lord of the Gandharvas, was standing there, how was Kṛṣṇa honored by you?
The aged hero Bāhlīka, the great car-warrior of the Kauravas; the son of Somadatta, the highly powerful Somadatta, the great car-warrior; Śakuni, the son of Subala; and the mighty King of Sindhu.
Having treated these [others] with contempt, how was Kṛṣṇa honored by you?

Madhusūdana is neither a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), nor a teacher (*ācārya*), nor a king; he is neither one who has completed his Vedic studies (*snātaka*), nor a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*). How was Kṛṣṇa honored by you?

O best of the Kurus, he has already been honored; what else could be desired? Or rather, if this Madhusūdana is to be honored by you, O Bhārata, what is the point of bringing these kings here only for their humiliation?
But we all pay tribute to this high-souled son of Kuntī neither out of fear, nor out of greed, nor because of conciliation,
since he is devoted to righteousness and desires to exercise the sovereignty of the earth.

"We offer him tribute, yet he does not even acknowledge us. What indeed is more insulting than this, that you have honored this Kṛṣṇa— who has not attained the marks of royalty— with the guest-offering in the assembly of kings?"
"Unexpectedly, the fame of the Son of Dharma as one whose soul is dharma has spread abroad. For who would offer such appropriate worship to one fallen from dharma,
he who was born in the Vṛṣṇi clan and yet slew the king in the past?"
"By acting unjustly toward the high-souled Jarāsaṃdha today, that evil-minded man has utterly cast away his righteousness, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
and by offering the guest-offering (*arghya*) to Kṛṣṇa, he has displayed a base and pitiable nature."
If the sons of Kuntī are afraid, wretched, and miserable ascetics,
yet they have offered you such great honor in the midst of kings,
surely you too must recognize the honor that Mādhava deserves.
Or rather, Janārdana, why did you, being unworthy of it, accept this worship offered by these wretched men? You hold in high regard a form of honor that is entirely unbecoming of yourself.
"Having obtained the overflow of the sacrificial offering, he is like a dog seeking to eat it in a deserted place.
This is not an act of insult directed at the lords of the earth;
rather, O Janārdana, it is clearly the Kurus who are deceiving you."

O Madhusūdana, the performance of marriage rites for a eunuch, or the sight of forms by a blind man— such is the honor you have received from one who is not a king, though treated as if he were a king. King Yudhiṣṭhira has been seen, and Bhīṣma has been seen exactly as he is.
"Vāsudeva has also been seen; all this is exactly as it is. Having spoken thus to them, Śiśupāla rose from his excellent seat and then departed from that assembly together with the kings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira rushed toward Śiśupāla and spoke these words to him, sweet and full of conciliation.
"O protector of the earth, what you have said is not proper; O King, it is supreme unrighteousness and useless harshness. For a ruler would never fail to understand what is the highest dharma."
But Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, said to him: "Do not disregard him otherwise than this.
Behold these many rulers of the earth who are far older than you;
they tolerate the offering made to Kṛṣṇa, and so you ought to forgive it as well."
"O Lord of Cedi, Bhīṣma truly knows Kṛṣṇa in his essential nature;
for you do not know him as the Kuru prince knows him.
Bhīṣma said:
"No conciliation should be offered to him, nor does he deserve any soothing words—
he who, toward Kṛṣṇa, the eldest in the world, does not acknowledge his due honor. A Kṣatriya, the best among those who wage war, having conquered a Kṣatriya in battle— "
He who, having brought another under his control, releases them, becomes their guru.
And in this assembly of kings, O protector of the earth, I do not see even a single unconquered monarch by the splendor of the son of Sātvatī.
For this Acyuta Janārdana is not only most worthy of worship for us; he is worthy of worship by all the three worlds as well. Indeed, by Kṛṣṇa many bulls among the Kṣatriyas were conquered in battle.
"The entire world is established in its entirety within the descendant of Vṛṣṇi.
Therefore, even though there are elders present, we worship Kṛṣṇa and no others.
You ought not to speak thus; let not your mind be such as this.
"O King, many who were advanced in wisdom have been attended by me;
O King, in the past, all those who knew his power were protected by him. While they were speaking, I heard of the virtues of that virtuous Śauri."
Among those assembled, I heard many accounts highly esteemed by the virtuous,
as well as the deeds of this wise man from his very birth,
which had been told repeatedly by men and heard by me once again.

O King of Cedi, it is not merely out of desire, nor by prioritizing our kinship, nor for any purpose whatsoever that we honor Janārdana— who has already achieved his own ends and who brings earthly happiness to those on earth— though he is already honored by the virtuous.
Having recognized his fame, heroism, and victory, we offer him this worship;
for here, not even a mere child has been honored by us without first being examined.
Since he surpasses the elders in his virtues, this monkey is considered most worthy of worship.
Among the twice-born, he is superior in knowledge; among the kṣatriyas, he is superior in strength;
among the vaiśyas, he possesses grain and wealth; and among the śūdras, he is so by birth alone.
Both of these reasons for being worthy of worship reside here in Govinda.
In this world, who among men possesses such knowledge of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, as well as immeasurable strength— except for Keśava? Indeed,
[who else has] generosity, dexterity, learning, heroism, modesty, fame, and supreme intelligence?
Humility, fortune, fortitude, contentment, and nourishment are eternally established in Acyuta.
You all ought to honor this man— who is endowed with every perfection, who is your teacher, father, and preceptor, and who is worthy of worship— now that he has been duly honored.
The officiating priest, the preceptor, the bridegroom, the bath-graduate, the king, and the beloved friend—all these are present in Hṛṣīkeśa; therefore, Acyuta is worshipped.
For Kṛṣṇa alone is indeed the origin and the dissolution of the worlds.
For this entire universe has been surrendered for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
he is the unmanifest primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the eternal agent. Because he is beyond all beings, the infallible Acyuta is the most ancient of all.
Intellect, mind, the Great One (Mahat), wind, fire, water, space, and earth—
as well as the fourfold classes of beings— all are established in Kṛṣṇa.
So too are the sun, the moon, the constellations, and the planets.
The cardinal directions and the intermediate directions—everything is established in Kṛṣṇa.
The Agnihotra is the foremost of the Vedas; the Gāyatrī is the foremost of the meters. The king is the foremost of men; the ocean is the foremost of rivers.
The moon is the foremost among the stars; the sun is the foremost among luminous bodies;
Mount Meru is the foremost among mountains; and Garuḍa is the foremost among those who fly. As far as the movement of the world extends—above, across, and below—[he is the foremost].
In all the worlds, including those of the gods, the Blessed One Keśava is the mouth;
he is Rudra, the soul of all, and he is the eternal Brahmā. As the imperishable one in the form of the perishable, he has assumed human birth.
But this foolish man Śiśupāla does not understand that Kṛṣṇa is everywhere and at all times; therefore he speaks in such a manner. For a wise man who would discern the supreme Dharma—
Indeed, he would see according to dharma, whereas this King of Cedi does not;
for among these kings, including the elderly and the children, as well as the high-souled ones—
who would consider Kṛṣṇa unworthy, or who would not honor him?
Then Śiśupāla resolved upon this improper worship;
he ought to act toward this improper act in accordance with what is right.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the son of Gaṅgā had spoken thus, Śiśupāla became enraged;
then Sahadeva, seeing Sunītha filled with anger, spoke to him at that time.
"O King of Cedi, all this has been done by me according to policy. I have no hesitation in this matter; hear now the reason for it. Kṛṣṇa is indeed the superior in strength among all the kings."
Therefore, you should all agree that he who is worthy of the *arghya* offering has been duly honored.
Or, if there is anyone among the kings, together with his army and vehicles, who cannot endure this,
let him quickly go forth to battle if he is capable of facing me in combat.
"I placed my left foot firmly upon his head.
When I had spoken thus, [the king] stated the reason; let him now give me the reply. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, when that path had been revealed in the midst of those wise, virtuous, proud, and powerful kings, not one among them uttered a word;
instead, a great rain of flowers fell upon the head of Sahadeva.
When Keśava had been addressed thus by Sahadeva, Sunītha’s eyes, which were already naturally red, became even redder still. Perceiving that his anger had flared up, the powerful Bhīṣma—
He spoke once more of the supreme qualities of Kṛṣṇa himself;
then, having addressed Sunītha and all those kings,
that best of speakers and foremost among the wise said this:
"O kings, understand that what Sahadeva has said regarding Keśava is indeed so; furthermore, listen to this."— thus spoke Vaiśampāyana.
Then, having heard those words of Bhīṣma at that time, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, the joy of the Kauravas, spoke to Bhīṣma:
"I desire to hear in full detail all the deeds of this god."
O Grandfather, tell me those [deeds] of the Blessed One so that I may hear them; O Lord, tell me the sequence of his actions and the manifestations of the All-pervading One.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"And what is the nature of Kṛṣṇa? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Thus addressed, Bhīṣma then spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the bull among men and slayer of foes, in that assembly of the kṣatriyas.
In the presence of Vāsudeva, who was like the god Śatakratu himself,
O lord of men, he recounted deeds difficult for others to perform before the listening kings and in the vicinity of Dharmarāja.
O lord of the people, O Indra among kings, that subduer of foes, Bhīṣma of terrible deeds— the best among the wise— then addressed the king of Cedi, Kṛṣṇa, with gentle words, and spoke this further.
Bhīṣma then spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus:
"O King Yudhiṣṭhira, listen to what has occurred and what is currently taking place."
This profound course of actions belongs to the Supreme Lord;
he who is the unmanifest, yet abides in manifest signs, is this Blessed One, the Sovereign,
the ancient god Nārāyaṇa, the self-existent Great-Grandfather.

The Puruṣa has a thousand heads; he is firm, unmanifest, and eternal. He is the all-pervading Lord with a thousand eyes, a thousand mouths, a thousand feet, and a thousand arms; he is the divine one who possesses a thousand names.
The god Sahasramukuṭa (Thousand-Crowned), Viśvarūpa (Universal Form), of great splendor, possessing manifold colors, the progenitor of the gods, stands indeed beyond the Unmanifest;
that Lord Nārāyaṇa first created the waters.
Then the Blessed One himself created Brahmā within the waters;
and the four-faced Brahmā himself created all those worlds. Indeed, in this manner, at the very beginning of time, there was the emergence of the entire universe.
Formerly, when the dissolution had arrived and all things mobile and immobile had perished;
when Brahmā and the others had dissolved away and the world of moving and unmoving beings had vanished;
when the universal deluge had occurred and the Great Principle (Mahat) had merged into primordial nature (Prakṛti).
One alone remains as the Self of all, the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
O Bhārata, all the gods are indeed the limbs of Nārāyaṇa;
his head is heaven, O King, his navel is the ether, and his feet are the earth.
The two Aśvins are the gods of his ears; the Moon and the Sun are his eyes;
Indra and Vaiśvānara are the gods of the mouth of that Great-Souled One;
and all other deities are the limbs of that Great-Souled One.
Having pervaded everything, Hari remained there like a thread amidst a cluster of jewels.
Then, at the end of the dissolution of all beings, seeing that everything was enveloped in darkness,
Nārāyaṇa— the great yogin, the omniscient one, and the possessor of the supreme self— [remained].
Having become Brahman, he himself created Brahmā as his own self. He is the overseer of all beings, the abundant source, the origin, and the imperishable.
[He created] Sanatkumāra, Rudra, Manu, and those whose wealth is austerity.
Brahmā created everything—both the worlds and the creatures—from that [seed].
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he emitted it there when the time had arrived;
from those high-souled beings, the eternal Brahman manifested in many ways.

O Bhārata, indeed many millions of kalpas have passed away; many millions of universal dissolutions (ābhūtasaṃplavas) have also elapsed. Throughout the ages of the manvantaras, there have been incessant cycles of cosmic intentions and universal dissolutions.

They revolve like a wheel; the entire world is pervaded by Viṣṇu. Having created the four-faced god, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign, dwells in the Ocean of Milk for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Brahmā is the grandfather of all beings and of the world;
beyond him is the divine Nārāyaṇa, the great-grandfather of all.
This Lord and Master, Nārāyaṇa, who is unmanifest yet abides in manifest forms, created the world, joined with its origin and dissolution;
having become Nārāyaṇa, he was Hari, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
He himself created Brahmā, the Moon, the Sun, and Dharma.
The Soul of all beings manifests in many ways for the sake of his purpose.
I shall now describe his divine manifestations, accompanied by hosts of gods.
Having slept for a thousand yugas,
he, the Lord of the gods and Master of the world, manifests when the thousand yugas are complete,
appearing as Brahmā, Kapila, and likewise Parameṣṭhin, intent upon his task.
In ancient times, the illustrious Lord of the gods, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire, created the seven Ṛṣis, Śaṅkara, Sanatkumāra, and Manu the Prajāpati.
By him [were slain] those two brothers, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were stationed in the midst of the ocean when all moving and stationary beings had perished,
when gods, asuras, and humans had vanished, and when serpents and rākṣasas had been destroyed—
those two most invincible ones, desiring to fight.
Having slain those two great Asuras who had previously been fashioned from clay by that powerful one, he granted them their chosen boon;
they were born from the ear-cavities of that high-souled Viṣṇu.
As they slept upon the great ocean, standing like the king of mountains,
Vāyu himself entered them, duly impelled by Brahmā. Those two great Asuras then grew in size, covering the very heavens.
Seeing those two, Vāyu and Prāṇa, Brahmā gently reflected: "Know one to be the softer; know the other to be the harder. Then that omnipresent Lord, born from the waters, gave them their names.
This one named Madhu was mild, while Kaiṭabha himself was harsh;
those two Daityas, having received their names, roamed about, arrogant in their strength.
O King, those two great Asuras once reached the entire celestial realm.
Then Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
desiring to fight, moved about entirely fearless, covering the entire sky and the whole world which was a single ocean.
Seeing those two asuras approach, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [observed them].
In that very mass of waters of the single ocean,
he vanished; he was born at the beginning from the navel-region of Padmanābha when a lotus had arisen there, and though it was a lotus, it was not born of mud.
Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, honored his dwelling;
both of them, Nārāyaṇa and the Four-faced One, remained within the womb of the waters,
and though lying in the water for many tens of thousands of years, they did not tremble.
Then, after a long time, both Madhu and Kaiṭabha arrived at that place where Brahmā was stationed. Upon seeing them, the Lord of the World’s eyes became bloodshot with rage.
Then, from his bed, the lotus-navelled one of great splendor leapt up;
at that time, a terrible battle took place between those two and him,
while the three worlds had become a single, dreadful ocean of water.
Then a tumultuous battle took place for thousands of years;
yet those two Asuras did not experience any fatigue in that conflict.
Then, after a long time, those two Daityas, intoxicated by the pride of war, [continued the struggle].
With delighted minds, they both spoke to the Lord, the divine Nārāyaṇa: "We are pleased by this battle of yours; you are a praiseworthy death for us.
Slay us before the earth is submerged by water."
"O best of gods, once we two have been slain, may we obtain the status of being your sons;
for whoever shall defeat us in battle, we two are ordained to be his sons.
Having heard those words of theirs, the Lord Nārāyaṇa then—
Seizing those two Daityas in battle with his arms, he crushed them;
with his two thighs, he brought about the death of both Madhu and Kaiṭabha. Having been slain, they leapt into the water and became one with their bodies.
As the two Daityas were being churned by the waves of water, they vomited fat;
that water was then pervaded by their fat, and it disappeared from view. And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa created various kinds of progeny.
O King, the entire earth was then covered by the fat of the two Daityas;
from that time forth, O son of Kuntī, the great earth has been known as Medinī. By the power of Padmanābha, it has been rendered eternal for mankind.
Bhīṣma said:
"Thousands of manifestations have passed away innumerable times;
however, I shall describe them to you according to my ability—listen to them, O joy of the Kurus."
Long ago, while Kamalanābha was sleeping upon the waters of the ocean,
the gods together with the hosts of ṛṣis were born from a lotus (puṣkara). This manifestation is celebrated as the Pauṣkarika.
Wherein the ancient [Purāṇa] is recounted, established in the Vedic revelation; wherein the manifestation of the Great-Souled One as the Boar (Vārāha) is the opening of the Śruti;
wherein Viṣṇu, the best of gods, assumed the form of a boar.
He lifted up the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, from the waters.

He whose feet were the Vedas, whose tusks were the sacrificial posts, whose teeth were the rituals, and whose mouth was the sacrificial altars; he whose tongue was fire, whose hair was the *darbha* grass, whose head was the Brahman, and who possessed great ascetic power.

The divine one has day and night for his eyes, the Vedas for his limbs, and the sacred scriptures for his ornaments; he has the clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his beak, and the chanting of the Sāmaveda for his great voice;
he is composed of dharma and truth, glorious, and honored by the prowess of his ritual actions.
The steadfast one consists of expiatory rites; he has the knees of sacrificial animals and is a great bull.
He bears the marks of the *udgātṛ* priest and the *homa* oblation; he is the great medicinal herb for the seed of sacrificial animals.
He is the inner self of the external world, with mantras for his bones, appearing serene in aspect.
The Veda is his shoulder, the fragrance of oblations is his scent, and he possesses the momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the *prāgvaṃśa* hall is his body, he is radiant, and he is laden with various initiations (*dīkṣā*);
the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is his heart, he is a yogin, and he is the great one consisting of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāsatra*).
With the *upākarma* ceremony as the luster of his lips and the *pravargya* rite as the ornament of his whorls,
accompanied by his consort Chāyā, he stood tall like the peak of a mountain of jewels. Thus did the eternal Viṣṇu become the sacrificial boar.

Then the Lord, having entered the waters of the single ocean, beheld the earth— his own goddess— with its mountains, forests, and groves, submerged in those waters and fallen into the expanse of the single ocean that bordered the sea.
While Mārkaṇḍeya looked on, he drew it up with his tusk;
having lifted this earth with his horn out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
the thousand-headed Lord of Gods, the Sovereign, fashioned the world anew.
Thus, in ancient times, by the Sacrificial Boar— the very soul of the past, the future, and the present— the divine Earth, who bears the waters of the ocean, was lifted up;
and all the Dānavas were slain by Viṣṇu, the God of gods.
This Vārāha incarnation has indeed been described; now listen to the Nārasiṃha, wherein Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by the Lord of Beasts after [the Lord] had become that.
Bhīṣma said:
O King, there was a powerful lord of the Daityas, an enemy of the gods, arrogant in his strength,
named Hiraṇyakaśipu; he was a thorn to the three worlds,
the primordial being of the Daityas, heroic, resolute, and mighty.

Having entered the forest, O King, he performed supreme austerity for ten thousand years and fifteen hundred more; his practice consisted of recitation and fasting, and he remained firm, motionless as a pillar, observing a vow of silence.
Then, O sinless one, because of his self-restraint, tranquility, and practice of celibacy, as well as his austerity and observance of rules, Brahmā became pleased with him. Thereupon,
O lord of the earth, the Blessed Lord Svayambhū himself came there.
In a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans,
together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and other deities,
as well as the Rudras, Viśvāsahāyas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kiṃnaras.
With the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, with the rivers and the oceans,
with the lunar mansions, the muhūrtas, and other planets moving through the sky,
as well as with the divine seers endowed with ascetic power, the Siddhas, and the Seven Seers;
Brahmā, the glorious teacher of all that moves and is stationary, was likewise surrounded by most meritorious royal sages, by Gandharvas, by hosts of Apsarases, and by all the gods.
Brahmā, the best among those who know Brahman, approached the Daitya and said:
"I am pleased with you, my devotee, because of this austerity, O observer of noble vows.
Choose a boon—may it be well with you—and obtain whatever desire you wish."
O best of gods, neither the gods, asuras, or gandharvas, nor the yakṣas, uragas, or rākṣasas, nor humans or piśācas could slay me, O Hiraṇyakaśipu.

"O Grandfather of the worlds, even the sages, though endowed with ascetic power, would not curse me with their wrathful spells; this is the boon I have chosen— that neither by weapon nor missile, nor by mountain nor tree, shall I be slain."
"O Grandfather, let there be no slaying of me by anything dry nor by anything moist, nor by anything else;
neither in the air nor on the earth, neither by night nor even by day,
neither within nor without— let there be no death for me."
O God of gods, if you grant me these boons, I choose that there shall be no [fear] from cattle, wild beasts, birds, or reptiles. O Brahmā, I choose this.
"O dear one, these divine and wonderful boons have been granted to you by me. You shall obtain all desired boons, of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One departed through the sky.
He shone in the world of Brahmā, attended by hosts of brahmin-sages.
Then the gods, the nāgas, the gandharvas, and likewise the sages,
having heard of the granting of the boon, approached Brahmā.
"O Blessed One, by means of this boon, that asura will oppress us.
Therefore, be gracious, O Blessed One; let a means for his destruction be devised."
O Blessed One, you are the self-existent, the original creator, and the all-pervading Lord of all beings; you are Bhīṣma,
the creator of the offerings to gods and ancestors, the unmanifest primordial nature, and the eternal.
Then, having heard those words for the benefit of the world, the Lord Prajāpati,
the Blessed One, spoke these words to all the hosts of gods: "O Thirty-three, he must necessarily obtain the fruit of his asceticism."
"At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa will bring about his death.
Having heard this from Brahmā regarding his destruction, all the gods,
filled with joy, departed for their own divine abodes.
As soon as that boon was obtained, it oppressed all living beings. The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, arrogant because of the granting of the boon,
ruled the kingdom as the lord of the Daityas, surrounded by hosts of Daityas.
By his might, he brought the seven islands and the region between the Lokāloka mountains under his control;
indeed, he obtained all the divine worlds and celestial enjoyments,
having defeated those gods who dwell in the three worlds.

Having brought the three worlds under his control, the Dānava dwelt in heaven. While that Dānava, intoxicated by the pride of his boon, resided in the celestial realm, that one of great strength then conquered all the worlds.
May I alone become Indra, Soma, Agni, and Māruta; may I be the water, the atmosphere, the constellations, and the ten directions;
may I be anger and desire, Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Yama.
The giver of wealth, the lord of riches, the Yakṣa, and the sovereign of the Kiṃpuruṣas— having said, "May I become these," he himself became so by force,
and having seized their positions, he took over their duties.
And he was praised in this world by the best of the gods and *kiṃnaras*, who were the foremost among those skilled in sacrifice.
Having brought those dwelling in hell up, he established them in heaven.
Having performed such deeds as these, the powerful lord of the Daityas—
In former times, he even assaulted the highly fortunate sages in their hermitages— those of firm vows, devoted to truth and righteousness, and self-controlled—
and he rendered the Daityas eligible for sacrifice while making the gods ineligible for sacrifice.
Wherever the gods went, he followed them there;
having seized the abodes of the deities,
he protected the kingdom for fifty-five million and sixty-one hundred thousand years.

Sixty thousand [demons] followed that evil-minded one; for sixty years, that lord of the Daityas enjoyed sovereign power and pleasures. Oppressed by that powerful lord of the Daityas, they [suffered].
All the gods, led by Śakra, went to the world of Brahmā;
having approached the Grandfather, the weary deities spoke with palms joined in reverence.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, protect us who have come here!
A terrible fear from the son of Diti prevails today, day and night.
O Blessed One, you are the self-born, the primordial creator, and the all-pervading Lord of all beings.
You are Brahmā, the creator of the offerings to gods and ancestors; you are the unmanifest, the primordial nature, and the eternal.
Listen to my distress, for even by me this situation is difficult to comprehend.
But Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣa of universal form and great splendor,
is unmanifest to all beings, inconceivable, omnipresent, and imperishable;
he is the supreme refuge for me as well as for you in times of distress.
Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; I am born from the unmanifest. From me were born the progeny, the worlds, and all those gods and asuras.
Just as I am to you, O gods, so is Nārāyaṇa to me.
"I am the grandfather of all, and that Viṣṇu is the great-grandfather.
O gods, it is certain that he, as Viṣṇu, will slay that Daitya."—
Bhīṣma.
"For him there is nothing indeed that is impossible; therefore, depart without delay.
Having heard the words of the Grandfather, O bull of the Bharatas, all those gods went together with Brahmā toward the Ocean of Milk.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and likewise the Viśvedevas and the Maruts;
the Rudras, the great ṛṣis, and the two Aśvins of beautiful form;
and whatever other divine beings there are, O King—all those gods together with their hosts.
Placing the four-faced one at their head, they arrived at Śvetadvīpa;
having gone to that ocean of milk, they reached the eternal, supreme goal—
the Lord who reclines upon Ananta, the infinite one of blazing splendor.
The thirty gods approached Viṣṇu, the eternal refuge,
the god consisting of Brahman, the sacrifice, the divine Brahman, the one of great power,
the lord of the past, present, and future, who is honored by the worlds.
The gods went for refuge to the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, the protector; "O Lord of Gods,
protect us today from the slaughter by Hiraṇyakaśipu!"
For you, O best of gods, are our supreme creator among Brahmā and the others;
O you with blossoming, stainless lotus-eyes, who strike terror into the ranks of the enemy,
you shall be the refuge for the destruction of the lineage of Diti.
Having heard the words of the gods, Viṣṇu of pure fame—
Viṣṇu— then [spoke].
Becoming invisible to all beings, he began to speak:
"O immortals, cast away your fear; I grant you freedom from fear.
Therefore, O gods, enter the celestial realm without delay."
"O Brahmā, here I am; I shall slay this lord of the Dānavas, who, arrogant because of the granting of a boon,
has become invincible to the lords of the immortals along with his host."
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, these gods are indeed greatly distressed.
O Viṣṇu, therefore slay the lord of the Daityas quickly; this is his time—do not delay."
"O gods, I shall swiftly and with haste bring about the destruction of the Daityas;
therefore, you and the deities must indeed ascend to heaven."—
Bhīṣma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One dismissed the lords of the three worlds; then,
