having made half his body human and half his body leonine,
he assumed the form of a man-lion (Narasiṃha) and crushed one hand with the other.
O King, the Lord Hari, of terrifying form and great splendor, with his mouth wide open like the God of Death,
went toward Hiraṇyakaśipu;
and the Daityas saw that mighty Narasiṃha as he approached.
Then, being greatly enraged, they rained down showers of weapons upon Hari; however,
Hari devoured the weapons discharged by them and slew many thousands of Daityas in battle.
Having slain all those furious and mighty lords of the Daityas, he,
highly enraged, rushed toward the lord of the Daityas who was arrogant of his strength;
he resembled a mass of clouds and possessed a voice like the thundering of clouds.
Like a cloud of blazing splendor, like a cloud of great velocity—
the wicked enemy of the gods, born of Diti— rushed toward the Man-Lion.
Seeing that exceedingly powerful Daitya, who possessed the prowess of an enraged tiger, [he approached].

It was guarded by arrogant hosts of Daityas, as well as by donkeys with claws for mouths. Then, having indeed fought with that Daitya, the highly resplendent Hari, at the time of twilight, hurriedly entered his abode.

Placing the lord of the Daityas upon his thigh, Hari, the best of the gods, struck him with his claws; he slew that foremost of Daityas, who was possessed of great strength and great heroism, and was arrogant due to the granting of boons, by means of his own power.
Having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu and all the Daityas at that time,
and having secured the welfare of the gods and their subjects, the immensely radiant Lord Hari rejoiced on earth, having attained his righteous purpose.
This Nārasiṃha incarnation has been recounted to you here, O son of Pāṇḍu; Bhīṣma said:
"Now listen to the manifestation of the Great-Souled One known as Vāmana."

O King, formerly in the Tretā Yuga, Bali, the son of Virocana, was the heroic sovereign of the Daityas; he was powerful, peerless in strength, and mighty. At that time, O great king, Bali was surrounded by hosts of Daityas.
Having swiftly conquered Śakra, he attained the station of Indra;
the gods, including the powerful Khaṇḍala and others, were terrified by him,
and they then went to the Ocean of Milk, placing Brahmā at their head.
Together they all praised the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa. Then Hari bestowed his grace upon those deities;
the birth of that Sovereign from Aditi, arising from his grace, is thus described.
Having attained the status of being the son of Aditi, this delighter of the Yādavas,
known as Viṣṇu, became the younger brother of Indra.
At that very time, however, there was a powerful and heroic lord of the Daityas.
He began to perform the horse sacrifice, the most excellent of rituals. While that sacrifice of the lord of the Daityas was then proceeding, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
Viṣṇu, having become a dwarf and remaining concealed, assumed the guise of a Brahmin.
Shaven-headed yet wearing the sacred thread, clad in a black antelope skin and bearing a topknot,
the dwarf of wondrous appearance took up a staff of *palāśa* wood and entered while the sacrifice of Bali was in progress, as he was bestowing the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
"Give me indeed three strides," he said to the lord of the Daityas. "Let only three paces be given," he said to the great Asura. Having promised "So be it," he then gave them to Viṣṇu.

Having obtained the earth by that means, Hari indeed yawned violently. O lord of the people, that infant, the Overpowering One, traversed all this— the sky including heaven and the earth— with three strides.
In ancient times, at the sacrifice of Bali, those unshakeable and mighty hosts of Daityas, led by Vipracitti, were shaken by the powerful Viṣṇu with his three strides,
even though they were full of wrath.
O King, they have various faces and massive bodies, wearing diverse garbs; they are fierce, bearing various weapons, adorned with diverse garlands and ointments,
and grasping their own arms as if blazing with splendor.
O Bhārata, as Hari strode there, they all gathered around him; having crushed all those Daityas with the soles of his feet and the palms of his hands,
he assumed a most terrifying form and swiftly seized the earth.
Having reached the sky and the celestial realm, he stood in the abode of the Sun; that soul of all beings, possessed of great power, outshone the Sun with his own splendor,
illuminating all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
That mighty-armed one shone forth, illuminating all the worlds. As he strode across the earth, the sun and moon were situated between his breasts;
and as he traversed the sky, they were said to have been positioned at his navel.
As Viṣṇu of immeasurable prowess was about to stride further, those two remained stationed at his knees; thus do the twice-born speak. Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he reached the shell of the cosmic egg.
From that opening, a flowing river issued forth from his foot;
that purifying stream, destined for the ocean, swiftly flowed toward the sea. Having slain the foremost of the Dānavas, it swept away the entire earth.
Having seized the splendor of the Asuras, that Janārdana cast the Asuras, along with their sons and wives, down into Pātāla across the three worlds;
[so too did he strike down] Namuci, Śambara, and the high-minded Prahlāda.
Shaken down by the falling of his feet, they were cast into the netherworld (pātāla).
O King, Hari— the self of all beings— manifested the great elements along with their specific derivatives, as well as time in its entirety, as the constituent parts of his own body.
Upon his body, the entire world appears as if brought together;
there is nothing in the worlds that has not been attained by that Great-Souled One. Indeed, such is the form of Upendra, [regarded] by gods, dānavas, and humans.
Seeing him, they all fainted, overwhelmed by the splendor of Viṣṇu;
the proud Bali was bound by the Great-Souled One in the sacrificial arena,
and the entire lineage of Virocana was cast down into Pātāla.
Having performed such deeds, he whose vehicle is Garuḍa did not experience any astonishment due to his supreme majesty;
having bestowed all the sovereignty of the immortals upon the Lord of Śacī, he remained as he was.
And Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Dānavas, gave the three worlds to Śakra.
This is the manifestation named Vāmana of the Great-Souled One;
this glory of Viṣṇu is indeed recounted by the twice-born who are knowers of the Vedas.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen, O great king, to how the manifestation of Viṣṇu among human beings occurred; hear further of the manifestation of that high-souled Viṣṇu.
There was a highly illustrious sage known as Dattātreya.
When the Vedas had been lost, as were the ritual acts and sacrifices,
when the four castes had become intermingled and righteousness had fallen into decay—
When unrighteousness increases, when truth has perished and falsehood prevails, when the subjects are wasting away and righteousness has fallen into disorder,
he indeed restores the Vedas along with their sacrifices and ritual acts.
The four castes were rendered unmixed by that great-souled one. Indeed, when he granted a boon to the lord of the Haihayas, Arjuna, the sovereign of the Haihayas, sought to propitiate him.
In the forest, he attended upon him properly, free from malice;
devoid of possessiveness and egoism, he gratified him for a long time. Having propitiated Dattātreya, he indeed received these boons.

From a trustworthy and most reliable Brahmin, a learned man [received] those [teachings] practiced by the wise; except for immortality, which was granted by the intelligent Brahmin Dattātreya through four boons, he there rejoiced in these [other gifts].
"May I be illustrious, wise, powerful, truthful in speech, and free from malice;
may I possess a thousand arms—this is my first boon.
[May I behold] all that is born from a womb or an egg, and everything mobile and immobile."
I wish to rule according to dharma; this is my second boon:
that I may worship the ancestors, the gods, the seers, and the brahmins with abundant sacrifices, and that I may strike down enemies on the field of battle with sharpened arrows.
"O Blessed One, Dattātreya, this is my third boon:
may there be no man equal to him—neither has been, nor will be, nor even is—whether here on earth or in heaven; he shall be my slayer."

That Arjuna became the preeminent son of Kṛtavīrya in battle; he grew up in Māhiṣmatī as the leader of a million warriors. Having conquered the entire earth, including the islands in the ocean, he ruled over it.
Like the sun blazing in the sky, Arjuna, by virtue of his meritorious deeds,
[reached] the lordly islands of Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmradvīpa, Gabhastimat, Gāndharva, Vāruṇa, Saumya, and Ārṣa.
Arjuna conquered islands never before subdued by his ancestors.
That supreme, excellent celestial chariot was entirely made of gold.
He divided the kingdom into four parts and, having divided it, protected each portion.
With one part he led the army, and with one part he dwelt at home;
that which was the third part of his, the king employed for the gathering of the people,
and being trustworthy and supremely auspicious, he performed sacrifices with it.
Those *dasyus* who wander through villages and those who dwell in the forest—
he repelled them all with a fourth part [of their spoils].
And from all his residents, Kārtavīrya exacted tribute.
Whatever was brought by his own forces, Arjuna disregarded it; whether it was a crow or even a mouse, he struck each one down. Furthermore, the gates in the kingdoms and the cities were not closed.
He himself was Rāṣṭrapāla; Arjuna became Strīpāla. He himself was Ajāpāla and he was Gopāla, O lord of the people;
as king, he protects all the fields of men.
But this [deed] of Kārtavīrya was unequaled by men;
neither kings of the past nor those of the future shall ever attain his state,
in that even as he proceeded across the ocean, his garment was not drenched.
Having governed the earth for a hundred thousand years,
Arjuna ruled his kingdom in this manner through the grace of Dattātreya;
thus he performed many deeds for the welfare of the world.
The manifestation known as Dattātreya is indeed Vaiṣṇava;
this has been told by Bhīṣma, O best of the Bharatas. Listen further concerning that Great-Souled One.
The reason for the birth of that Great Soul in the lineage of Bhṛgu,
and the purpose for which he appeared as the manifestation of Viṣṇu known as Jāmadagnya—
O King, he was the powerful son of Jamadagni named Rāma.
O King, that Rāma, the slayer of the Haihayas and the best among the strong,
as well as Kārtavīrya of great heroism who was peerless in might,
was slain by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, because he acted with treachery.

Having struck down King Kārtavīrya, the subduer of the Haihayas and a ruler seated upon his chariot, Rāma slew him in battle; for he was the destroyer of Jambha’s sacrifice and had even slain a sacrificial priest upon the ritual grass.
The breaker of Jambha’s head and the slayer of Śatadundubhi—
this very Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, the heroic one, has been born among the Bhṛgus to uproot the thousand-armed [Kārtavīrya] who is victorious in battle.
The highly illustrious one conquered sixty-four hundred thousand Kṣatriyas assembled on the Sarasvatī with his bow; in that slaughter of those who hated the Brahmins, fourteen thousand were slain.
Once again he seized [his weapon], and that bull among men brought an end to the heroes;
then, having first broken ten thousand,
that subduer of enemies struck a thousand with his mace and cut down another thousand.

Having caused fourteen thousand [Kṣatriyas] to drink the smoke of chaff, and having conquered the remaining haters of Brahman, the descendant of Bhṛgu then performed his ablutions while being hailed "Rāma! Rāma! by the Brāhmaṇas who had been oppressed by the Kṣatriyas.
The powerful Rāma, with his axe, struck down ten thousand [demons];
for he could not endure those words uttered so piteously by the distressed twice-born ones who were crying out, "O Rāma, son of Bhṛgu, come to our aid!"
The Kāśmīras, Daradas, Kuntīs, Kṣudrakas, Mālavas, and Śakas; the Cedis, Kāśikas, Karūṣas, Ṛṣīkas, Krathakaiśikas;
and the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Māgadhas, Kāśis, and Kosalas.
Having struck down the Rātrāyaṇas, Vītihotras, Kirātas, and Mārttikāvatas— these and thousands of other lords of kings in various lands—
with sharpened arrows, he offered them as a gift to Vivasvat.
Covered by millions of *kṣatriyas* and adorned with Meru and Mandara,
the earth was rendered devoid of *kṣatriyas* twenty-one times by him;
having thus cleared the earth of *kṣatriyas*, that highly illustrious descendant of Bhṛgu—
He filled the rivers and the lakes with blood that was the color of cochineal insects and resembled the *jīvañjīvaka* bird; there,
among those waters and upon those grounds, the hero performed the libations for his ancestors.
Having brought all eighteen islands under his control, that descendant of Bhṛgu performed thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of human-sacrifices,
and then gave the earth, bounded by the ocean, to Kāśyapa.
He circumambulated her, making the ground free of dust before him;
then, regarding that which was brought about by Time as true, those people who are knowers of the Purāṇas even sing this verse here concerning the high-souled Bhārgava:

Kāśyapa accepted from Rāma Jāmadagnya an altar eighteen cubits high and made of gold, exceeding the height of a man. Having thus performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, the mighty-armed one—
For another hundred years, O Rāma, Saubha fought against Sālva.
Then that lord, a tiger among the Bhṛgus, while fighting from that Saubha,
mounted his chariot Subandhura, O King, O bull of the Bharatas.
He overheard naked young maidens singing:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, enhancer of the Bhṛgu lineage's fame!
Lay down all your weapons; you shall not destroy Saubha."
"With discus in hand and mace in hand, the granter of fearlessness to the terrified,
Kṛṣṇa shall destroy Saubha in battle along with Pradyumna and Sāmba.
Having heard that, the tiger among men departed from that very spot for the forest.
Having laid aside all his weapons and awaiting his time, the highly illustrious Rāma, that supreme ascetic,
established his chariot, armor, weapons, arrows, axe,
and bows in the waters and performed intense penance.
Having established himself in modesty, wisdom, prosperity, fame, and splendor— the destroyer of enemies,
whose soul is rooted in Dharma— dispatched that chariot. For the Lord, dividing time, set it in motion at the beginning of the age.
It was not out of faith that he destroyed Saubha, nor was the illustrious one incapable;
for he who is known as the son of Jamadagni is the venerable Rishi Bhīṣma.
That Bhārgava, world-renowned, performed austerities as his portion. Listen, O King, likewise to the manifestation of the high-souled Viṣṇu in the twenty-fourth age, preceded by Mārkaṇḍeya.
On the ninth lunar day, the imperishable Viṣṇu, the mighty-armed one, having divided himself fourfold, was likewise born from Daśaratha,
renowned in the world as Rāma and equal to the sun in splendor.
For the sake of the world’s adornment, Viṣṇu, the eternal one,
was born there, O son of Kuntī, as one of great fame solely for the sake of dharma;
they call him too the lord of men, the very body of the Lord of all beings.
O Bhārata, having then created an obstacle to Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice, Subāhu was slain by him; Mārīca was severely struck,
and weapons were bestowed upon him by the wise Viśvāmitra.
For the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods, which were irresistible even by the deities themselves, while the sacrifice of the high-souled Janaka was then proceeding,
the bow of Maheśvara was broken with supreme ease as if in mere play.

Then, having performed the marriage of Sītā, that beloved of the Raghus returned once more to the city and rejoiced there with Sītā. After some time had passed, however, he was urged by his father to go there.
Seeking to do what was pleasing to Kaikeyī, he entered the forest; that Rāma,
who dwelt for fourteen years in the woods, knowing all duties,
followed by Lakṣmaṇa, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
O Bhārata, having performed austerities in the forest for fourteen years,
that Lakṣmī— who was formerly his constant companion and whom people call Sītā— followed her husband in embodied form.
Dwelling in Janasthāna, he performed the work of the gods;
having slain Mārīca, Dūṣaṇa, Khara, and Triśiras,
as well as fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of terrible deeds.
The righteous Rāma, desiring the welfare of all creatures,
slew Virādha and Kabandha, two Rākṣasas of cruel deeds;
and at that time, Rāma also slew two Gandharvas who had been afflicted by a curse.
He caused the cutting off of Rāvaṇa’s sister’s nose,
and having suffered that separation from his wife, he wandered through the forest searching for her. Then, having passed beyond the Pampā lake, he went to that Mount Ṛśyamūka.
Having seen Sugrīva and Māruti, he indeed established a friendship between the two. Then, having gone to Kiṣkindhā together with Sugrīva,
he slew Vālin, the mighty lord of monkeys, in battle.
Then Rāma consecrated Sugrīva as the lord of the monkeys.
Thereupon, O King, that valiant one, being eager and hastening,
had the region of Laṅkā searched for by the son of the Wind-god, who then reported it back.
Then, having built a bridge across the ocean together with the monkeys,
Rāma, seeking the whereabouts of Sītā, entered Laṅkā.
Indeed, [he was there] amidst the hosts of gods, serpents, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and birds.
There stood Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, invincible and difficult to defeat in battle,
joined by tens of millions of Rākṣasas and resembling a mass of crushed collyrium;
he was hard for even the hosts of gods to behold, puffed up with pride because of the granting of a boon.

In ancient times, Rāma, the lord of beings, slew Rāvaṇa along with his ministers and his kin in battle— that hero who was the thorn of the three worlds, possessed of a massive body and great strength— having destroyed Rāvaṇa together with his hosts.
Having consecrated that high-souled Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, right there in Laṅkā, Rāma then granted him immortality; then,
O Pāṇḍava, Rāma took Sītā and ascended the Puṣpaka chariot.
Having returned to his own city, Śabala protected the kingdom of Dharma. O King,
the exceedingly powerful Dānava named Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu,
was slain by Śatrughna at the command of Rāma.
Having performed many such deeds for the welfare of the world,
Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, ruled the kingdom according to the sacred ordinances;
he performed ten horse-sacrifices, as well as the Jyotiḥ and Ukthya sacrifices consisting of multi-day sessions.
While Rāma ruled the kingdom, no inauspicious words were heard, nor was there any calamity for living beings; there was no fear born of wealth,
nor did living beings have any fear arising from water or fire.

No woman was a widow, nor did any become destitute; while Rāma governed the kingdom, everyone was satisfied. The social classes did not engage in intermixture, nor did any person perform the work of a plowman.

The elders did not perform the funeral rites for the young; the Vaiśyas attended to the Kṣatriyas, and the Kṣatriyas did not oppress the Vaiśyas. Men did not overstep their wives, nor did wives overstep their husbands.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, there was no cultivation of small plots in the world;
likewise, people lived for thousands of years and possessed thousands of sons.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, all living beings were free from disease.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, there was a cohabitation upon the earth among the ṛṣis, the deities, and likewise the humans;
for all were then satisfied in form, O lord of the people.
While that king Rāma ruled the kingdom on earth, governing the entire world according to dharma, everyone was devoted to austerity and all were observant of dharma.
There was no man anywhere who was unrighteous toward living beings while Rāma ruled the kingdom;
indeed, the people who know the ancient lore sing this verse concerning him: "While Rāma governed the realm, the out-breath and in-breath of all creatures remained perfectly balanced."
Dark-complexioned and youthful, with reddish eyes like a bull among elephants,
his arms reaching to his knees, handsome-faced, lion-shouldered, and possessed of great strength;
for ten thousand years and ten hundred years [he remained].
Having obtained the kingdom and its enjoyments, he ruled this earth;
"Rāma, Rāma, Rāma" were the conversations among the subjects. While Rāma governed the kingdom, this entire world became Rāma.
At that time, there were no twice-born ones deficient in the Ṛg, Yajur,
and Sāma Vedas. Having dwelt in Daṇḍaka, that bull among men performed the task of the thirty gods against the descendant of Pulastya, who had previously wronged him in battle.
The powerful one, endowed with virtues and blazing with his own splendor, struck down the enemy of the gods, Gandharvas, and Nāgas;
even so was that mighty-armed one, the enhancer of the Ikṣvāku lineage.

"Having slain Rāvaṇa along with his hosts, the Overlord ascended to heaven. Thus is celebrated the manifestation of the high-souled son of Daśaratha. Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, who grants fearlessness to those who are afraid—
O King, in the twenty-eighth yuga, he who was marked with the śrīvatsa was born;
he was graceful, generous, and highly esteemed among men in the world.
He possessed mindfulness, knew the proper place and time, and bore the conch, the discus, the mace, and the sword.
Known as Vāsudeva, he is always the benefactor of the worlds;
born in the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the Earth,
he is renowned as the slayer of Madhu and the bestower of fearlessness upon men.

It is said that he destroyed the abodes of Śakra, Arjuna, and Rāma; he slew Kaṃsa and other Daityas in human form in battle. This manifestation of the Great-Souled One was for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Furthermore, at the end of the Kali age, when dharma has fallen into decay, Hari will again be born as Kalkī Viṣṇuyaśas for the sake of slaying the hosts of heretics, O bull among the Bharatas.
For the sake of increasing the Dharma and out of a desire for the welfare of the Brahmins—
these and many other divine beings, accompanied by hosts of gods— [spoke thus],
Vaiśampāyana said.
"The manifestations [of the Lord] are sung of in the Purāṇas by those who discourse on Brahman.
Having been addressed thus, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and the joy of the Pauravas, then [spoke].
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, spoke again to Bhīṣma:
"O best of speakers, O lord of men, I desire to know once more the birth of the illustrious Upendra among the Vṛṣṇis."

O Grandfather, tell me how Janārdana, possessed of great intelligence, was born here on earth among the Mādhavas; and for what purpose did that one of great splendor, whose eyes are like those of a bull, take up the form of cows?
The protector of the worlds protected [them] from the slaughter by Kaṃsa;
and whatever was performed by Govinda while playing in his childhood—
Vaiśampāyana [related it].
"O best among the wise, O grandfather, tell me that.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Keśava, Bhīṣma then [spoke].
Bhīṣma.
The valiant one then declared his birth among the Mādhaveyas. "Behold, O Yudhiṣṭhira, descendant of Kuru, I shall relate to you exactly how the birth of Nārāyaṇa occurred here among the Vṛṣṇis."

O Great King, formerly, while the Kṛta Yuga was prevailing in the world, there occurred a battle famous throughout the three worlds known as Tārakāmaya. In it were Virocana, Maya, Tāra, Varāha, and Śveta.
Lamba, Kiśora, Svarbhānu, Ariṣṭa, and Kṣara;
Vipracitti, Pralamba, Vṛtra, Jambha, Bala, and others; Namuci, Kālanemi, and the one renowned as Prahlāda.
These and many other hosts of Daityas by the thousands,
O King, bearing various weapons and possessing diverse ornaments and vehicles,
stood facing the deities— the Daiteyas and Dānavas.
But those gods, fighting in the battle, advanced against the Dānavas—
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts;
Indra, Yama, Candra, Varuṇa, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
The two Aśvins of great heroism and whatever other hosts of deities there were,
engaged in a most terrible battle with the Dānavas in due order;
and as they fought, the gods encountered the Daityas and Dānavas.
Then that battle became terrible, crowded with gods and dānavas;
a tumultuous conflict then arose between those two forces. Then the gods and dānavas advanced, scattering sharp weapons.
The gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Cāraṇas, were being struck down;
then, while being slaughtered by the Daityas in battle, those hosts of gods,
utterly exhausted and with their weapons depleted, fled from the field of combat.
In their minds, they sought refuge with the Lord, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Protector. In that very interval, the Lord Hari arrived there,
illuminating the earth with his radiance and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Seeing Viṣṇu, who is honored by the worlds, arrive mounted upon Garuḍa,
all the gods in the battle were filled with joy and cast off their fear;
once again, all the deities engaged in combat with the Daityas and Dānavas.
That battle became terrible, inconceivable, and hair-raising. All the gods, led by Śakra, slew the Daityas in combat.
Being slaughtered by the gods, those Daityas and Dānavas fled.
O Bhārata, seeing the Dānavas fleeing in that battle,
a Dānava known as Kālanemi then appeared;
he was terrible, possessing a hundred weapons, a hundred arms, and a hundred faces.

The glorious one stood with a hundred heads, like a mountain with a hundred peaks; his crown had the form of the sun, and his armlets and ornaments jingled. He had smoke-colored hair and a golden beard, and his face was characterized by bitten lips.
Bearing a vast body that pervaded the space between the three worlds,
threatening the gods in battle and shrouding the ten directions,
he rushed forward in great fury like Death with his jaws wide open.
Then, with a rain of weapons, he overpowered the gods in battle.
Thereupon, O Yudhiṣṭhira, those Daityas and Dānavas once again advanced against all the gods, assailing the deities in the conflict with fury.
O great king, being slaughtered in battle by Kālanemi and by the Daityas as well, those gods fled together in all directions. Seeing the gods thus routed, the great Asura Kālanemi—
Having conquered by force Indra, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Ravi, as well as these and others, he accomplished their tasks;
having swiftly defeated them all, the great Asura Kālanemi—
In the sky, he beheld Viṣṇu of great splendor seated upon Garuḍa;
seeing him, his eyes copper-red with rage, he then advanced while threatening him,
raising his hundred arms which grasp every weapon in battle.
Out of rage, O Bhārata, the lord of the Daityas hurled [the weapon] at the chest of Viṣṇu;
and all the Daityas and Dānavas, led by Maya,
seized their own weapons and struck Viṣṇu.
Though being struck by the exceedingly powerful Daityas with all their weapons raised,
Hari did not waver in battle, remaining as unshakable as a mountain.
Then, filled with rage, Kālanemi once again raised his firm mace.
O King, in that battle he struck both Viṣṇu and Garuḍa. Seeing that Garuḍa was exhausted, Hari raised his discus and severed the hundred heads and arms of Kālanemi.
In that battle, O King, he struck down all those other Daityas and Dānavas;
only three Daityas escaped from that conflict:
Virocana, Maya, and the great Asura Svarbhānu.

Having slain all the Daityas and Dānavas without exception, Viṣṇu indeed restored their own respective positions to the gods and the sages; having bestowed this favor upon the deities, O Bhārata, he attained great joy.
Then Hari went to the world of Brahmā together with Brahmā. Having entered the world of Brahmā, the Lord Nārāyaṇa then [went to] the divine hermitage of Nārāyaṇa, the secret abode of the ancients.
Then, having entered while being praised by the great seers, the God,
becoming thousand-headed, proceeded to his bed;
the primordial God, the ancient Self, fell under the power of sleep.
The imperishable Viṣṇu, deluding the world, always sleeps happily;
thirty-six thousand years passed while that high-souled one was thus reclining, according to human calculation here on earth.
Then, at the end of the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages,
Viṣṇu— being praised by Brahmā and the other gods as well as by the great ṛṣis— leaped up from his bed together with Brahmā and the deities.
For the benefit of the gods, he went toward the assembly hall of the gods—
that auspicious, blazing hall situated upon the peak of Meru—
and all the deities entered it together with Brahmā, O Bhārata.
They went there and sat down; at that time, the earth became silent.
Then the Earth, speaking piteously out of weariness, said:

"O gods, I am utterly exhausted and severely oppressed by the armies of powerful kings; constantly weary from carrying burdens, I indeed live in misery. And in every city, a monarch is surrounded by forces numbering in the tens of millions."
In kingdom after kingdom, there were hundreds of villages and thousands of clans;
with the thousands of those lords of the earth and the forces of their armies, and with tens of thousands of villages and kingdoms, I was rendered free of all rivals.
Some were born among the Daityas, and some from the wombs of Rākṣasas;
therefore, I am not able to sustain these people,
for they are constantly oppressed by the evil-minded lords of the Daityas.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard those words of the Earth, the Lord Nārāyaṇa then [spoke].
Bhīṣma.
Having commanded all those gods to dwell upon the earth, he set his mind upon that which the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, born of the lineage of Vasudeva,
was about to perform; O King, I shall tell you all of that in its entirety— listen.
The majesty and the life-story of Vāsudeva, who is of great splendor,
[were told] for the benefit of gods and mortals, and indeed for the welfare of the worlds;
for when that Blessed One, O dear one, did not find delight in heaven, he became the all-pervading Lord.
Then, having assigned the various beings to their tasks on earth— bringing worldly happiness—
he then indeed urged the Maruts, the Vasus, and both the Sun and the Moon to subdue the Daityas.
"O Gandharvas and Apsarases, Rudras, Ādityas, and likewise the two Aśvins—
you who are the great lords of all beings, take birth in the world of men!
For the large-eyed one has created mobile beings from himself by means of his own self."

"Let it be born," Govinda said, even to those belonging to the animal realm. Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, all those inhabitants of heaven— the omniscient Lord of the Gods together with the gods— [responded].
The slayers of the Daityas and Dānavas, the lords of the world, were born;
then, in the lineage of the wise Vasudeva,
who was born of the race of Yayāti, the Lord Nārāyaṇa took up residence, performing deeds of merit and renown.
Having commanded [the gods] for the sake of pleasure, Hari, O dear one, having made himself manifold by himself, was born in the lineage of Yadu; indeed,
for the sake of pleasure alone, that Supreme Person protected those cows.
O Ajātaśatru,
O lord of the earth, listen as I relate how this Bhīṣma was born on earth, O bull of the Bharatas, my dear son.
The oceans trembled, and the mountains shook with joy;
the fires, though blazing, became tranquil as Janārdana was being born. Auspicious winds blew, and the dust settled into peace.
When Janārdana was being born, the celestial lights shone forth,
and the drums of the gods resounded loudly in the sky;
then Nārada, having arrived, rained down showers of flowers.
With auspicious hymns, they praised Madhusūdana; then, filled with joy at his manifestation, the great seers worshipped him. Then, having beheld those sages headed by Nārada, [he looked upon them].
The hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases danced and sang;
and the thousand-eyed Lord of Śacī approached Govinda.
Then the radiant one, honoring the great seers, addressed them.
"Having performed his duties and the rites of the gods for the welfare of the world,
the god who created the worlds returns again to his own realm by means of his splendor.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Three Heavens departed together with the sages.
Having granted permission to them all and concealing his supreme nature,
Kṛṣṇa dwelt for many years in the family of the cowherd Nanda. Then Vasudeva beheld the newborn infant, who resembled the sun.
O King, out of fear, he had hidden Hari within the family of the cowherd Nanda.
Then, on one occasion, having left that infant sleeping beneath a cart,
Yaśodā went to the Yamunā river.
Then, performing the play of a child, Kṛṣṇa threw his own hands and feet about and wept sweetly, stretching his legs upward;
then Keśava supported the cart with his big toe.
Then, having overturned it with one foot, the infant lay on his back, longing for the breast, and he cried out;
seeing the cart overturned and its jars and pots shattered, [the people were amazed].
The people were filled with the utmost wonder at that infant;
before the very eyes of the Śūrasenas, a great marvel was witnessed:
the bird had been slain by the infant of fierce splendor while he lay still.
And Pūtanā, who possessed a massive body and enormous breasts, was also slain by Vāsudeva while all the gods were looking on, O Bhārata. Then,
O great king, in the course of time, Rāma and Keśava became engaged in combat.
Both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa then became two wrestlers,
like the sun and moon in the sky swallowed by each other’s rays;
with arms like the coils of serpents, they then glided everywhere.

O King, Bhārata, with their limbs smeared with dust, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa then ran about; sometimes touching the ground with their knees as they played here and there in the forest, and drinking from streams of curd while the churning was being performed.
Then that boy Govinda was seen there by the cowherd women as he was devouring that inexhaustible butter; subsequently,
Kṛṣṇa was bound with a rope to a mortar by the cowherd women.
Then, O King, by that child, both those Arjuna trees were broken along with their roots and branches; it was like a marvel. Thereafter, both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa passed beyond childhood.
In that very place where they had lived as cowherds, the two of them became seven-year-old boys;
wearing blue and yellow garments and anointed with yellow and white unguents,
both became cowherds bearing the side-locks of youth.
Playing leaf-instruments that were pleasing to the ear, those two fair-faced ones shone as they moved through the forest like two exalted serpents;
they had ears like peacock feathers and wore crowns of young shoots.
Encircled by forest garlands, they rose up like two young *sāla* trees; adorned with lotus wreaths and wearing cords as sacred threads,
those heroes carried baskets and gourds and played upon their cowherd flutes.
Sometimes laughing with one another and playing here and there in the forest, sometimes sleeping together on beds of leaves, and sometimes seeking intervals of sleep,
the two of them— protecting the calves and beautifying the great forest— wandered on.
O King, thus did those two auspicious ones wander and sport at that time;
then, having gone to Vṛndāvana, both sons of Vasudeva [remained there],
O Bhīṣma.
O son of Kuntī, there they both roamed about, tending the cattle in Govraja.
Then, on one occasion, Govinda— possessing a beautiful form and a lovely countenance— wandered through that delightful forest without his elder brother Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Wearing side-locks of hair, glorious, dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotuses,
his chest marked with the *śrīvatsa* like the moon with its spot;
he was a youth wearing a yellow garment and a cord used as a sacred thread.
With his limbs smeared with white sandalwood paste and his hair dark and curly,
he was adorned with a silver peacock feather that trembled in the gentle breeze;
at times singing, at times playing, at times dancing, and at times laughing.
Blowing his cowherd flute most sweetly and according to his desire,
that radiant Lord, the youth, went at times to the forest for the sake of delighting the cows; thus he wandered through Gokula during the rainy season.

O bull of the Bharatas, Kṛṣṇa found great joy in those most delightful regions, amidst the rows of forest trees in the woods, as he played. Once, while wandering through that forest together with the cattle, he—
Then, O sinless one, having seen the banyan tree named Bhāṇḍīra, the great Lord Keśava then resolved to dwell in its shade along with the cowherd boys who were his equals in age.

Kṛṣṇa took his delight there during those days, just as he had formerly done in the city of heaven. While Kṛṣṇa was thus sporting, the many cowherds dwelling at Bhāṇḍīra then delighted him with various esteemed toys.
Some cowherds, their minds full of joy, sang along;
others, those forest-dwellers among the cowherds, sang of Kṛṣṇa alone.
While they were thus singing, Keśava played his instrument for them.

Amidst the sounding of leaf-instruments, flutes, and lutes made of gourds, Kṛṣṇa thus sported with the cowherd boys through various games. O son of Kuntī, even as a child, he then performed that which is for the welfare of the world.
O Bhārata, while all beings were looking on, Vāsudeva sported upon the head of the serpent in that lake within the Nīpa forest;
having thus subdued Kālīya, he did so while the whole world watched.
Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva, took his rest there. O King, at that time in the Tāla forest, the fierce Daitya Dhenuka, who had the form of a donkey, was indeed slain by Baladeva.
Then once, O son of Kuntī, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
those two of auspicious countenance, went to the forest; tending the flourishing herds of cattle, they wandered about filled with joy, beholding the woods.
Making playful sounds, singing aloud, and examining the trees, calling out the names of the calves and the cows, those two subduers of enemies,
unconquered, moved about engaged in sports well-known to the world.

Those two gods, honored by the immortals, assuming human initiation, wandered through the forest with diversions suited to their birth and qualities. Then the immensely radiant Kṛṣṇa went to the cow-pen.
Śauri, the Lord who creates all beings, partook of that very *giri-yajña* under preparation with the cowherd boys— the milk-rice (*pāyasa*)—
and seeing him, all the cowherds worshipped Kṛṣṇa alone.
Then, being honored by the cowherds, he assumed a divine form;
that mountain named Govardhana was held up for seven days by the infant Vāsudeva, the crusher of enemies, for the sake of the cows.
While playing at that time, Kṛṣṇa performed a difficult feat;
it was like a marvel to all the world, O Bhārata. Having descended to the earth, the God of gods saw Kṛṣṇa and was filled with joy.
Having addressed him as "Govinda," Purandara indeed consecrated him;
having spoken thus and embraced Govinda, Puruhūta ascended to heaven. Then [he encountered] a Daitya known as Ariṣṭa, who had the form of a bull.

O King, O Pārtha, out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures, Kṛṣṇa swiftly slew the Daitya named Keśin, who had assumed the form of a horse; likewise, he slew that horse which possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants while it was wandering in the forest.
Seizing him, Puruṣottama struck down the son of Bhoja;
he slew the Andhra wrestler Cāṇūra, that great asura, and Sunāman,
the slayer of enemies, who was placed at the head of the entire army.
O Bhārata, assuming the form of a deer, he terrified Govinda; and at the assembly, Muṣṭika was effortlessly slain by Baladeva. Furthermore, O Bhārata, Kaṃsa was then struck with fear by Kṛṣṇa.
Just as one might slay a bull among elephants, Kṛṣṇa killed Airāvata, who was eager for battle, while Kuvalayāpīḍa looked on; then,
while everyone watched, that slayer of enemies killed Kaṃsa.
Having consecrated Ugrasena, he prostrated at the feet of his parents.
Janārdana indeed performed such deeds as these,
Bhīṣma said.
Thus, even in their childhood, the two of them sported with cowherds;
thereafter, O dear one, they went again to their preceptor Sāndīpani,
devoted to service to their teacher, knowers of dharma, and practitioners of dharma.
Observing a rigorous vow, those two high-souled ones wandered through the Avanti country;
within sixty-four days and nights, they mastered the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs. Both of those delights of the Yadus also attained proficiency in writing and calculation.

They both acquired the entire and wonderful science of music (gāndharvaveda), and they mastered the training of elephants and horses in twelve days. Then those two heroes went again to their teacher, Sāndīpani.

Desiring to learn the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), those two knowers of dharma who practiced righteousness approached and bowed before a preeminent teacher of missiles and weapons. O King, having been honored by him, they traveled through the land of Avanti.
Within fifty days and nights, they both acquired the ten-limbed Dhanurveda in its entirety, well-established along with its secret doctrines;
seeing that they had accomplished their purpose, the lord of brahmins urged them to perform service for their teacher.
Then the powerful Sāndīpani requested a favor from Govinda:
"My son was carried away into this ocean by a timi fish.
Bring back my son; may prosperity be yours, for he has been devoured by the timi."
There, for his distressed preceptor, he promised to perform a difficult task—
one impossible for anyone else in the three worlds to accomplish—
O bull of the Bharatas, he who had slain the son of Sāndīpani.
That asura was struck down by those two in battle into the ocean;
then, through the grace of the one of immeasurable luster, the son of Sāndīpani,
who had remained a ghost for a long time, once again possessed a body.
Seeing that which was impossible, inconceivable, and a truly great marvel,
amazement arose among all living beings;
as did [the sight of] all sovereign powers, cattle, horses, and wealth.
Rāma and Keśava brought all of that to their preceptor.
Keśava attained supreme preeminence in combat with maces and clubs, as well as in the use of all weapons; he became renowned throughout all the worlds.

And who other than Nārāyaṇa could mount the chariot of the Lord of Śacī, which is adorned with every kind of jewel and resplendent like the sun? And his peerless charioteer is the beloved friend of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Mātali said:

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, dear one, even Kaṃsa, the son of King Bhoja, was held in check by none other than the Supreme Person; he was equal to Kārtavīrya in his knowledge of weapons, in strength, and in heroism."
From that son of the lord of the Bhojas, the enhancer of the Bhoja kṣatriyas,
all kings were terrified, just as serpents tremble before Suparṇa; for he was a warrior armed with a variegated bow, a sword, and a spotless spear.
O Bhārata, that king of the Bhojas had one hundred times a hundred thousand foot soldiers,
and eight hundred thousand brave warriors who never retreated,
all bearing banners made of gold.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, his elephants, adorned with golden and yellow girths,
numbered as many thousands; they were elephants that never retreated in battle,
resembling mountains and bearing variegated banners and flags.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the elephants of King Bhoja were always exceedingly joyful; indeed, the great force of that king’s swift, well-adorned female elephants was twice as large as that.
He indeed had sixteen thousand horses with the hue of *kiṃśuka* flowers; furthermore,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there was another great array consisting of colts,
well-equipped with excellent riders and invincible by any force.
That army of sixteen thousand, led by Kaṃsa’s brothers,
was entirely protected on all sides by Sunāman for Kaṃsa’s sake,
O Yudhiṣṭhira; and his horses were of every color.
That host, known as Miśraka, is said to consist of sixty thousand [beings].
It is like a river with the great force of the wrath of Kaṃsa, with banners as its marshy trees,
with rutting elephants as its great crocodiles, and following the dominion of Vaivasvata.
A river with a great mass of foam consisting of weapons, possessing a mighty current of swift horses,
with maces and iron clubs for its pāṭhīna fish, various armors for its moss, great whirlpools of chariots and elephants, and mud of various kinds of blood.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, who else but the singular Nārāyaṇa— the slayer of Kaṃsa— could [cross] that terrible river of great battle, whose colorful bows, arrows, and swords were its fish, whose chariots and horses were its turbulent eddies, and whose roar was the tumultuous whirlpools of combat?

Standing upon Śakra’s chariot, O Bhārata, he scattered those armies of the son of Bhoja like the wind dispersing great clouds. Having slain Kaṃsa along with his kinsmen, together with his ministers, while he was seated in the assembly hall—
Having honored Devakī— who was worthy of honor— along with her circle of friends,
and having saluted Yaśodā and Rohiṇī again and again,
Janārdana consecrated King Ugrasena.
The Lord, the younger brother of Vāsava, was honored by the leaders of the Yadus;
then Bhīṣma [beheld] the king approaching together with all the monarchs.
On the banks of the Sarasvatī, Puruṣottama defeated Jarāsaṃdha;
leaving Śūrasena-pura, Keśava, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of all the Yādavas, returned to Dvārakā.
The lotus-eyed one accepted vehicles and many jewels from the Nairṛtas according to their merit;
there, the Daityas along with the Dānavas created obstacles.
The mighty-armed one slew those great asuras who had been granted boons; there,
a Rākṣasa named Naraka—
who terrifies the hosts of gods and is known by you for his power— created an obstacle.
Stationed upon the earth in the form of a *mūrti-liṅga*, he, the destroyer of all gods and asuras,
then acted with hostility toward both humans and sages.
Then Bhauma went to Kaśeru, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ.
On the fourteenth day, he seized Rucirāṅgī in the form of an elephant;
having crushed her, he carried her off, and having abducted her, Naraka said:
Naraka.
Then the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, with his grief, fear, and affliction destroyed,
took possession of whatever various jewels exist among gods and men,
as well as all that the entire earth and the oceans contain.
"From this day forward, O Goddess, all the Nairṛtas,
along with the Daityas and Dānavas, shall bring offerings to you alone.
Thus [they shall offer] many excellent jewels and various [treasures]."
O Bhārata, at that time Bhauma carried off those jewels among women;
and Nāraka forcibly carried off the daughters of the Gandharvas,
as well as those belonging to gods and men, and the seven groups of Apsarases.
Fourteen thousand two hundred and one women,
all wearing single braids and devoted to the path of the virtuous, were gathered there;
Bhauma had their inner apartments constructed upon the Jewel Mountain.
Undaunted in spirit, he [advanced] toward the domain of Mura in the watery region;
and those ten sons of Mura, the king of Prāgjyotiṣa,
along with the foremost Nairṛtas, waited upon him while protecting [the realm].
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this very son of Mahī, who had been granted a boon at the conclusion of his ascetic penance,
once overpowered Aditi for the sake of her earrings;
yet in former times, that deed could not have been accomplished even by all the hosts of Asuras joined together.
That great Asura, whom the goddess Earth brought forth and whose capital was Prāgjyotiṣa, had previously performed a most terrible deed;
he possessed four frontier guardians who were intoxicated with the pride of war.
Having blocked the path leading to the gods, they stood surrounding [the city] together with hideous Rākṣasas who terrified the hosts of deities—
Hayaśiras, Niśumbha, and the formidable Pañcajana.
The great asura Mura, who had been granted a boon and possessed a thousand sons,
was slain by him; for that purpose, the mighty-armed Janārdana, the wielder of the discus, mace, and sword, was born among the Vṛṣṇis as Vāsudeva from Devakī.
O dear one, you know well that Dvārakā is the primary residence of this lord of men, whose splendor is renowned throughout the world;
for the city of Dvārakā is exceedingly beautiful, surpassing even the abode of Vāsava.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it truly shines forth pre-eminently upon the earth; you have seen it with your own eyes. That assembly hall, which takes refuge in the Vṛṣṇis, resembles a city of the gods;
it is renowned as the Dāśārha hall, extending for a yojana in both length and breadth.
There, all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, led by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
remained protecting this entire course of worldly affairs.
While they were all seated there, O bull of the Bharatas, on one occasion—
Divine fragrances wafted through the air and showers of flowers fell.
Then, a mass of light of great wonder, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns,
appeared for a moment in the sky and thereafter established itself upon the earth.
In the midst of that splendor, Vāsava was seen mounted upon a white elephant, surrounded by all the hosts of gods;
and Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and the king were there together with the hosts of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Suddenly leaping up, they offered their salutations to him.
Descending quickly from his elephant, he embraced Janārdana,
and likewise embraced Baladeva and King Āhuka.
Uddhava, Vasudeva, and the high-minded Vikadru; Pradyumna, Sāmba, Niśaṭha, Aniruddha, and Sātyaki;
Gada, Sāraṇa, Akrūra, Bhānu, Jhilli, and Viḍūratha.
Having embraced Kṛtavarman and Ārudeṣṇa, the leaders of the Daśārhas, and having looked upon them, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings,
then embraced the great leaders of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, just as Vāsava would.
Having accepted the worship offered by them, O dear one, the Blessed Lord Pākaśāsana,
Janārdana, at the word of Aditi and for the sake of the earrings,
spoke with great joy, "O Lord, slay Bhauma."
Bhīṣma said:
Then the mighty-armed Janārdana, being pleased, spoke to him:
"Having slain Naraka, the son of the Earth, I shall recover the two earrings."
Having spoken thus, Govinda addressed Rāma,
as well as Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Sāmba, who was peerless in strength;
having then addressed them there, the highly illustrious Vāsudeva—

Then, having mounted Garuḍa, Hṛṣīkeśa— bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the sword— departed out of a desire for the welfare of the gods. As that slayer of enemies was proceeding, the gods, together with Purandara, [followed him].
Following behind, they joyfully praised the imperishable Viṣṇu. Having slain the fierce hosts of Rākṣasas and the great Asuras of Naraka,
he beheld six thousand nooses of Mura, which were as sharp as razors.
Having severed his bonds with his weapon and slain Mura along with his progeny,
he passed through the masses of rocks and crushed Niśumbha—
he who alone, equal to a thousand, had fought all the gods.

The Lord, the son of Devakī, of immeasurable splendor and invincible, the delighter of all the Yādavas, struck down that horse-necked one of great heroism and immense strength in the midst of the Lohitagaṅgā.
In Audakā, Madhusūdana slew Virūpākṣa and the five terrible Pañcajanas, those great Asuras of Naraka.
Then [he went] to the city named Prāgjyotiṣa, which was as if blazing with splendor.
He reached the city, and there a battle took place—
a great battle between gods and asuras, O bull of the Bharatas, such as has never occurred before; a battle that would cause wonder to the world.
Then, cut down by discuses and plows, and struck by spears and swords, the Dānavas fell there upon encountering Janārdana;
eight hundred thousand Dānavas, O scorcher of foes!

Having slain [the demon], that tiger among men, the Supreme Person, went to the abyss of Pātāla; the exceedingly radiant Madhusūdana, the best of men, fought with Madhu, terrifying the hosts of gods, as if he were Naraka himself.
O Bhārata, that battle between the high-souled Naraka and Bhauma, fought for the sake of the earrings of the Lord of the Gods, became terrible. Then,
after sporting with Naraka for a moment, Madhusūdana—
The powerful one forcibly crushed his revolving wheel with his own wheel; his head, its body destroyed, fell suddenly to the earth like Vṛtra when struck by the thunderbolt.
But seeing him fallen upon the ground, she indeed gave him the two earrings;
and having given them to the mighty-armed one, she spoke these words:
"O Lord, Madhu was created by you alone, and by you alone was he slain."
Sporting as you wish, protect the subjects in that manner.
Vāsudeva [said]:
"Of the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and the high-souled ones..."
Hateful to living beings, a hater of Brahman, the lowest of men, loathed by the world, your son is an enemy of the gods and a thorn to the world;
powerful, he oppresses Aditi, who is worthy of the homage of all the worlds.
"O proud one, that Asura was then slain by me for the sake of your earrings;
O beautiful lady, you should not feel any resentment toward me for what I have done. And it is through my power that your son has attained the highest state."
"Therefore, O highly fortunate lady, depart; the burden has been laid down. Bhīṣma, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, having slain Naraka, the son of the Earth—"
Accompanied by the world-protectors, he beheld the abode of Naraka. Then, having reached the residence of the illustrious Naraka,
he saw inexhaustible wealth and various kinds of jewels.
Jewels, pearls, and corals, as well as objects fashioned from lapis lazuli;
diamonds, sun-crystals, and pure crystals;
and those made of Jāmbūnada gold and Śātakaumbha gold.
[There were] things with the brilliance of blazing fire and others with the luster of cool rays;
a beautiful, white inner chamber of golden hue;
and whatever wealth was seen in the house for that purpose—the vast riches of Naraka.
Indeed, even in the palaces of Mahendra, such a vast accumulation of wealth as that of King Kubera had never been seen before;
when Bhauma and Nisumbha were slain, Vāsava, together with his hosts, said:
Having brought these jeweled earrings to the seated Lord of the Daśārhas,
[he presented] these various precious gems, riches, golden necklaces,
magnificent girth-bands, and lances belonging to those renowned for their valor.
There were elephants of fearsome appearance with trappings of coral,
spotless banners, and various garments;
they numbered twenty thousand, and twice as many female elephants.
Eight hundred thousand excellent horses born in the land, as well as cows, unaltered sheep, and vehicles at your pleasure— O Janārdana,
O subduer of enemies, I shall deliver all this to you at the abode of the Vṛṣṇis.
There were fine woolen beds and seats,
birds of lovely appearance that warbled at will,
and various vehicles mixed with sandalwood and agallochum.
O subduer of enemies, I shall cause you to obtain that wealth which you have earned through righteousness alone in the three worlds,
including the jewels of the gods and Gandharvas, and those born of the Daityas and Asuras, as well as the abode of the Vṛṣṇis.
Whatever jewels exist here in the abode of Naraka,
Vāsava, having quickly placed all of them upon Garuḍa,
arrived at Maṇiparvata together with the Lord of the Daśārhas.
There, auspicious winds blew and wondrous, brilliant lights shone;
as the hosts of gods looked on, they were filled with amazement—
along with the thirty deities, the sages, and likewise the moon and sun in the sky.
By its radiance, it became as if indistinguishable from that mountain. Permitted by Rāma and by Vāsava, the mighty-armed Keśava, feeling great joy, entered the mountain of jewels.
There, Madhusūdana beheld gates and sanctuaries with arched portals and banners, possessing the hue of lapis lazuli;
that mountain of jewels shone like a mass of variegated clouds.
Adorned with palaces featuring banners variegated with gold, and with spacious mansions possessing staircases of jewels,
Madhusūdana beheld women of exquisite complexion dwelling therein.
Then the beloved daughters of the chiefs of the Gandharvas and Asuras surrounded that mighty-armed, unconquered one as he stood in a place equal to heaven, those women wearing single braids.

All were clad in saffron robes, and all had their senses fully restrained; no sorrow born of the heat of ascetic vows afflicted any among them. And they wore spotless garments, even those made of silk.
Having approached the lion of the Yadus, all those lotus-eyed women joined their palms in reverence before him; and they all spoke thus to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Supreme Person, this has been related to us by Nārada."
Govinda will come for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods;
having slain the asuras Naraka, Nisumbha,
and Mura, as well as Bhauma with his retinue and the dānava Hayagrīva.
"Likewise, he shall obtain the wealth of Pañcajana, which is inexhaustible; in a very short time, he will become your husband. Having spoken thus, the wise celestial sage Nārada then departed.
"Constantly thinking of you, we have performed severe austerities;
when time has passed, O mighty-armed one, when shall we behold Mādhava?"—
having formed this resolve in their hearts, O best of men.
"We constantly practice austerities while being guarded by the Dānavas;
therefore, perform for us the favor of marriage through the Gāndharva rite.
Then, for the sake of our desire for what is dear, the Blessed Maruta himself—
As Nārada had said, that will soon come to pass:
the gods and Gandharvas beheld those supreme women with the bull-eyed one placed at their head, like a bull leading a herd of young cows.
Beholding his moon-like face, their senses filled with joy and greatly delighted, they spoke these words to the mighty-armed one:
"Truly, Vāyu spoke this to us here in the past!"
Even the great seer Nārada is grateful for all beings;
so too is the divine Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the conch, discus, mace, and sword.
Having slain Naraka, the son of the Earth, he will indeed become your husband.
By good fortune, the word of that great-souled chief of sages, Nārada, must surely come true from the very moment we have seen it;
for behold, we see your beloved face, which resembles the moon!
"Today we have achieved our life's purpose by the sight of this great-souled one.
To all those women who were filled with passion, that best of the Yadus said:
"O large-eyed ones, speak as you wish; all of that shall be yours."
Then, having caused all those jewels to be carried by his servants,
and having caused the women— the daughters of gods, sages, and kings— to be carried as well,
Kṛṣṇa placed that supreme mountain of gems upon the arm of Vainateya.
The Blessed One, the son of Devakī, quickly climbed [the mountain], which was filled with flocks of birds, elephants, wild beasts, and serpents;
frequented by troops of monkeys; and possessed of grassy meadows and rocky surfaces.
Frequented by *nyaṅku* deer, boars, and *ruru* deer,
possessing great peaks with precipices and teeming with various peacocks—
upon that mountain, Śauri, the younger brother of Mahendra, placed Garuḍa.
While all beings looked on, the one of great strength uprooted the mountain of jewels,
along with Upendra, Baladeva, and the mighty Vāsava,
as well as that incomparable mass of gems and the mountain itself.
Carrying the divine, auspicious, and nectar-like umbrella of Varuṇa, which resembled the moon, Garuḍa—
resembling the peak of a great mountain through the forceful flapping of his own wings—
raised a roar in all directions as he flew.
Shattering the mountain peaks and uprooting the trees, he swept away the great clouds as he ascended the path of Vaiśvānara,
eclipsing the splendor of the planets, constellations, stars, and the host of the Seven Sages.
Having transcended the mass of radiance and traversed the path of the sun and moon,
Madhusūdana reached the central peak of Meru and beheld all the abodes of the gods, O bull of the Bharatas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O scorcher of foes, having passed beyond the radiant realms of all the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the Aśvins,
that subduer of enemies reached the most holy station, the world of the gods.
Having reached the abode of Śakra and descended from it, Janārdana paid homage at the feet of Diti, being honored by all the deities as well as by the Prajāpatis,
led by Brahmā and Dakṣa.
Then the Lord gave the two divine earrings of Aditi;
and Keśava, together with Rāma, accepted all those most precious jewels, and so did Aditi, [who accepted] the younger brother of Vāsava.
Free from her feverish distress, Śacī, the queen of Mahendra, then paid homage to the descendant of Daśārha and to Rāma; and taking Satyabhāmā, the queen of Kṛṣṇa, she presented her to Aditi.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to Kṛṣṇa,
Aditi,
the mother of the gods, being free from all anxiety, granted a boon to Satyabhāmā, who was intent upon serving her.
"O beautiful one, you shall not grow old as long as Kṛṣṇa remains among men.
Bhīṣma said:
"O lovely-faced one, you shall be endowed with the qualities of all fragrances."
Having stayed there together with Śacī, the slender-waisted Satyabhāmā,
being permitted by Śacī as well, departed for Kṛṣṇa’s abode;
he was honored by the thirty gods and attended by hosts of great sages.

Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of enemies, departed from the world of the gods for Dvārakā. Having traversed a long distance, the mighty-armed Acyuta reached the gate of the city of Vardhamāna, that most excellent of cities.
Beholding that city of Dvārakā, filled with every prosperity, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari,
being delighted, prepared to enter it.
He beheld many delightful groves of trees grown in gardens throughout Dvāravatī, endowed with various flowers and fruits;
[he saw them] with houses resembling the sun and moon, like the peaks of Mount Meru.

Dvārakā was constructed by Viśvakarman with beautiful and skillful craftsmanship; it was adorned with moats as radiant as the Gaṅgā and Sindhu rivers, filled with clusters of lotuses and frequented by swans.
With its radiant white wall, glowing like the sun,
situated at the summit of the sky, it was like the heavens themselves enshrouded by clouds;
and with groves resembling the Nandana and Miśraka gardens, [it shone].
It shines like the divine Caitraratha forest, the grove of the Grandfather (Brahmā); and with trees resembling those of Vaibhrāja, overflowing with blossoms of every season,
Dvārakā shines like the sky studded with stars in the firmament.

The Raivataka mountain shines with its beautiful ridges and great courtyards; it is the ornament of Dvārakā in the delightful eastern direction. To the south, the five-colored Latāveṣṭa mountain resplendent.
Resembling Indra’s banner,
the silver mountain Sukakṣa, with its great forest of variegated flowers, rests upon the western quarter; likewise, the Veṇumān mountain shines in the northern direction.
O bull among the Pāṇḍavas, that white mountain resembling Mount Mandara shines toward Raivataka; likewise, the forest of Pāñcajanya, possessing the hue of a variegated woolen blanket,
as well as the Sarvartuka forest, shine there.
Encircled on all sides by a winding vine, the great abode of Meruprabha shines forth; likewise, the Tālavana forest, the Puṣpaka, the Puṇḍarīki,
and the great Citrapuṣpa forest surround this Sukakṣa.
The Śatapatra forest, as well as Karavīra and Kusumbha,
shine forth; and likewise Caitraratha and the great forest of Nandana, along with Ramaṇa,
Bhāvana, and Veṇumān on every side.
O Bhārata, in the eastern direction shines the beautiful Puṣkariṇī lake,
measuring one hundred *dhanus* in circumference, belonging to the high-souled Keśava;
it is joined with fifty gates leading to the great city of Dvāravatī.
He entered the beautiful Dvārakā, which illuminated everything on all sides—
immeasurable, of great height, overflowing with vast depths,
endowed with the finest palaces, and adorned with white mansions.
He beheld the city of Dvārakā, equipped with sharp *śataghnī* engines and networks of mechanical devices, as well as great iron wheels;
and upon its rampart were eight thousand chariots adorned with small bells.
With banners raised high, it was like a city of the gods;
he beheld the city of Dvārakā, eight *yojanas* in width, twelve *yojanas* in length, and twice that in its surrounding settlement, standing firm and immovable.
The great enclosure of the eight-fold path, with its sixteen great squares,
was thus laid out by Uśanas himself;
within the arrays, there were seven paths and great thoroughfares.
There, that city was directly fashioned by Viśvakarman;
it was endowed with golden staircases of jewels, bringing joy to the people,
and was auspicious with excellent palaces resounding with the great noise of singing.
In that most excellent city of the illustrious Daśārhas,
the blessed Indra, the subduer of Pāka, rejoiced upon seeing the mansions with their uplifted banners fluttering like waves.
With golden peaks shining like the summits of Mount Meru,
with ridges as white as plaster and encased in gold,
and with mountain-caves and peaks adorned with jewels and embellished with every kind of gem.
[The city was] with palaces possessing half-moons and turrets,
with balconies, crowded with mechanical houses, and like mountains containing precious minerals; likewise, it had floors made of jewels and gold, polished with lime.

With gates made of Jāmbūnada gold and bolts fashioned of lapis lazuli, with furnishings of great value that were pleasant to the touch in every season, they resembled wonderful mountains with lovely peaks, slopes, and caves.
With five-colored golds, possessing a radiance like a shower of flowers,
equal to the roar of rain-clouds, appearing like clouds of various hues,
and resembling the peaks of Mount Mahendra, they were fashioned by Viśvakarman.
With those great elephants of the Daśārhas, which were as radiant as the moon and sun and seemed to be painting the sky,
that palace-lake shone like Bhogavatī with its terrible lakes teeming with fierce serpents.

It was adorned with houses like clouds, featuring black banners as their vehicles, red with the weapons of the Daśārhas, possessing Vṛṣṇis as their great peacocks, crowded with thousands of women as their offspring, and having Vāsudeva as their Indra and Parjanya.
Dvārakā appeared exceedingly beautiful, like the sky shrouded by clouds;
they beheld the manifest abode of the Lord of Gods, constructed by Viśvakarman, extending for four yojanas.
And it was just as vast and immeasurable, filled with great wealth, endowed with excellent palaces, and joined by mountain-like mansions—
this which the mighty-armed Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned at the bidding of Vāsava.
A palace of Padmanābha, one *yojana* long on all sides,
rising like a peak of Mount Meru and adorned with ten thousand pieces of gold—
this was the preeminent dwelling provided for Rukmiṇī by that high-souled one.
Satyabhāmā, moreover, always dwells in a white palace with variegated jeweled staircases,
which is known as "The Cool," and is adorned with banners having the luster of the stainless sun.
With its great banners visible on all four sides, it was surrounded by forest regions;
and that preeminent palace there, adorned for Jāmbavatī,
seemed to illuminate the three worlds with its splendor and variegated ornaments.
But he who had the appearance of a white color, situated between those two,
Viśvakarman fashioned him so that he resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa,
with his summit blazing like Jāmbūnada gold and appearing like a flaming fire.

Standing like the ocean, he was renowned as Meru. On that mountain lived the daughter of the king of Gāndhāra, a woman of noble lineage known by the name Sukeśī, who had been bestowed there by Keśava.

Known as Padmakūṭa, it is lotus-colored and possesses great radiance; O mighty-armed one, it is the highly honored abode of Suprabhā. Furthermore, that which is called the excellent palace Sūryaprabha—
O best of the Kurus, that palace, possessing the hue of excellent lapis lazuli and a green luster, was bestowed upon Lakṣmaṇā by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
it was established right where the networks of bridges were located.
O Bhārata, he whom all beings know as Hari—
Vāsudeva, who is worshipped by hosts of gods and ṛṣis— dwelt there with his queen Mitravindā as the ornament of all dwellings.
Furthermore, that most excellent palace constructed here by all the artisans,
which was exceedingly beautiful, stands here as if laughing;
for it belongs to Suvāsas, who was honored by all the artisans on account of Sudattā.
O dear one, the palace of Vāsudeva, the consort of the Great-Souled One, is renowned as Ketumān; it is called Viraja, free from passion, belonging to that high-souled being,
and it serves as the assembly hall of the Great-Souled Keśava.
But as for that foremost palace there, which Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned for the Lord—
measuring one yojana in length and breadth and composed entirely of jewels—
all its pillars were made of gold and adorned with banners.
In the abode of Vāsudeva, banners that inspire the path were raised; likewise,
networks of bells were placed in every dwelling by that lion of the Yadus, who brought the great Vaijayantī mountain.
That peak of Haṃsakūṭa, where the great lake Indradyumna is located— sixty *tāla* trees in height and half a *yojana* in width,
resounding with the great cries of *kiṃnaras*— that too belongs to the one of immeasurable splendor.
While all beings were looking on,
that supreme peak of Meru, which traverses the path of the sun,
made of divine Jāmbūnada gold and renowned throughout the three worlds, [was seen].
Kṛṣṇa also uprooted that [palace] and brought it to his own residence;
it was formerly radiant there, adorned with all kinds of medicinal herbs,
which Śauri, the scorcher of foes, had brought from the abode of Indra.
There Keśava established that Pārijāta tree,
which was attended by hundreds of attendants with ointment in their hands and adorned with golden celestial chariots;
thus were the great trees of Brahmasthala created by Vāsudeva.
Possessing waters crowded with lotuses, fragrant gems, and blue water-lilies; with sands of jewels and pearls, there are lotus-pools and lakes,
whose supreme banks are adorned by great trees.
Sāla, tāla, and aśvakarṇa trees, as well as rohiṇas with a hundred branches, bhallātakas, kapitthas, candravṛkṣas, and campakas,
along with date palms and ketakās, were planted on all sides.
The trees that grow in the Himalayas as well as those born in the Nandana grove were brought by that lion of the Yadus and planted there—
trees with foliage appearing red, yellow, and crimson, and bearing white blossoms.
In those various forest groves, they were filled with the fruits of all seasons;
there were thousand-petaled lotuses and *mandāra* trees by the thousands,
as well as *aśoka*, *karṇikāra*, *tilaka*, and *nāgamallikā* trees.
Kurava trees, nāgapuṣpas, campakas, and tṛṇagulmaka shrubs;
saptaparṇas, kadambas, nīpas, and likewise kuravakas; ketakyas and kesaras, as well as hintālas, talas, and taṭakas.
Tāla trees, priyaṅgu, bakula, piṇḍika, and bījapūraka; grapes, āmalaka, dates, mṛdvīkā, and jambuka; likewise mangoes, jackfruit trees, aṅkola, sesame, and tinduka.
Likucas, āmrātakas, and likewise kṣīrikās and kaṇṭakīs;
nālikeras and iṅgudas, as well as forests of utkrośakas;
and forests of plantains, along with jasmine, mallikā, and pāṭala trees.
And there were ponds and thousands of wells filled with white and blue lotuses;
and everywhere there were *bhallātaka*, *kapittha*, *tinduka*, *bandhujīvaka*, *priyaṅgu*, *aśoka*, *kāśmarya*, and *prācīnāmalaka* trees.
With *priyaṅgu*, *badarī*, and barley; with *spandana* and *candana*; with *śamī*, *bilva*, and *palāśa*; with *pālāśa*, *vaṭa*, and *pippala*;
and with *udumbara*, *bilva*, *pālāśa*, and *pāribhadraka*.
With *indravṛkṣa*, *arjuna*, and *aśvattha* trees,
with *ciribilvaka* and *saubhañjanaka* trees, with *bhallāṭa* and those called "horse-like" (*aśvasāhvaya*), as well as with *sarja* trees, betel vines, cloves, and *kramuka* nuts.
And there, on all sides, various types of bamboo were planted;
whatever trees grew in the Nandana grove and those in the Caitraratha forest,
they were all planted on every side by the Lord of the Yadus.
The great ponds were crowded together, filled with red sand;
in that excellent palace, there were rivers and lakes of clear water,
abounding in blooming lotuses and various kinds of trees.
In that excellent palace, there were rivers with sands of jeweled pebbles;
flocks of intoxicated peacocks and cuckoos filled with passion were present;
and all the mountains of the world became endowed with supreme excellence.
Right there were herds of elephants, and likewise cattle and buffaloes;
and there dwellings were established for boars, deer, and birds. That mountain, fashioned by Viśvakarman, served as the rampart for his residence.
Clearly one hundred *kiṣkus* in height and possessing a radiance equal to the moon,
he [encircled] those great mountains, rivers, and lakes,
as well as the palaces, forests, and groves.
Thus did those three bulls among men— Upendra, Baladeva, and the highly illustrious Vāsava— survey Dvārakā.
Then Śauri, standing upon the head of Garuḍa,
joyfully blew that white conch shell, which caused the hair of his enemies to stand on end;
by the sound of that conch, the ocean was violently agitated.
The entire sky resounded, and that was a wondrous sight at that time. Upon hearing the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch and seeing Garuḍa, the Kukuras and Andhakas were freed from their grief.

Seeing Kṛṣṇa, who held a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, was seated upon the head of Suparṇa, and possessed a splendor like that of the rising sun, they rejoiced. Then there arose the sounding of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums.
And a lion’s roar arose from all the city-dwellers. Then all those Daśārhas and all the Kukuras and Andhakas,
filled with joy, gathered together upon beholding Madhusūdana.
Placing Vāsudeva at their head, accompanied by the sounds of flutes and conchs,
King Ugrasena went to the residence of Vāsudeva; meanwhile,
Devakī moved about within her own quarters to rejoice.
"Rohiṇī and all the women of Āhuka, as well as those who were slain, have been restored; all enemies of the Brahmins are destroyed, and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis are victorious.
Thus addressed by the women, Madhusūdana remained unhurt.

Then Śauri, on his vehicle Suparṇa, returned to his own abode; there the Lord fashioned Mount Maṇi according to the intended design. Then Madhusūdana placed wealth and jewels within the assembly hall.
Having set him down, the lotus-eyed one, longing for a sight of his father,
first touched the water before Sāndīpinī; then the highly illustrious,
large-armed, and broad-copper-eyed youth, being filled with joy, paid his respects to him.
With his eyes filled with tears and his heart overcome with joy,
the younger brother of Vāsava, together with Rāma, paid homage to his father;
and Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, was smelled on the head by the two of them.
Having approached the Sātvatas in order of seniority, Adhokṣaja, the joy of the Yadus,
called out the names of all the Daśārhas.
Then he [bestowed] all their riches and all that consisted of jewels.
Then Bhīṣma, the joy of the Yadus, distributed those [treasures] among all of them,
together with the great ministers of Keśava, headed by Mahendra.
It shone with those tigers among the Vṛṣṇis, like a mountain cave with lions;
then the lord of the gods, the highly illustrious Mahendra, seated upon his throne, addressed them all with auspicious words that gladdened their hearts.
I shall relate in brief that which was done by Vāsudeva— the purpose for which the high-souled Kṛṣṇa took birth among humans— concerning the leaders of the Kukuras and Andhakas, and that King Āhuka.
Having slain hundreds of thousands of Dānavas,
this lotus-eyed subduer of enemies entered the cavernous depths of Pātāla—
that which had not been attained even by Prahlāda, Bali, and Śambara of old.
This wealth has been brought here for you by the wise Śauri, who overcame Mura along with his noose and blew the Pāñcajanya conch;
having bypassed the masses of rocks, he slew Nisumbha together with his hosts.
The powerful Dānava Hayagrīva was slain by the valiant one;
Bhauma was crushed in battle, and the two earrings were recovered once more.
Thus Keśava attained great glory among the gods in heaven.

Free from sorrow, fear, and affliction, relying on the strength of Kṛṣṇa’s arms, the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis performed various sacrifices with Soma offerings; and once more, upon the slaying of Bāṇa, Śauri was honored by the Ādityas together with the Vasus.
"The Sādhyas shall come to Madhusūdana through my mouth.
Having spoken thus, and having taken leave of all the Kukuras and Andhakas,
Vāsava embraced both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, as well as Vasudeva.
The slayer of Vṛtra, having honored Pradyumna, Sāmba, Niśaṭha, Aniruddha, and Sāraṇa, as well as Babhru, Jhilli, Gada, Bhānu, and Cārudeṣṇa,
addressed Sātyaki once more, along with Sāraṇa and Akrūra.
He embraced Āhuka, the king of the Vṛṣṇis and lord of the Kukuras,
as well as Kṛtavarman the Bhoja and others among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis; then,
having taken leave of them, Vāsava, the foremost of gods, [departed] from the younger brother of Vāsava.
Then, while all beings looked on, the Lord, the husband of Śacī, mounted the elephant Airāvata, who resembled a white mountain,
as he traversed the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavens.
Repeatedly filling the air with the resonant sounds from its mouth-ornaments,
it possessed great golden side-pieces for its harness, golden horns,
was spread over with a beautiful rug, and was adorned with every kind of jewel.
Adorned with hundreds of banners featuring many jewels, and with a constant flow of rut-fluid dripping like a cloud pouring rain,
he was mounted upon the great elephant of the quarter, the Mahāmātra, who wore a golden garland.
Standing upon the peak of Mount Mandara, he shone like the scorching sun;
then, seizing his formidable thunderbolt, that supreme goad,
the Lord of Śacī went forth with the powerful Pāvaka.
The hosts of Maruts followed behind him with female elephants, herds of male elephants, and celestial chariots; likewise, Kubera, Varuṇa, and the Planets followed with joy.
Having ascended the path of the wind, he reached the path of Vaiśvānara (fire).
Having reached the path of the sun, the god vanished right there. Then,
those women who belonged to all the Daśārhas and to Āhuka—
Yaśodā, the world-renowned queen of Nandagopa;
the highly fortunate Revatī; the devoted Rukmiṇī;
both Satyā and Jāmbavatī; Gāndhārī; and Śiṃśumā as well.
Viśokā, Lakṣmaṇā, the virtuous Sumitrā, Ketumāt,
and other queens of Vāsudeva, accompanied by Śrī, then departed,
those excellent women desiring to behold the majesty of Keśava.
Filled with joy, they went to the assembly hall to behold Acyuta. Devakī and Rohiṇī, honored by all the goddesses,
beheld the god Kṛṣṇa seated together with the wielder of the plow.
Having first approached Rohiṇī and offered her salutations,
the two gods Rāma and Keśava greeted Devakī;
and Devakī [greeted] the seven goddesses and their mothers according to their seniority.
