The Blessed One, the younger brother of Vāsava, together with Rāma, paid his respects to him. Then, having obtained an excellent seat, Devakī, preceded by the wives of the Vṛṣṇis,
took both Rāma and Keśava onto her lap.
Then she shone with those two bull-eyed sons,
just as Devakī, the mother of the gods, shines with Mitra and Varuṇa;
and immediately thereafter, Yaśodā’s daughter indeed arrived.
O Bhārata, she who was exceedingly radiant with her form and splendor,
whom they call the maiden Ekānaṅgā, capable of assuming any form at will— it was for her sake that the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu) slew Kaṃsa along with his hosts.
Then the Blessed Rāma, having approached that beautiful woman,
smelled her head and took hold of her with his left hand;
and having embraced her there like a dear and equal friend, he [consoled her].
With the tip of his right hand, Mādhava took hold of her;
they beheld that sister of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in the midst of the assembly,
reclining upon a golden lotus like the goddess Padmā between two supreme elephants.
Then, with a great rain of unbroken grains, parched grain, flowers, and clarified butter,
the Vṛṣṇis— along with their children, elders, kinsmen, families, and relatives— joyfully showered Saṃkarṣaṇa and Janārdana.
The Vṛṣṇis, filled with joy, sat down near Madhusūdana;
being honored by them, the mighty-armed Madhusūdana, that tiger among men who increases the delight of the citizens, entered his own residence.
Together with Queen Rukmiṇī, he rejoiced happily in happiness; and thereafter, O Bhārata, the best of the Yadus enjoyed himself at all times with Satyabhāmā, Jāmbavatī, and all his other wives.
And Hṛṣīkeśa went to the residence of Rukmiṇī.
O dear one, O mighty-armed one, this is the victory of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
and it is for this purpose that they say the high-souled one was born among human beings.
Then,
O great king, the highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa, having found happiness with his own wives day and night in Dvārakā, rejoiced greatly.
For the sake of his grandson, he then performed that which was for the benefit of the gods—
something difficult to overcome even by all the deities led by Indra, O bull of the Bharatas. The powerful Bāṇa, the eldest son of Bali, became king.
O best of the Bharatas, that powerful one possessed a thousand arms;
then, O King, with a mind fixed on truth,
he performed intense asceticism and propitiated Rudra for many years.
Many boons were granted to him by the high-souled Śaṅkara;
having obtained from him those boons difficult for even the asuras on earth to attain, Bāṇa ruled his kingdom in Śoṇitapura, peerless in strength.
And all the gods were terrified by that arrow, O Pāṇḍava. Having conquered all the deities, including Indra, Bāṇa ruled for many years over a vast kingdom like Kubera, O Bhārata.
For that purpose, the wise Uśanas Kāvya made an effort through his supernatural powers;
then, O King, there was Bāṇa’s daughter named Uṣā,
who was peerless in beauty in the world, like the daughter of Menakā.
Then, O Kaunteya, by means of a stratagem, the highly effulgent Aniruddha,
the son of Pradyumna, having obtained Uṣā, rejoiced there in secret.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the immensely powerful Bāṇa was there at that time.

Having discovered that secret dwelling, he took Pradyumni along with his daughter and forcibly compelled him to dwell in a prison cell. Then, though tender and worthy of happiness, he experienced great suffering.
O King, tormented by Bāṇa, Aniruddha fainted. At that very moment, O son of Kuntī, Nārada, the bull among sages, arrived at Dvārakā; having seen Kṛṣṇa, he spoke these words.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who increase the fame of the Yadus! Your grandson Aniruddha, being oppressed by Bāṇa of immeasurable splendor,
has fallen into distress and remains constantly confined within the maiden’s chamber.
Having spoken thus, the celestial sage indeed went to the city of Bāṇa. O King, having heard the words of Nārada, Janārdana then summoned Baladeva and the highly effulgent Pradyumna.
Janārdana ascended Garuḍa together with those two;
then, having mounted Suparṇa, those three bulls among men,
possessed of great heroism, went in anger toward the city of Bāṇa.
Then, O Great King, having reached that city, they beheld it:
encircled by copper walls, adorned with silver gates,
crowded with golden palaces, and variegated with pearls and gems.

Abounding with gardens and groves, adorned with dance and song, filled with arched gateways and birds, and beautified by lotus ponds— that city, resembling heaven itself, was crowded with happy and well-nourished people.
Seeing that golden city filled with joy, they were struck with the utmost wonder. The deities Maheśvara, Guha, Bhadrakālī, and Pāvaka were always stationed at the gates of that city of Bāṇa.

O King, these deities indeed always protected that city. Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the highly effulgent Kṛṣṇa, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, became greatly enraged and forcibly overcame the gatekeepers in battle.
He reached the northern gate, which was protected by Śaṅkara; there stood the great-splendored Maheśvara, wielder of the trident,
having taken up his Pināka bow along with arrows out of a desire for Bāṇa’s welfare.
Knowing that Kṛṣṇa had arrived like Death with his mouth wide open,
Vāsudeva and Maheśvara then engaged in battle.
That combat was terrible, inconceivable, and hair-raising.
Desiring victory over one another, those two gods hacked at each other and discharged divine weapons in their wrath. Then Kṛṣṇa fought for a moment with the wielder of the trident.
Having conquered that Mahādeva in battle, Janārdana then defeated the others guarding the gates and entered that supreme city. Having entered, Janārdana then approached Bāṇa there.
Enraged by that arrow, O Pāṇḍava, he waged a great battle with him;
and Bāṇa too, O bull of the Bharatas,
being highly incensed in that combat, brought down all his sharp weapons upon Keśava.
Again, raising a thousand weapons with all his arms,
Bāṇa, filled with rage, released them toward Kṛṣṇa on the field of battle.
Then, O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa cut down all those weapons.
O King, after fighting with Bāṇa for a moment,
Adhokṣaja then raised his divine discus,
the supreme among weapons, and severed the thousand arms of Bāṇa, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
Then, O Great King, Bāṇa, severely afflicted by Kṛṣṇa,
fell down quickly with his arm severed, like a tree stripped of its branches (viśākha). Having struck down that son of Bali, Kṛṣṇa, filled with haste, [acted].
Then Govinda liberated the son of Pradyumna, who had been cast into Rājagṛha; having freed the son of Pradyumna along with his wife,
he seized all of Bāṇa’s innumerable jewels.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, the enhancer of the Yadus' fame, forcibly seized the cattle-wealth and all the possessions from Bāṇa’s abode;
thereafter, Madhusūdana, having taken all the jewels, departed.
He quickly placed his entire wealth upon Garuḍa; then,
with haste, O son of Kuntī, he [placed] the mighty Baladeva,
the highly heroic Pradyumna, and the immensely radiant Aniruddha.
O King, having placed Uṣā and Sundarī along with the groups of servants and maidservants,
as well as all these various jewels upon [the chariot],
the mighty one of great splendor, clad in yellow garments, was filled with joy.
With his limbs adorned with divine ornaments and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword,
he mounted Garuḍa like the sun ascending the eastern mountain;
then, having mounted Suparṇa, he set out toward Dvārakā.
Having entered his own city accompanied by the Yādavas, Kṛṣṇa then rejoiced,
O King, like Vāsava dwelling in heaven; so too did Bhīṣma rejoice at that time.
The nooses of Mura have been destroyed; Niśumbha and Naraka have been slain. The path leading toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa has been made secure once more.
O bull of the Bharatas, the protectors of the earth have been terrified by Śauri.
O bull of the Bharatas, by the twanging of his bow and the sound of the *pāñcajanya* conch, and by his armies resembling clouds, Keśava terrified Rukmin, who was surrounded by the Southerners.
Then, with a chariot possessing the roar of rain-clouds and the splendor of the sun,
this wielder of the discus and mace carried off his queen Bhojyā.
Jārūthya, Āhṛti, Krātha, and Śiśupāla were all conquered.
Vakra, along with Śaibya, and the Kṣatriya Śatadhanvan; Indradyumna was slain in anger, as was the Yavana Kaśerumān;
and Sālva, the lord of Saubha, was killed together with Krathadhanvan.
And with his discus, Puruṣottama, the lotus-eyed one, split a thousand mountains and fought against Dyumatsena; they moved across the peak of Mount Mahendra in the blink of an eye.
O best of the Bharatas, he seized both Varuṇa and Abhitashcaru in the Irāvatī; both of these were equal in strength to Agni and Sūrya. Gopati and Tālaketu were slain by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
In the throwing of the axle and on the path of the wheel-rims and the swans,
both those Surāṣṭras were struck down by Kṛṣṇa;
and Vārāṇasī was burnt, O dear one, by the high-souled Keśava.
The bull among the Kāśīs, along with his followers and his kingdom, has been slain. Having reached the city of Prāgjyotiṣa, the best of cities, which was filled with many Asuras,
and having encountered the peaks of red minerals, Varuṇa was conquered by Kṛṣṇa.
Invincible and unassailable, the world-protector of great splendor,
Indradvīpa was guarded by Mahendra himself, by Maghavan; yet,
O Pārtha, the Pārijāta tree was carried away by the more powerful Keśava.
Janārdana slew Pāṇḍya, Pauṇḍra, Mātsya, and Kaliṅga— all together— and Mādhava slew the King of Aṅga. And he,
having slain one hundred and one of the foremost Kṣatriyas with his chariot...

The bull among the Yādavas, Kṛṣṇa, carried away Gāndhārī as his queen. Then, O best of the Bharatas, the powerful Madhusūdana defeated the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow for the sake of sport in the presence of Kuntī.

O bull of the Bharatas, seeking to do what was pleasing to Babhru, this wielder of the discus and mace defeated Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Bhīmasena, and Suyodhana together during his circuitous journey.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, Madhusūdana conquered the entire earth— abounding in horses, chariots, and elephants— which had been brought under the power of Veṇudāri and used as his wife. He uprooted her from Veṇudāri’s control.
O Bhārata, having obtained through asceticism heroism, strength, and vital energy,
Bāṇa terrified all the lords of the gods along with their hosts,
who repeatedly sought to frighten him with thunderbolts, lightning, maces, and nooses.
He could not have met death in battle even at the hands of the gods led by Indra;
yet he was overcome and slain by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
after his thousand arms had been severed by the great-souled Govinda.
This mighty-armed Janārdana, the slayer of Madhu and possessor of great fame, slew Pīṭha, Kaṃsa, Paiṭhaka, Atiloman, Jambha, Airāvata, and Virūpa.
O best of the Bharatas, he slew Śambara, the crusher of enemies. O bull of the Bharatas, having gone to Bhogavatī and defeated Vāsuki,
this lotus-eyed one liberated the son of Rohiṇī.
Thus, while still a child, Janārdana, the lotus-eyed one, performed many deeds with Saṃkarṣaṇa as his companion; in this manner,
he acted in every respect against both the Asuras and the Suras.
Kṛṣṇa, the lord and master of all the worlds, who brings both fear and fearlessness—
thus this mighty-armed teacher of all the wicked,
having accomplished immeasurable benefit for the gods, shall return to his own abode.
This one of great fame, having brought the delightful Bhogavatī, beloved of the sages,
and Dvārakā under his own control, shall cause them to enter the ocean—
that beautiful city, rich in merit, adorned with shrines and sacrificial posts.

He will enter Dvārakā, the abode of Varuṇa, together with its forests— that beautiful city, resembling the residence of the Sun, which was built by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and abandoned by Vāsudeva; the ocean shall submerge it.
Among gods, asuras, and humans, there has never been, nor will there ever be anywhere,
any king who could occupy that throne except for Madhusūdana.
Yet the children of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, those great chariot-warriors, were shining brilliantly.
Those whose life-breaths have departed shall attain the back of the firmament, having reached that which is favored by him.
Thus, having ordained this ritual for the Daśārhas according to the prescribed rule,
Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself shall become Soma and the Sun.
Immeasurable and beyond injunction, going wherever he pleases and self-controlled,
the Blessed One rejoices with living beings as a child does with toys;
this Lord did not undergo conception, nor did he dwell in a womb.
By the power of his own splendor, Kṛṣṇa provides the path for all beings;
just as a bubble, having arisen, dissolves back into that very same source,
so too do all moving and unmoving creatures always [return] into Nārāyaṇa.
"O Bhārata, the mighty-armed Keśava cannot be measured;
for beyond this supreme form, nothing else exists that possesses such universal form.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the highly illustrious Bhīṣma then fell silent.
Thereupon, Sahadeva uttered these meaningful words as a reply concerning Keśava,
the slayer of Keśin, whose prowess is immeasurable:
"O kings, he among you who cannot endure Kṛṣṇa being worshipped by me— having recognized Kṛṣṇa as the Lord of all worlds, the Supreme Person—
let him quickly go forth for battle here against me in combat, if he is capable."
"I have placed this foot upon the heads of all who are strong.
When I have spoken thus, let him give a proper reply;
for he alone shall be slain by me, without a doubt.
"Let those kings who are wise acknowledge this teacher, father, and guru— who is worthy of honor, has been honored, and deserves worship. Then,
not one among those intelligent and virtuous men spoke.
When his station was thus revealed in the midst of proud and powerful kings, a rain of flowers fell upon Sahadeva’s head;
and invisible voices also cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!"

Nārada, who speaks of what is to be and what has been, the dispeller of all doubts and knower of all worlds, brandished his black antelope skin and spoke these words most clearly in the midst of all living beings: 02,036.007a He who speaks of the future and the past, Nārada, the resolver of all doubts and knower of all worlds, 02,036.007c brandished his black antelope skin and spoke these words most clearly in the midst of all living beings.
"Those men who shall not worship Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals...
Vaiśampāyana said:
"They should be known as dead while yet alive; they are never to be spoken to."
There, all the hosts led by Sunītha, having been summoned, arrived;
they were seen to be filled with rage and their faces were pale. They [discussed] the consecration of Yudhiṣṭhira and the honoring of Vāsudeva.

"It must not be so; such is the task," they all said at that time. From their extraction of the matter and their firm resolve, all those kings, overcome with anger, spoke there out of despondency and their own determination.
The bodies of those who were being restrained by their friends shone like roaring lions that have been drawn away from their prey;
they beheld that boundless flood of troops, an inexhaustible ocean of kings.
Then Kṛṣṇa perceived that Sahadeva was making a solemn vow for battle;
having honored those worthy of honor, especially the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas,
Sahadeva, the god among men, completed that ritual act.
When Kṛṣṇa had been thus honored, Sunītha, the subduer of enemies, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to the lords of men:
"I stand here as your commander-in-chief; what do you intend to do now?"

"Let us stand together in battle, having girded ourselves against the assembled Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas. Having thus incited all those kings, that bull among the Cedis then consulted with the monarchs regarding the obstruction of the sacrifice.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having beheld that ocean of kings resembling the [actual] ocean—
terrible like the sea agitated and struck by the winds of universal destruction— *0365_01*
Then Yudhiṣṭhira,

the slayer of foes possessed of great splendor, spoke out of anger to Bhīṣma— the eldest grandfather of the Kurus and the best among the wise— just as Puruhūta, the destroyer of enemies, spoke to Bṛhaspati.
"This great ocean of kings has been stirred up by anger;
O Grandfather, tell me what should be done in this matter,
so that there may be no obstacle to the sacrifice and welfare may prevail for the subjects."
"O Grandfather, tell me today all that regarding everything everywhere," said Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma who knows the law. When he had spoken thus,
Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, then spoke these words.
"Do not fear, O tiger among the Kurus; a dog cannot slay a lion.
An auspicious and well-trodden path has been chosen here by me long ago. For while the lion is fast asleep, dogs may well gather there."
All these lords of the earth stand together here,
positioned before this sleeping lion of the Vṛṣṇis;
O dear one, they bark in great anger like dogs in the presence of a lion.
For as long as he has not awakened, O Acyuta, he remains like a sleeping lion;
yet this was already known to you when you desired to offer praise.
Therefore, that bull among the Cedis, a lion among men, makes these others appear like lions.
O best of kings, the small-minded Śiśupāla desires to lead all monarchs, O dear one, by every means to the abode of Yama;
surely Adhokṣaja wishes to reclaim this [kingdom] once again.
O Bhārata, that splendor which resided in Śiśupāla remains [within him],
O best of the wise; and his intellect has become deranged, O son of Kuntī— blessings be upon you— as it has for all the kings of the earth, including the King of Cedi.
For whenever this tiger among men desires to seize whatever he wishes,
his opponent's intellect fails, just as it did for the Lord of Cedi;
so it is with Mādhava regarding all four classes of beings in the three worlds.

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma is indeed the source of all things and their destruction as well. Having heard these words of his, O Bhārata, the king, the lord of Cedi, then addressed Bhīṣma with harsh-syllabled speech.
Śiśupāla said:
"Why do you, being an old man and a disgrace to your lineage, not feel shame while terrifying all the kings with so many many threats?"
"It is fitting that you, who abide by the third nature (the forest-dwelling stage), should speak words devoid of righteousness; for you are the best of all the Kurus.
You are like a boat tied to another boat, or as one blind man follows another."

"O Bhīṣma, the Kauravas of whom you are the leader have indeed become such [as you describe]. By your recounting his deeds— especially those beginning with the slaying of Pūtanā— our minds have been further shaken."

"O Bhīṣma, how is it that your tongue does not split into a hundred pieces, you who are so arrogant and foolish, yet desire to praise Keśava? O Bhīṣma, it is for such a person that insults ought to be directed by even the most childish of men."
Being advanced in wisdom, you wish to praise this cowherd;
yet if a bird was killed by him in his childhood, what is so wonderful in that?
As for those two—the horse and the bull—O Bhīṣma, they were not experts in combat.
O Bhīṣma, if this tree, devoid of consciousness,
was felled by him with his foot, what wonderful feat was performed there?
If those two trees, as large as Arka trees, were felled by him, [what is so marvelous?]

And since the Naga was cast down by him, what cause for wonder is there? O Bhīṣma, if he held up Mount Govardhana— which is no larger than an anthill— for seven days, then in my opinion, that is not considered a marvel.
"Much food was eaten by him while playing on the mountain peak"—
hearing this, O Bhīṣma, they were struck with great wonder;
for wise and virtuous men of good character never speak thus.
O knower of dharma, that this powerful Kaṃsa was slain by him whose food he had consumed is not at all a great wonder;
for he was a slayer of goats, a slayer of birds, a slayer of calves and serpents, and likewise a slayer of donkeys.
O Bhīṣma, you who are like fire and a magician, how is it that you, being worthy, do not receive the highest honor? Surely you have not heard this from the virtuous as they speak,
O knower of unrighteousness, lowest of the Kuru clan, for I shall address these words to you.
One should not let weapons fall upon women, cows, or Brahmins;
nor upon one whose food one eats, nor upon one who has come for refuge. Thus do the virtuous, the noble, and the righteous always instruct.

"O Bhīṣma, all that is seen in this world appears false when compared to you. O best of the Kurus, while praising Keśava— who is superior to me in age, in wisdom, and in stature— you speak as if you were ignorant of him."
O Bhīṣma, being a killer of cows and a killer of women, how does he deserve praise?
If he is honored merely because of your word,
O Bhīṣma, then such is the nature of this man.
If Janārdana, this lord of the world who is the best among the wise, should honor [this] merely because of your words,
thinking "all this is so," then all that is certainly false.
A verse does not instruct the singer, even if he sings many;
all beings follow their own nature, just like the bhūliṅga bird.
Surely this nature of yours is base; there is no doubt about this.
Because they are the sons of a river, their minds are known to be fickle and not steady;
therefore, even among the Pāṇḍavas, this [conduct] is considered most wicked—
those for whom Kṛṣṇa is the most worthy of worship and you are the guide.
"You speak of dharma while being ignorant of it, having fallen away from the path of the virtuous. For who that is the best among the wise, knowing himself to be righteous,
would act as you have done, O Bhīṣma, while claiming to regard dharma?"
If you truly understand the Dharma, and if your mind is indeed wise, O knower of the Dharma, then why was this maiden— who desires another—
taken by hand according to the ritual of marriage by the wise King Śālva, who fancies himself so intelligent?
"Blessings to you! How was she who is named Ambā carried off by you?
O Bhīṣma, your brother Vicitravīrya, who followed the conduct of the virtuous, did not desire that maiden whom you had abducted."
While you, who pride yourself on being wise, looked on as another fathered children upon his two wives, offspring have been born to you upon a path practiced by the virtuous;
for there is no merit in you, Bhīṣma, this celibacy is in vain.
Whether you maintain this out of delusion or out of cowardice, there is no doubt about it;
yet, O knower of dharma, I do not see any increase in your merit anywhere,
for you have not served the elders who speak thus of dharma.
Sacrifices performed, gifts given, the Veda studied, and sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees— all this is not worth a sixteenth part of the merit of having offspring,
O Bhīṣma, even that which has been accomplished through many vows and fasts.
All that shall certainly become fruitless for one who has no offspring;
and being childless and aged due to teaching false dharma,
you too will now meet your death at the hands of your kinsmen, just like the swan.

"O Bhīṣma, other men who were knowers of wisdom have indeed spoken thus in the past; I shall relate that to you properly as you listen. Long ago, it is said, there was a certain aged swan living on the shore of the ocean."
Though his speech was righteous, he acted otherwise; he indeed instructed the birds, saying, "Practice righteousness, not unrighteousness"—such were his words.
You have entered into a terrible illusion; therefore, wake up, wake up!

"Non-violence is the supreme dharma"— this was indeed the speech of that Bhīṣma, who constantly spoke of dharma, which the birds heard. Having heard those words of the swan, all the birds were filled with joy.
Then the birds, having surrounded the swan on all sides, said to him:
"Please explain to us briefly that dharma which pertains to birds."
"O best of the twice-born, tell us: who indeed is the one who speaks the supreme dharma?
The Swan replied:
"O flocks of birds, non-violence toward living beings is indeed dharma; violence is not dharma."
"This alone is to be understood as dharma and adharma in brief.
Having heard these words of the aged swan, those birds remained closely attentive.
The birds—
And those birds, longing for righteousness, spoke as if smiling:
"O bird, he who always practices righteousness in this world is the wisest of birds;
he is a *haṃsa*."
Tell us here in truth,
O righteous-souled one, where that man goes who constantly practices dharma in this world, remaining established in virtuous conduct—
[O] birds!
O best of the twice-born, having understood both dharma and adharma, that swan indeed travels through all the worlds in this world eternally; such is the certainty,
O birds.
Why do you not go to that heavenly world which is so difficult to attain? O young birds, you do not understand the subtlety of Dharma—
that Dharma which one who possesses a virtuous mind constantly practices in this world.
And at the end of his life, having cast off his own body, he goes to heaven.
And I too, O twice-born ones, having cast off this body in due time—
Śiśupāla.

"I shall go to the heavenly world; this indeed is the course of dharma. Thus did that swan discourse extensively on dharma for the birds, O Bhīṣma; those birds constantly heard nothing but dharma from him.
Then, O Bhīṣma, we have heard that other egg-born creatures dwelling in the waters of the ocean brought food for him for the sake of dharma;
they deposited their eggs everywhere in his very vicinity.
O Bhīṣma, as those birds were sporting in the waters of the ocean, they rejoiced;
yet that evildoer, remaining vigilant in his own task, devoured the eggs of them all while they were heedless. That swan was ever watchful in his own duty.
Then, as those eggs were being destroyed, another egg-born being of great wisdom became apprehensive; he once beheld that [being] and thought,
"Could this be his deed?"
Then, when all the swans had departed to wander about, he remained there, having concealed his own self; then,
when all the swans had departed, he wandered about at that time.
Standing there, he had covered himself; at one point, he indeed beheld him.
Then, having seen the offense of the swan, that bird—afflicted by supreme sorrow on behalf of all birds—related it to them.

Then, O best of the Kurus, having seen him with their own eyes as he had gathered those birds together, they slaughtered that swan of deceitful conduct. "In the same way as that swan, you too shall now meet your death at the hands of your kinsmen."
The aged swan was killed there by that evil-minded one of false conduct;
O Bhīṣma, these lords of the earth, being enraged, might likewise slay you, who share the nature of a swan, just as those birds slew that bird.
O Bhīṣma, descendant of Bharata, I shall relate to you in full that verse which people who know the ancient lore sing regarding this:
"When the inner self has been established..."
O bird,
you roar falsely; your impure act of eating eggs exceeds your words.
Śiśupāla said:
"That king Jarāsaṃdha of great strength was highly esteemed by me,
for he did not wish to engage in battle with him, considering him a mere slave in combat."
Regarding that which was done by Keśava at the time of Jarāsaṃdha’s slaughter,
as well as by Bhīmasena and Arjuna— who considers that act to be righteous?
For it was performed by one who professes the Veda, yet entered through a non-gate by means of a stratagem.
The power of the wise Jarāsaṃdha was witnessed by Kṛṣṇa, who,
though recognizing himself as one devoted to Brahman,
did not wish to offer water for the feet first to that evil-minded man.
"Let it be eaten," Jarāsaṃdha said to Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Dhanañjaya, O Kauravya; yet Kṛṣṇa performed a transformation. "If this one were the creator of the world, as you, fool, imagine him to be..."
Why does he not correctly understand his own self as a Brahmin?
But this is a source of wonder to me: that these Pāṇḍavas, having been led astray by you from the path of the virtuous, consider that to be right.
"Or rather, O Bhārata, this is no wonder for those of whom you are the one who,
though aged and possessing the nature of a woman, is the instructor in all matters.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those many harsh words, consisting of harsh syllables,
the powerful Bhīmasena, the best among the strong, became enraged. His eyes, which were naturally long and wide, resembled lotuses.
Furthermore, his two eyes became blood-red, inflamed with rage;
and all the kings beheld a three-pronged frown upon his forehead,
like the triple-pathed Gaṅgā resting upon the three peaks of Mount Triśṛṅga.
As he gnashed his teeth in rage, they beheld his face like that of Time itself at the end of an eon, desiring to consume all beings;
but as the high-minded one sprang up with speed, [Bhīma] seized him.
Just as the Lord restrains Mahāsena, so did the mighty-armed Bhīṣma restrain that Bhīma;
O Bhārata, as he was being checked by his elder with various words, Bhīma’s anger was pacified.
For that subduer of enemies did not transgress the word of Bhīṣma,
just as the great ocean, though swollen at the end of the rainy season, does not overstep its shore.
But Śiśupāla, O lord of men, became enraged at Bhīmasena.
The hero, established in his own manliness, did not waver then;
though the subduer of foes leaped at him again and again with great force,
he paid it no mind, just as a lion disregards a small animal.
And laughing, the powerful king of Cedi spoke these words, seeing Bhīmasena, who possessed terrible prowess, filled with extreme rage:
"Release him, Bhīṣma! Let the lords of men behold him."
"Consumed by the fire of my prowess, like a moth by a flame.
Then, having heard those words of the Lord of Cedi,
Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus and foremost among the wise, spoke this to Bhīmasena.
"This is not the intellect of the Lord of Cedi, that he should thus challenge Acyuta. O mighty-armed Bhīmasena, his resolve is fixed on the slaughter of Kṛṣṇa.
Bhīṣma said:
Born in the royal family of Cedi, this three-eyed, four-armed youth let out a roar and a cry resembling the braying of a donkey;
because of that, his parents and their kinsmen were struck with terror.
Seeing that transformation, the two of them resolved to abandon him.
Then, an incorporeal voice spoke to the king, who was with his wife, ministers, and domestic priest, and whose heart was bewildered by anxiety:
"O King, this glorious and mighty son has been born to you;
therefore, you must not fear us. Protect the infant with an undisturbed mind. Neither you nor Death himself have arrived as his end."

"Death shall slay him with a weapon, O lord of men; he has already been born. Having heard these words uttered by the invisible being, the mother, tormented by affection for her son, spoke these words:
I bow with palms joined to him by whom this speech was uttered concerning my very own son; let him speak further words,
whether he be the Blessed Lord or another, according to the truth.
Having said, "He is of great strength, he is a great being," [the voice] spoke again further:
"I wish to hear what shall be the death of this son. Then that hidden being spoke these words once more.
When he is taken onto one's lap, both his arms, which are exceedingly long,
will fall to the surface of the earth like two five-headed serpents;
and this is the third eye of the child, situated upon his forehead.
"Upon seeing whomsoever he sinks down, that person shall become his death.

Having heard this and what was thus proclaimed, all the kings on earth approached, desiring to see him. He who has three eyes and four arms was likewise described. Upon hearing this, all the rulers of the earth went forth, eager for a sight of him.
Having honored those kings who had arrived according to their rank,
that lord of the earth then placed his son upon the lap of each king one by one;
thus he did for thousands of kings, individually and in due order.
A child mounted upon his lap did not perceive that illustration. Having heard this very thing in Dvāravatī, the two of great strength,
Saṃkarṣaṇa and Janārdana, then arrived at the city of Cedi.
Then the two Yādava heroes went to see their paternal aunt, that Yādava woman;
having seen her and comforted their father’s sister, those long-armed ones saluted King Dāmaghoṣa in due order.
Having saluted those kings according to custom and according to their seniority, and having inquired after their welfare and health, Rāma and Keśava sat down;
then the two heroes were honored with even greater affection.
The Goddess herself placed her son upon the lap of Dāmodara. As soon as he was set upon his lap, both of his extra arms fell away,
and that eye born from his forehead sank back into its place.
Seeing that, distressed and terrified, she entreated Kṛṣṇa for a boon:
"O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, grant a boon to me who am afflicted by fear;
for you are the consolation of the distressed and the granter of fearlessness to those who are afraid."
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the Yadus, spoke; then,
having seen that two-eyed one and comforted him, the mighty-armed one,
who grants fearlessness to his devotees, listened to the words of his paternal aunt.
"Do not fear," Janārdana said to his father's sister.
"What boon shall I grant you, or what may I do for you, O paternal aunt? Whether it be possible or impossible, I shall carry out your word."
Having been addressed thus, she then spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the joy of the Yadus:
"O you of great strength, may you forgive the offenses of Śiśupāla;
O tiger among the Yadus, O Lord, know that this is my boon requested for my sake."
Thus addressed, the lotus-eyed one of great strength replied.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O paternal aunt, I shall indeed forgive a hundred offenses of his."
"Do not set your mind on grief for your sons who deserve death;
O Vṛkodara, this is how it happened in the past regarding this child.
Knowing his own death at the hands of Kṛṣṇa, the bringer of joy to the Yadus,"
Bhīṣma said:
"O hero, it is thus that this sinful King Śiśupāla, of very dull intellect and arrogant because of the boon granted by Govinda, challenges you."
Bhīṣma said:
"This is not the king of Cedi’s own idea by which he challenges Acyuta;
surely this is the settled resolve of Kṛṣṇa himself, the sustainer of the world."
"For what king on earth today deserves to insult me as Bhīmasena does, his soul possessed by fate, this defiler of his lineage?
For he is surely a portion of the splendor of Hari, O mighty-armed one."
O tiger among the Kurus, Hari, the one of vast renown, desired once again to seize that very [bow] by which this evil-minded king of Cedi roars excessively like a tiger, disregarding all of us.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the King of Cedi could not endure those words of Bhīṣma;
filled with rage, he spoke this further reply to Bhīṣma.
Śiśupāla said:
"O Bhīṣma, let this power of Keśava—
which you always stand up for like a bard to praise— belong to our enemies!"
O Bhīṣma, your mind always delights in praising others;
if you would praise kings, then set aside this Janārdana and praise Darada Bāhlīka, this best of monarchs.

O Bhīṣma, praise this Karṇa, who at his birth caused the earth to tremble, who is equal in strength to the thousand-eyed Indra, the sovereign of the realms of Vaṅga and Aṅga, and the drawer of the great bow.
O mighty-armed one, he who possesses these two divine earrings born with him and fashioned by the gods, as well as this armor with a luster like the rising sun— by means of these,
Jarāsandha, who is exceedingly difficult to conquer, has become the equal of Vāsava.
He was defeated in hand-to-hand combat and brought to the dissolution of his body;
praise Bhīṣma, whose arms and thighs were like those of a bull, and the two heroes renowned on earth—
Droṇa and the son of Droṇa, father and son, both great chariot-warriors.
"O Bhīṣma, praise these two most excellent of the twice-born, who are worthy of praise, for they should be constantly lauded.
O Bhīṣma, it is my conviction that if either one of them were enraged, he could reduce this entire earth, with all its mobile and immobile beings, to ashes."

"O Bhīṣma, I do not see any lord of men who is equal to Droṇa in battle, nor likewise to Aśvatthāman; yet you do not wish to praise these two. Why then do you not praise Śalya and the other lords of the earth?"
"O Bhīṣma, if your mind is always inclined toward praise,
what indeed can I do, O King, since you surely have not heard what was said of old by the elders who speak of dharma?"

Self-reproach and self-praise, as well as the disparagement of others and the praise of others— this fourfold conduct is not practiced by the noble ones. Since this is something that ought to be censured, you constantly praise me out of delusion and devotion.

O Bhīṣma, no one approves of that [view] regarding Keśava. How can you, out of mere personal whim, place the entire world under a wicked-souled man of the Bhoja clan who acts as a mere protector of a herd?
"Or perhaps, O Bhārata, this devotion of yours does not return to its natural state,
just as I previously described in the case of the bird called Bhūliṅgaśakuni.
This bird named Bhūliṅgaśakuni lives on the far side of the Himavat mountains."
O Bhīṣma, her words are always heard to be contemptible in meaning; she indeed constantly cries out, "Do not act rashly! while she herself acts with extreme rashness, unaware of it.
O Bhīṣma, that small-minded creature indeed takes away from the mouth of a devouring lion whatever morsel of meat has become stuck between his teeth;
for she lives, O Bhīṣma, at the will of that lion, without a doubt.
In the same way, O Bhīṣma, you who are ignorant of dharma always utter such words, even while the lords of the earth desire that you live;
for there is no one else equal to you in performing deeds loathed by the world.
02,041.024 Vaiśampāyana said: 02,041.024a Then, O King, having heard those bitter words from the lord of Cedi, Bhīṣma spoke these words while the king of Cedi listened.
"Indeed, I live only because these rulers of the earth desire it;
for I do not count these lords of men as anything more than blades of grass.
When Bhīṣma had spoken thus, the kings then became enraged.
Some there rejoiced, while others censured Bhīṣma;
having heard those words of Bhīṣma, some great archers said, "This Bhīṣma is sinful, arrogant, and old; he does not deserve forgiveness."
"Let the evil-minded Bhīṣma be slain like an animal by all the kings acting together in fury; or let him be burned in a straw fire!
Having heard these words of theirs, the grandfather of the Kurus then [spoke].
The wise Bhīṣma spoke to those very lords of the earth:
"I do not perceive an end to all that has been said here;
however, O lords of the earth, listen to everything that I shall say."
"Either my being slaughtered like an animal, or my being burned by a fire of straw—
having heard this in the assembly of kings,
the righteous-souled Bhīṣma then spoke these words to those kṣatriyas."
"Let this entire footprint placed upon your heads by me be honored;
here stands Govinda, the Infallible (Acyuta), worshipped by us. Whose mind hastens toward death, let him [approach] Mādhava."
"Let him challenge Kṛṣṇa today in battle, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the mace, so that,
being struck down, he may enter the very body of this god.
For who indeed could be his equal upon this earth bounded by the oceans?"
Passing over Duryodhana, the lord of kings and mighty-armed one,
and King Jayadratha, who was skilled in weapons and possessed firm valor,
[he passed] Druma, the preceptor of the Kimpuruṣas, whose prowess is celebrated throughout the world.
Passing over the one of great heroism, why do you praise Keśava? Passing over the aged preceptor of the Bharatas as well as Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat,
why do you praise Keśava, despite his lack of great heroism?
Passing over Rukmin, the best among archers and a supreme man of great heroism, why do you praise Keśava? And [why do you praise] the highly heroic Bhīṣmaka and King Dantavakra?
Bhagadatta, whose banner bears the sacrificial post, Jayatsena of Magadha, both Virāṭa and Drupada, Śakuni, Bṛhadbala,
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and the excellent Śveta, the Pāṇḍya king.
Having bypassed the highly fortunate Śaṅkha, the proud Vṛṣasena,
the valiant Ekalavya, and the great car-warrior Kāliṅga—
all of whom possess great heroism— why do you praise Keśava?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, upon hearing Bhīṣma’s words, the king of Cedi, possessed of great prowess and desiring to fight with Vāsudeva, spoke to Vāsudeva.
"I summon you, Janārdana; come to battle with me, so that today I may slay you along with all the Pāṇḍavas. For with you, O Kṛṣṇa, the Pāṇḍavas must be slain by me in every way."

"O Kṛṣṇa, it is my opinion that those who have bypassed the kings and honored you— who are not a king— those foolish ones who, out of childishness, worship you as a slave and a non-king, treating one unworthy as if he were worthy, deserve to be slain."
Having spoken thus, that tiger among kings stood roaring in indignation,
while the powerful Śiśupāla,
enraged for battle, was equipped with armor in the presence of all those rulers of the earth.
Sunītha set out swiftly with the intent to destroy the sacrifice of the son of Pṛthā.
Then Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, Hari, holding his discus and mace in hand,
mounted his chariot equipped with a banner and well-adorned by Dāruka.
With Bhīṣma as his guide, he stood ready for battle;
at that time, Kṛṣṇa, stationed upon a single prepared chariot, approached all those kings who had been provoked to anger by that man of sinful nature.
Then all the kings beheld Acyuta, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose banner bore the emblem of Garuḍa, appearing like the rising sun;
and having seen Kṛṣṇa approaching, as if scorching with his splendor.
Seated upon a divine flower-chariot like another Puṣpaketu,
the mighty-armed destroyer of great asuras addressed those who, being powerless, had behaved toward Keśava according to their respective merits.
Then, O King, that hero of the Vṛṣṇis, the slayer of enemy heroes, spoke consolingly:
"Depart with your forces, all of you, having been comforted by my command. Let not this wicked man defile all these kings."
When this had been said, Kṛṣṇa then spoke these words, gentle in their tone,
to all the kings and in the presence of the Pāṇḍavas:
"O kings, this son of Sātvatī is our most extreme enemy."

That cruel-souled man was not well-disposed toward the Sātvatas who had done him no harm. Knowing that we had gone to the city of Prāgjyotiṣa, that perpetrator of cruelty seized the wife of Babhru while the Yādavas were looking on.
At that time, he began to strike him, yet it did not break; then,
for his sake, the king’s existence was [directed toward] slaughter,
and thus the kings were restrained.
Having taken her solely because of the fault of over-extension,
he previously gave her to Babhru while you all were looking on;
this occurred long ago on Mount Gomanta after the Māgadha had been slain.
O lords of men, it is said that this jackal did not indeed tread upon this [ground] before;
therefore, during the journey to Kuṇḍina, he committed many unpleasant acts against me,
all of which I shall not be able to enumerate.
By the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit, all this destruction of my enemies has occurred;
in this very conflict, millions of kings have been slain by me.
Today, I shall forgive them out of compassion.

O kings, just as he abducted the wife of a wicked man, so too, O lords of men, this [Kṛṣṇa]— though he was my sister’s son— burned Dvārakā; yet I shall do something even greater to please my father’s sister.
While the Bhoja princes were sporting on Mount Raivataka,
he killed and captured them all and formerly returned to his own city.
He [also seized] the sacrificial horse released for the Aśvamedha, which was surrounded by guards.

That man of evil intent stole from my father his horse for the purpose of obstructing his sacrifice; furthermore, out of delusion, he abducted the wife of the illustrious Babhru while she was on her way to the Sauvīras, even though she was unwilling and had already departed from here.
This cruel-doer, disguised by illusion, abducted Bhadrā, the ascetic daughter of King Viśāla of Vaiśālī, for the sake of Karūṣa—
she who was chosen as his wife by my father.
Having formed an alliance with Karūṣa out of a desire to seize [the city],
this man of sinful intent approached, having entered in haste, intending to plunder the wives of the Vṛṣṇis and slay the Kukuras and Andhakas.
Relying upon Jarāsaṃdha, he has done many things displeasing to me;
O lords of men, I am not able to enumerate them all.
Thus, this sinful man has acted limitlessly toward the Vṛṣṇis.
"From the very beginning, this most upright man has acted thus for us;
we must forgive a hundred offenses deserving of death. I am bound by terrible oaths made in the presence of his mother."
Thus, I have endured a hundred such [insults] from us, which bring about my destruction;
however, at this time of my death, there are two whom I must by no means forgive:
the one who obstructs the sacrifice and the enemy of the Pāṇḍavas, whom I shall slay.
"Such is the state of my mind; how indeed may I transcend it?
For the sake of my father’s sister, I am enduring this very great suffering.
Fortunately, however, this is taking place today in the presence of all the kings."
"You all see today this great transgression committed against me; but listen now to those deeds which were done behind my back.
However, I shall not be able to forgive this particular transgression of his today."
One should predict a disturbance in the kingdom from the untimely appearance of flowers and fruit.
When a tree— whether being honored, already honored, or even unhonored—
is broken by the wind, split, or even bent down, [it portends such a calamity].
One should know that there is danger from both fire and wind, or else even the most excellent [of men] perishes;
all the quarters blaze, and disturbances among kings arise. When a tree splits while being felled, it also emits a sound.

The entire kingdom falls along with him; one should not bring down that tree. If some forest-dweller, provoked to anger, should cut it down, the cutter, the breaker, and the master shall quickly perish.
The falling of deities, the collapsing of pavilions,
the trembling of mountains, and the instances where images dance, roar, and laugh— these are the signs of defeat.
If stones open and close like eyes, one should predict a disturbance in the kingdom;
if they exude oily substances born of water,
or if anything else undergoes such a transformation, that is a sign of impending danger.
Either the high ministers die, or the king along with his retinue;
or there may be disease in the city, and disturbances in the kingdom and the country;
or [these signs appear] in the abodes of the deities, or in the palaces of the kings.
When honey is found in a storehouse or an armory,
one should indicate that every location where it is being struck by a stronger force will be subject to an impending danger from an external enemy.
Furthermore, wherever a tree exudes red blood from its roots,
or likewise an elephant from the tips of its tusks, or a bull from its horns—
there will be the ruin of the kingdom from the tree, and the downfall of the king from the elephant.
If it is indicated that a bull will perish, there will be the destruction of cows and Brahmins.
Wherever the king's umbrella falls to the surface of the earth, O King,
the monarch together with his kingdom will very quickly perish.
If a deformity is seen in temples, or where there is a king's palace, or in the dwellings of elephants,
there will be suffering for that region, whether for the king or for the people of the realm.
One should predict a terrible fear of drought and extreme famine resulting from the arrogance of one who deserves death throughout the entire circle of kings;
for this fool, who is about to die, there was a longing for Rukmiṇī.

"And that fool did not obtain it, just as a Śūdra does not obtain the hearing of the Vedas. Having heard this and other such words from Vāsudeva regarding the censure of Śiśupāla, all those lords of men then gathered together.
Seeing the King of Cedi on the seat of his chariot, bow in hand and fixing arrows with fury,
they reproached him upon hearing the words of Vāsudeva;
utterly agitated, they abandoned the King of Cedi at the head of the army.

But seeing all those lords of the earth— along with their horses, infantry, chariots, and elephants— fleeing in all directions, shattered by the Vṛṣṇi hero, terrified by his vast prowess, and struck down by the splendor of Kṛṣṇa;
O King, Śiśupāla, his eyes copper-red with rage like a moth toward a flame, advanced alone on his chariot against Keśava. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira,
the best among the wise, seeing the King of Cedi prepared for battle, spoke to Nārada.

In the atmosphere and upon the earth, there is nothing whatsoever unknown to you. Whatever terrestrial and celestial omens arise here for the destruction of kings, as well as various kinds of portents— none escape your knowledge.
"O great sage, I wish to hear this in its entirety from you," said the wise Brahmin to the intelligent King of the Kurus. Thus spoke the wise one.
To him who questioned him, the highly illustrious Nārada, with undistracted mind, related everything:
his prowess, his path, his encounter, and his exaltation.
O best of the Kurus, there is ascending and gliding against one another,
the crossing of reins, physical exertion, and the suppression of vital functions; likewise,
there is appearing and disappearing, as well as the sighting of those who are invisible.
One skilled in the planets should examine all of this: the waning and waxing, the decrease, the position in the zodiacal signs, and the strength and weakness of the planets;
for the terrestrial planets first come into motion, and after them, the celestial ones.
And when portents created by the gods arise in this world,
and when the shadow of all living beings does not turn back even after the sun has set, that is a sign of impending defeat.
Where there is no shadow, yet a pure shadow is perceived as if it were a reflection,

and where there are sacred trees (*caityaka-vṛkṛkṣa*), one should know that there is great danger. Furthermore, when the sacred trees have withered leaves and sprouts, or their leaves have become dry, [one should know that there is great danger].
Where coral trees are withered, one should indicate the absence [of the deity] there;
but where shrines are seen with glossy leaves and sprouts,
and where [the deities] are seen striving, there is existence— of this there is no doubt.
A flower might be born from a flower, or fruit might depend upon a fruit; likewise,
a king or one of royal rank may be reborn for the sake of death at any time— during the rainy season, autumn, winter, or spring.
One should predict upheaval in the kingdom from flowers and fruit produced out of season;
the flow of rivers at an improper time indicates great danger.
Whether being honored or even unhonored, a lord of the forest [should be treated with respect].
When it is shattered by the wind, split, or even bent,
one should know that both fire and wind are at fault, or else the most excellent [king] perishes therein;
all the quarters blaze and disturbances arise for the king.
When a tree, being cut down, cries out even after it has been felled,
and the entire kingdom wails with it, one should not fell that tree; rather,
if someone should cut down such a lord of the forest in anger, [he incurs great sin].
The one who cuts, the one who breaks, and the lord himself will surely perish quickly.
The falling of deities, the collapsing of pavilions,
and the trembling of mountains— these are the signs of defeat.
If a rainbow is seen at night, from that also great fear arises;
O bull of the Bharatas, the terror belongs only to the one who sees it, not to others.
Having seen a rainbow at night, one should abandon that kingdom.
Where deities dance, roar, and laugh;
where they open and close their eyes—one should predict a disturbance in the kingdom.
Where rocks exude oily substances and moisture born of water; [one should predict a disturbance in the kingdom].
Or any other such portentous anomaly is a sign of impending danger;
perhaps a high minister dies along with the king and his retinue,
or there may be an epidemic in the city, and turmoil in the kingdom and the realm.
When honey is found in the dwelling of deities, or in the palace of kings, or in a storehouse or an armory,
one should burn that entire place when it is being attacked by a more powerful force.
One should indicate that there will be an external danger in that place; likewise, if a tree there exudes red blood,
or if an elephant does so from the tips of its tusks, or a bull from the tips of its horns.
From a tree, one should predict the ruin of the kingdom; from an elephant, the downfall of the king;
from a bull, the destruction of cattle and Brahmins. One should likewise indicate that for whom the royal parasol falls to the surface of the earth, [the same fate awaits].
That king, together with his kingdom, will swiftly perish if something deformed is seen in temples, in the royal palace, or again in the dwellings of the *nāgas*.

There will be suffering for that region, whether for the king or the countryside; one should predict a terrible fear of drought and famine. But if there is a fracture of an arm, there will be danger from the gods and the planets.
One should know that when a weapon is broken, it portends the destruction of the commander-in-chief.
When a consecrated image of a deity does not find a place within [the city],
the king shall abandon that city within six months.
Where the earth splits open, where it roars and sinks down,
there the king dies and that kingdom perishes.
[One should avoid] those born from the tracks of the enī-deer, or snakes, or *ḍuṇḍubha* lizards, or *dīpyaka* insects.
Where a frog swallows [the king], there the king perishes. Where food is accumulated that is either undivided or uncooked, it is not enjoyed;
rather, people waste away or die from that food.
And at a well where the waters swell, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
they flow forth among stationary objects and then emerge from them again—
whether footless, three-footed, two-headed, or four-armed.
Where women give birth [to such creatures], one should predict defeat there.
If a female elephant, a buffalo, a cow, a donkey, a camel,
or a sow gives birth to such [beings], one should know that defeat is imminent there.
Goats, sheep, women, cows, horses, and other species as well—
when these are born deformed, there is defeat in that place;
where a river flows upstream with turbid water.
Nārada said:
"The quarters of the sky do not shine; that is a sign of defeat.
These, O Bhārata, as well as other such omens—"

From Keśava alone are born all things terrestrial and aerial; O Bhārata, the moon, the sun, the planets, and the stars likewise arise from Janārdana; so too do wind, fire, water, and earth originate from him.
Whatever region he wishes to cause to decline or to prosper,
in that very place he produces various omens;
O dear one, this destruction of the Lord of Cedi has now arrived.
Govinda informs [us] by his own means; of this there is no doubt.
This earth has trembled, and inauspicious winds are blowing.
O Lord of the People, Rāhu has also fallen upon the Moon out of season.
Meteors fall accompanied by thunderclaps, and a profound darkness arises.
Vaiśampāyana said:
This Hari yawns for the destruction of the King of Cedi.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Nārada fell silent.
As that battle between those two lions among men was about to commence,
the lords of the earth beheld many terrible portents.
There, O Bhārata, as they were being watched from all directions,
inauspicious cries of jackals were heard at that time, O King;
and the entire earth, with its trees, cities, and mountains, resounded.
At midday, on an inauspicious day, Svarbhānu swallowed the sun; and from the sky,
O scorcher of the foe, a sharp-beaked vulture fell from the top of the Cedi king’s banner, which was adorned with every kind of gem.
Wild and domestic beasts and birds alike, filled with joy,
let out a terrible cry as that battle drew near.
Such were the dreadful omens, both terrestrial and celestial, that appeared.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the wielder of the Śārṅga bow became enraged, portents were seen;
then the King, the lord of Cedi, drew his great bow with a loud twang.
About to advance, he spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa, the slayer of Madhu:
"You alone are my enemy; therefore, O Mādhava, having slain you today, I shall thereafter rule the earth bounded by the oceans."
That duel which I have long desired has now arrived before me. Oh, by good fortune, after such a long time, O Vāsudeva,
I shall today slay you along with Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍavas!
Having spoken thus, the King of Cedi pierced that bull among the Yadus in battle with sharp-pointed, keen-edged arrows; those arrows,
fletched with heron feathers, were released from the bow of the Cedi king.
Then they entered Kṛṣṇa like serpents entering a mountain; yet,
whether the King of Cedi was taking up his arrows or even discharging them,
none of them could perceive any opening or movement in him, as if he were the wind in the sky.
Then the great cloud that was the King of Cedi rained down a mass of arrows upon Dhṛṣīkeśa, like a rain-cloud showering a mountain.
Thereupon, Acyuta, the slayer of enemies, took up his Śārṅga bow along with an arrow.
The mighty-armed slayer of enemy heroes addressed Sunītha:
"O King of Cedi, this sharp and great arrow of mine is capable of piercing you with its force,
like a massive thunderbolt striking a mountain."
When Govinda had spoken thus, the Lord of Cedi then again released many sharp arrows toward Kṛṣṇa. Then Kṛṣṇa, afflicted by those arrows, drew his radiant Śārṅga bow.
Then he released sharpened arrows by the hundreds and thousands;
but the King of Cedi cut those arrows down with showers of his own shafts,
and that bull among the Cedis swiftly struck Keśava with six other arrows.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, suddenly released his weapon;
the mighty-armed King of Cedi destroyed that very weapon with another weapon.
Then [he struck him] with a hundred thousand straight-knotted arrows.
Then, having completely overwhelmed Śauri Dāmodara from all sides,
the powerful and majestic Śiśupāla, filled with rage, let out a roar;
and that slayer of enemy heroes, highly incensed, spoke these words to Keśava:
Today, O dear one, my arrows shall pierce your limbs in battle;
having slain you along with your sons, ministers, and the swift Pāṇḍavas,
I shall today attain freedom from my debt to the wise Jarāsaṃdha.
"Of Kaṃsa, of Keśin, and likewise of Naraka"—
having spoken thus to Janārdana with eyes copper-red with rage, Śiśupāla,
becoming invisible, completely covered him from all sides with a shower of arrows.
Then, with that very weapon, the Blessed One cut down the many arrows;
having severed all those shafts, he proceeded to make himself invisible.
As the two heroes of great strength entered into invisibility, they shone resplendently.
"Excellent! Excellent! the beings in the sky honored him, saying, "Never before have we seen such a battle as this.
Then Śiśupāla quickly struck Kṛṣṇa with three arrows.
Kṛṣṇa also pierced Sunītha with five arrows in the battle;
then the powerful Sunītha struck him back with seventy iron shafts. Thus deeply pierced by Kṛṣṇa, Sunītha was overcome with rage.
He pierced Vāsudeva between the breasts with sharpened arrows;
having struck Kṛṣṇa again with three shafts, the king let out a roar at that opportune moment.
Then, they suddenly engaged in an exceedingly fierce battle with their arrows.
Like two tigers with their claws, two noble elephants with their tusks,
two five-faced lions with their fangs, or two cocks with their beaks,
those two tore at each other in battle with their sharp arrows.
Then, filled with rage, the two of them released an unsurpassed shower of arrows.
Having cut down those very arrows with their own arrows, those two bulls among men engaged in a terrible,
superhuman battle consisting of divine weapons.
The powerful Śiśupāla released the Āgneya weapon,
which Keśava neutralized by means of the Vāruṇa weapon.
Then the King of Cedi suddenly discharged the Kaubera weapon.

The Lord of the world suddenly destroyed the Kāubera weapon; then, enraged and deluded by Time, he released the Yāmya weapon. By means of the application of the very Yāmya weapon, he neutralized the Yāmya weapon.
The Lord overcame the Gāndharva weapon with the Gāndharva, the Mānava with the Mānava,
the Vāyavya with the Vāyavya, the Raudra with the Raudra,
the Aindra with the Aindra, and the Vaiṣṇava with the Vaiṣṇava.
Thus employing their weapons, the two of great strength fought on.
Then the powerful son of Damaghoṣa, manifesting his illusory power (*māyā*),
unleashed a rain of maces and clubs, as well as spears, lances, and arrows.
The King of Cedi loosed a shower of axes and clubs,
which the blessed Keśava destroyed with his infallible weapon (*amogha-astra*).
Then he rained down a most terrible shower of stones upon Keśava.
Enraged by the Vajra weapon, the Lord reduced it to powder;
then the bull among the Cedis unleashed a terrible downpour of water,
which the Blessed Hari dispersed into hundreds of fragments with the Vāyavya weapon.
Having destroyed all the illusions of Sunītha, Janārdana,
that great car-warrior, quickly engaged in a duel for a moment;
while fighting with arrows, he rebuked the King of Cedi.
The son of Damaghoṣa spoke boldly to the joy of the Yadus:
"Today let my arrows make Kṛṣṇa non-Kṛṣṇa.
Having spoken thus, the evil-minded one loosed a shower of arrows upon Janārdana.
Assuming that terrible form, that tiger among men released [his power]; however,
in an instant, that joy of the Yadus, that Supreme Person, with his limbs mangled by arrows, bled profusely.

Neither the driver, nor the chariot, nor even the horses—which were like mountains—could be seen, as they were completely covered by arrows; the world became agitated. Seeing Keśava in that state, all living beings cried out.
Then Dāruka, the slayer of enemy heroes, said to Keśava:
"O Mādhava, never before have I seen such a battle as this which I have witnessed; yet, by your power, O Lord, I remain standing."
"Otherwise, O Janārdana, my life-breaths would not remain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reflected thus, O Govinda, bring about his death immediately.
Thus addressed by the charioteer, Keśava spoke these words:
"In ancient times, this exceedingly powerful Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was the enemy of the gods, the lord of the Daityas, who had become arrogant through the granting of boons."
Then there was a lord of the Rākṣasas named Rāvaṇa, possessed of exceeding prowess;
by that very strength and heroism, he disregarded my power. And I shall become the death of that evil-minded one at the proper time.
"O charioteer, you must not fear; while I am standing here, he is nothing at all.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, whose banner bears Garuḍa, let out a roar;
Keśava blew his great conch, Pāñcajanya.
Having confounded him, the Blessed One took up his divine discus and,
in the battle, severed Sunītha’s head with that discus.
Then, having heard those words, the powerful Śiśupāla—
Laughing with a loud sound, he laughed and said this:
"O Kṛṣṇa, proclaiming Rukmiṇī as having been won by me before others in assemblies—
especially among kings— how is it that you feel no shame?"
For what man among the virtuous,
O Madhusūdana, would ever proclaim another’s wife as having belonged to someone else?
Whether you grant me forgiveness or not, O Kṛṣṇa, forgive me.
"Whether he be angry or even pleased, what will come of you to me? Even as he was speaking thus, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana saw that evil-minded Śiśupāla approaching.
Taking the wheel that was lying at his side, he sent it toward that evil-minded one;
having observed all of his hundreds of offenses from every perspective,
O sinless one, he then took up a vessel of water for the sake of the wheel.
The wheel, which shone like molten gold, was hurled at that evil-minded one; and it, appearing with the luster of black iron,
likewise stripped away his unsurpassed limb.
Having fallen upon the earth with its earrings, it shone;
a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the assembly hall.
Then he thought in his mind of the discus that destroys the hosts of Daityas.
At that very moment, when the wheel had come into his hand,
the Blessed One, skilled in speech, spoke these words aloud:
"Let the protectors of the earth hear from me why this has been forgiven by me."
"One hundred offenses of this very man, as he begs for them, must be forgiven. O kings, that which was requested by me has indeed been granted in its entirety.
Now, while you all look on, I shall put him to death."

Having spoken thus, the best of the Yadus, the subduer of enemies, in a moment of rage, severed the head of the King of Cedi with his discus. That mighty-armed one fell like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.

Then, O great king, the monarchs beheld a supreme radiance rising from the body of the Lord of Cedi, like the sun ascending from the sky. Then [they saw] Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who is worshipped by the world.
He paid homage to that unborn, all-pervading Lord, who is worthy of praise, worshipped by the three worlds, and yet remains unstudied;
and at that moment, O King, he entered into that splendor.
Seeing this, all the rulers of the earth considered it a marvel.
When that splendor entered the mighty-armed Supreme Person,
the sky rained down though cloudless, blazing thunderbolts fell,
and the earth trembled when the King of Cedi was slain by Kṛṣṇa.
Then some of those kings said nothing at all;
as the time for speech had passed, they gazed only at Janārdana.
Others, filled with indignation, rubbed their palms together with their hands.
Others, frantic with rage, bit their lips with their teeth;
some kings, however, praised the descendant of Vṛṣṇi in private,
while others were incensed, and still others remained neutral.
Those hosts of gods and gandharvas, and those kings renowned upon the earth,
they all offer salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa, the Great Soul;
as do those kṣatriyas here who have arisen from the faction of the asura hosts.
Those evil-minded ones, whose lives are spent, revile Hṛṣīkeśa;
as do the hosts of Prajāpatis who are indifferent toward that Great Soul,
as well as the Brahmarṣis, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Cāraṇas.
They indeed praise Govinda with divine hymns accompanied by auspicious rites;
they dance among one another to various songs and attend upon the Great Soul, Govinda, filled with joy.
Greatly delighted, the great seers approached Keśava while offering hymns of praise;
likewise, the high-souled Brāhmaṇas and the mighty kings,
all being at ease, extolled him upon seeing the prowess of Kṛṣṇa.
The Pāṇḍava, however, spoke to his brothers with courtesy:
"Accomplish the task against the heroic son of Damaghoṣa, the lord of the earth; do not delay.
Hearing the words of the Kuru king, those brothers were filled with haste.
And so, they then carried out the command of their brother;
and Pārtha, together with those lords of the earth, consecrated his son as the sovereign of the Cedis and the lord of the land.
Then the sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja proceeded,
its obstacles and disturbances pacified by worship, and crowded with throngs of great seers.

When that sacrifice had commenced, those skilled in speech and proponents of logic, desiring to defeat one another, uttered many reasoned arguments. The kings beheld that supreme ritual of the sacrifice.
O Bhārata, Sahadeva constructed there archways like those fashioned for Upendra; they were made of golden palm-wood,
blazing as if with fire and resembling the radiant sun in its brilliance.
With those sacrificial arches and the planets, that sacrifice shone like the sky;
and there were many beds, seats, and pavilions provided with abundant wealth,
along with jars, vessels, cauldrons, and pitchers on every side.
O King, there was nothing there that those monarchs did not see made of gold;
the Brahmins, highly honored, dwelt at that sacrifice,
engaging in many conversations and watching actors and dancers.
And as the Brahmins were eating various kinds of delicious food, the great sound of those joyful men was heard there incessantly:
"Give! Give! Eat! Eat!"
Such conversations were constantly heard there:
"There are various transformations of rice, delicious and diverse;
and very many kinds of foods to be chewed, as well as sweet drinks."

The king’s servants constantly gave [food] to the twice-born at that great sacrifice. When a full hundred thousand brahmins were then eating, a signal was established there: a conch shell was blown incessantly.
O Bhārata, the sound of that conch resounded repeatedly;
hearing that supreme sound of the conch, they were filled with wonder.
While the sacrifice proceeded in this manner, tens of thousands of people were satisfied and well-nourished.

O King, there were many mounds of food, as high as mountains; and the people beheld streams of curd and lakes of clarified butter. Indeed, the entire continent of Jambūdvīpa, filled with various provinces, was there.
O King,
in that great sacrifice of the monarch, thousands of men were seen gathered from here and there, bringing wealth to that king’s grand rite.
There, kings wearing garlands and polished jeweled earrings served those brahmins by the hundreds and thousands with various kinds of food and drink, as well as diverse foods to be licked.
They gave to the brahmins those various kinds of foods fit for a king’s enjoyment, as well as sweet flowers and fruits;
they gave these and sweet syrups to the brahmins here.
Having continuously partaken of these [offerings] at that sacrifice, all the twice-born and others attained supreme delight, rejoicing intensely at that time.
Thus, everything was gathered together, abounding in cattle, wealth, and grain.

Having seen the sacrificial enclosure, the kings were filled with the utmost wonder. And the officiating priests, all the performers of the sacrifice, offered oblations for the son of Pāṇḍu during the great Rājasūya ritual at the proper times, in accordance with the scriptures.
And all those learned in the scriptures, thoroughly trained in every discipline— Vyāsa, Dhaumya, and the others— all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), according to the rules,
performed their respective duties for the Pāṇḍava’s great sacrifice.

Among those present, there was no member of the assembly who was not learned in the six Vedāṅgas, nor anyone who was not deeply versed in scripture; no one was lacking in vows, nor lacking a preceptor, nor was there any who was wicked or intolerant. Furthermore, there was no one there who was miserable, nor did any person become impoverished.
Whether hungry or suffering, or even a common man,
Sahadeva of great splendor always caused food to be given to those seeking food, by the command of the king.

And the officiating priests, skilled in the ritual arrangements and possessing the eye of knowledge regarding the meaning of the scriptures, performed all the rites day after day according to the sacred texts; meanwhile,
the Brahmins, learned in the Vedas and the Shastras, held discourses at all times.
And at the conclusion of the discourse during that great sacrifice,
all beheld that sacrificial altar, strewn with gods, twice-born brahmins, and great seers accomplished in the Vedas;
it then shone like the stainless sky filled with stars.
Then the highly effulgent Sahadeva caused sacrificial stakes made of gold and adorned with all kinds of jewels to be fashioned for the sake of beauty;
there they beheld the archways made of golden palm trees.
With those archways and those celestial bodies, that sacrifice shone like the sky;
with its golden archways of palm trees, it was as if the quarters of the world were adorned with the tusks of the elephants of the directions,
or as if the suns themselves were stationed in every direction with their splendors.
Then that assembly hall of the high-souled Pāṇḍava shone, crowded with kings wearing crowns,
as well as with other gods, yakṣas, serpents, celestial humans,
and hosts of vidyādharas.
That Rājasūya sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja shone brightly;
it was thronged by hosts of Gandharvas, graced by throngs of Apsarases,
and adorned with the songs of Kimpuruṣas and Kiṃnaras.
There, Nārada sang, as did the highly effulgent Tumburu,
Viśvāvasu, Citrasena, and others skilled in song;
they delighted them all during the intervals between the sacrificial rites.
There, all the Apsarases— beautiful and lovely to behold—
constantly danced and sang during the intervals between activities,
as well as [recited] the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and all kinds of narratives.
Then, those experts in the science of sound spoke during the intervals between the rituals:
"The kettledrums, the clay drums, the *duṇḍuka* drums, and the *gomukha* horns,
as well as the conchs, flutes, and lutes, are heard by the thousands."
In this world, all the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras in their entirety,
as well as all the Mlecchas and those born of all castes— whether at the beginning, middle, or end—
assembled from various lands and belonging to diverse tribes.
This world, as it were, is contained within Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence:
all the Kurus, including Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Suyodhana,
as well as the entire host of Vṛṣṇis and the Pāñcālas in their entirety.
Like servants at a sacrifice, they performed all the rites as was appropriate. Thus commenced that sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja; O mighty-armed one, it shone like the sacrifice of Soma himself.
There, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira constantly bestowed garments, woolen blankets, and outer cloaks at all times, as well as golden neck-ornaments, vessels made of gold, and every kind of jewelry.
Whatever excellent wealth he had obtained there from the lords of the earth,
he then bestowed all those jewels upon the Brahmins. Thereafter, that sacrifice of the Kuru king was endowed with every prosperity.
O King, it shone forth, bringing joy to the youths, possessed of vast energy;
with obstacles stilled and undertakings made easy, it abounded in wealth and grain,
was rich in food and many delicacies, and was well protected by Keśava.
And he brought that great sacrifice, the Rājasūya,
to completion. Throughout its duration until its conclusion, the mighty-armed Lord Janārdana, Śauri, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace, protected that sacrifice.
He bestowed ten billion gifts upon high-souled brahmins;
no other lord of the earth in this world will ever do such a thing.
And the officiating priests were constantly satisfied with all their desires and wealth.
Then, having performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), that king, the son of Pāṇḍu, being purified,
[honored] Vyāsa, Dhaumya, and the high-minded Nārada,
as well as Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and Vaiśampāyana.
He honored Yājñavalkya, Kaṭha, and the highly powerful Kalāpa,
as well as all the foremost of Brahmins, treating them with due respect.
"It is through your power that this great sacrifice, the Rājasūya, has been attained."
"By the power of Janārdana, my heart's desire has been fulfilled.
Then, having completed the sacrifice at its conclusion, he worshipped Mādhava,
Baladeva— the lord of gods— and the foremost of the Kurus, headed by Bhīṣma.

Then, having approached King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, after he had performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the entire assembly of kings spoke these words:
"By good fortune you prosper, O Knower of Dharma; you have attained imperial sovereignty, O Lord."
"O descendant of Ajamīḍha, the glory of the Ajamīḍhas has been increased by you through this deed, O Indra among kings; and a very great merit has been performed.
Having been well honored with all our desires, we now take our leave, O tiger among men."
"We shall go to our own kingdoms; you should grant us permission for this.
Having heard these words of the kings, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, honored the monarchs as was fitting and spoke to all his brothers.
"All these kings have come to us out of affection;
having taken leave of me, those subduers of enemies are now departing for their own kingdoms.
Follow these best of men to the border of our realm—may prosperity be yours."
Having understood their brother’s words, the dharma-practicing Pāṇḍavas followed those foremost of kings one by one as was appropriate;
the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna quickly followed Virāṭa.
The great car-warrior Dhanañjaya [approached] the high-souled Yajñasena;
and the mighty Bhīmasena [approached] Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
and the highly intelligent Vidura.
The great car-warrior Sahadeva [confronted] the high-souled Saṃjaya,
as well as Droṇa and the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), together with their ministers and circles of friends,
and the heroic Droṇa along with his son.
O King, Nakula advanced against Subala and his son;
Satyaka, the slayer of enemy heroes, against the heroic Śalya and his son;
and [he also opposed] King Bhagadatta and Bṛhadbala of Kosala.
The son of Hiḍimbā followed Bhīṣmaka along with his son, as well as his highly intelligent maternal uncle,
and all those from the south;
the sons of Draupadī, together with the son of Subhadrā, followed the mountain-dwelling kings.
In the same manner, those bulls among Kṣatriyas followed other Kṣatriyas. Thus, having been duly honored, both the kings and all the Brahmins departed from every side.
O bull of the Bharata race, when all those lords of the earth had gone...
Seeing the Pāṇḍava king seated upon the throne, his purpose accomplished, shining with the splendor of great Indra, the powerful Vāsudeva spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O descendant of Kuru, I take my leave of you; I shall go to Dvārakā.
By good fortune, you have successfully performed the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices.
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja spoke to Madhusūdana.
"O Govinda, through your grace I have indeed attained this sacrifice;
through your grace, the entire earthly warrior class has come under my control and stands before me, having brought the foremost tribute."
"O sinless one, how can my voice utter words for the sake of your departure?
O hero, without you, we shall not find any pleasure here in any way whatsoever.
Yet, you must certainly go to the city of Dvāravatī."
Thus addressed, the righteous Hari of wide renown, accompanied by Yudhiṣṭhira, approached Pṛthā and spoke with joy:
"O paternal aunt, your sons have today attained universal sovereignty."
"May you be successful and prosperous; may you attain joy. With your permission, I am eager to go to Dvārakā.
Having spoken thus to his sister, Śauri then [addressed] his father's [sister].
Keśava honored Subhadrā and Draupadī;
then, having emerged from the inner apartments accompanied by Yudhiṣṭhira,
he bathed, performed his prayers, and had the Brahmins recite blessings.
