Then, O great king, having yoked a well-prepared chariot that resembled an excellent cloud, Dāruka presented himself before him. Seeing the chariot standing ready, with its banner bearing the foremost of birds (Tārkṣya), [he approached].
With Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna placing their hands upon him,
the high-minded lotus-eyed one circumambulated the chariot, ascended it, and then departed for the city of Dvāravatī.
Then Sātyaki and Kṛtavarman, having quickly mounted their chariot,
fanned Hari there with two chowries;
so too did Baladeva, the lord of gods, and thousands of Yādavas.
Honored by the son of Dharma, they all departed like kings. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous ruler, leaving his esteemed golden throne, followed him on foot.
Accompanied by his brothers, the illustrious one approached the mighty Vāsudeva— Viṣṇu, the lord and teacher of all— who had assumed a human form for the sake of his task,
while the Wind-god proceeded ahead with a gait resembling that of a messenger-man.
Then, having halted that excellent chariot for a moment, Hari,
the lotus-eyed one, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī:
"O lord of people, remain ever vigilant and protect the subjects."

"May your kinsmen depend upon you, as living beings depend on the rain-cloud, as birds depend on a great tree, and as the immortals depend on the thousand-eyed Indra. Having thus made this mutual agreement, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava [departed].
Having taken leave of one another, they both departed for their respective homes.
O King, when Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of the Sātvatas, had gone to Dvāravatī,
the great king Yudhiṣṭhira then entered the city.
O Bhārata, King Duryodhana alone, as well as Śakuni the son of Subala,
the Sūta’s son Rādheya, along with Duḥśāsana and the others,
were honored with all objects of desire and sensory enjoyments.
Those two bulls among men dwelt in that divine assembly hall.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that most difficult-to-attain and supreme sacrifice, the Rājasūya, had been completed—
Surrounded by his disciples, Vyāsa appeared before him;
he quickly rose from his seat, surrounded by his brothers,
and honored his grandfather with water for his feet and the offering of a seat.
Then, having sat down upon an excellent golden throne, the Blessed One said to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, "Be seated. Then the king, surrounded by his brothers, sat down.
The blessed Vyāsa, who was skilled in various forms of speech, said:
"By good fortune you prosper, O son of Kuntī, having attained this sovereignty so difficult to obtain;
all the Kurus have been raised up by you, O upholder of the Kuru lineage."
"I take my leave of you; I shall depart, having been honored by you, O lord of the people.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, saluted and clasped the feet of his grandfather and then spoke.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of bipeds, a most difficult doubt has arisen within me;
O bull among the twice-born, there is indeed no one other than you who can resolve it.
"The venerable seer Nārada has declared three kinds of portents, O Grandfather: those celestial, those atmospheric, and those terrestrial.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Moreover, due to the fall of the King of Cedi, a great and ominous portent had occurred;
having heard the words of the king, the lord Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the son of Parāśara, spoke these words.

"O King, O Lord of the people, for thirteen years the great fruit of these portents will result in the destruction of all the Kṣatriyas; this shall come about through Time, O bull of the Bharatas, making you alone the cause."
O Bhārata, the assembled host of kṣatriyas shall go to their destruction through the transgression of Duryodhana and by the power of Bhīma and Arjuna.
O Indra among kings, at the end of the night you shall see the bull-bannered god in a dream.
[Namely: Nīlakaṇṭha, Bhava, Sthāṇu, Kāpālin, Tripurāntaka,
Ugra, Rudra, Paśupati, Mahādeva, Umāpati,
Hara, Śarva, Vṛṣa, Śūlin, Pinākin, and Kṛttivāsas.

O lord of the people, you shall see such a dream as this: Śiva seated upon a bull that resembles the peak of Mount Kailāsa, constantly gazing toward the direction presided over by the King of the Ancestors (Yama).
"Do not grieve for his sake, for time is difficult to overcome.
May it be well with you; I shall depart for Mount Kailāsa.
Vaiśampāyana said:

"Remaining vigilant, self-controlled, and steadfast, protect the earth. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa departed for Mount Kailāsa along with his disciples who followed the sacred scriptures.
When the grandfather had departed, the king was filled with anxiety and grief;
sighing hot breaths repeatedly and reflecting upon that very matter, he wondered:
"How indeed might destiny be thwarted by human effort?"
"What was spoken by the supreme ṛṣi will certainly come to pass.
Then the highly energetic Yudhiṣṭhira said to all his brothers,
"O tigers among men, you have indeed heard what Dvaipāyana told me."

Then, having heard those words, her mind was resolved upon death: "If I am intended by Time, O father, to be the cause of the destruction of all the kṣatriyas, what purpose is there for me in living?"
To the king who was speaking thus, Phālguna replied:
"O King, do not fall into this terrible despondency which destroys the intellect.
Having reflected deeply, O Great King, perform that which is appropriate."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, whose resolve is truth, spoke to all his brothers, reflecting upon the words of Dvaipāyana right there: "From this day forward, may prosperity be yours; listen to my vow."
"O dear one, thirteen years have passed; what purpose is there for me to live? I shall not speak harshly to my brothers or other kings;
remaining under the command of my kinsmen, I shall apply myself while reciting that [instruction]."

As I conduct myself in this manner toward my own sons and others alike, no dissension shall arise in the world; for conflict is rooted in division. Keeping strife at a distance and acting only with kindness, [I shall maintain peace].
"O bulls among men, I shall not become an object of reproach in the worlds.
Having heard those words of his elder brother, the Pāṇḍavas,
devoted to the welfare of Dharmarāja, acted accordingly.
O lord of the people, having made an agreement with his brothers in the assemblies, the King of Dharma, having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods according to the rules,
and having performed auspicious rites, was surrounded by his brothers.
O bull of the Bharata race, when all those lords of the Kṣatriyas had departed,
Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his ministers, entered that best of cities;
so too did Duryodhana, O great king, and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
In that very same delightful assembly hall, the lord of men remained.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O bull of the Bharata race, Duryodhana was dwelling in that assembly hall.
Slowly, together with Śakuni, he beheld that entire assembly hall;
there the joy of the Kurus saw celestial designs such as he had never seen before in the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Once, in the midst of the assembly hall, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth,
having reached a crystal floor, suspected it was water;
deluded in his intellect, the king proceeded to lift up his own garment.
There, too, when the people saw him, the Pāṇḍavas then laughed;
dejected and with his face turned away, he wandered about that assembly hall.
Then the king, dejected and ashamed, fell down upon the dry ground.
Then, thinking a pond with crystal-clear water and adorned with crystal lotuses to be dry land, he fell into the water while still wearing his clothes.
Seeing him fallen into the water, the servants laughed heartily.
And by the king's command, they presented him with beautiful garments;
Suyodhana laughed, and his servants laughed as well.
But seeing him in such a state, the mighty Bhīmasena—
Then Arjuna and both the twins— all of them— laughed aloud.
Thereupon, in another part of the assembly hall, King Duryodhana,
being intolerant, could not endure their derision.
Guarding his outward appearance, he did not look at them;
lifting up his garment again as if about to step onto dry land,
he then ascended, whereupon all those people laughed once more.
But when the lord of the earth saw another door made of crystal that appeared to be closed,
he struck his head as he entered and stood there as if dazed;
he saw yet another such door with large panels of crystal.
Striking with both hands, he emerged and fell down before him;
thinking that the door was closed,
though it had opened of its own accord, he turned back from the doorway.
O lord of the people, having thus encountered various deceptions there,
King Duryodhana, permitted by the son of Pāṇḍu,
then attended the great Rājasūya sacrifice with a heavy heart.
Having witnessed that miraculous supernatural power, he departed for Hastinapura.
As King Duryodhana traveled— burning with envy at the prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas and exhausted by his brooding— an evil thought arose within him.
But King Duryodhana, having witnessed that splendor of the sacrifice of the illustrious Pāṇḍavas, was not satisfied; at that time, he departed for his own home, leaving behind all others.
As he watched, dejected by his suffering, a sinful thought arose within him,
O bull of the Kurus, upon seeing the sons of Pṛthā with cheerful minds and the kings submissive to their will, and the entire world, down to its children, brought under their influence.
Moreover, upon hearing of the supreme majesty of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, became pale;
wandering with a distracted mind, he brooded only over the assembly hall.
Then Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, being intoxicated by the incomparable splendor of the wise Dharmarāja,
did not respond to Subala’s son, even though he spoke again and again.
Seeing him thus distracted, Śakuni addressed him:
"Duryodhana, why do you walk along sighing as if from some root cause?
Duryodhana said:
Having seen this entire earth subject to Yudhiṣṭhira’s authority,
the celestial ṛṣis, yakṣas, and gandharvas come there constantly;
yet Kṛṣṇa, being ill-at-ease, increases their prosperity.
There, those afflicted by disease are led forth, as are those who deal in legal disputes and words; there, the sellers of perfumes do not go, nor do those of great splendor,
nor the sellers of donkeys, camels, horses, goats, and rhinoceroses, nor kings.
In this world, the name "Kaurava" circulates only there; however,
the gate of the city of Hariprastha is always kept firmly closed by the constant mounting of men upon chariots, elephants, horses, and other vehicles.

O maternal uncle of great splendor, having seen that sacrifice of the high-souled Pārtha— conquered by the prowess of his weapons and resembling that of Śakra among the gods— occurring in such a manner, [he was amazed].
Filled with indignation and burning day and night,
I am drying up like a small pool of water during the onset of the hot season;
behold, Śiśupāla has been struck down by the chief of the Sātvatas!
And there was not a single man there who followed in his footsteps;
for the kings, being consumed by the fire arising from the Pāṇḍava,
endured that offense— who indeed would be able to endure it?
That great deed was thus performed by Vāsudeva,
and it was accomplished through the prowess of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas;
for indeed, the kings, having brought various jewels, [honored] the king.
They wait upon the son of Kuntī like Vaiśyas paying tribute;
seeing such splendor blazing as it were within the Pāṇḍava,
I am overcome by indignation and burn with grief, though I am undeserving of it.
Having thus made this resolution, he then spoke these words once more to the King of Gāndhāra, as if burning with fire:
"I shall either enter the fire or consume poison."
I shall even enter the waters, for I shall not be able to live.
For what man of spirit indeed in this world would endure seeing his rivals prospering and his own ruin?
Thus, I am neither woman nor non-woman, neither man nor even non-man,
since I endure today such sovereign power over the earth and such immense wealth as has come to me.
Seeing such a sacrifice as that, who like me would not burn with anguish? I am alone and powerless to acquire that royal splendor,
and seeing no allies, I contemplate death.
"I consider destiny alone to be supreme, while human effort is useless,
having seen that radiant prosperity brought thus to the son of Kuntī.
Previously, O son of Subala, I made every effort for his destruction."
Having transcended all that, like a lotus in the water, that aged man [has emerged];
therefore, I consider destiny to be supreme and human effort to be useless,
for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are declining while the sons of Pṛthā are constantly prospering.

Having seen that splendor and that assembly hall of such a kind, and having been subjected to that mockery by the guards, I am consumed with grief as if by fire. Therefore, O maternal uncle, grant me leave today, for I am deeply distressed.
"Report to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that indignation has taken possession of him.
Śakuni said:
"Duryodhana, you should not harbor indignation toward Yudhiṣṭhira."

For the Pāṇḍavas always enjoy their own rightful portions; indeed, their supreme destiny is ordained by fate in manifold ways. Furthermore, in the past, you repeatedly employed numerous stratagems against them.
O Great King, O subduer of enemies, even when an undertaking has begun, men who possess perseverance do not falter in their tasks;
and those tigers among men, favored by fortune, remain liberated.
By them, Draupadī was obtained as their wife, along with Drupada and his sons;
and the heroic Vāsudeva became their ally in the conquest of the earth—
he who is indeed unconquerable by all beings, including gods, asuras, and humans.
He has flourished through their splendor; what cause for lamentation is there in that? O Lord of the Earth, you have obtained your paternal inheritance and have not been overcome;
it has grown by their power—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Having gratified the Fire-god, Dhanañjaya obtained the Gāṇḍīva bow, two inexhaustible quivers, and divine weapons; by means of that preeminent bow and his own prowess of arm—
The rulers of the earth have been brought under his control; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Having liberated both the people from the danger of fire and the Dānava Maya, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, caused that assembly hall to be constructed.
And by that very Māyā, the Rākṣasas named Kiṃkaras were commanded;
those terrible ones carry that assembly hall—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
And as for what you said, O King, descendant of Bharata, regarding your lack of assistance:
That is false; for these brothers of yours are great car-warriors who are your allies:
Drona, the great archer, together with his wise son, the Suta's son Radheya, and Gautama, the great car-warrior.

That single mighty-armed one will defeat all the Pāṇḍavas along with the Somakas in battle; what need have you for allies? For there is Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, and Gautama, the great chariot-warrior.
The powerful Jayadratha, skilled in weapons and firm with his bow,
myself along with my brothers, and the heroic son of Somadatta—
if you are joined by all these, conquer the entire earth.
Duryodhana said:
"O King, accompanied by you and these other great chariot-warriors,
I shall surely defeat them, if you grant me your permission."
"When these have been conquered today, the earth shall be mine;
all the protectors of the earth, as well as that assembly hall with its great wealth.
Śakuni said:
Dhanañjaya, Vāsudeva, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira,
Nakula, Sahadeva, and Drupada along with his sons—
these cannot be conquered in battle by force, even by the hosts of gods themselves.
They are great car-warriors, mighty archers, skilled in weapons, and fierce in battle;
yet I know, O King, how Yudhiṣṭhira himself can be conquered— learn that from me and accept it.
Having heard the words of Śakuni, the Kuru king spoke to him.
Duryodhana said:
"Through the vigilance of our friends and other high-souled men..."
"If they can be conquered by you, then tell me so, uncle.
Śakuni said:
"The son of Kuntī is fond of gambling, yet he does not know how to play."
Once challenged, that lord of kings will not be able to turn back;
victory can be achieved through stratagem, for he is incapable of conquering otherwise. I am skilled at gambling, and there is no one on earth equal to me.
"O son of Kuntī, challenge that man to a game of dice within the three worlds!
O King, being skilled at the dice, I shall undoubtedly win back for you his kingdom and that radiant prosperity, O bull among men."
"O Duryodhana, report all this to the king:
'Once permitted by your father, I shall conquer him; of this there is no doubt.
Duryodhana said:
"O son of Subala, you yourself must report this to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the chief of the Kurus, according to what is proper; I am not able to speak it myself.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having witnessed that great Rājasūya sacrifice of King Yudhiṣṭhira, he, accompanied by the sons of Gāndhārī,
entered Hastināpura according to the counsel of Duryodhana.
"So be it," the bird Śakuni firmly resolved in his heart.
And seeing that state of unease in the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the evil-doer,
that wicked man, approached those lords of the earth with that sinful soul.

Having previously ascertained that intention of Duryodhana’s, which was intended for the destruction of the Bharatas and the ruin of kings, that evil-minded one, harboring in his heart the desire for the slaughter of all the world, acted for the destruction of those wicked-souled men.
Then Śakuni, the son of Subala, impelled by fate and by destiny itself, a doer of cruel deeds, spoke to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, as he sat before the one whose eye is wisdom (Droṇa),
having heard the words of Duryodhana.
Approaching the one of great wisdom, Śakuni spoke these words:
"O Great King, Duryodhana is pale, wan, and emaciated; he is dejected and lost in thought—know this, O bull of the Bharatas."
"You do not indeed examine properly that which arises from an enemy and is unbearable;
why do you not perceive the grief of your eldest son?
Thus addressed by Śakuni, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, [remained silent].
Having summoned Duryodhana, he spoke these words.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Duryodhana, my son, what is the root cause for which you are so deeply distressed?"
"If that matter is something I must hear, then tell it to me, O joy of the Kurus.
Śakuni has told me that you are pale, wan, and emaciated;
yet, even as I reflect on it, I do not perceive the cause of your grief."
"O son, indeed all great sovereignty has been entrusted to you.
Your brothers and your friends likewise do nothing that is displeasing to you;
both Gāndhārī and I myself enjoy only what is given by you."
"You wear fine robes and eat meat with rice;
noble steeds carry you—why then are you pale and emaciated? You have costly beds and delightful women."
Your virtuous dwellings and pleasure gardens are at your disposal as you wish;
everything is yours, like that of the gods, bound only by your word—of this there is no doubt.
Why then, O son, do you grieve like one who is wretched, though you are invincible?
O dear son, you have attained that which is remembered as the supreme duty of a mother and a father toward their son: you have arrived as the entirety of our family's prosperity,
like Vāsava himself present in heaven with all his desires fulfilled.
With various and excellent foods and drinks, why indeed do you grieve? He was learned, accomplished in knowledge, dear to me, and cherished at home;
he possessed mastery of Nirukta, Nigama, and Chandas, along with the six auxiliary sciences and the treatises on meaning.

You have studied and mastered the sciences through the eight grammars; out of compassion, you learned the science of weapons from Halāyudha and from Droṇa. Since your eldest brother stands established in the kingdom, why do you grieve, my son?

That food and clothing which are so abundant and beyond compare for ordinary men— O son, you enjoy them as a lord while being praised by bards and panegyrists. O you of known wisdom, how can this root of sorrow belong to you?
"In this world, tell me, my son, who else possesses such supreme fortune as mine?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, Manda, following the sway of anger, [replied].
Revealing his own intention, he replied thus to his father.
Duryodhana said:
"I eat and I clothe myself just like an ordinary man."
Bearing fierce indignation while enduring the passage of time, one who,
being intolerant of his own subjects' transgressions, overcomes them and stands firm against his enemies, desiring to liberate his people from suffering— he indeed is called a man.
"Contentment indeed destroys prosperity, as does arrogance, O Bhārata;
and both compassion and fear—being possessed by these, one does not attain greatness.
Seeing the prosperity of Yudhiṣṭhira, that which I have enjoyed no longer sustains me."
Seeing my own self declining while my rivals prospered, that [weapon] appeared as if blazing before the son of Kuntī, causing me great distress;
and though it remained invisible to the son of Kuntī, I saw it as if it were raised against him.
Therefore, I am pale, dejected, wan,
and emaciated. Yudhiṣṭhira supports eighty-eight thousand householders who are *snātakas*, each of whom has thirty slave-girls.
Ten thousand others constantly eat the finest food there from golden plates in Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence;
yet, because of the enemy's extraordinary prosperity, Virūpa was deprived of food.
The King of Kamboja sent him blankets made of the skins of the *kadalī* deer, as well as those that were black, dark-blue, and reddish, all of the highest quality;
he also sent hundreds and thousands of chariots, women, cattle, and horses.
And three thousand female camels roam about as well;
for the kings, having brought tribute, have assembled in this royal abode,
O lord of the earth, bringing various kinds of jewels.
Bringing vast quantities of wealth in abundance for this foremost of sacrifices for the son of Kuntī,
I have never seen nor heard of anything like the influx of riches at the sacrifice of the wise son of Pāṇḍu.
"O King, if all this is untrue, you ought to ask Saṃjaya about it. O Lord, having seen that boundless flood of wealth belonging to the enemy, I find no peace at all as I reflect upon it incessantly."
Brāhmaṇas and Vāṭadhānas, possessing herds of cattle by the hundreds,
stand at the gate having brought a tribute of three *kharvas*, but they are kept waiting.
They have brought beautiful water-pots made of gold.
Having thus presented the offering, they then obtained entrance;
the Ocean, the son of Varuṇa, brought for him that very Kāṃsya vessel from which the celestial women withhold the honey for Śakra.
Taking up a preeminent conch shell, which was capable of withstanding a thousand gold pieces and adorned with many jewels, Vāsudeva consecrated him.
And upon seeing all that, it appeared to me like a fever.
Taking that [water], they go to the eastern and southern oceans;
likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, they go to the western ocean,
taking jars for the sake of water there, O king of kings, those Rākṣasas.
They went in all directions to fetch water, avoiding only the northern quarter;
for, my son, they do not go to the north except for birds.
Having gone there, Arjuna brought back a staff and immeasurable wealth.
O Bhārata, I saw a lotus pond constructed by Maya with jewels from the Bindu-sarovara, covered with crystal and filled with water as it were;
and as Vāsava lifted up my garment, Vṛkodara laughed at me.
The servants and the guardians of the assembly hall laughed, O bull of the Bharatas;
for the sake of their parents, they especially staked their lives there.
"If I were able in that situation, I would have had Vṛkodara slain."
O Bhārata, that laughter of my rival indeed burns me;
for there, O lord of men, thinking it to be a pavilion with a lotus-pond, I fell into a crystal pool adorned with crystal lotuses.
There Bhīma, along with Pārtha, laughed aloud at me,
and Draupadī, together with the women, mocked me, causing my heart to sink. And the servants, urged by the king, drenched my clothes in water.
They gave me other garments, and that was even more painful for me.
O King, pillars stood there by the hundreds of thousands like if they were without support; and I, O Lord, was struck there within the crystal.
Shadows stood like pillars by the hundreds and thousands; then, emerging through what was not a door, yet appearing as if it were the form of a gateway,
I struck a stone and was once again wounded in the forehead.
Touching it and seeing that it was certainly not the way, O King, I entered another path;
and there, upon seeing me, the women laughed at me in such a manner, saying to me, "This is the door, O King, this is the door! and "This is not the door! regarding me.
Standing before them, Vṛkodara spoke these words with a smile,
O bull among men, causing laughter to all those members of the assembly:
"There are no jewels anywhere that I have not heard of or seen."
I have seen those things there; therefore, I am tormented and distressed.
I shall enter the fire, or I shall enter the great ocean. For a man of honor, infamy is worse than death.
And hear from me as I relate this wonder that occurred there:
when a full hundred thousand brahmins had been served their meals,
a signal was established there such that a conch shell would be blown constantly.
O Bhārata, as that conch shell resounded again and again,
I heard its most excellent sound, and my hair stood on end;
the assembly hall was crowded with many kings who were eager to see [the spectacle].
O Great King, it shone like the stainless sky with its stars;
for all kinds of jewels were brought together at the sacrifice of that wise son of Pāṇḍu, O lord of men.
Like Vaiśyas serving the twice-born, the protectors of the earth served him;
that splendor belonging to Yudhiṣṭhira, O King, was not possessed by the king of the gods, nor by Yama, nor by Varuṇa, nor even by the lord of the Guhyakas.
Even for Viṣṇu himself, the Lord,
or even for the sovereign of the Rākṣasas,
having seen that supreme splendor of the son of Pāṇḍu, I [am filled with envy].
I find no peace, for my heart is burning;
until I have attained the sovereignty of the Pāṇḍavas, tranquility does not exist for me. Either I shall obtain this fortune through my arrows, or I shall lie dead, slain by my enemies.
"O scorcher of enemies, what is the use of life for one such as I?
O King, the Pāṇḍavas are prospering while we remain stagnant.
Śakuni said:
"O you of true prowess, hear from me the means for attaining that supreme fortune which you have seen in the Pāṇḍava. O Bhārata, I am renowned on earth as well for my skill with dice."
He knows the heart of others, he knows the stakes, and he knows the distinctions of the game;
though the son of Kuntī is fond of gambling, he does not know how to play. Summoned, he will certainly come; say to him, "Let us play."
"O Lord, by employing deceit, I shall certainly defeat him in both gambling and battle;
thus I shall bring back that prosperity."
02,045.039 Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Śakuni,
King Duryodhana then spoke these words to Dhṛtarāṣṭra without a moment’s delay.
"O King, this man, skilled in dice, is capable of winning back the fortune of the son of Pāṇḍu through gambling; therefore, you ought to grant him permission. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The wise minister Kṣattṛ stands under his command; by meeting with him, I shall learn the final decision regarding this matter.
For he, being far-sighted, places righteousness foremost and seeks the highest welfare."
He will speak what is appropriate for both sides, providing a definitive determination of the matter.
Duryodhana said:
"If this Kṣattṛ (Vidura) comes to us, he will cause you to turn back."
Alternatively, you should summon either Vāsudeva or Bhīṣma for the determination of what must be done, and hold counsel with them as to how [the matter] is resolved;
for once you have withdrawn, O Indra among kings, I shall undoubtedly die.
"O King, when I am dead, you shall be happy with Vidura;
you shall enjoy the entire earth—what will you do with me?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those piteous words spoken out of affection by him,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, remaining steadfast in the opinion of Duryodhana, spoke to his servants:
"Build for me a vast assembly hall with a thousand pillars and a hundred gates."
"Let the artisans quickly fashion it so that it is beautiful and pleasing to behold. Then, having strewn it with jewels and scattered dice upon it on all sides,
report to me slowly when it has been well-constructed and easy of access."
Having resolved that it was for the sake of pacifying Duryodhana,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great king, dispatched Vidura;
for indeed, he had no decision whatsoever without consulting Vidura.
Though he knew the evils of gambling, he was drawn away by affection for his son.
Hearing that, the wise Vidura, perceiving that the gateway to the Kali age had arrived and that the mouth of destruction had opened, rushed toward Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Approaching his high-souled elder brother, the younger brother bowed his head at the feet of his elder brother and spoke these words:
"O King, O Lord, I do not approve of this resolve of yours."
"O Vidura, act in such a way that no division among my sons arises on account of the dice-game.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Kṣattṛ, there shall be no quarrel between my sons and their cousins."

"The gods in heaven will undoubtedly show us favor (02,045.053c). Whether it be inauspicious or auspicious, beneficial or harmful, let this friendly game of dice proceed; this is ordained by destiny, there is no doubt. (02,045.054)
While I am present here, as well as Bhīṣma, that bull among the Bharatas,
this misfortune ordained by fate shall not come to pass in any way. Go now, mounting the chariot drawn by horses equal to the wind in speed.
"Bring Yudhiṣṭhira to Khāṇḍavaprastha this very day. Vidura, I tell you this: my resolve is not to be thwarted. I consider destiny alone to be supreme, by which all this comes to pass."
Thus addressed, the wise Vidura, reflecting that this could not be so,
spoke these words:
"This entire lineage, along with its kinsmen..."
Extremely distressed, he approached the son of the River (Bhīṣma), who was possessed of great wisdom.
Janamejaya said:
"How did that disastrous gambling match among the brothers come about?"
Where was that calamity encountered by my grandfathers, the Pāṇḍavas?
And who were the kings present there as members of the assembly, O best of those who know Brahman?
Who approved of it, and who opposed it?
"O twice-born one, I desire this to be told by you in detail;
for this, O best of the twice-born, is the very root of the destruction of the earth.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the king, the powerful disciple of Vyāsa,
who was a knower of all the Vedas, related everything exactly as it had happened.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen to this story from me in detail, O best of the Bharatas,
O great king, if your mind is set upon hearing it further.
Having learned the opinion of Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā— "
In that secluded place, he spoke these words again to Duryodhana:
"Enough with this gambling, O son of Gandhārī; Vidura does not praise it.
For that man of great intelligence would never speak what is harmful to us."
"I consider that which Vidura speaks to be the highest benefit;
O son, let all of that be done, for I believe this is for your own welfare.
It was the celestial sage, the preceptor of Vāsava, who spoke thus to the wise King of the Gods."
Whatever scripture the illustrious Bṛhaspati of noble intellect has spoken,
all that— along with its secret doctrines— the great poet Vidura knows;
and I too, my son, always abide by his word.
O King, whether it be the wise Vidura, esteemed as the foremost of the Kurus, or the highly intelligent Uddhava, honored among the Vṛṣṇis—
enough of that gambling, my son; for in gambling, dissension is seen.
In division lies the destruction of a kingdom; therefore, my son, avoid it. Half of the Kurus' realms is already recognized as yours here;
together with your kinsmen and brothers, you shall enjoy happiness.
"That which is indeed considered the supreme duty for a son toward his father and mother has been fulfilled by you, my dear;
you have attained that station belonging to your fathers and grandfathers. You have studied, you are accomplished in the scriptures, and you were constantly cherished at home."

"O mighty-armed one, you stand in the kingdom as the eldest brother; what is there that is not auspicious for you? You have obtained food and clothing of the highest quality, which ordinary people cannot even attain; why then do you grieve, my son?"
O mighty-armed one, you shine like the Lord of the Gods in heaven, constantly commanding this vast and prosperous kingdom of your fathers and grandfathers;
such sovereignty as yours is very difficult for others to attain.
"O King, those objects of enjoyment have already been described by me;
O you of known wisdom, how is it that this root of sorrow has arisen for you? You ought to explain to me that which is so exceedingly painful."
Duryodhana said:
"O King, a sinful man perceives only that 'I eat' and 'I am clothed,' whereas a man of noble character perceives others who are superior to himself."
That man who harbors resentment is considered the lowest of men.
O Indra among kings, O Lord, this common prosperity does not please me;
seeing the blazing fortune in the son of Kuntī, I am deeply pained.

"Having seen the entire earth brought under the sway of Yudhiṣṭhira, I am firm in my resolve that I shall live; this I tell you out of sorrow. The Caitrikas and Kaukurakas appear as if they have been humbled and are now submissive."
The Kāraskaras and Lohajaṅghas were in Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence; likewise, those from the Himalayas, the coastal regions of the ocean, and all mines of precious gems— all these,
including even the lowest castes, were present in Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence.

O lord of the people, thinking of me as the eldest and the most excellent, Yudhiṣṭhira honored me and appointed me to receive the jewels; indeed, I was charged with appraising the finest jewels presented there,
which were of the highest value.
O Bhārata, neither the farthest limit nor the nearest edge could be seen there;
my hand was no longer sufficient for receiving that wealth as it was brought from afar, and they continued to present it even when I was exhausted.
O Bhārata, I saw a lotus pond constructed by Maya with jewels from Lake Bindu and covered with crystal, appearing as if it were full of water;
while I was lifting up my garment, Vṛkodara laughed at me.
O bull of the Bharata race, the servants and the hall-keepers laughed at him,
who was bewildered by the extraordinary prosperity of his enemy and deprived of jewels.
"If I were able there," [he thought], "I would have struck down Vṛkodara."
O lord of men, if I were to undertake the fierce task of slaying him,
our fate would undoubtedly be like that of Śiśupāla;
for that mockery by my rival burns me, O Bhārata.
And again, O lord of men, thinking that very same pond, so rich with water-born flowers, was solid stone, I fell into the water;
there Kṛṣṇa, together with Pārtha, laughed aloud at me.

And Draupadī, along with the women, distresses my heart; and whatever group of servants there was, O sinless one, they too are mocking me. And the servants, urged by the king, are [handling] the wet clothes in the water.

They gave me other garments, and that was even more painful for me. O lord of men, hear now another deception as I tell it: as I was departing by a way other than the gate, [I was stopped] by one who had the appearance of being stationed at the gate.
Having struck a stone again, I was wounded in the forehead;
and seeing me there in such a state, O King, the women laughed at me, saying, "This is the door, this is not the door. Thus did they speak to me.
Standing before them, Vṛkodara spoke these words with a smile:
"There, the two twin-born sons of Yama, seeing me from afar, were indeed filled with joy;
both together, they embraced me with their arms while grieving."
Sahadeva, as if feeling astonishment, said there to me again and again, "O King, this is the door; go from here. And Bhīmasena spoke there, addressing him as "Son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Having awakened and smiled, O Lord of Men, he said:
"The names of these jewels have not been heard by me before from this gate;
that I have seen them there causes my mind to burn with grief."
I shall enter the fire, or I shall enter the great ocean;
for the infamy of one who has been highly esteemed exceeds death itself.
O Indra among kings, this occurred in that assembly during the great Rājasūya sacrifice.
Duryodhana said:
"O Bhārata, hear that which was seen by me regarding the Pāṇḍavas:
for the foremost treasures were brought from here and there by the lords of the earth."
"O Bhārata, having seen that wealth of my enemy, I find no firm peace of mind, whether it be in terms of its fruits or its land; therefore, take possession of it.
Take the sheep-skins, the deer-skins, and those adorned with gold."
The King of Kamboja gave as wealth excellent cloaks and skins;
three hundred horses, speckled like partridges and with noses like parrots;
and three hundred female camels well-nourished on *pīlu*, *śamī*, and *iṅguda* plants.
The cow-herders, the Brāhmaṇas, and the Dāsamīyas from all quarters—
those highly fortunate ones, desiring to please the high-souled Dharmarāja,
stood at the gate with three hundred billion offerings, having been turned away.
Brāhmaṇas and Vāṭadhānas, possessing herds of cattle by the hundreds,
arrived taking along beautiful water-pots made of gold,
as well as jewels, silver, and pure gold alone.
Delighted, with a serene soul, and surrounded by his own kinsmen,
Traikharva, the lord of the foremost chariots, personally presented himself to the Pāṇḍava;
and he who had been introduced to the king by the chief of the twice-born was Śaṅkha.
Given with affection by Kuṇinda to the wise Dharmarāja,
all his brothers presented that conch shell to their brother, the wearer of the diadem; Bībhatsu accepted that water-born shell adorned with a golden garland.
It was adorned with a thousand gold coins, radiant with its own splendor,
beautiful, lovely to behold, and fashioned by Viśvakarman;
and Dharma, bowing down again and again, bore it.
He who roars even when not eating then roared exceedingly;
at that roar, the kings fell away from their own splendor, rendered inferior—
namely Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāṇḍavas, Sātyaki, and Keśava as the eighth.
Established in courage, endowed with heroism, and acting kindly toward one another, they saw the kings unconscious and laughed at me; then,
being greatly delighted, Bībhatsu gave away cows with golden horns.
O Bhārata, five hundred oxen were sent as a preeminent tribute by Sumukha to Ajātaśatru for that foremost of the twice-born; and Kuṇinda likewise sent gold and various kinds of garments.
The King of Kaśmīra, taking pure *mādhvīka* wine and honey as flavorful as nectar,
brought the entire tribute and presented it to the Pāṇḍava; likewise,
the Yavanas brought horses of great speed from the mountains.
They stand at the gate, barred from entry, with highly precious seats, costly woolen blankets— new, variegated, fine, most excellent, and beautiful to behold— as well as various other jewels.
Śrutāyu, the king of Kaliṅga, [possessed] the unsurpassed jewel-gem;
the women of Aṅga were beautiful, adorned with gold;
and King Vaṅga [possessed] couches made of Jāmbūnada gold by the hundreds.
O Bhārata, from the vicinity of the southern ocean, he brought more than a hundred *prāvāra* cloths, aquatic gems, and tribute,
and presented them to the Pāṇḍava before the other kings.
Pāṇḍya gave to the Pāṇḍava ninety-six *bhāras* of the finest Dārdara sandalwood, as many conch shells,
and an infinite amount of sandalwood, agallochum, pearls, lapis lazuli, and variegated gems.

Both Cola and Kerala indeed gave [presents] to the Pāṇḍava; Aśmaka gave ten thousand cows adorned with gold, possessing golden horns, yielding milk, accompanied by their calves, and providing pots for milking.
The king of the Saindhavas gave twenty-five thousand horses from the Sindhu region,
adorned with golden garlands; and the Sauvīra king gave thirty excellent chariots yoked with elephants.
Having brought ornaments of gold adorned with precious gems,
which were like the midday sun in brilliance and seemed as if they possessed incomparable splendor,
he presented the entire tribute to the Pāṇḍava.
O Bhārata, the King of Avantī brought as tribute thousands of various jewels, excellent necklaces and armlets, diverse ornaments, and even ten thousand female slaves.
O best of men, the King of Daśārṇa, the King of Cedi, and the heroic Śūrasena stand at the gate of the assembly hall, desiring to see you;
they have brought their entire tribute and presented it to the Pāṇḍava.
O King, the powerful [king] was joyfully presented by the King of Kāśī:
eighty thousand cows, eight hundred elephants,
and ten thousand river-born horses adorned with golden garlands.
And the King of Kāśī gave various jewels as tribute; likewise,
the Vaideha king Kṛtakṣaṇa and Bṛhadbala of Kosala each gave fourteen thousand of the finest horses.
Śaibya, together with the Vasātis, and Trigarta, along with the Mālavas,
each of those kings gave him immeasurable jewels—
exquisite necklaces, pearls, and various kinds of ornaments.
Having thus presented the offering, they then obtained entry.
There were a hundred thousand female slaves dressed in cotton garments—
dark-complexioned, slender, with long hair, and adorned with golden ornaments.
Śūdras brought skins of the ranku deer, fit for the most excellent Brahmins;
all of them stood at the gate, desiring to see the son of Pāṇḍu,
while the inhabitants of Bharukaccha brought their entire tribute.
O Great King, they presented horses born in the land of Gandhāra—
those men who live by the mouths of rivers where grain is cultivated by Indra’s plows,
and those born in the coastal gardens and along the Indus.
Those Vairāmas, Pāradas, and Vaṅgas, together with the Kitavas,
having brought various tributes and diverse jewels,
as well as goats, sheep, cattle, gold, donkeys, camels, and honey produced from fruit, [waited upon the king].
Various kinds of woolen blankets stand at the gate, barred from entry.
The heroic lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, the powerful ruler of the Mlecchas,
King Bhagadatta, a great chariot-warrior, stands there accompanied by his Yavana troops.
Taking swift, noble steeds with the speed of the wind,
and bringing the entire tribute, he stands at the gate, barred from entry.
He carries vessels made of iron and swords with hilts of pure ivory.
Then Bhagadatta, the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa, having given that [elephant] away, departed;
he was followed by those with two eyes, those with three eyes, those with eyes on their foreheads, who had gathered from various directions—
those wearing turbans, those without clothing, the Bāhukas, and the man-eaters.
And there I saw one-footed beings barred at the gate,
who were giving much gold and silver as tribute to him;
kings of various complexions, having brought tribute, [stood] there in great numbers.

They brought ten thousand well-trained donkeys, black-necked and large-bodied, capable of leaping great distances; they were famous in all directions, endowed with the proper proportions and color, and born on the banks of the Vaṅkṣu.
Having been granted entry, they arrived at Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence—
[steeds] with the hue of indragopaka insects, the color of parrots, swift as thought,
resembling rainbows, and even like the clouds of twilight.
Having captured wild horses of many colors that were as swift as thought,
the Ekapādakas gave him gold of priceless value;
then King Siṃhala, having accepted that great wealth, [departed].
Gośīrṣaka, Padmaka, Hari, and Śyāma sandalwood—
each weighing a hundred *bhāras*— stands held back at the gate,
O King, as do those from the land of the Nagnas and the renowned Barbaras.
O Great King, a hundred thousand maidservants and thousands of woolen blankets, having been brought forth, stand at the gate, barred from entry;
so too do the kings of Pauṇḍra and Dāmalipta, who act according to their own will.
Taking with them kāleyaka, silver, and various articles of personal use, as well as aloe-wood, crystal, ivory,
nutmegs, *takkola*, cloves, and camphor, those of great strength set forth.
Having brought various other articles, they stood waiting; all these great-souled ones remained at the gate, held back. Then King Śaileya, having taken hold of fine woolen cloths, [approached].
Standing at the gate, O Great King, he was turned back by the gatekeepers;
[he saw] the Cīnas, Hūṇas, Śakas, Oḍras, and those dwelling among the mountains,
as well as the Vārṣṇeyas, Hārahūṇas, Kṛṣṇas, and the people of the Himalayas.

I am unable to describe those Niṣādas, Pārasicas, and dark-skinned people from the Himalayas, who were of various kinds and barred at the gate; I cannot recount those diverse folk who arrived and were turned away at the entrance.
To provide him with strength,
they brought ten thousand well-trained donkeys, famous throughout the quarters, which were black-necked, massive in body, capable of traveling a hundred leagues, and appeared in many diverse forms.
Rich with the touch of the passion for fine measurements, those born in Bāhlīca and Cīna,
as well as the Kharvaṭas and Tomaras— brave men likewise from Vardhanaka—
stood at the gate, holding various kinds of garments, though they were held back.
The Prākoṭas, the Tāṭakeyas, the Nandināgarakas,
the Tāpitas, the Traipuras, the Pañcameyas along with the Urus,
and likewise all the Aṭavikas, with their various goods and equipment—
Having taken them with them, O Great King, they stand at the gate, barred from entry;
[carrying] woolen cloths, those made of ranku-deer hair, as well as those produced from insects and from silk,
and likewise others, thousands of pieces, ground fine and possessing the luster of lotuses.
Smooth cloth made of non-cotton and wool, soft skins of antelope, sharpened long swords, spears, javelins, and battle-axes,
as well as sharp axes produced in the western regions.
Having brought various juices, diverse fragrances, and thousands of gems,
as well as the entire tribute, they stood at the gate, barred from entry.
These were the Śakas, Tukhāras, Kaṅkas, Romaśas, and the horned men.

Having brought as tribute various offerings— including many great and far-ranging horses numbering in the hundreds of millions, and gold measured by the *padma* in countless crores— they stand at the gate, held back.
There were highly precious seats, vehicles, and couches,
variegated with jewels and gold, as well as those made of ivory; there were also costly coats of mail and various kinds of weapons.
And chariots of various forms, adorned with gold,
equipped with well-trained horses and covered with tiger-skins;
and variegated rugs and jewels by the thousands.

Having given iron arrows, half-nārāca arrows, and various other weapons— this great wealth— the king who was the sovereign of the eastern region entered the sacrificial hall of the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
With joy, he gave to the son of Pṛthā two thousand garments of black deer-skin, ten thousand fine linen cloths, bronze vessels, highly precious rugs, and various other jewels.
O King, other men dwelling by the ocean brought various kinds of jewels and gave them to the Pāṇḍava; and then, O King,
the Mālavas also presented various gems.
O Indra among kings, having taken ten million *droṇas* of wheat and various other kinds of grain,
the mighty one gave them to the Pāṇḍava with affection and entered the great sacrifice.
Taking many various jewels, O Great King, the king who was the lord of Surāṣṭra brought ten thousand *droṇas* of jars filled with oil,
as well as sweet white sugar-candy by the thousands of carts, O King.
Taking all of these, he gave them to the son of Kuntī.
And other kings, O King, who had gathered from various lands,
having taken diverse jewels, gave them to the descendant of Kuru.
In the entirety of Jambūdvīpa, including its kingdoms, forests, and mountains,
there is no king who does not pay tribute to Pārtha;
nor is there any man among the seven regions who has not come to his sacrifice.
Crowded with various groups of people, it shone like the assembly hall of Śakra.
Duryodhana said:
"O sinless one, hear from me as I describe the various gifts he bestowed upon him."
That great accumulation of wealth given by kings for the sake of sacrifice,
which those [ascetics] enjoy under the delightful shade of the *kīcaka* bamboos along the Śailodā river between the mountains Meru and Mandara— [all that was lost].
The Khaśas, Ekāśanas, Ājyohas, Pradaras, and Dīrghaveṇus; the Paśupās, Kuṇindas, Taṅgaṇas, and Parataṅgaṇas—
they indeed possess that which is called Pipīlika, granted as a boon by the ants.
The kings brought gold measured by droṇas in heaps;
black, white, and moon-bright yak-tails with beautiful markings;
and much sweet honey produced from Himalayan flowers.
They brought away garlands from the Northern Kurus with water,
and from the northern Kailāsa, medicinal herbs of great power; having brought these and other tributes from the mountain regions, they stood bowed before him.
They stand barred at the gate of King Ajātaśatru—
those kings who dwell beyond the Himavat on the Sunrise Mountain,
those along the shore of the Vāriṣeṇa ocean, and those all around the Lohitya river.
O Lord, I also see those Kirātas who subsist on fruits and roots, who are clothed in skins,
who wield cruel weapons, and who perform cruel deeds; and I see loads of sandalwood, aguru wood, and kālīyaka.
O Lord of the people, having brought heaps of skins, jewels, gold, and perfumes, as well as ten thousand Kairātika slave-girls and charming creatures— beasts and birds— from distant lands;
Having brought gold of great luster gathered from the mountains and having taken their entire tribute, they stand at the gate, barred from entry—
these Kāyavyas, Daradas, Dārvas, and the heroic Vaiyamakas.
The Audumbaras, who are difficult to distinguish [from others], the Pāradas along with the Bāhlikas,
the Kāśmīras, the Kundamānas, the Paurakas, the Haṃsakāyanas, the Śibis, Trigartas, Yaudheyas, the Rājanyas, and the Madrakas and Kekayas.
The Ambaṣṭhas, Kaukuras, Tārkṣyas, and Vastrapas along with the Pahlavas;
the Vasātis with the Mauleyas, together with the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas;
and the Śauṇḍikas, Kukkurās, and Śakas, O lord of the people.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, Śānavatyas, and likewise the Gayas—
noble-born, organized into guilds, and preeminent, with weapons in hand—
these Kṣatriyas brought wealth by the hundreds to Ajātaśatru.
The Vaṅgas, the lords of Kaliṅga, the Tāmraliptas along with the Puṇḍrakas;
the Draviḍas, Oḍras, and Pāṇḍyas, as well as the Colas and Kulyas;
[they brought] fine linen, silk from Kośala, woven leaf-fiber cloth, and even heavy cloaks.

O Bhārata, many there were who wore ear-flaps; they were mountain-dwellers from whom [the king] took what was not to be taken away, yet they did not feel great affection [for him]. The kings of the borderlands gave him tribute, yet they did not come [to pay homage].

There, by the king's command, they were addressed by the gatekeepers: "Having performed your task and being well-adorned with ornaments, you shall then obtain entrance. [Enter] those elephants with tusks like plowshafts, girths of gold, lotus-colored, and covered with blankets."
Having given one thousand armored elephants at each gate— elephants resembling mountains, ever-intoxicated, and stationed all around Lake Kāmyaka—
they then entered through the gateway. These elephants were patient and of noble breed.
The Surasas, with their sandalwood juices, were stationed in golden jars;
and there were the Vaidehakas, the Puṇḍras, the Goleyas, and the Tāmraliptakas;
the Marukas, the Kāśikas, the Dardas, and the Bhaumeyas, along with actors and dancers.
The Karṇāṭas, the Kāṃsyakuṭṭas, the Padmajālas, the Sutīvaras,
the Dākṣiṇātyas, the Pulindas, the Śambaras, the Kaṅkaṇas, the Khaṣas,
the Barbaras, the Yavanas, as well as the Gurjaras and the Ābhīras.
The Pallavas, Śakas, Kārūṣas, Tumbaras, and likewise the Kāśikas—
these and many other hosts have assembled here from all directions;
and other jewels have been brought here by those high-souled ones.
The Gandharva named Citraratha, a follower of Vāsava,
gave four hundred horses with the speed of the wind. And the Gandharva Tumburu, being greatly delighted, [gave] a hundred steeds.
O lord of the people, O descendant of Kuru, the skillful king gave away hundreds of boars with skins the color of mango leaves and adorned with golden garlands;
he also gave away a great many of the finest elephants.
Virāṭa, the king of the Matsyas, brought two thousand rutting elephants adorned with golden garlands for the sake of tribute;
and from the kingdom of Pāṃśu, King Vasudāna presented twenty-six elephants.
O King, lord of men, he presented two thousand horses adorned with golden garlands— youthful, endowed with speed and strength—
and having taken the entire tribute, he offered it to the Pāṇḍavas.
O lord of the people, Yajñasena gave fourteen thousand female slaves and ten thousand male slaves together with their wives,
as well as twenty-five thousand horses adorned with golden garlands.
King Bāhlīka gave to the high-souled Pāṇḍava twenty-six chariots yoked with elephants, O great king,
and he offered his entire kingdom to the sons of Pṛthā for the sake of the sacrifice.
Vāsudeva, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, out of respect for Kirīṭin,
gave fourteen thousand of the finest elephants;
for Pārtha is indeed the self of Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa is the self of Kirīṭin.
Whatever Arjuna might say to Kṛṣṇa, he would do it all without doubt;
Kṛṣṇa would even renounce the heavenly realm for the sake of Dhanañjaya,
and likewise, Pārtha would even sacrifice his life for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Fragrant juices of sandalwood contained in golden jars; heaps of sandalwood and agallochum produced on Mount Sahya and growing on Mount Dardura; radiant jewels and gems, gold, and fine garments.
Even Caula and Pāṇḍya, though they arrived at the gate, did not obtain entrance;
O Great King, it is for this reason that my inner soul finds no peace,
for it appears as if a yoke were tied to a horse in reverse.
O bull of the Bharatas, even though he is inferior in qualities to you,
the younger ones are prospering while the eldest son languishes;
they say this is due to the devotion of the wise son of Kuntī.
All the Kṣatriyas, endowed with their own strength and proud of their honor,
as well as those kings among the Mlecchas who paid tribute at his sacrifice,
were exceedingly delighted; so too were the sons of Pāṇḍu, those great chariot-warriors.
The Siṃhalas brought there hundreds of sea-essences, lapis lazuli, pearls, and conch shells,
as well as elephant blankets; they were dark-complexioned with copper-hued eyes, adorned with necklaces of jewels.
Having seized them there, the men stood at the gate, holding them back;
for the sake of pleasing [the king], the Brāhmaṇas and the conquered Kṣatriyas brought offerings, as did the Vaiśyas and even the Śūdras who were intent on service.
Out of affection and great respect,
all the Mlecchas— belonging to all castes, including those born at the beginning, middle, and end [of the social order]—
as well as those who had come from various countries belonging to diverse tribes, approached Yudhiṣṭhira.

This world seems as if overturned within Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence; seeing the many diverse tributes sent by kings— which are themselves the sorrows of my enemies— a desire for death arises in me today.
O Bhārata, I shall now describe to you those who were the servants of the Pāṇḍavas,
for whom Yudhiṣṭhira provided both raw and cooked food:
ten thousand and three padmas of elephant-riders together with their cavalry.
There were also a hundred million chariots and many foot soldiers; they began to be slaughtered, cooked,
and likewise cast away elsewhere amidst the very sounds of auspicious proclamations.

In Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence, I did not see anyone among all the social orders who had not eaten, who was not joyful, or who was not well-fed in any way. There were eighty-eight thousand *snātaka* householders.

But those noble kings who are true to their word and observe great vows— each one of whom Yudhiṣṭhira supports with thirty maidservants— they too, being well-pleased and fully satisfied, pray for the destruction of his enemies.
Ten thousand other ascetics with vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas) eat from golden vessels in Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence; they consume everything—
whether already eaten or not yet eaten, prepared or unprepared— even including those who are hunchbacked or dwarfish.
O lord of the people, while she did not eat, Yājñasenī watched closely;
O Bhārata, two [kings] did not pay tribute to the son of Kuntī—
the Pāñcālas on account of their marriage alliance, and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis on account of their friendship.
Duryodhana said:

"Those noble kings who are true to their word and firm in their great vows, who have mastered all branches of knowledge, who are eloquent speakers, and who have performed the final purificatory bath of the Vedānta— [they are here]."
Resolute, restrained by a sense of shame, righteous in soul, and illustrious—
those consecrated kings wait upon him,
having been brought by other monarchs for the sake of sacrificial gifts, with milch cows that yield from bronze vessels.
O Bhārata, I saw there thousands of wild cattle here and there; the kings, having personally lifted them up with respect,
brought them for the sake of the consecration, as well as various vessels without distraction.
Bāhlīka brought the chariot adorned with gold;
Sudakṣiṇa yoked it with white horses born in Kamboja.
The highly illustrious Sunītha attached its peerless undercarriage.
The lord of Cedi quickly seized the raised standard himself;
the Southerner took the armor, and the King of Magadha took the garland and the turban;
and Vasudāna, the great archer, took a lordly sixty-year-old elephant.
Matsya fastened the dice, Ekalavya the sandals, and the king of Avanti likewise brought various kinds of water for the consecration. Cekitāna presented a quiver, and the king of Kāśī offered a bow.
Then Dhaumya and Vyāsa, of great ascetic merit, consecrated Śalya with a sword that had a golden hilt, a shaft made of śaikya iron, and was adorned with gold;
they did so while placing Nārada, Devala, and the sage Asita at their head.
The Brahmins, endowed with knowledge and resembling the sun in brilliance, approached with joy the best of sages, Yājñavalkya— the son of Brahmā whose senses were conquered—
to attend his consecration. The great seers stood before him full of affection.
Accompanied by the son of Jamadagni and other masters of the Vedas,
they approached that high-souled king, who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees according to the sacred mantras,
just as the Seven Sages approach the great Indra, the lord of the gods, in heaven.
Then Sātyaki, whose valor is truth, held his umbrella; Dhananjaya and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava both held two fans;
and the twins then took up two pure white yak-tail whisks.
The ocean brought for him that conch of Varuṇa, which Prajāpati had taken for Indra in a former age;
it was fashioned by Viśvakarman and adorned with a thousand gold coins.

When I was consecrated there by Kṛṣṇa, a faintness came over me, O Indra among kings. There, for the sake of water, the Rākṣasas took up jars and went from the eastern ocean to the western and even to the southern.
But they could not proceed further toward the north without their winged steeds, O dear one.
There, for the sake of auspiciousness, they blew conchs by the hundreds; as those were blown, their sound resounded, and my hair stood on end.
The kings, bowing down, fell as if deprived of their own splendor;
yet Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāṇḍavas, Sātyaki, and Keśava as the eighth—
established in goodness, endowed with heroism, and acting for one another's welfare— remained firm.
Seeing the kings unconscious and seeing me as well, they then laughed aloud.
Then, overjoyed, Bībhatsu gave away cows with golden horns,
reddish-brown in color, accompanied by their calves, and yoked to carts weighing a hundred *suvarṇas* of gold.
O Bhārata, having likewise given one thousand [cows] adorned with cloths and foot-ornaments,
along with five hundred oxen to the foremost of the twice-born,
neither the slayer of Śambara, nor Yauvanāśva, nor Manu attained such [merit].
Neither King Pṛthu Vainya, nor Bhagīratha,
nor Yayāti, nor even Nahuṣa was like King Yudhiṣṭhira,
O son of Kuntī, who is endowed with such extraordinary and supreme splendor.
Having thus attained the Rājasūya sacrifice like the lord Hariścandra, you were not one who failed in his duties toward the Sāṃnāhikas nor likewise toward the Ākṣiṇeyas; for,
O Lord, having beheld this prosperity in Pārtha, it is as if it were in Hariścandra himself.
"How indeed do you see my life as superior, O Bhārata?
O lord of men, it is like a yoke tied by a blind man, turned upside down;
the younger ones prosper while the elder ones decline, O Bhārata."
Seeing this, O hero of the Kurus, I find no peace even upon careful reflection;
it is for this reason that I have become so emaciated.
[He saw] their paleness and their state of grief.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O son, you are indeed the eldest and the son of the eldest; do not hate the Pāṇḍavas."

For the hater takes upon himself misery just as he does death itself. O bull of the Bharatas, how could one such as you hate Yudhiṣṭhira, who is unaggressive, shares your goals, is your equal friend, and harbors no hatred toward you?
"O King, O son, how can you, being equal in lineage and prowess to your brother, desire his royal splendor out of delusion? Do not be thus; be peaceful here for the sake of what is right.
Or, O bull among the Bharatas, if it is that sacrificial glory you desire,"
Let the officiating priests perform for you the great seven-threaded sacrifice;
the kings shall also bring you abundant wealth,
as well as jewels and ornaments, out of affection and great respect.
For this earth is indeed a cow that milks all desires, and she is called the wife of the hero;
likewise, the earth, when supported by a hero, fulfills one's heart's desire. If you too possess such valor, you shall surely obtain this earth.

O dear one, the practice of what is harmful— namely, the intense longing for another's property— brings suffering in both worlds and the contempt of friends. He who is self-contented and established in his own duty truly prospers in happiness.
Non-interference in the affairs of others, constant diligence in one's own duties,
and effort in protecting one's own interests— this is the mark of greatness.
A man who remains unperturbed in calamities, who is skillful, and who is always industrious [attains it].
The vigilant man who has disciplined his self always beholds auspicious things.
Do not cut off these [sons] as one would arms; the sons of Pāṇḍu are just like that to you. Therefore, for the sake of wealth, do not commit treachery against your brothers.
O King, do not harbor hatred toward the sons of Pāṇḍu here; likewise, their entire paternal wealth belongs to you. My dear son, there is great unrighteousness in betraying a friend.
Those who were your grandfathers are also theirs;
therefore, the great dharma is proclaimed as being [the avoidance of] treachery toward friends.
For he who was your grandfather is indeed the same for them as well.
"Bestowing wealth within the sacrificial altar, experiencing beloved desires,
and sporting with women without fear— be at peace, O bull of the Bharatas.
Duryodhana said:
Knowing [the truth], you indeed delude me, like one boat tied to another on a ship. Do you lack attention to your own interest, or do you perhaps hate me?
For he who possesses no innate wisdom, though he be merely very learned, [is like this].
He does not understand the meaning of the scriptures, just as a ladle does not know the taste of the soup.
These sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra do not exist for whom you are an instructor;
you always speak of future matters as if they were your own duty.
For how could those who follow his footsteps find the path if he is led by others, lacks leadership, and is confused about the way?
O King, one whose wisdom is fully developed, who serves the elders, and has conquered his senses— [should be followed].
"You utterly delude us who are intent upon our own duties. Bṛhaspati has said that the conduct of kings is different from the conduct of the world;
therefore, a king must always consider his own interest with great effort."
O Great King, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya is centered on victory.
Whether that be dharma or adharma, O bull of the Bharatas, let it be so within his own duty;
he should drive all the directions before him, as a charioteer does with a whip.
O bull of the Bharatas, he who desires to seize the blazing glory of his enemy—
whether by secret or open means— that strategic application which destroys the foe is indeed the true weapon for those skilled in weapons; it is not considered a weapon that merely cuts.
Neither an enemy nor a friend should be recorded in writing, nor even in a register, O King;
for he who causes one distress is called an enemy.
Lack of contentment is the root of prosperity; therefore, I desire it.
O King, he who strives for elevation is the supreme statesman.
Indeed, one should not cultivate a sense of "mine-ness" regarding sovereignty or wealth;
for others seize what was previously acquired—this, they know, is the duty of a king.

Having made a pact of non-aggression, Śakra severed the head of Namuci; for that is considered by him to be the eternal conduct toward an enemy. The earth swallows these two, just as a snake swallows creatures dwelling in holes.
O lord of the people, there is no such thing as an enemy by birth for a man, provided he does not oppose the king and does not exile a Brahmin;
he with whom one shares a common livelihood is the enemy, and no other person.
He who, out of delusion, neglects an enemy faction that is prospering,
cuts off his own root, just like a disease that has been allowed to grow. For even a minor enemy, if his prowess increases excessively, [will destroy him].
Like an anthill growing from its base, it devours the tree from within;
O descendant of Ajamidha, O Bharata, let not the prosperity of the enemy please you. This burden rests upon the heads of those possessed of strength; this is the policy of the virtuous.
He who desires the growth of his wealth like the increase of his progeny truly prospers among his kinsmen; for such prowess indeed brings immediate advancement.
Until I have attained the sovereignty of the Pāṇḍavas, there will be no peace for me.
"Either I shall attain that prosperity, or I shall lie slain in battle.
O lord of men, what is the use of life to one such as I today?
The Pāṇḍavas are constantly increasing, while our own growth has come to a standstill."
Śakuni said:
"That prosperity which you see in Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, and because of which you suffer, I shall take it away from him; let the opponent be challenged to a game of dice."
"O King, let Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, be summoned.
Without entering into danger and without fighting at the head of the army, I shall cast the dice and, remaining unhurt myself, achieve victory over the ignorant through my own wisdom."
"Know, O Bhārata, that the stakes are my bows, and the dice are my arrows. Know that the heart of the dice is my bowstring, and the chariot is my quiver.
Duryodhana said:
"O King, this man, skilled in dice, is capable of seizing the fortune from the sons of Pāṇḍu by means of gambling; therefore, dear father, let that be pleasing to you. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I abide by the teaching of my high-souled brother Vidura;
having met with him, I shall learn the final decision regarding this matter.
Duryodhana said:

"O Kaurava, Vidura— free from doubt and devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, not so much to mine— will destroy your understanding. O lord of the people, that steward (Kṣattṛ) is even superior to Kṛṣṇa in intelligence."

He spoke only of dharma, not as a means for victory; and likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, policy devoid of dharma is the same. Therefore, for one who seeks to conquer through discipline, both of these are mutually contradictory.
A man should not undertake his own task through the agency of another;
O joy of the Kurus, there is no equality of intellect between two people regarding their undertakings.
A fool, avoiding fear and protecting himself, [acts thus].
Like a sodden mat in the rainy season, one perishes while remaining [in this state].
Neither diseases nor Yama wait for the attainment of the highest good;
as long as one is capable, so long should one practice what is beneficial.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O son, I do not at all approve of your conflict with those who are powerful;
for enmity creates a transformation that is indeed a weapon made of no iron."
O Prince, you mistake what is harmful for what is beneficial;
this weaving together of most terrible strife has indeed begun in some manner or other.
And he would also release his swords and arrows.
Duryodhana said:
"In ancient times, the practice of gambling was established by the ancients."
In that matter, there is no transgression and no conflict. Therefore, let the words of Śakuni be pleasing to you today;
quickly issue the command for the assembly hall here.
The gate to heaven is distinguished for those who gamble;
it is likewise appropriate for those who abide therein.
For in this way, it would indeed be equal to oneself.
"Engage in a game of dice with the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The words you have spoken do not please me."
"O lord of men, let that which is pleasing to you be done; otherwise, you will suffer later for having undertaken such speech, for words of this kind are not consistent with dharma."
For this very thing was foreseen by Vidura,
who followed his wisdom and knowledge long ago;
and now that same fate comes upon him against his will.
"A great danger that destroys the seed of the Kṣatriyas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
Considering fate to be supreme and insurmountable,
the king— his mind bewildered by destiny— stood firm in his son's words and loudly commanded his men.
A supreme assembly hall of mine, one *krośa* in length, adorned with a thousand pillars of gold and lapis lazuli, possessing a hundred doors and pinnacles of crystal on its archways.
"Let those who are diligent, having heard his words, quickly make it wide, acting with haste and without hesitation"; the wise and skillful ones then made it so swiftly.
All kinds of materials were brought to the assembly hall,
and thousands of artisans were employed; then, in a short time, it reached completion.
They informed that king with confidence of his beautiful assembly hall, filled with many jewels and wonderful, furnished with various golden seats.
Then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, spoke thus to the wise Vidura, the chief minister:
"Go indeed to Prince Yudhiṣṭhira."
"By my word, bring here quickly that assembly hall of mine,
which is variegated with many jewels and furnished with costly beds and seats."
"Let her come together with her brothers and let a friendly game of dice proceed here"—
having understood this wish of his son, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, [acted accordingly].

Considering fate to be insurmountable, the king acted accordingly. Thus addressed unrighteously by his brother, Vidura— the best among the wise— did not approve of his words and spoke these words to him:
"O King, I do not welcome this command;
do not act thus, for I fear the destruction of our lineage.
With sons divided, conflict will surely arise."
"I suspect this, O King, was done for the sake of gambling.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Kṣattṛ, this quarrel here will not cause me grief."
If destiny were not adverse,
for this entire world indeed moves under the control of what has been ordained by the Creator and is not independent.
"O Vidura, having reached the king today by my command,
quickly bring the invincible Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Vidura set forth with noble horses— swift, powerful, well-trained,
and strong— having been dispatched by force by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having set out on that path and reached the king’s city, he of great intelligence entered into the presence of the wise Pāṇḍavas, being honored by the twice-born.
Having reached Rājagṛha, which resembled the abode of Kubera,
that righteous-souled one approached Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
The high-minded king, firm in truth, [received him].
Having received Vidura with due honor and respect, Ajātaśatru, the descendant of Ajamīḍha,
then inquired after Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons.
Yudhiṣṹṭhira said:
"I perceive that there is no joy in your mind;
O Kṣattṛ, have you returned in safety?"
"Are the sons of the elder [king] compliant with him? And are the subjects also obedient to his will?
Vidura said:
The high-souled king is well, along with his sons;
he dwells surrounded by kinsmen who are like Indra,
O King, and is delighted by his well-disciplined sons.
Free from sorrow, delighting in the self, and firm in soul—
this is what the Kuru king said to you, after first inquiring after your welfare and your well-being.
"This assembly hall is equal in form to your own;
go there, my son, and behold it, O Pārtha, having met with your brothers in that place."
"Let a friendly game of dice be played and let us enjoy ourselves; we take pleasure in your company,
as do all the Kurus who have assembled here."
You will see those gamblers who have been appointed there by the high-souled King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, already seated and ready for play.
"Thus have I come, O King; please accept that.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṣattṛ, in gambling there is strife for us."
Who indeed, being wise, would take pleasure in gambling? Or what do you consider to be the most appropriate course? We all stand ready to abide by your word.
Vidura said:
"I know that gambling is the root of calamity,
and I have made every effort to prevent it."
"The king has sent me to you;
having heard this, O learned one, do what is most beneficial here.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who were the other gamblers playing there besides the sons of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
I ask you, Vidura; tell us who they were."
"With whom we play, having assembled by the hundreds.
Vidura said:
"O lord of the people, Śakuni, the king of Gandhāra,"
Rājātideva, Kṛtahasta, Matākṣa,
Viviṃśati, Citrasena, King Satyavrata, Purumitra, and Jaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The gamblers who have assembled here are full of great danger; they are players who employ deceitful stratagems."
"This world is indeed under the control of what is ordained by the Creator;
it was not by those gamblers that I was made to play today.
Nor did I [play] at the command of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
O sage, I do not wish to go to the gambling match;
for a father is always beloved by his son, and I shall do exactly as you, Vidura, have told me.
I would not have played with Śakuni against my will,
nor would he have dared to challenge me in the assembly hall had he not done so; once challenged, I never turn back.
"Therefore, that eternal vow has indeed been undertaken by me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to Vidura, the King of Dharma—
Having quickly ordered all the provisions for the journey,
on the following day he set out with his attendants and followers,
accompanied by the women, headed by Draupadī.
"Destiny steals away one's wisdom, just as a falling flash of light blinds the eye;
and man falls under the power of the Creator, as if bound by snares.
Having spoken thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira departed together with Kṣattṛ.
Unable to endure that challenge, Pārtha,
the subduer of enemies and slayer of hostile heroes, mounted the chariot given by Bāhlīka; thus clad in armor, the son of Pāṇḍu set forth together with his brothers.
Then he dispatched messengers toward the city called Nāgāhvaya;
those tigers among kings then carried out the king’s command.
Thereafter, the king of great splendor, together with Dhaumya and his retinue, [set forth].
Having had the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions, he went out from the palace;
having given wealth to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule for their journey,
and having given wealth to others as well, he prepared to depart for that place.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, worthy of a king, and accompanied by his retinue—
the great king mounted that lordly elephant, sixty years of age,
and sat upon a supreme golden seat on the elephant’s neck.
Wearing a golden diadem, radiant as gold, and adorned with every ornament,
O King, Pārtha shone with supreme royal splendor,
like a wise fire blazing upon a golden altar.
Then the king departed, with his men and mounts filled with joy,
filling the expanse of the sky with the great roar of his chariot,
while being extolled with hymns of praise by bards, genealogists, and panegyrists.
Surrounded by a great army like the sun with its own rays,
King Yudhiṣṭhira shone with a white parasol held over his head, like the lord of stars on a full-moon night.
Seated upon his elephant between both wings, the joy of the Kurus,
blazing with royal splendor, proceeded with Brahmā at his head,
while yak-tail whisks with golden handles were fanned on all sides.

O bull of the Bharatas, the son of Pāṇḍu received with due propriety the blessings of victory from the joyful men along the road. Others, being composed, [honored] the Kuru king as he proceeded on the path.
Men constantly praise his happiness with the sounds of beasts and birds;
likewise, O King, the soldiers who follow the king—
their tumultuous roar stands pervading the very heavens.
The mighty Bhīma, mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant, went before the king;
on both sides of the king were two well-equipped elephants with their seats, and the twins (Yama) also proceeded, O bull of the Bharatas, having likewise ascended them.
Both of them, resplendent in form, graced the great army;
behind them followed the wise Pārtha, the best among wielders of weapons,
having mounted the chariot given by Agni and taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow with his white horses.
O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, marched into the midst of the army;
while the women, headed by Draupadī, accompanied by their attendants and with all their belongings,
mounted upon various palanquins and wagons.
O King, at that time, a great army marched ahead of the king;
it was abundant with men, elephants, and horses, adorned with banners, chariots, and standards,
equipped with chariots and swords, and resounded with the noise of foot soldiers.
Resounding with conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, flutes, and lutes,
O King, that army of the Pāṇḍavas shone as it marched forth at that time,
like Kubera in Laṅkā in days of yore with his supreme splendor.
He went with his venerable friend accompanied by a great army;
likewise Pārtha also proceeded with great magnificence and a very prosperous host, just like Vaiśravaṇa.
