O great king, he passed by lakes, rivers, forests, and groves, and eventually arrived at the city; indeed,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the Kurus, drew near to Hastināpura.

"With that prince who is unworthy [of such status],
I shall play with you as if with one who is dear, though he is not.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, Śakuni, determined and resorting to deceit,
said to Yudhiṣṭhira, "I have won.
Śakuni said:
"O King, these two beloved sons of Mādrī have been won by me for you;
yet I consider Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya to be even dearer to you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"You surely practice unrighteousness, you who do not regard the rule of conduct;
O fool, you who wish to create a division among us who are of one mind.
Śakuni said:
The intoxicated man falls into a pit; the heedless man strikes against a pillar.
O King, you are the eldest and the most excellent; salutations to you, O bull among the Bharatas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, they do not see those things either in sleep or while awake.
"Like intoxicated gamblers when they are playing, they prattle on like those who have lost their senses.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"He who, like a boat, leads us across the ocean of battle;"
O Śakuni, I shall play with that Phalguna, the son of a king, who is swift, a conqueror of his enemies, and a hero of the world, though he is undeserving of such a match.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, Śakuni, resolute and resorting to deceit,
addressed Yudhiṣṭhira, saying, "I have won."
Śakuni said:
"This archer among the Pāṇḍavas, this Savyasācin, has been defeated by me."
"O King, stake Bhīma, your beloved,
for what remains of yours, O Pāṇḍava, that can be played by the son of Kitava.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
He who is our leader, he who is our guide in battles; like the wielder of the thunderbolt, the sole enemy of the Dānavas,
that high-souled one with his side-long glance and knitted brows.
He who has the shoulders of a lion and is ever intolerant of insult,
to whom no man is equal in strength,
the foremost among mace-bearers here, the crusher of enemies.
"O King, I shall play with that prince Bhīmasena, who is unworthy [of such a stake].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, Śakuni, resolute and resorting to deceit,
said to Yudhiṣṭhira, "I have won.
Śakuni said:
"You have lost much wealth, as well as your brothers along with their horses and elephants.
Tell me, O Kaunteya, if there is any wealth remaining that has not been lost.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I am the most distinguished among all my brothers and likewise beloved by them;
once we have been defeated, we ourselves shall perform the labor during the calamity.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, Śakuni, resolute and resorting to deceit,
said to Yudhiṣṭhira, "I have won.
Śakuni said:
"You have committed this most wicked deed, that you have defeated yourself, O King, while wealth still remained. To defeat oneself is a sin.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Śakuni, the master of dice, defeated all those world-heroes who stood at the gambling match, challenging each one individually. Śakuni said:
"Indeed, you have one beloved queen who remains undefeated as a stake;
bet Kṛṣṇā of Pañcāla and win yourself back with her.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Neither short nor tall, neither too dark nor too ruddy,
with eyes reddened by passion— with her, whose eyes are like the petals of an autumn lotus and whose scent is that of an autumn lotus, I play with you.
With a beauty equal to Śrī, she would be like one who dwells among autumn lotuses; likewise, she would possess such benevolence, such perfection of form,
and such excellence of character as a man might desire in a woman.
For a man who desires the attainment of virtue, pleasure, and wealth should seek a woman endowed with all virtues— affectionate, sweet-spoken, and such as this:
she who goes to rest last and wakes up first.
From the cowherds and shepherds on down, he knows everything that has been done and left undone.
His face shines like a lotus when perspiring and like a jasmine flower;
standing in the center of the sacrificial altar, she has long hair, copper-colored eyes, and is not overly hairy.
"O King, with this very Draupadī, the princess of Pañcāla, who is slender-waisted, beautiful-limbed, and of such a nature, I shall play for the stake— alas, O son of Subala!
Vaiśampāyana said:

When these words had been spoken by the King of Dharma, O Bhārata, the cry of "Fie! Fie! issued forth from the elders present in the assembly. That assembly was agitated, O King, and various conversations arose among the monarchs.
Sweat broke out upon Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others;
Vidura, clutching his head, became like one whose life-force had departed,
sitting with his face cast down, meditating and sighing like a serpent.
Bāhlīka, Somadatta the son of Pratīpa, along with Saṃjaya,
the son of Droṇa, Bhūriśravas, and Yuyutsu the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
washing their hands with downcast faces, they sighed like serpents.

But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with joy, asked again and again, "What has been won? What has been won? for he could not conceal his outward expression. Karṇa, along with Duḥśāsana and the others, rejoiced exceedingly.
But from the eyes of the other members of the assembly, tears fell.
Saubala, however, appearing victorious and intoxicated with pride, did not hesitate;
crying out "I have won," he once again took up those dice.
Duryodhana said:
"Come, Kshattri, bring Draupadi here—
the beloved wife who is highly esteemed by the Pandavas."
"Let her sweep the house and depart quickly;
let there be joy for us along with our female slaves.
Vidura said:
It is difficult for one such as you to discern; O dull-witted one, bound by your fetters,
you do not realize that you are hanging over a precipice.
Out of extreme childishness, you provoke tigers;
upon your head are venomous serpents, full of poison and great in their power. Do not be angry, O dull-witted soul; do not go to the abode of Yama.
"O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇā has not truly entered into slavery,
for it is my opinion that she was staked by a king who was no longer his own master.
This man [Duryodhana] bears himself like a bamboo that brings about its own destruction."
The fruit belongs to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son; for this gambling leads to enmity and great peril, yet like one who is ripe, he does not perceive it at the time of his end.
One should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor a speaker of cruel words;
one should not take from another what belongs to a lowly person,
nor that speech by which another would be agitated.
One should not utter that harsh speech which leads to worlds of sin, for abusive words issue from the mouth,
and by them one who is struck grieves day and night.
They fall upon the vital spots of another;
a wise person should not discharge them at others.
Indeed, it is said that once a goat dug up a weapon.
Just as one who has lost his sword might painfully dig into the earth with his feet to sever his own throat,
so too, do not dig up this enmity with the sons of Pāṇḍu.
They do not declare any blameworthy sin in one who dwells in the forest or a householder,
whether he be an ascetic or one whose knowledge is fully perfected.
Indeed, these dog-like men are always barking thus at the most terrible and crooked gate of hell;
yet you do not perceive it, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Many followers of the Kurus, along with Duḥśāsana, will follow you at this rise of the dice-game;
gourds sink and stones float.
Boats are constantly deluded upon the waters;
so too is the foolish King, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
for he does not listen to my words which are like wholesome medicine.
"Surely this end of the Kurus will come—
a most terrible, all-consuming destruction—
for these poetic words of well-wishers, though appearing as wholesome advice," [he said].
"Nothing is heard [of them]; only greed increases.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Cursing the Kṣattṛ, he spoke thus:"
Intoxicated with pride, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son glared at Prātikāmī in the assembly hall and spoke to him in the midst of the most noble men.
"O Prātikāmin, bring Draupadī here;
you have no cause for fear from the Pāṇḍavas.
This Kṣattṛ is merely a coward who keeps on disputing."
"And he is never desirous of our prosperity.
Having been addressed thus, that charioteer Prātikāmī,
having heard the king's words, departed quickly.
Having entered like a dog into a lion’s den,
the Prātikāmī approached the queen of the Pāṇḍavas and spoke.
"While Yudhiṣṭhira was intoxicated by the madness of the dice-game,
Duryodhana won you, O Draupadī.
Therefore, go now to the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"I am taking you for the ritual, O Yājñasenī.
Draupadī said:
"How can you speak thus, O Prātikāmī?"
"What prince indeed would gamble with his wife?
The king is a fool, intoxicated by the madness of gambling;
or rather, he has no other stake whatsoever."
The messenger said:
"When there was no other stake left for him,
then the Pāṇḍava Ajātaśatru played."
"O princess, his brothers were previously surrendered by that king, and now he has surrendered himself as well.
Draupadī said:
"Go, O son of a Sūta; having gone to the assembly hall, ask that gambler:
'Which did you lose first, yourself or me, O Bhārata?
Having learned this, return and then lead me there, O son of a Sūta."
"Having learned what the king intends to do, I shall go forth in sorrow.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to the assembly hall, he then repeated those words of Draupadī.
Standing in the midst of the lords of men, Draupadī spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Whose master were you when you lost us?
First, did you lose yourself, or rather me?"
"Thus spoke the daughter of the great king, O lord of the people;
Yudhiṣṭhira, however, became motionless, as if his life-force had departed,
and did not answer the charioteer with a word, whether good or bad."
Duryodhana said:
"Let Kṛṣṇā, the princess of Pañcāla, come here and speak this question. Let everyone right here hear her words and his."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to the royal palace, acting under the command of Duryodhana,
the charioteer Prātikāmī spoke to Draupadī as if trembling.
"O princess, these courtiers are calling out;
I believe the destruction of the Kauravas has arrived.
A weak man indeed cannot maintain prosperity."
"O princess, as you are about to enter the assembly hall," Draupadī said,
"it was surely thus that the Ordainer ordained."
Both the wise and the foolish touch the two kinds of contact; however,
the Sage has declared that there is one supreme Dharma in the world, which,
when preserved, will bring us peace.
This very dharma has not reached the Kauravas;
go to the members of the assembly and ask them for my word regarding what is righteous.
Whatever they tell me, I shall certainly do.
O Sūta, having heard those words of Yājñasenī, those virtuous, wise,
and most excellent men went to the assembly hall and then spoke these words.
With their faces cast down, they said nothing at all;
perceiving that persistence of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
Vaiśampāyana said:
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard what Duryodhana intended to do, Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched a messenger approved by Draupadī;
she was clad in a single garment, her lower cloth disarranged, weeping, and in her menses.
Having entered the assembly hall, the princess of Pañcāla stood before her father-in-law.
Then, seeing the princess of the royal house arrive in the hall,
all the members of the assembly inwardly censured the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O King, having gone quickly to the palace of Kṛṣṇā, that wise messenger announced the firm resolve of Dharmarāja. And the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were dejected and filled with sorrow.
With their limbs enveloped by truth, they did not look up at all.
Then, beholding their faces, King Duryodhana spoke joyfully to his charioteer.
"Bring her right here, Prātikāmin;
let the Kurus speak to her face to face. Then the Sūta, obedient to his will, [acted].
Terrified by the wrath of Drupada’s daughter,
he cast aside his pride and spoke again to the members of the assembly: "What shall I say to Kṛṣṇā?"
Duryodhana said:
"O Duḥśāsana, this son of a charioteer of mine,
being small-minded, is terrified of Vṛkodara."
"Seize Yājñasenī yourself and bring her here;
what can your rivals do to you when they are powerless?
Then that prince rose up.
Having heard this, his gaze clouded with anger toward his brother,
he entered the residence of those great chariot-warriors and spoke thus to the princess Draupadī:
"Come, come, O Pāñcālī! You have been won, O Kṛṣṇā!
Cast off your shame and look upon Duryodhana. Serve the Kurus, O lady with eyes like broad lotuses!"
"You have entered this assembly hall by right;
depart from here. Then, rising up with a deeply troubled mind, she wiped her pale face with her hand.
Distressed, she fled toward where those women of the aged king, that bull among the Kurus, were; then,
out of rage, he pursued her with speed.
Then Duḥśāsana, roaring at her,
seized the queen of the king by her long, dark, and wavy hair.
Those who were sprinkled with water purified by mantras during the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the great Rājasūya sacrifice—
those [waters] have now disregarded the prowess of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having forcibly seized her, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having touched that Kṛṣṇā of exceedingly dark hair, brought her into the vicinity of the assembly hall.
Duḥśāsana dragged her, who had a protector yet was like one without a protector, as the wind drags a distressed plantain tree; being dragged,
her slender body bent low.
She spoke softly: "O dull-witted one, today I am in my courses; furthermore, O ignoble man, you ought not to lead me, clad in but a single garment, into the assembly."
Then, having violently seized her by her black hair, he spoke to Kṛṣṇā,
as well as to Kṛṣṇa, Jiṣṇu, Hari, and Nara.
I cry out for protection; indeed, I am leading you away—O Govinda, dweller of Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa, beloved of the gopīs!
O Keśava, do you not know that I have been humiliated by the Kurus?

I, the chief queen of the sons of Pāṇḍu, a bride in the lineage of Ajamīḍha— such as I am, O Keśava, have been seized by the hair while you were still alive! Or perhaps, O Yājñasenī, you have become menstruating [and thus defiled]?
Clad in a single garment or even naked,
defeated at dice and made a slave, you may enjoy your desires among the slave-women as you please.
With her hair disheveled and her garment half-fallen,
she was being violently shaken by Duḥśāsana;
modest as she was, she burned with indignation.
Kṛṣṇā spoke these words slowly:
"These men in the assembly have been instructed in the scriptures;
they are all performers of ritual action and are like Indra himself."
All those who occupy the position of elders are indeed venerable;
I cannot bear to stand before them in such a manner,
O you of cruel deeds and ignoble conduct!
"Do not strip me naked; do not drag me away!
Your princes would not tolerate this, even if the gods led by Indra were your allies."
The king, the son of Dharma, remained established in dharma;
yet dharma is subtle and can only be perceived through refined discernment.
Even regarding a word of his master, [one must not transgress] by so much as an atom.
I do not wish to find fault while casting aside my own virtues;
yet this is ignoble, that you drag me along in the midst of the Kuru heroes while I am in my courses.
"And yet no one here offers you worship;
surely they have followed this opinion of yours. Fie! The lineage of the Bharatas is indeed ruined."
The duties of the Kṣatriyas and their conduct are likewise [lost],
where all the Kurus in the assembly witness the transgression of the boundaries of Kuru-dharma.
There is no courage in Droṇa or Bhīṣma; likewise, it is certain that this great-souled king also lacks it, since he thus commits this fierce unrighteousness.
The elders and leaders of the Kurus do not perceive this;
therefore, you all, members of the assembly, answer this question:
O lords of the earth, do you consider me defeated or undefeated?
Speaking thus piteously, the slender-waisted woman caught sight of her husbands,
the Pāṇḍavas, with their eyes fixed on her and their bodies overcome with anger.
She inflamed him with her sidelong glances;
yet it was not so much by the kingdom, nor by wealth, nor even by the finest jewels that she had been taken away, that he was thus moved.
Just as there was suffering from the angry glance of Kṛṣṇā, impelled by her righteous indignation,
so too did Duḥśāsana, upon beholding Kṛṣṇā, [experience distress].
Looking at those wretched husbands,
she shook her with force until they were nearly unconscious;
then the fierce one spoke as if laughing, "You are a slave!"
But Karṇa,
the king of the Gāndhāras and son of Subala, being exceedingly delighted by those words, honored them with a loud laugh.
In the same way, he welcomed Duḥśāsana;
as for the other members of the assembly who were there, they did so with the exception of those two and Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Seeing Kṛṣṇā being dragged into the assembly hall, they were overcome with extreme sorrow; yet he,
who was detached from worldly ties and learned in all the scriptures, recognized it as destiny.
The high-minded Bhīṣma, who understood that intention, spoke to Draupadī.
Bhīṣma said:
"O blessed lady, it is not possible to explain [this] because of the subtlety of dharma."
I am able to answer this question of yours correctly;
for one who possesses no property is unable to stake another's wealth,
having observed that women are under the control of their husbands.
One might abandon the entire earth in its full prosperity,
but Yudhiṣṭhira would never abandon the truth;
for the Pāṇḍava has already declared, "I am defeated."
Therefore, O blessed lady, I am unable to distinguish this; that Dharma is so subtle that it cannot be discerned by the son of Pāṇḍu, who has thus been defeated.
In dice-play, Śakuni is without equal among men; yet that high-souled son of Kuntī, having surrendered his will to him, did not consider it a deception.
"Therefore, I do not ask you this question.
Draupadī said:
"The king, having summoned me to the assembly by those skilled in debate..."
He has not exerted much effort against those who are evil-minded, deceitful, ignoble, and fond of gambling; why then is he now permitted to follow his own desires?
That foremost of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, being of pure nature, did not perceive their deceitful conduct; for although he was defeated by all of them acting in concert, he remained unaware.
And yet,
you have resorted to this deceit; here stand the Kurus in the assembly hall,
who are likewise the lords of their sons and daughters-in-law.
Having considered all this and my own words as well,
answer this question of mine correctly:
"Have I been defeated by him, or have I not?"
That is no assembly where there are no elders;
they are not elders who do not speak the Dharma;
that is not the Dharma where truth is not found.
"That which is permeated by deceit is not truth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As she was speaking thus, weeping piteously;
As she looked back at those husbands again and again,
Duḥśāsana spoke harsh, unpleasant, and indeed unpalatable words.
Seeing her being dragged along— menstruating, with her upper garment slipping, and undeserving of such treatment— Vṛkodara looked toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Appearing deeply distressed, he gave way to great anger.
Bhīma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, in this land there are harlots who belong to gamblers."
They do not gamble with those [dice], for there is indeed compassion toward them as well. As for the tribute that the King of Kāśī brought, and whatever other excellent goods,
as well as the jewels that other rulers of the earth presented— [all these were set aside].
Our vehicles, wealth, armor, and weapons,
as well as our kingdom, ourselves, and even we ourselves, have been won by the enemies through gambling;
yet I felt no anger toward them, for you are the lord of us all.

But this I consider an extreme transgression, that Draupadī is being staked as a prize; for this young woman, who deserves no such fate, having obtained the Pāṇḍavas as her husbands, is now being tormented by the Kauravas— those base, cruel men who delight in deceit— all because of you.
"O King, this wrath is being directed at you on her account;
I shall consume your arms—bring the fire of Sahadeva!
Arjuna said:
"O Bhīmasena, never before have you spoken such words. Surely your reverence for dharma has been destroyed by cruel enemies.
One must not fulfill the desires of others; rather, one should practice only the highest dharma."
One ought not to transgress against an elder brother who is righteous;
for when challenged by enemies, a king who remembers the duty of a Kṣatriya plays at dice according to the desire of the opponent— that brings us great fame.
Bhīmasena said:
"O Dhanañjaya, if I were to know that this had been done by him,
I would have forcibly burnt both his arms in a blazing fire."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus seen the Pāṇḍavas in such distress and the princess of Pañcāla being tormented, Vikarṇa spoke these words.
"O kings, speak out regarding those words spoken by Yājñasenī; through our failure to discern the meaning of her speech, hell shall await us this very instant.
Both Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra are the two eldest among the Kurus."
Having assembled, the high-minded Vidura said nothing;
nor did Bhāradvāja, the preceptor of all, nor Kṛpa himself— these two best of the twice-born likewise offered no answer to the question.
"But those other rulers of the earth who have assembled from every direction,
having cast aside desire and anger, let them speak according to their own judgment regarding these words that the auspicious Draupadī has spoken repeatedly."
"O kings, having reflected, tell me which side belongs to whom;
give your answer. Thus he spoke many times to all those members of the assembly, yet those protectors of the earth said nothing to him, whether good or bad.
Having thus spoken repeatedly to all the lords of the earth, Vikarṇa, wringing his hands together and sighing, said this:
"O protectors of the earth, either speak your word or remain silent; do not hesitate in any way."

"O Kauravas, I shall indeed say what I consider to be the right course in this matter. O best of men, they say there are four vices of kings: hunting, drinking, gambling, and excessive addiction to sensual pleasures."
For a man attached to these [vices] lives having abandoned dharma;
and the world does not regard an action performed by one so engaged as valid.
Therefore, this son of Pāṇḍu, while deeply immersed in calamity, [acted thus].
Challenged by the gamblers, he staked Draupadī as the wager;
she was the blameless common wife of all the Pāṇḍavas,
and this stake had been proposed by that Pāṇḍava after he himself had previously been defeated.
"And this Kṛṣṇā was offered as a stake by the son of Subala, who sought a wager;
having considered all this, I believe she has not been won.
Upon hearing this, a great roar arose from those in the assembly.
While Vikarṇa was speaking and censuring the son of Subala,
that noise ceased; then Rādheya, overcome with rage,
raised his beautiful arm and spoke these words.

Indeed, many abnormalities are seen in Vikarṇa; born from that very source, they lead to his destruction, just as fire produced from the fire-drill consumes its own origin. Even when fully developed within the body, disease destroys one's strength.
"Beasts trample upon grass, and the Kauravas have trampled their own kin.
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, the high-minded Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Gāndhārī— all these are wiser than you."
"Though urged by Kṛṣṇā, these men have not said anything at all;
I consider them to think that the daughter of Drupada has been won according to dharma.
But you, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are being torn asunder by sheer childishness alone."
"What you say in the midst of the assembly— that I am a child speaking like an elder—
is not so; O younger brother of Duryodhana, you do not know dharma according to its true nature,
you dull-witted one, when you claim that Kṛṣṇā has been won when she is not won."
"How indeed, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, can you consider Kṛṣṇā as unconquered,
when the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas staked all his possessions in the assembly hall? And Draupadī, O bull of the Bharatas, was included within those possessions."
"If you consider Kṛṣṇā thus won by Dharma, how can you think she is not won?
Draupadī was named [as the stake] in words and was permitted by the Pāṇḍavas;
for what reason do you consider her unwon?"
Or if you think that she was brought into this assembly wearing but a single garment by means of unrighteousness— even in that regard, hear my further reply:
O joy of the Kurus, the gods have ordained only one husband for a woman.
But this woman is known to be under the sway of many men and is certain to be unchaste;
it is my opinion that bringing her into this assembly is not surprising,
whether she wears but a single garment or is even entirely naked.
Whatever wealth they possess, whatever women they have, and the Pāṇḍavas themselves—
all that property has been won here by Saubala in accordance with dharma. Duḥśāsana, this Vikarṇa is but a child who speaks like a wise man.
"Bring forth the garments of the Pāṇḍavas and also those of Draupadī. O Bhārata, having heard that, all the Pāṇḍavas cast off their upper garments and sat down in the assembly hall.
Then, O King, Duḥśāsana, having forcibly seized Draupadī’s garment in the midst of the assembly, proceeded to drag it away.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O Govinda, O Kṛṣṇa who dwells in Dvārakā, beloved of the cowherd women! O Keśava, do you not know that I have been humiliated by the Kurus— I, the queen of the sons of Pāṇḍu and the bride of the lineage of Ajamīḍha?
"O Keśava, even while you are alive, I have been subjected to this seizing of my hair.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As her garment was being pulled away, Draupadī thought of Hari.
O Govinda, dweller of Dvārakā, O Kṛṣṇa, beloved of the gopīs! O Keśava, do you not know that I have been humiliated by the Kauravas? O Lord, O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of Vraja, O destroyer of suffering!
O Janārdana, lift me up as I am submerged in the ocean of the Kauravas!
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Great Yogin, Soul of the Universe, Creator of the World! O Govinda, protect me who have sought refuge in you and am perishing in the midst of the Kurus.
Having thus called to mind Kṛṣṇa Hari, the Lord of the three worlds,
that beautiful woman, O King, wept in her distress, covering her face.
Hearing the words of Yājñasenī, Kṛṣṇa was deeply moved.
Leaving her bed and seat, the compassionate Yājñasenī approached on foot; out of pity, she cried out for the sake of protection to Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hari, and Nara.
Then the Great-Souled Dharma,
having vanished, covered her with a multitude of various garments;
at that time, her mind was fixed entirely upon Govinda.

"Save me, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"—this was uttered by me in my distress. While I was being protected by you, my lion-like lord, that wicked man dragged away my garment in the very presence of the Kurus, as if I were unprotected.
As her garment was being pulled away, she lamented in great distress,
repeatedly calling out, "Govinda! Kṛṣṇa!"—
O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, O Acyuta whose home is Dvārakā!
"O Govinda, O lotus-eyed one, protect me who have come to you for refuge!
I have learned that which was sung of old by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha:
'When a great calamity has arrived, the Blessed Lord Hari should be remembered.'"
In her mind, Draupadī meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa,
the sovereign Kṛṣṇa, the great-grandfather of the worlds, who grants fearlessness in times of distress.
"Alas, Kṛṣṇa, dweller of Dvārakā! Where are you, O delighter of the Yādavas?
Why do you disregard me as I have fallen into this state, left without a protector?"—O lord of the people, while Draupadī’s garment was being dragged away.
In that very manner, another garment appeared repeatedly.
By the grace of Draupadī,
even as her clothing was being dragged away, she pulled forth garments until there were one hundred and eight.
Then, O Lord, garments of various colors and devoid of passion appeared by the hundreds through the preservation of the Dharma;
thereafter, a tumultuous roar, a terrible sound, arose there.

Seeing that most wonderful sight among all the rulers of the earth, they there praised Draupadī while censuring the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, uttering inauspicious words against the Kaurava: "Fie! Fie! on him.
There, in the midst of the kings, Bhīma, his lips quivering with rage and wringing his hands together, uttered this curse in a loud voice:
"O Kṣatriyas dwelling in this world, take these words of mine to heart!"
"O lords of the earth, this has never been spoken by other men before, nor will anyone else speak it; if, having spoken thus, I do not act accordingly,
may I not attain the destination of all my ancestors."
"If I do not forcibly pierce the chest of this sinful man, this base-born outcaste of the Bharatas, and drink his blood in battle,"—
having heard those words of his, which brought joy to all the world, [the warriors were filled with delight].
They performed extensive worship while reviling the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
but when a heap of garments had been piled up in the middle of the assembly hall,
Duḥśāsana, exhausted and ashamed, sat down.
Then, seeing the sons of Kuntī there, a hair-raising cry of "Fie! arose from the members of the assembly and the lords of men,
saying, "The Kauravas do not answer this question."
That crowd there cried out, censuring Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
then Vidura, the knower of all dharma, raising his arms and silencing the members of the assembly, spoke these words.
Vidura said:
"Having thus posed this question to Draupadī, she indeed laments like one who is helpless. Yet you, O members of the assembly, do not answer that question; herein dharma is being violated."
For an afflicted man approaches the assembly hall like a blazing sacrificial fire;
indeed, the members of the assembly must extinguish him with truth and righteousness.
Then, being distressed, the man shall state his inquiry regarding dharma before the members of the assembly.
There, those who have transcended the power of desire and anger should answer that question.
O lords of men, just as Vikarṇa has answered the question according to his wisdom,
you too should answer that question according to your own judgment.
For he who, having entered an assembly, does not answer a question while perceiving the truth,
partakes of half the fruit that results from falsehood. Furthermore, he who, having entered an assembly, speaks falsely while perceiving the truth [partakes of the full fruit].
"It is certain that one obtains the entire fruit of falsehood.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between Prahlāda and the sage of Aṅgiras."

The lord of the Daityas named Prahlāda had a son, Virocana. Desiring a maiden, he once approached Sudhanvan, the son of Aṅgiras, saying, "I am the elder! I am the elder! out of his longing for the girl.
"We have heard that there was once a dispute between those two gods over their vital breaths. A debate regarding questions arose between them, and they both questioned Prahlāda:
'Which one of us is superior? Answer our question; do not speak falsely.'"
Fearing the dispute, he indeed looked toward Sudhanvan.
Enraged and blazing like the staff of Brahma, Sudhanvan said to him:
"O Prahlāda, if you speak falsely, or if you do not speak at all,"
"The wielder of the thunderbolt will strike your head into a hundred pieces with his vajra," Sudhanvan said; and having been told this, the Daitya, trembling like a leaf of the holy fig tree,
went to the highly powerful Kaśyapa to question him.
Prahlāda said:
"O highly wise one, you are indeed the knower of the dharma pertaining to the gods and the asuras here in this world; O Brāhmaṇa, hear now this dilemma regarding dharma."
"Whoever indeed does not answer a question, or should point out what is false—what worlds await him hereafter? Tell me that as I ask you.
Kaśyapa said:
One who, knowing the answer, fails to declare it due to desire, anger, or fear,
binds himself with a thousand nooses of Varuṇa. Likewise,
a witness who declares testimony falsely, moving about with ears as loose as those of an ox, incurs the same fate.
A thousand nooses of Varuṇa are cast upon oneself;
when a full year has passed, one single noose is released.
Therefore, one who knows the truth should speak the truth straightforwardly.
When Dharma, pierced by Adharma, enters an assembly and the members of that assembly do not extract its barb,
then one quarter of the guilt falls upon the perpetrator and one quarter falls upon the witnesses.
One quarter of the sin falls upon all the members of the assembly, one quarter falls upon the king,
one quarter is indeed taken by the chief [judge],
and one quarter remains among those who do not condemn what is blameworthy.
By this, one becomes preeminent, and the members of the assembly are liberated from sin; for where the one deserving of censure is censured, the guilt goes to the perpetrator.
But those who speak falsely when Dharma is questioned by Prahlāda, O Prahlāda—
They destroy one's merit from sacrifices and charitable works, as well as seven generations both preceding and following.

Indeed, the grief felt by one whose property has been seized, or by one whose son has been killed, or the grief felt toward a debtor, or that felt by one who has been swallowed up by the king— all these are equal.

The sorrow of a woman bereft of her husband, and that of one who has strayed from the caravan; the sorrow of a childless woman, and that of one seized by a tiger; the sorrow of a woman whose husband has taken another wife, and that of one defeated by witnesses.
The lords of the thirty gods have declared these indeed to be equal misfortunes:
he who speaks falsely incurs all of those misfortunes. Testimony is based on what was seen with one's own eyes, what was heard, and what was retained in memory.
"Therefore, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from dharma or artha.
Vidura said:
"Having heard the words of Kaśyapa, Prahlāda spoke to his son."
"Sudhanvan is indeed superior to you, and likewise Aṅgiras is superior to me;
Sudhanvan’s mother is also superior to your mother.
O Virocana, this Sudhanvan is the master of your life."
Sudhanvan said:
"Since you have abandoned affection for your son and remain established in dharma, I grant permission regarding your son; let him live for a hundred years."
Vidura said:
"Having thus heard this supreme dharma, all you members of the assembly,
what do you consider to be the final answer to Kṛṣṇā’s question?"
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Vidura, the kings said nothing at all;
but Karṇa said to Duḥśāsana, "Take Kṛṣṇā, a slave-woman, to the house."
Duḥśāsana dragged that poor woman into the midst of the assembly while she was trembling, filled with shame, and lamenting for the Pāṇḍavas. Draupadī said:
"What was to be done by me previously has not been done; what remains must now be accomplished. I have been rendered distraught by this powerful one who drags me away by force.
Wait a moment, O evil-minded Duḥśāsana, lowest of men!"
"I offer my salutation to these elders in the assembly of the Kurus;
let there be no fault in me for this which was not performed by me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Shaken by that [wind] and overcome with grief, the ascetic woman, though unworthy of such treatment, fell down and lamented thus in the assembly hall. Draupadī said:
I, who was seen by kings assembled in the arena at my self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*),
have never been seen elsewhere before; that same I have now entered this assembly hall—
she whom neither the wind nor the sun had previously beheld within my home.
I, who formerly could not endure even being touched by the wind in my home, am today seen in the midst of the assembly hall within the council of the Kurus;
the Pandavas now tolerate me being touched by this evil-minded man.
"These Kurus tolerate this; I consider it a reversal of time, that they allow their daughter-in-law and daughter, who is undeserving of such suffering, to be thus afflicted.
But what could be more miserable than this, that I, though a virtuous woman, am [forced to suffer]?"
Today I enter the midst of this assembly; where indeed is the righteousness of the rulers of the earth?
We have heard that in former times they did not bring virtuous women into the assembly hall. That ancient, eternal dharma has perished among the Kauravas.
"How indeed can the wife of the Pāṇḍavas, the sister of the son of Pṛṣata, and the friend of Vāsudeva, come to the assembly hall of these kings? How can she,
the wife of the King of Dharma, born of a lineage equal to his own— "
"Tell me, O Kauravas, whether I am a slave or not a slave; I shall do accordingly.
For this base man, who destroys the fame of the Kauravas, has out of malice and in his cruelty, without even considering the facts, treated me with such harshness."
Even in the presence of his elders, she was devoted to her vows of chastity;
yet King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having set out upon an improper course, led her— who was unable to endure such distress— into the midst of the assembly while those learned in dharma looked on.
"O Kauravas, I am not able to endure this affliction for long.
O kings, whether you consider me defeated or undefeated, whatever you think, I desire a response accordingly; I shall do that, O Kauravas."
Bhīṣma said:
"O blessed lady, I have described the supreme goal of dharma;
even by high-souled brahmins, it is not possible to reach it in this world."
Just as a powerful man perceives what is right in this world,
so too is that considered dharma at the time of its application when asserted by others;
yet, I am unable to resolve this question of yours with absolute certainty.
Because of Pāṇḍava’s approval, because of its subtlety, and because of the gravity of the task;
and because of the subtlety and profundity of this matter, as well as its weightiness,
surely the end of this lineage will come before long.
For indeed, O auspicious lady, all the Kurus, though born into noble families, have become utterly devoted to greed and delusion and are severely struck down by calamities;
yet they do not deviate from the paths of dharma, as you, our daughter-in-law, remain steadfast.
"O Pāñcālī, this conduct of yours is truly worthy:
that even when you have fallen into such hardship, you still look only toward dharma.
These elders, Droṇa and the others, are likewise people who know the dharma."
They remain with their bodies empty, bowed down as if their life-breaths had departed.
It is my opinion that Yudhiṣṭhira alone is the authority regarding this question;
he himself ought to declare whether she has been won or not won.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus seen her in such a state, crying out repeatedly like a distressed osprey, he spoke.
Fearing the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the kings did not speak a word, whether good or even bad;
yet they beheld those sons and grandsons of the rulers of the earth.
While they remained silent, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as if smiling, then addressed these words to the daughter of the Pāñcāla king.
Let this question rest regarding the noble-souled Bhīma, Arjuna, and likewise Sahadeva,
as well as your husband Nakula, O Yājñasenī.
Let these men speak words issued from you,
proclaiming Yudhiṣṭhira to be powerless in the midst of the noble ones, for your sake, O Pāñcālī.
"Let them all speak untruth to the King of Dharma;
O Pāñcālī, you shall be released from slavery. The high-souled King of Dharma remains established in righteousness."
Let him who is like Indra himself, or your lord— if he indeed has power over you— speak this;
then quickly choose one [of us] according to his word.
For all these Kauravas in this assembly, though situated in the midst of suffering,
do not speak as they truly are because of their noble nature.
And having observed that their husbands were so unfortunate,
all the members of the assembly there then loudly praised the words of the Kuru king.
They also made whirling movements with their garments, shouting aloud;
and there too, the cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Having heard those heart-stealing words, [he...]
There was defiance among the Kauravas in the assembly hall,
yet all the kings were filled with joy,
honoring the righteous best of the Kurus.
Having heard these words spoken by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
all those kings looked intently at Yudhiṣṭhira, thinking, "May this [proposal] always be consistent with righteousness."
"What indeed will the knower of dharma say? they asked with their faces turned sideways;
"What indeed will the Pandava Bibhatsu, unconquered in battle, say? And what will Bhimasena and the twins say?"—thus they spoke, filled with intense curiosity.
When that noise had ceased, Bhīmasena spoke these words,
raising his massive, rounded arm which was smeared with sandalwood paste:
"If this Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira is our elder..."
He would no longer be the master of this family, nor would we tolerate it;
for he is the lord of our meritorious asceticism and even of our very lives—
if he considers himself victorious, then we have been defeated.

"Indeed, no one who remains alive shall escape from me after touching these locks of hair of the princess of Pañcāla with his foot, he being subject to the laws of mortality. Behold my two long and rounded arms, like iron clubs."
"Having come between these two, even Śatakratu could not escape;
yet, bound by the noose of dharma, I do not encounter such peril,
restrained as I am by my own dignity and by Arjuna’s restraint."
"Released by the King of Dharma, I would crush these wicked sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with my palms and sword, like a lion crushing small animals.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one throbbed again and again.
Then Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura said to him:
"Let it be forgiven; everything is possible for you.
Karṇa said:
"Three, it is said, are without property: the slave, the pupil, and the dependent woman.
You are the wife of a slave; you are his property, O blessed lady."
The lowly lord, the male slave, the wealth, and the female slave— these three, it is said, are truly possessed of wealth in the assembly: Bhīṣma, the Kṣattṛ, and the preceptor of the Kauravas.
Those who speak ill of their most wicked master, yet desire his prosperity and do not abandon him—
entering here, enjoy yourself with us and our attendants.
Therefore, having entered this house, you must accomplish what remains to be done for you.
O princess, we are all masters under your command; it is the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who are yours, not the sons of Pṛthā.
"Choose another husband quickly, O beautiful woman,
one whom you will not lose to gambling. For a woman's conduct toward husbands is indeed subject to her own desires."
"Let it be known to you that Nakula, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, Sahadeva, and Arjuna have all been conquered and shall remain my slaves forever."
"Enter as a slave-girl, Yājñasenī! Your husbands have been defeated and no longer exist.
What indeed do you think is the purpose of your own self?"
In this matter, O Pārtha, one must consider the prowess and manliness of Drupada, the King of Pañcāla, whose daughter he won by gambling excessively in the midst of the assembly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that, Bhīmasena, filled with extreme indignation and appearing deeply distressed, then sighed heavily.
"Bound by the snares of dharma and following the king,
Bhima, his gaze clouded with anger as if burning him, said:"
"O King, I do not feel anger toward the Sūta’s son;
this is the true nature of a servant's duty that has entered him.
Or rather, why should my enemies hold me back today?"
"O King, you would not be a god if it were not for her.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of the son of Rādhā, King Duryodhana then—
He spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, who remained silent and bewildered:
"O King, Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins stand here under your command;
therefore, put your question to Kṛṣṇā if you consider her unconquered."
Having spoken thus to the son of Kuntī, he cast off his own garment and,
as if smiling, looked at the princess of Pañcāla, deluded by the intoxication of power—
she who was like the trunk of a plantain tree and honored with every auspicious mark.
Resembling an elephant’s trunk and possessing a weightiness like that of a thunderbolt,
he smiled broadly at the son of Rādhā as if to challenge Bhīma,
and while Draupadī looked on, he displayed his left thigh.
Then Vṛkodara, beholding that, widened his bloodshot eyes and spoke in the midst of the kings as if making it resound throughout the assembly:
"May Vṛkodara never attain the same world as his ancestors!"
"If I do not shatter this thigh of yours with my mace in the great battle,
I shall not go to those worlds, nor even to the most meritorious realms of merit. If I were to crush even your crown with my foot..."
"If I do not strike him down in battle, then I shall enter the fire. From all the orifices of that enraged man, flames of fire issued forth like those from the hollows of a tree burning.
Vidura said:
"Behold the supreme danger from Bhīmasena;
take heed, for he is like the noose of King Varuṇa."
"Surely this was ordained by fate from the beginning;
a further misfortune has arisen among the Bharatas.
This excessive gambling has been committed by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
For you who dispute over this woman in the assembly,
a great danger to your security and well-being is seen;
the Kurus are deliberating upon evil counsels.
"O Kurus, understand this matter quickly;
if this were wrongly perceived, the assembly would fall into great corruption.
Had the gambler staked this first,"
If he were the master, his self being unconquered,
then this wealth won in a dream would indeed be real; but I think it is so for him whose master gambles away.
Having heard the words of Gāndhārī’s son,
"O Kurus, do not deviate from this Dharma," Duryodhana said:
Just as I stand by the words of Bhīma and likewise those of Arjuna,
so too do I stand by those of the twins;
yet if they declare Yudhiṣṭhira to be powerless, [I shall follow them].
"Then you shall be released from slavery, O Yājñasenī.
Arjuna said:
"The king was formerly our master in the matter of the stake."
The high-souled Dharmarāja, son of Kuntī,
is the lord; yet this man’s soul has been defeated—
know this, O Kurus, all of you.
Karna said:
"O Duḥśāsana, listen to these words spoken by me:
O hero, why delay? Take the daughter of Drupada away."
"Enjoy yourself as a slave and do as you please, O giver of honor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śakuni, the son of the king of Gāndhāra, spoke.
"Excellent, O mighty-armed Karṇa! Let it be done as you wish.
Then Duḥśāsana quickly began to forcibly bring in the daughter of Drupada, and that evil-minded one dragged her along.
Then the princess of Pañcāla, of celestial beauty, cried out with great urgency:
"Save me, Bhīṣma! O Droṇa, O son of Droṇa, and likewise Kṛpa!
Save me, Vidura, you who are most righteous and devoted to dharma!"
O Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, do indeed protect your daughter-in-law! O illustrious Gāndhārī, you who are all-knowing and all-seeing, protect me, O Queen, for I am tormented by the fear of Suyodhana.
"O noble lady, mother of heroes, O Yādavī, why do you look upon me thus? Why do you not protect me, your own daughter-in-law, as I am being tormented by ignoble men?"—
to me, who was thus lamenting, no one said anything at all.
Alas, I am destroyed, I who am so dull-witted, having fallen under the power of Duryodhana! Neither King Pāṇḍu, nor Dharma, nor the Lord of the Gods,
nor Vāyu, nor even the two Aśvins, truly protect a daughter-in-law.
Vidura:
Alas, what misery! That I, an unfortunate woman devoted to my husband, must still live and hear these words of yours, O princess.
These sons of Pṛthā do not say anything at all;
therefore, for the sake of what is pleasing to you, listen to these words:
that which is called "evil-minded" and "ungrateful."
If Suyodhana, together with his followers, that most wicked one,
along with the king and his son,
were to hear these great words being spoken...
"The evil-minded and most wicked one shall not hear [this]," having spoken thus to Drupada’s daughter,
Vidura—
The Steward spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Let not the daughter of Drupada suffer.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O prince, you shall not see your enemies.
Having spoken thus to him, Vidura first addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"O Great King, if you thus afflict Draupadī,
before long your wicked son, who acts to the detriment of the Pāṇḍavas, shall perish along with his ministers."
"From Bhīma and Arjuna, who are enraged, and from the two sons of Mādrī, restrain your son; do not contemplate his destruction. Vaiśampāyana said:

Having heard this, the dull-witted one did not utter any reply. Then Duryodhana, there, overcome by the power of fate and delusion, disregarded the words of the Kṣattṛ and, with wide eyes, was filled with joy.
The wicked one repeatedly showed his thighs to Draupadī. When his thighs were being gazed upon, Vṛkodara, seeing Suyodhana, rolled his eyes bloodshot with rage.
Having observed this humiliation within himself,
that powerful and proud younger brother of the king, restraining his wrath in the assembly of the Kauravas, [spoke].
As he was departing, Bhīma spoke these words:
"I shall be the slayer of Duryodhana; Dhanañjaya shall be the slayer of Karṇa;
and Sahadeva will kill Śakuni, that gambler with the dice."
And I shall further utter these great words in the midst of the assembly:
"When the battle occurs, the gods will make it true;
I shall slay this wicked Suyodhana with my mace in combat."
And with my foot, I shall trample his head upon the ground;
having pierced the chest of that brave but evil-minded man—
Arjuna!

I shall drink the blood of Duḥśāsana like a lion; O Bhīmasena, there are none who harbor enmity toward you who are dull-witted enough to dwell happily in their homes, unaware of the great danger that looms.
O Bhīma, the resolve of the virtuous is not known by mere words;
yet if they stand in battle in accordance with the duty of the Kṣatriyas,
[it shall be seen] against Duryodhana, Karṇa, and the evil-minded Śakuni.
The earth shall drink the blood of those enemies— Duḥśāsana as the fourth— who are false, exultant, and evil-minded;
at your command, O Bhīmasena, I shall slay Karṇa in battle.
In battle, I shall slay Karṇa and his followers with feathered arrows;
and whatever other kings, through delusion of intellect, shall fight against me,
I will lead them all to the abode of Yama with my sharp shafts.

For even the Himalayas might move from their place, and the sun might lose its radiance, and the coolness of the moon might perish, if my truth were to waver. Vaiśampāyana said: [The above constitutes the verse.]
When Pārtha had spoken thus, the illustrious and powerful Sahadeva, son of Mādravatī, grasping his massive arm and desiring the slaughter of Saubala, spoke these words:
With eyes bloodshot with rage and hissing like a serpent,
Sahadeva said:
"O fool, destroyer of the Gāndhāras' fame, those dice which you consider so important— "
These are not dice, nor are they sharpened arrows, which you have grasped in battle;
rather, as the noble one has spoken concerning you and your kinsmen,
"I shall perform that deed," so do you carry out all your duties in every respect.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O son of Subala, if you will stand in battle according to the duty of a Kṣatriya," having heard these words of Sahadeva, O lord of the people, Nakula also [spoke].
Nakula,
the most handsome among men, spoke these words:
"This daughter of Yajñasena was won at this gambling match by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

I shall send those who, standing as favorites of Duryodhana, caused the words of Kṛṣṇā to be heard— the wicked sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, driven by Time and desiring death— to the abode of Vaivasvata in great numbers.
"And I shall slay in battle that evil-minded Ulūka, the beloved son of Saubala, that lowest of men and my enemy,
acting upon the command of Dharmarāja while following the path of Draupadī."
Draupadī said:
"I shall, before long, make this earth free from the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
since you show me your thigh and since you gaze upon your thigh."
Therefore, O most unrighteous one, death shall come to you through your own thigh;
and because this evil-minded brother of yours thus torments me,
Vṛkodara shall surely drink his blood.
And Dhanañjaya shall slay this most wicked-minded Karṇa, along with his sons, kinsmen, ministers, and retinue, as well as Śakuni, who is base in character, deceitful, and evil-hearted.
"O Vaiśampāyana,
Draupadī, who perceives the dharma, spoke these words: 'Sahadeva, enraged in battle, will slay him along with his kinsmen.'"
Then, from the sky, a great rain of flowers fell;
it appeared upon the head of the princess of Pañcāla, and the cry of "Excellent! arose on all sides.
Having heard these words, Arjuna then made a firm vow.
"I shall slay Karṇa in battle, along with his sons and his kinsmen—
he under whose protection the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself roars;
I shall destroy that powerful Sūta together with his very roots."

"And those others, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kings, who shall fight—I will slay them all; I swear this by my weapon in truth. This very day, I shall kill all these members of the assembly."
Seeing this daughter of Drupada, my anger becomes exceedingly great. What indeed shall I do, since the king is ever compassionate?
Or rather, in a mere moment, I [shall subdue] the entire circle of kings.
"With my arrows, I shall lead [him], the crusher of enemies, to the abode of Yama.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard their words, the members of the assembly did not speak.
O King, because of Arjuna’s fear, there was indeed silence there. Having heard Draupadī’s words, Dhanañjaya then became enraged;
with his eyes copper-red from anger, he spoke these words.
"But this Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira is restraining me.
Having said this, the valiant Savyasācin, his eyes copper-red with anger, took up his bow,
sprang forward, and glared at those enemies.
There, all the kings beheld Phalguna rising up like the fire at the end of an eon burning all the worlds,
looking on with bow in hand and sighing again and again.

Seeing him thus, like the wrathful Rudra desiring to slaughter the sacrificial animals at Dakṣa’s rite, the kings were despondent with terrified minds; for they knew the prowess of Dhanañjaya and had then lost all hope for their lives.
They all became as if dead, with eyes that seemed unblinking;
the kings gazed intently at Arjuna and the son of Dharma.
And seeing Arjuna enraged, the earth itself trembled.
The beings who roam the sky were indeed terrified and overcome with fear;
then the sun did not shine, nor did the wind blow;
neither the moon nor the stars appeared, and neither the heavens nor the directions could be discerned.
The entire world, both mobile and immobile, became utterly agitated.
Leaping up, Pārtha shone like the sun in the sky.
Seeing Pārtha in their midst, enraged and resembling Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time, [the enemies were struck with fear].
Filled with joy, Bhīmasena set his mind solely upon battle;
and Pāñcālī then beheld Dhanañjaya, highly enraged and desirous of slaying all his enemies, like Suparṇa [Garuda] toward serpents.
Enraged and blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, he became difficult to behold.
Seeing him possessed by such splendor, the city-dwellers trembled.
Then, they beheld Dhanañjaya leaping up with great speed.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the eldest Dharmarāja, who was compassionate, seized him just as Puruhūta seized Hari. Yudhiṣṭhira spoke.
"O Pārtha, do not act rashly; do not go to your destruction and lose your fame.
I am capable of burning this evil-minded charioteer, yet upon seeing his feet, my anger subsides."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Pāṇḍava, restrain this anger for the sake of the world.
Thus addressed by the king, Dhananjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu, then [replied].
Pārtha stood facing the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, completely subduing his anger. When that heroic Pāṇḍava Phalguna had thus become tranquil,
the entire world, both mobile and immobile, became filled with joy.
Seeing that Pārtha had been restrained by his brother, Vṛkodara became dejected, O King; indeed, there was silence there. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, in the house of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
a jackal howled loudly at the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
O King, the donkeys brayed in response to it.
And from all sides, fierce birds [were crying out]; Vidura, the knower of truth, heard that terrible sound, as did the daughter of Subala.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the learned Gautama also cried out loudly, "May there be well-being! May there be well-being!
Then the wise Gāndhārī and Vidura likewise spoke.
Observing that terrible portent, they then reported it to the king in a state of distress;
thereupon, the king spoke these words.
"You are slain, O dull-witted Duryodhana,
you who, being ill-behaved, addressed a woman in the assembly of the bulls among the Kurus!"

Having spoken thus to his wise son Dhṛtarāṣṭra— who was specifically seeking the welfare of his kinsmen by averting their misfortune— the sage said further regarding Draupadī, his lawful wife: "02,063.026a" [The remainder of the verse follows].
Having reflected upon this with his wisdom, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose intellect was fixed on the truth, spoke to the dark-complexioned Pāñcālī with words of consolation:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Choose a boon from me, O Pāñcālī, whatever you desire;
for you, being a virtuous woman devoted to dharma, are the most distinguished among my daughters-in-law.
Draupadī said:
"If you grant me a boon, O bull among the Bharatas, I choose this:
let the illustrious Yudhiṣṭhira, who follows all dharma, be no longer a slave."—
Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Let it be as you desire; let Yudhiṣṭhira be no longer a slave.
Choose another boon, O daughter, O devoted wife!
Let not the young boys say that he is lacking in spirit."

"O Bhārata, this one who has come as Prativindhya— having formerly been a prince such as no other man anywhere, cherished [by us]— will surely perish if he perceives himself to be the son of a slave."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"So be it, O auspicious lady, just as you speak. O blessed one, I grant you a second boon; choose it from me."
"For my mind wavers; you do not deserve to choose only one boon.
Draupadī said:
"Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya, together with their chariots and their bows—"
"I choose Nakula and Sahadeva as my second boon.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"So be it for you, O highly fortunate one, just as you desire, O Nandinī."
"Choose a third boon from us; you have not been sufficiently honored by these two alone. For you, as a practitioner of dharma, are the most excellent among all my daughters-in-law.
Forgive me now for this shedding of tears; indeed, it makes the house feel empty."
Draupadī said:
"O Blessed One, greed leads to the destruction of dharma; I do not venture to accept a third boon, O best of kings, for I am unworthy to receive it."

They say that a Vaiśya may have one husband, a Kṣatriya woman two husbands, and a king three husbands, O Indra among kings; but for a Brāhmaṇa, there are a hundred husbands. Having been inferior men, these husbands of mine have now crossed over [to higher states].
"And they shall surely attain auspicious things, O King, by means of their meritorious deeds.
Karna said:
"Those women who have been heard of among men as being highly esteemed for their beauty—"

We have never heard of such deeds performed by any woman when the sons of Pṛthā and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were overcome with rage; yet Kṛṣṇā Draupadī became the source of peace for the sons of Pāṇḍu in this world.
"For those sinking in water without a boat, for those drowning where there is no firm ground,
this Pāñcālī became a ship that carried the sons of Pāṇḍu to the further shore.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having heard that, Bhīmasena, extremely intolerant in the midst of the Kurus and deeply distressed in mind, said, "The sons of Pāṇḍu have women as their only refuge. Devala indeed declared that there are three lights for a man.

Not turning one's back in battle, not retreating when challenged, and the protection of one's wife— these are the three lights. Offspring, action, and knowledge— from these, all creatures are produced.
In this body— which is impure, devoid of life, empty, and abandoned by kinsmen— these three things arise for a man:
that light of ours has been struck down by the touch of his wife.
"O Dhanañjaya, how indeed might there be offspring born from one who has been touched [by a curse]?
Arjuna said:
"Harsh words, whether spoken or unspoken by an inferior person,"
The Bhāratas, who are always superior men, speak thus:
they remember only good deeds and not the hostilities committed; being virtuous and discerning, they act once they have gained confidence in themselves.
Then Bhīma, filled with rage, spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O King, give me leave to subdue these evil-minded ones.
Bhīma said:
"Right here I shall slay all these swift enemies who have assembled; or else, O Indra among kings, O Bhārata, go forth and cut them down by the roots.
What is the use of our debating here? What is the use of our distress, O Bhārata?"
"Right now, let us slay them here; rule this earth!
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Bhīmasena was surrounded by his younger brothers.
Like a lion in the midst of deer, he repeatedly glared at his iron club;
though being consoled and fanned by Pārtha of unwearied deeds,
the mighty-armed and heroic one perspired from an internal burning.
O lord of men, from the apertures of that enraged man— his ears and so forth—
a fire arose, accompanied by smoke and sparks of flame.
His face became difficult to behold due to the knitting of his brows.
When the end of the age had arrived, like Death personified,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the mighty-armed one, restrained him with his own arm and said to him,
"Do not do this; remain silent," O Bhārata.
Having restrained his mighty-armed father, whose eyes were bloodshot with anger,
he stood before Dhṛtarāṣṭra with palms joined in reverence.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, what shall we do for you? Command us, for you are our lord. O Bhārata, we desire to remain forever under your command.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Ajātaśatru, may it be well with you; go in safety and security.
Having been granted permission, rule your own kingdom together with your wealth.
However, this instruction of mine, an old man, must be understood.

"O Yudhiṣ�ṭhira, you know in its entirety that which has been declared by wisdom— the beneficial and the supreme good— and you understand, my dear, the subtle course of all duties. You are humble, O man of great intelligence, and a devoted attendant of the elders."
"Where there is wisdom, there is peace; go to tranquility, O Bhārata!
A weapon does not strike wood that is already dry; a weapon is brought down only upon wood.
Those who possess wisdom do not recognize enmities; they see virtues, not faults."

Those who do not encounter opposition are the supreme persons; being virtuous, they act for the sake of others without looking for anything in return. O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is the lowest of men who speak harsh words during a dispute.
But those who are moderate, when addressed with harsh replies,
do not speak such harmful and abrasive words, whether spoken or unspoken; indeed, the wise and supreme among men always respond in this way.

The virtuous remember only good deeds, not even the hostilities committed against them; for the noble ones, who clearly understand and have gained confidence in themselves, maintain unbroken boundaries of purpose and are pleasant to behold.
"O dear one, do not take to heart that harshness of Duryodhana regarding the conduct shown by you, the noble one, in this assembly of the virtuous;
nor [take offense] toward your mother Gāndhārī, nor toward me, who longs for your virtues."
"Behold, O Bhārata, your aged and blind father standing before you.
Desiring to see my friends and the relative strength of my sons, I previously overlooked this game of dice with deliberate intent."

The Kurus, O King, for whom you are the ruler, are not to be grieved for; nor is the wise Vidura, your minister, who is learned in all the scriptures. In you resides righteousness, in Arjuna prowess, and in Bhīmasena valor.
Faith and service to their elders were present in those two foremost of men, the twins.
O Ajātaśatru, may it be well with you; enter Khāṇḍavaprastha. May there be brotherly affection between you and your brothers, and let your mind be fixed upon dharma.
02.065.016 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and best of the Bharatas,
performed all the customary rites of the noble and set forth together with his brothers.
Mounting chariots that resembled clouds, they set out for Indraprastha, the most excellent of cities, together with Kṛṣṇā, their minds filled with joy. Janamejaya said:
Having learned that they had been granted permission along with their stores of jewels and wealth,
what was the state of mind of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra toward the Pāṇḍavas at that time?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having learned that they had been granted permission by the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
Duḥśāsana quickly went to his brother Duryodhana, who was accompanied by his ministers, O bull of the Bharatas.
Afflicted by grief, O best of the Bharatas, he spoke these words:
"That old man is destroying what has been brought together with great difficulty;
the Pāṇḍavas have departed, O King, along with their followers, vehicles, and wealth."
"O great car-warriors, take note: they are equipped with bows and quivers;
O great car-warriors, take note: these are the weapons intended for the destruction of the enemy.
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala—"
Having come together in secret, those proud men, acting in concert against the Pāṇḍavas,
approached the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Vicitravīrya,
and spoke these gentle words with great urgency.
Duryodhana said:
"O King, you have not heard that which the learned Bṛhaspati,
the priest of the gods, spoke while expounding the policy of Śakra."

"O crusher of enemies, all foes must be destroyed by every possible means before they can cause you harm through war or force. Therefore, we shall honor all those kings with the wealth of the Pāṇḍavas."
If we fight them, what will be lost for us? Who would dare cast away angry, venomous serpents that have approached to bite, having placed them around one's neck or on one's back?
"O dear one, the Pāṇḍavas, having taken up their weapons and mounted their chariots, are enraged;
like angry venomous serpents, they will leave nothing of us remaining.
Indeed, Arjuna goes forth fully armored, having slung his two great quivers over his shoulders."
"Taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow, Pārtha, the best among wielders of weapons, being filled with rage,
will in no long time leave us nothing remaining.
I do not see how one can turn back Bībhatsu when he is enraged in battle."
He repeatedly takes up the Gāṇḍīva bow, sighing and looking about;
in a very short time he will leave us nothing remaining.
I see no one who can withstand the enraged Bībhatsu in battle.
Bhīṣma and Droṇa, Karṇa and the son of Droṇa, the best among chariot-warriors;
Kṛpa and Vṛṣasena, Vikarṇa and Jayadratha;
Bāhlīka and Somadatta, Bhūri and Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
Śakuni along with his sons, the kings, and the other Kauravas—
all these, though striving in battle, were unable to withstand Pārtha;
for there is no archer in the world equal to Arjuna in prowess.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Who is that man, a hero whose prowess is equal to that of Arjuna, whom you have mentioned as being like the many-armed Arjuna despite having only two arms?"
Duryodhana said:
"O son, tell me of that one of great prowess; I wish to hear it.
There was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms."
The heroic lord of the Haihayas, Pāñcadaśya, was Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the grandfather of Kārtavīrya; O son of Gāndhārī, [know] all those to be the grandfathers of Kārtavīrya.
Duryodhana said:
"Tell me that king's history in due order; O King, hear now the life-story of the high-souled Kārtavīrya."
Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, has his origin in the Unmanifest;
from Brahmā was born the learned Atri, and the son of Atri was Niśākara (the Moon). Budha was the son of Soma, and Purūravas was the son of Budha.
His son was Āyu, and the son of Āyu was Nahuṣa.
Nahuṣa’s son was Yayāti, and Yayāti’s son was Yadu. O great king, the son of Yadu was renowned as Sahasraujas.
O King, the son of Sahasraujas was renowned as Cakradāsa.
The heir of Cakradāsa was the monarch named Hehaya. The son of Hehaya was known as Dharmanetra.
The son of Dharmaketu was Kārtavīrya,
and from Kārtavīrya was born Arjuna, the best among the strong.
And that Arjuna, O Great King, performed severe austerities.
Having performed most difficult austerities for more than ten thousand years,
Arjuna propitiated the sage who was the son of Atri;
Datta indeed granted four boons to that king.
Previously, when you were taking pleasure in unrighteousness, the first boon requested by the virtuous was that you be restrained therein;
now, having conquered the earth through righteousness, you must delight it through righteousness alone.

Having conquered many battles and slain enemies by the thousands, even as he strove in combat, his death in battle came from one superior to him; for it is said, O Bhārata, that he possessed a thousand arms while fighting.
"A chariot and a banner were produced; thus have I heard in the past.
In the same way, O King, the earth with its seven continents and its cities, together with its oceans and mines, was indeed conquered by the fierce Bālin, my dear."
Then that radiant Arjuna became the lord of the seven islands;
and that king of great strength performed great sacrifices—
Duryodhana.
Having conquered the entire earth many times over numerous years,
O King, Arjuna, the lord of Māhiṣmatī,
once went with his wives to the Narmadā river to bathe, O best of the Bharatas.
Then, O King, having gone to the river and joyfully entered the water,
he proceeded to engage in water-sports;
at that very moment, however, Rāvaṇa arrived with his rākṣasas.
O dear one, the powerful lord of Laṅkā went to that region. Then, seeing Arjuna on the Narmadā, the heroic Daśānana— who was constantly prone to anger— was deluded by the granting of a boon.
Highly incensed, he rushed forward like Śambara against Mahendra;
then Arjuna, seeing Rāvaṇa, likewise repelled him. Thereupon, both Rāvaṇa and Arjuna indeed engaged in combat.

Then, O King, having fought and conquered by force in battle that lord of the Rākṣasas— the hero Durjaya, who was arrogant due to the granting of a boon— the lord of men bound him with his bowstring and entered his own city.

Having heard that Rāvaṇa had been bound, Pulastya then released him; for he had previously seen Arjuna in the city and had not seen him there at that time. Then, on one occasion, the powerful and radiant Kārtavīrya-Arjuna—
Then, having gone to the seashore and wandering about, deluded by pride,
O Bhārata, he covered the ocean with hundreds of arrows.
The ocean, having paid homage to him with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him.
"O hero, do not release these swift arrows; tell me, what may I do for you? For the beings who have taken refuge with me would be destroyed by your great shafts."—Arjuna.
O tiger among kings, they are being oppressed; O Lord, grant them freedom from fear.
O Lord of the Sindhu, give me battle this very day with haste!
[Thus spoke] the Ocean.
Or else, I shall afflict you; therefore, do not delay. O King, there are many of great prowess dwelling in this world;
O Indra among kings, O one of mighty strength, engage in battle with even one of them.
Arjuna said:
"If there were anyone anywhere who, bearing excellent weapons, was my equal in battle,
he would be like the ocean."
Tell me of him who exists, O King, who might withstand Jamadagni, the great seer, in a great battle— if indeed he is renowned,
O Duryodhana.
"His son indeed deserves to give battle to you in the proper manner.
Having heard the words of the ocean, the king who was the lord of Māhiṣmatī,
overwhelmed by great wrath, first roared together with his ministers.
Then, O Bhārata, he departed quickly with his anger;
having reached that hermitage, he sought out Rāma and,
together with his kinsmen, began to act in opposition to him.
He caused distress to the high-souled Rāma;
then the splendor of Rāma, who possesses immeasurable energy, blazed forth,
as if burning the armies with his brilliance like the sun with its rays.
Then those two engaged in battle like Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Thereupon, seizing his axe, Rāma suddenly cut down the king who possessed a thousand arms, as one might fell a tree with many branches.
Seeing him slain and fallen, all his kinsmen gathered together; taking up swords and spears, they opposed Rāma. Rāma, too, mounting his chariot, quickly drew his bow.
Discharging supreme weapons, he scattered the royal army;
then, O King, the Kṣatriyas, tormented by the fear of Jamadagni’s son,
entered mountain fastnesses like deer fleeing from the fear of a lion.
Because they did not perform their own prescribed duties out of fear of them,
and because of the absence of Brāhmaṇas, the subjects fell into the state of *vṛṣalatva* (degradation).
Thus became the Draviḍas, the Kāśas, the Puṇḍras, along with the Śabaras.
For they had fallen into the state of outcasts (*vṛṣalatva*), their kṣatriya duties having been severed.
Then, when the kṣatriya women were repeatedly struck down and the heroic warriors slain, the twice-born raised up the kṣatriya lineage; and Rāma, having destroyed those [enemies], [restored it].
Then, on the twenty-first occasion, a divine, sweet voice, audible to all the world, spoke to Rāma:
"Rāma, Rāma, turn back! Behold now these virtues!"
Having repeatedly deprived these kinsmen of their lives,
those sages, headed by Ṛcīka, likewise spoke thus to that high-souled one: "Rāma, Rāma, O great hero, turn back!"
But Rāma, unable to endure the slaughter of his father, spoke to those sages:
"O fathers,
indeed you ought not to restrain me."
"O best among victors, you ought not to slay these wretched kshatriyas. For such slaughter is not fitting for you, who are a true brahmin.
Duryodhana:
"Indeed, such destruction is not appropriate for you, being as you are a virtuous brahmin."
Having heard the words of his ancestors, that descendant of Bhṛgu abandoned his anger;
having performed thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of human-sacrifices,
he gave the earth, bounded by the ocean, to Kāśyapa.
O dear one, Dhanañjaya is the equal of that Rāma in battle;
Pārtha is undoubtedly equal to Kārtavīrya in combat. Having displayed his prowess in battle, O Indra among kings, it is impossible to defeat Pārtha.
Duryodhana said:
"Listen, O King, to the inconceivable feats of prowess performed by Arjuna in the past;
Arjuna, the best among archers, committed a difficult deed long ago."
O King, in the city of Drupada, during the svayaṃvara of Draupadī, amidst the clamor of all classes from children to the elderly gathered there with all the kṣatriyas present,
the swift-acting [Arjuna] cast a fish into the water that was difficult to behold.
That excellent bow, which was impossible for all the kings to string,
he made ready in an instant while all the Kṣatriyas looked on. Then the mighty Phalguna, having pierced the mechanical device, [won] the marriage.
His shoulder was encircled by Kṛṣṇā with a golden garland;
then, seeing Pārtha thus surrounded by her, all those kings—
mighty heroes filled with rage— took up all their weapons.
Placing Vaikartana at their head, they all rushed toward Pārtha. Seeing all those kings enraged, the mighty Pārtha checked them with sharp arrows and conquered them there himself.
Having conquered all those rulers of the earth led by Karṇa,
Pārtha then obtained the auspicious Kṛṣṇā through his prowess and strength in battle,
just as Bhīṣma formerly did Ambā before the entire assembly of Kṣatriyas.
Then, at one time, Bībhatsu himself set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
There, he approached Ulūpī, who had been born auspiciously as the daughter of a king of the Nāgas,
and he obtained her among the foremost of the Nāgas, having requested her according to the proper custom.
Then he bathed in the Godāvarī and the Kāverī rivers;
thereafter, having reached the Pāṇḍya kingdom, he obtained his daughter. Having found joy there, Jiṣṇu then departed toward the southern direction.
Having gone to the southern shore of the ocean, Arjuna reached the Kumārī-tīrtha of the Apsarases and,
by means of his supreme heroism and strength, liberated five [nāgas] who had assumed the forms of crocodiles.
Having reached Kanyātīrtha, he then proceeded to Dvāravatī; there,
at the command of Kṛṣṇa, Phalguna obtained Subhadrā,
and having placed her upon the seat of his chariot, he set out toward his own city.
Then, when Pārtha had departed taking [the earrings], all the Yādavas heard of it and,
filled with rage, rushed toward him like a pride of tigers toward a lion. Pradyumna, Kṛtavarman, Gada, Sāraṇa, and Sātyaki [also pursued him].
Āhuka, Sāmba, Cārudeṣṇa, Viḍūratha,
and all the other Yādavas, led by Baladeva—
with the sole exception of Kṛṣṇa— were accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, having encountered Dhanañjaya as he was proceeding through the forest,
many millions of Yādavas, filled with great rage, surrounded him and waged war;
yet Pārtha alone fought a most terrible battle against them all.
For a moment, indeed, an equal battle took place between them;
then, O Indra among kings, the heroic Pārtha, having checked all of them in battle with sharp arrows,
overcame all those Yādavas by his might.
Taking Subhadrā with him, Duryodhana entered Śakraprastha.
Listen further, O Great King, to the daring deed of Phalguna.
And Bībhatsu granted the Khāṇḍava forest as requested by Agni. O King, as soon as it was obtained by him, the blessed Lord Havyavāhana then began to consume the Khāṇḍava forest.
Then, O king of kings, as Vibhāvasu was indeed devouring him, the mighty Savyasācin,
a lordly charioteer armed with bow and arrows and equipped with his quiver,
protected himself by his own prowess.
Then, having heard that, Mahendra gave orders to those clouds.
Thus commanded by him, those masses of clouds rained down with excessive showers. Thereupon, Pārtha [Arjuna] [assailed] the hosts of clouds from all sides with volleys of arrows.
The birds warded them off, and it was like a marvel.
Hearing that the masses of clouds had been repelled, Purandara became enraged;
mounting his white elephant and surrounded by all the hosts of gods, he advanced.
He went forth to fight with Pārtha for the sake of protecting Khāṇḍava;
and then, O Bhārata, the Rudras, the Maruts, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, the Ādityas, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas [also followed].
The Gandharvas together with other hosts of gods,
all those lords of the immortals, equipped with weapons and blazing with their own splendor, rushed forward desiring to slay Dhanañjaya.
O lord of the earth, all those most terrible omens that appear at the end of a Yuga were seen there;
then all the hosts of gods rushed toward Pārtha.
But seeing those gods and that divine army, Phalguna remained unperturbed; quickly grasping sharp-pointed, swift-flying arrows,
