he stood like Time itself at the end of an eon, gazing upon Śakra and the gods.
Then all the hosts of gods, together with Purandara,
O lord of the earth, covered that mortal man, Bībhatsu, with showers of arrows.
Thereupon, the highly energetic Pārtha quickly seized the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Then, with volleys of arrows, he warded off the shafts of the gods;
but all the mighty deities, enraged once more,
rained down various weapons upon that mortal, Savyasācin, in the battle, O lord of the earth.
Then Pārtha, with his sharp arrows, cut those showers of weapons released by the gods into two or three pieces while they were still in the air;
and again, Pārtha, filled with rage, drew his bow into a circle.
He struck the hosts of gods on all sides with sharp arrows. Then,
O bull of the Bharatas, all the hosts of gods, having fought repeatedly with Pārtha and realizing him to be impossible to defeat in battle, [withdrew].
Afflicted by the arrows of Pārtha, all those gods were pacified;
abandoning Vāsava along with his elephant, they fled in every direction.
In the battle, the Rudras with the Gandharvas fled toward the east, and the Maruts toward the south.
Terrified, the Vasus and the two Aśvins fled toward the western quarter;
the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas likewise fled facing northward.
And the Sādhyas, their faces turned upward, fled in fear, reflecting upon the arrows of Pārtha.
Thus all the hosts of gods fled in every direction, looking back again and again at Pārtha with his bow. Seeing those throngs of deities fleeing in battle, Purandara—
Then, filled with rage, the one of great splendor covered Pārtha with arrows;
Pārtha, though a mortal, likewise pierced Śakra, the lord of the gods. Thereupon, that lord of the gods unleashed a rain of stones.
Then Arjuna, filled with great indignation, countered that shower of arrows;
thereupon, the King of the Gods also increased that downpour,
desiring to test further the prowess of Savyasācin.
And that Pāṇḍava, gladdening the subduer of Pāka (Indra), caused that shower of stones of great velocity to vanish with his arrows; then,
seizing with both hands a mountain named Aṅgada—
Desiring to slay the one of white horses, Śakra unleashed a mountain covered with trees;
then Arjuna, with thousands of swift, blazing,
and straight-flying arrows, shattered that king of mountains.
And Pārtha forcibly checked Śakra in battle with his arrows.
Then, O great king, Śakra, realizing that the hero Dhanañjaya was endowed with energy and strength and could not be conquered in combat, [withdrew].
At that moment, Vāsava attained supreme joy there on account of his son’s heroism; O King, there was no one of great renown in heaven capable of defeating him, not even Prajāpati himself.
Then Pārtha, having slain the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas with his arrows,
the one of great splendor caused them to fall continuously into the blazing fire. No one there was able to restrain Pārtha.
Having seen Śakra turned back along with the hosts of gods in heaven,
Pārtha, having conquered the deities just as Suparṇa once did for the sake of Soma in the past, gratified the sacrificial fire.
Then Arjuna, having gratified the Fire-god by his own prowess,
[obtained] the chariot, the banner, the horses, the divine weapons, and the assembly hall;
as well as the Gāṇḍīva, the best of bows, and two quivers with inexhaustible arrows.
O Bhārata, Bībhatsu obtained these and acquired fame;
listen further, O Indra among kings, as Pārtha went toward the northern direction.
O bull of the Bharata race, having conquered the nine regions along with their cities and mountains, and having brought the entire Jambūdvīpa under his control,
he defeated all the kings by force and established them as tributaries.
Having taken all those jewels and returned once more to the city,
O Bhārata, he then caused the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, to perform the Rājasūya, the most excellent of sacrifices.
Arjuna performed these and other deeds in the past;
there is no man anywhere in the world equal to Arjuna in valor—
not among gods, dānavas, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, or rākṣasas.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the other Kuru great chariot-warriors,
as well as all the kings in the world and other heroic archers—
these and many others, O lord of the earth, surrounded him.
O Kauravya, though they were all prepared, they were unable to fight against Pārtha alone in battle; for I have constantly beheld Phalguna as the most excellent of men,
and having reflected upon him, I am deeply agitated by fear of him.
O father, in every house I always see Pārtha,
equipped with his arrows and the Gāṇḍīva bow, like the Destroyer himself with noose in hand;
O Bhārata, I see thousands of Pārthas and am filled with fear.

This entire city appears to me as if it were Pārtha; for even in this secluded place, O dear descendant of Bharata, I see only Pārtha. Having seen Pārtha appearing in my dream, my mind is as if bewildered.

Names beginning with the letter ‘a’—such as *arjuna*, *aśva*, and *aja*—cause my heart to tremble with fear; for these words, O dear one, produce terror in me when I think of that heroic enemy, the son of Pṛthā. There is no fear for me other than from that enemy hero.
For Vijaya would surely slay even Prahlāda or Bali in battle;
therefore, O Great King, a war with him would lead to the destruction of our people. Knowing his power, I live in constant sorrow.
Just as there was formerly fear of Mārīca in the Daṇḍaka forest, so too,
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
shall there be fear for me from the highly heroic Pārtha [Arjuna] when Rāma is present.
"I know well this invincible prowess of the great hero Jishnu,
O dear one; do not do anything displeasing to that heroic son of Pṛthā,
whether it be through gambling, combat with weapons, or harsh words at any time."
If you act thus toward these [sons], there will indeed be conflict between them.
Therefore, my son, always behave with affection toward Pārtha.
And whatever man on earth conducts himself through his relationship with Pārtha—
O Bhārata, he has no fear whatsoever in the three worlds;
therefore, O child, you should always treat Duryodhana with affection, as you would Jiṣṇu.
O descendant of Kuru, in that gambling match, deceit was practiced against the son of Pṛthā through trickery.
Therefore, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you must slay him then, for there shall be no other means for us.
O Bhārata, you must not employ stratagems against the Pāṇḍavas.
My child, many stratagems were previously employed by you against the sons of Pṛthā;
the sons of Kuntī have on numerous occasions overcome those harmful schemes.
Therefore, my dear child, if you wish to act for the welfare of our life, our family, and our people, then together with your friends, your kinsmen,
and your brothers, conduct yourself always with affection toward Pārtha.
Having heard the words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King Duryodhana then reflected for a moment and, impelled by fate, spoke.
We have heard that Vṛkodara, having swiftly raised his heavy mace and quickly yoked his own chariot, has set forth;
and Nakula, taking up his sword and shield adorned with eight moons, has likewise departed.
Sahadeva and the king signaled their intent through gestures.
Then, all of them, mounting chariots equipped with many weapons and accoutrements, set out for the mobilization of the army, striking down the throngs of enemy chariots.
For they will never forgive us, having been so greatly wronged by us; and who among them could possibly forgive the suffering of Draupadī?
Let us gamble again with the Pāṇḍavas—for your good—so that they may go into exile in the forest.
"O bull of the Bharatas, we shall thus be able to bring them under our control. Either they, defeated at dice, or we ourselves, shall enter the great forest for twelve years, clad in deerskins."
"Let us live for thirteen years among people in disguise,
and then, once recognized, for another twelve years in the forest;
let the game of dice proceed accordingly."
"Having cast the dice, let the Pāṇḍavas play this game once more.
O King, O bull of the Bharatas, this is our most important task;
for this Śakuni knows the entire science of the perfection of dice."
Having secured allies, we are firmly rooted in our kingdom;
and having honored our vast and powerful army, which is difficult to overcome,
they will complete their vow in the thirteenth year.
"O King, scorcher of the foe, we shall conquer them; may this be pleasing to you.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Bring them back quickly, even if they have already gone far on their journey, according to your wish."
"Let them come again; let the Pāṇḍavas engage in this gambling match.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Droṇa, Somadatta, and the great car-warrior Bāhlīka—

Vidura, the son of Droṇa, and the heroic son of the Vaiśya woman, Bhūriśravas, the son of Śāntanu, and the great car-warrior Vikarṇa—all of them spoke thus: "Let there be no gambling; let there be peace in every way."
While they were dwelling there according to their pleasure,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, out of love for his son, issued a challenge to the Pāṇḍavas to engage once more in gambling, despite the fact that all his well-wishing friends who perceived the truth were unwilling.
Then, O great king, Gāndhārī, emaciated by grief, spoke words consistent with righteousness out of affection for her son to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men;
and when Duryodhana was born, the high-minded Kṣattṛ spoke [as follows].
"Let this disgrace to the family be led forth to the other world;
for as soon as he was born, O Bhārata, he howled like a jackal. Surely this is the end of our lineage; O Kurus, understand this!"
Do not sink into the great waters through your own fault, O Bhārata; do not,
O Lord, approve the counsel of the ignorant and undisciplined,
lest you become the cause of the terrible destruction of your lineage.
Who indeed would break a dam that has been built, or blow upon a fire that has been extinguished? O Bhārata, who would provoke the Pārthas again after they have been established in peace?
O descendant of Ajamīḍha, remembering you, I shall remind you once more.

A scripture does not instruct one of evil intellect, whether for their welfare or otherwise. O King, an elder should by no means possess the mind of a child. Let your sons have you as their guide; let them not, being shattered, abandon you.
"Therefore, at my word, let this defiler of the family be abandoned. O King, lord of men, you did not act accordingly out of affection for your son;
know that the fruit of that has now arrived, leading to the end of your lineage."
May that wisdom born from your understanding of the Dharma through tranquility toward others be ever with you, and never contrary to it. That is no strength which is opposed by gentleness.
One should diligently cultivate the friend that is the Dharma; for prosperity gathered through cruelty is perishable, whereas that which is gentle and mature passes down to one's sons and grandsons.
Then the great king spoke to Gāndhārī, who perceives the dharma:
"Let there be the end of this family's desire; I shall not be able to prevent it.
Let it be exactly as they wish; let the Pāṇḍavas return."
"Let my men play dice once again with the Pāṇḍavas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the messenger Prātikāmī approached Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pṛthā, who had already traveled far on his journey.
By the command of the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he said:
"O King Yudhiṣṭhira, the assembly hall has been prepared; the dice have been cast. Come, O Pāṇḍava, play! Thus your father speaks to you, O Bhārata."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By the decree of the Creator, living beings experience both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
there is no turning back from those two if one must gamble again."
"Even though I know that a challenge to a game of dice, especially one issued by an elder,
leads to ruin, I do not venture to disregard it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Speaking thus, the Pāṇḍava returned with his brothers;
yet, knowing the magic of Śakuni, Pārtha went to the gambling match once more,
for a being made of gold is impossible.
Nevertheless, Rāma lusted after the deer;
for generally, the intellects of those who have met with calamity become most perverted.

Those great car-warriors, the bulls of the Bharata race, entered that assembly hall once again; though they sat as they pleased, those best of the Bharatas agitated the hearts of their friends for the sake of resuming the game of dice.
Oppressed by fate for the destruction of the entire world, they arrived;
seeing them come so piteously, Akṣa quickly spoke.
Śakuni said:
"The elder has released for you that wealth which was already considered won;
however, O bull of the Bharatas, hear from me about one great-stake wager:
for twelve years, we shall be defeated by you at dice."
Clad in the skins of the ruru deer, we shall enter the great forest for thirteen years, remaining unrecognized among people;
and once recognized, we shall spend another twelve years in the forest.
"Either you have been defeated by us, or you shall dwell in the forest for twelve years together with Kṛṣṇā, clothed in deerskins;
and when the thirteenth year has passed, you may return once more as is fitting."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, you must regain your own kingdom either by these means or by others. With this resolve, O Bhārata, come and play again at dice with us, having cast the dice."
Then, in the midst of the assembly, all the members of the court, with their hands raised high and their minds agitated by intense emotion, spoke. Indeed,
all the members of the assembly said:
"Alas! Shame! These kinsmen do not awaken him to this great danger;
though it must be understood through intelligence, these bulls of the Bharata race do not perceive it themselves.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Hearing these many rumors of the people, the lord of men,
Pārtha, out of shame and attachment to dharma, went to gamble once again;
though he knew better, the one of great intelligence engaged in the game anew.
Thinking, "May this destruction of the Kurus not come to pass," Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How indeed can a king like me, while observing his own duty, [act]?"
"Challenged, I shall turn back and play with you, O Śakuni.
Śakuni said:
"Cattle, horses, many milch cows, and boundless goats and sheep."
The elephants, the treasury, the gold, and all the male and female slaves—
O Pāṇḍavas, this alone shall be our single stake for living in the forest:
either you or we, being defeated, shall dwell taking refuge in the woods.
"And for the thirteenth year, we shall remain unrecognized among people;
with this resolve, O bull of the Bharatas, let us play,
O Bhārata, with a single throw of the dice for exile in the forest."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Pārtha accepted that stake, and the son of Subala took it up;
"It is won! Śakuni thus addressed Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus possessed by the power of destiny, O Bhārata, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was restrained by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, as well as by the wise Vidura, Yuyutsu, Kṛpa, and Sañjaya.
[He was accompanied] by Gāndhārī and Pṛthā, as well as Bhīma, Arjuna, and the Yamas;
by the heroic Vikarṇa, by Draupadī, and likewise by the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman);
and by Somadatta as well as the wise Bāhlīka.
Though he was constantly and most earnestly restrained, the King did not desist;
and even though he was thus being forbidden out of a desire for his welfare, Kuntī’s son,
for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods’ work, allowed the Kali age to enter him for a moment.
Possessed by Kali, O King, he addressed Śakuni, saying,
"Let it be so," as he then played for exile in the forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Defeated, the sons of Pṛthā resolved to dwell in the forest;
they took up deerskins as upper garments in due order.
Seeing those subduers of enemies, deprived of their kingdom and clad in deerskins, [the people were moved].
Then, as they were setting out for their forest exile, Duḥśāsana said:
"The wheel of the high-souled King Dhṛtarāṣṭra has begun to turn;
the sons of Pāṇḍu have been defeated and have fallen into the utmost calamity."
Today the gods have set forth upon even paths that are free of obstacles; for we, though superior in merit and senior in status,
have been cast into endless hell by our enemies for a long duration of time.
Deprived of happiness and fallen from their kingdom for eternal years— those who,
intoxicated by their strength, once mocked the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
those Pāṇḍavas, now defeated and stripped of their wealth, shall go to the forest.
Let them cast off their variegated armor and put on celestial, radiant garments;
let them all don deer skins.
Just as those who had accepted the stake of Saubala were always of such a firm conviction that "there are no men like this in the worlds," so too were they.
"Today these Pāṇḍavas shall know their own true nature;
in times of adversity, they will prove to be as fruitless as sterile sesame seeds.
Even that old man of dull intellect [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] was present at that *svayaṃvara*."
O Kaurava, let there be no such vain-mindedness in you regarding this old Yajñasena, for he is the very source of the dwelling place for high-spirited men such as these.
Behold the deerskins of the powerful Pāṇḍavas, though they are uninitiated;
even this old man of dull intellect [acted thus] at the *svayaṃvara*.
While the kings were looking on, Yajñasena Somaka, who was possessed of great wisdom, appeared to have a vain intellect before the Pāṇḍavas.
Yajñasena Somaka was truly of great intelligence.
Having given the Pāñcāla maiden to the Pāṇḍavas,
he has indeed committed a wicked deed; for the sons of Pṛthā are not eunuchs, yet they are the husbands of Yājñasenī.
As she beheld them, their limbs covered in deerskins— wearing fine upper garments and urged on by deerskins—
she saw them in the forest, destitute and without support.
"O Yājñasenī, what pleasure will you find?
Choose another husband here, whomever you desire!
For all these Kurus are assembled here."
"Patient, self-controlled, and endowed with great wealth—
choose one of these as your husband;
let not this reversal of fortune cause you distress."
Just as sterile sesame seeds are fruitless, just as deer made of leather are [mere illusions],
so too are all the Pāṇḍavas, like mere chaff for crows. Why do you wait upon the fallen Pāṇḍavas?
"Effort spent upon serving eunuchs is as fruitless as sesame seeds without kernels.
Thus did the cruel son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra cause harsh words to be heard by the Pārthas.
Having heard that, the exceedingly intolerant Bhīmasena,
having rebuked him loudly and restrained him out of rage, approached him suddenly and said this:
"Like a Himalayan lion toward a jackal," Bhīmasena said,
"you speak harshly to one who is unaccomplished and frequented by cruel, sinful people."
"Indeed, you boast in the midst of the kings by means of your Gāndhāra lore;
just as you here pierce our vital spots intensely with the arrows of your words,
so shall I remind you of them, cutting through your vital spots in battle."
"And those who follow you, driven by the power of desire and greed— those protectors along with their followers— I shall send to the abode of Yama.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As he spoke thus— clothed in deerskins,
overcome by sorrow, yet bound to the path of righteousness— he danced in the midst of the Kurus.
Calling out "O cow! O cow! and casting off all shame, Bhīmasena said:
"O Duḥśāsana, you are capable of such cruel, harsh, and ruthless deeds."
For who, having obtained wealth through deceit, ought to boast?
Let not Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, go to the worlds of the righteous,
if he does not drink your blood in battle after rending your chest.
"Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle while all the archers look on, I shall attain peace before long; I tell you this as the truth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Duryodhana, the dull-witted king, out of joy imitated with his own gait the playful movement of Bhīmasena as he moved like a lion.
As the Pāṇḍavas were departing from the assembly hall,
Vṛkodara, turning his body halfway around, said to him, "This much alone has not been accomplished."
"For I shall remind you of this and answer you, O fool, once you have been swiftly struck down along with your followers—
having considered this humiliation within yourself."
Restraining his wrath, the powerful and proud Bhīma, following the king, spoke these words as he was departing from the assembly of the Kauravas.

"I shall be the slayer of Duryodhana; Dhanañjaya shall be the slayer of Karṇa; and Sahadeva will kill Śakuni, that gambler with the dice. Furthermore, I shall speak these great words once more in the midst of the assembly.
"The gods will surely bring it to pass that there shall be war between us;
I shall slay this wicked Suyodhana with my mace in battle,
and I shall place my foot upon his head on the earth."
"I shall drink the blood of this harsh and evil-minded Duḥśāsana, who is a hero only in words, just as a lion drinks the blood of its prey.
Arjuna said:
"O Bhīma, the resolve of the virtuous is not fully understood by mere words;
they shall see what will come to pass after fourteen years from now.
O Bhīmasena, there are none who possess enmity toward you."
Intoxicated by their power over the planets, they do not perceive the great danger;
the earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana, Karṇa, the evil-minded Śakuni, and Duḥśāsana as the fourth.
"O Bhīmasena, at your command, I shall slay Karṇa in battle— that envious speaker who releases evil-minded men. Thus does Arjuna pledge his word, desiring to do what is pleasing to Bhīma.
I shall slay Karna and his followers in battle with my feathered shafts;
and whatever other kings, through delusion of intellect, shall fight against me,
I will send them all to the abode of Yama with my sharp arrows.
Himavat might indeed move from its place, the sun might lose its radiance,
and coolness might vanish from the moon, if my truth should waver;
yet in the fourteenth year from now, the rulers of the earth shall be witnesses [to my fulfillment].
"If Duryodhana does not grant us the kingdom fourteen years from now, this shall indeed come true, provided that he treats [us] with honor. Vaiśampāyana said:
When Pārtha had spoken thus, the illustrious and powerful Sahadeva, son of Mādravatī, grasped his massive arm and,
desiring the slaughter of Saubala, spoke these words:
With eyes bloodshot with rage and hissing like a serpent, [he said]:
"O fool, you who destroy the fame of the Gāndhāras, those which you consider to be dice are not dice;
they are sharpened arrows chosen by you for battle."
Just as Bhīma spoke concerning you and your kinsmen, saying,
"I shall perform that deed;
carry out all your preparations," so shall I slay you along with your followers in battle by my own prowess and speed.
"O son of Subala, if you will stand in battle according to the duty of a Kṣatriya,"—
having heard these words of Sahadeva, O lord of the people, Nakula, the most handsome of men, spoke these words:
This daughter of Yajñasena was won at this gambling match by those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who,
standing there for the sake of Duryodhana’s pleasure, were made to hear harsh words;
those wicked sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, impelled by Time, are now on the verge of death.
I shall show you the abode of Vaivasvata most abundantly;
I shall slay in battle that cruel and vilest of men, the evil-souled Ulūka, the beloved son of Saubala.
"By the command of the King of Dharma, following the path of Draupadī,
I shall before long make the earth free of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Thus spoke all those tigers among men, with their long arms.
Having made many formal pledges, they approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I take my leave of the Bharatas, as well as our aged grandfather."
King Somadatta, the great king Bāhlika,
Droṇa, Kṛpa, other monarchs, and Aśvatthāman himself;
Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
[He addressed] the son of Somadatta of great heroism, the highly intelligent Vikarṇa,
Yuyutsu, Saṃjaya, and likewise the other members of the assembly;
as well as the illustrious Gāndhārī and his mother Pṛthā.
"Having taken leave of you all, I depart; I shall see you again upon my return.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Out of shame, those virtuous ones said nothing at all to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"With their minds alone, they should have conceived what was beneficial for that wise one.
Vidura said:
"The noble Pṛthā, a princess, ought not to go to the forest."
"She is delicate, aged, and always accustomed to comfort.
The Pāṇḍavas said,
"O sinless one, saying 'So be it,' they all replied, 'We shall do exactly as you tell us.'"
"You are our paternal uncle, equal to a father, and we are devoted to you.
O learned one, do as you command, for you are our supreme preceptor. Furthermore, O high-minded one, please ordain whatever else must be done."
"This auspicious woman shall dwell here in my house, honored with all due respect"—know this, O sons of Pṛthā; may you be free from ailment in every way.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, bull of the Bharatas, understand this to be my word.
No one who has been defeated by unrighteous means suffers from that defeat;
for you indeed understand the laws of righteousness, Dhanañjaya is the knower of battle,
Bhīmasena is the slayer of enemies, and Nakula is the gatherer of wealth.

Sahadeva, a god among men, will always follow behind you; fierce in battle, he will exist for the destruction of all calamities. Sahadeva shall be the charioteer, while Dhaumya, the supreme knower of Brahman, will be the priest.
Draupadī is skilled in both dharma and worldly affairs and is a practitioner of righteousness;
all of you are dear to one another and likewise speak kindly to each other. You are indivisible by enemies and contented—who here would not envy you?
O Bhārata, this indeed is the most auspicious of all meditative absorptions (samādhi) for you;
even an enemy equal to Śakra cannot withstand it, O Acyuta. In former times, you were instructed in this on Mount Himavat by Merusāvarṇi.
You have heard of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana in the city of Vāraṇāvata,
of Rāma on the Bhr̥gutuṅga peak, and of Śambhu by the river Dr̥ṣadvatī;
and you have also heard concerning the dark great seer Añjana.
"Residing on the banks of the Kalmāṣī, you went into discipleship under Bhṛgu;
you were a constant witness to Nārada, and this Dhaumya is your priest. Do not abandon that wisdom, honored by the ṛṣis, when it comes time for the next world."

O Pāṇḍava, you surpass Purūravas, the son of Ila, in intelligence; you surpass other kings in power, and the sages in the practice of dharma. Your mind is fixed on victory like that of Indra, and on the restraint of anger like that of Yama.
In the region of Kubera for the act of renunciation, and in that of Varuṇa for self-restraint;
the gift of oneself, gentleness, and subsistence from the waters;
the forbearance of the earth, and the entire splendor from the solar orb.
"Know that the strength of the wind arises from yourself and from all living beings. May you be free from disease; may blessings be upon you; I shall see you when you have returned.
Furthermore, in times of calamity, in difficulties regarding dharma or wealth, or in all undertakings,"
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should proceed according to what is right from time to time.
You have been questioned here, O son of Kuntī; may you attain well-being, O Bhārata. We shall see you returned again, having accomplished your purpose and being endowed with prosperity.
"Indeed, no one knows of any transgression whatsoever committed by you in the past.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, the Pāṇḍava of true prowess replied, "So be it."
Having paid homage to Bhīṣma and Droṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira set forth. Then, when King Dharmarāja had departed from there,
all the people, without haste, climbed up to see him.
Then, having climbed upon the excellent palaces, the peaks of the celestial chariots,
all the gate-towers, and all the other trees on every side,
the illustrious people looked out with indifference.
Indeed, those streets crowded with many people could not be traversed in that manner; therefore,
they climbed upon them so that, being distressed, they might behold the son of Pāṇḍu on foot,
deprived of his umbrella and stripped of his garments and ornaments.
Then, seeing Pārtha clad in bark garments and deerskins,
the people,
their hearts overwhelmed by grief, spoke many kinds of words.
The great fourfold army that used to follow him as he traveled—
now the Pāṇḍavas followed him in this manner, together with Kṛṣṇā,
the four brothers, and the family priest Dhaumya.
Having restrained Bhīma and Arjuna by deceit and left them with their bows unstrung, he who remained steadfast in righteousness—
that high-souled one by whom she could not previously even be looked upon, even by beings moving through the sky— [has now revealed her].
Today, the people walking along the royal highway behold that Kṛṣṇā,
who was accustomed to body-unguents and used red sandalwood paste;
having endured the rain, the heat, and the cold, she will soon become discolored.
Today Queen Pṛthā surely speaks out of being possessed by truth;
yet the queen ought not to see her sons and daughter-in-law today. How could even a son devoid of merit be made to witness such sorrow?
How much more so for one who has conquered this world through conduct alone?
Kindness, compassion, fortitude, good character, self-restraint, and tranquility—
these six qualities adorn that best of men, the son of Pāṇḍu.
Therefore, by his affliction, all living beings are deeply tormented,
like aquatic creatures in the summer when the water has dried up;
for the entire world is afflicted by the suffering of that Lord of the World.
By the destruction of the very root, the tree that bears flowers and fruit is destroyed.
For this King of Dharma, possessed of great splendor, is the root of human beings;
other people are his flowers, fruits, leaves, and branches.
"Like brothers, let us quickly follow with our sons and kinsmen the Pāṇḍava as he departs,
abandoning our gardens, fields, and homes."
Sharing in the same sorrow and joy, we follow the highly righteous Pārtha;
our vehicles have been overturned, our courtyards laid in ruins,
and all our wealth and grain have been seized, their essence stripped away from every side.
Covered in dust and abandoned by the deities,
they were overrun by rats scurrying from their holes; devoid of water and smoke, and lacking any sweeping or cleaning.
The offerings, sacrifices, mantras, oblations, and recitations have all perished;
like vessels shattered by an evil age,
these dwellings abandoned by us— let the son of Subala take possession of them.
"Today let the forest where the Pāṇḍavas go become a city,
and let our abandoned city become a forest. Let all the caves belong to fanged beasts, and the dwellings to wild animals and birds."

Let the elephants and lions, terrified by fear of us, abandon even their forests; let them seek out regions untouched by us and forsake those they frequent. Let them leave behind the lands containing grass, meat, and fruit, along with the deer and elephants.
"O Vaiśampāyana,
we shall dwell happily in the forest together with the sons of Pṛthā,"—
such were the various words uttered by people of diverse origins.
Pārtha heard it, and having heard it, his mind was not shaken. Then, from all sides, in house after house,
the women of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who were situated upon the palace [terraces]—
Then, having torn down the lattices of the palace and its enclosures,
they beheld the Pāṇḍavas, dejected and clad in garments of bark and deer-skins,
and they saw Kṛṣṇā, whom they had never seen before, walking on foot.
Seeing her clad in a single garment, weeping, with disheveled hair and in her menses,
all the women then became deeply pale-faced;
afflicted by grief and sorrow, they lamented in many ways out of their bewilderment.
"Alas, alas! Fie, fie! they cried, shedding tears from their eyes.
Then, having heard the words of the people, the king, together with his brothers, set out for forest life, his resolve firmly made.
02.070.001 Vaiśampāyana said: When he had departed, Kṛṣṇā, afflicted by intense grief, approached the illustrious Pṛthā and took leave of her as well as the other women there.
Having offered salutations and embraces as was appropriate, she desired to depart;
then a great clamor arose within the inner apartments of the Pāṇḍavas.
And Kuntī, deeply distressed upon seeing Draupadī departing, [cried out].
With a voice overwhelmed by grief, she spoke these words with great difficulty:
"O child, you should not grieve now that this great calamity has befallen you;
for you are well-acquainted with the duties of women and are likewise possessed of virtuous character and conduct."
"O lady of pure smiles, I ought not to instruct you regarding your husbands;
for both your families are adorned by your possession of the virtues of a virtuous wife. Fortunate indeed are these Kurus, O sinless one, that they have not been consumed by your [wrath]."

"Go on your path safely, for you are strengthened by my meditation. For virtuous women do not fall into despondency when a future purpose is at hand; protected as you are by your weighty duties, you shall swiftly attain prosperity."
"And my son Sahadeva, while living in the forest, must always be looked after by you,
so that even having encountered this calamity, his great mind does not sink. Having said, "So be it," that queen, her eyes clouded with flowing tears, [departed].
Clad in a single garment stained with blood and with her hair disheveled, she went forth.
As she departed wailing in grief, Pṛthā followed after her. Seeing Pṛthā, all the women wept, overcome by intense sorrow.
Then she saw all her sons, stripped of their ornaments and garments,
their bodies covered in deerskins, their faces slightly downcast with shame;
they were surrounded by exultant enemies and mourned by their friends.
Approaching all her sons who were in that state, she, being exceedingly affectionate,
embraced them and spoke many things out of grief, lamenting:
"How [can this be] regarding those adorned with the practice of true dharma, conduct, and steadfastness?"
"O noble ones, firm in devotion and ever intent upon the worship of the gods, a calamity has come upon you; what is this reversal of fate?
By my insight, I perceive this offense against you as being born from the ill-will of someone."
"Yet this must be the fault of my own ill fortune, that I have given birth to you— who,
though endowed with the highest virtues, now suffer excessive pain and exhaustion—
and how will you live in the difficult forests, deprived of all prosperity?"
"Neither emaciated by vigor, courage, strength, zeal,
nor splendor— if I had known this would surely be your dwelling in the forest,
I would not have come from the Hundred-Peaked Mountain to Hastināpura after Pāṇḍu’s death."

I consider your father to be blessed, endowed as he was with asceticism and wisdom, for even without attaining the desire for a son, he formed his beloved wish for heaven. And blessed is this supreme state attained by you, who possess knowledge beyond the reach of the senses.
Today I consider Mādrī alone to be truly virtuous and a knower of dharma in every respect,
for she has surpassed me in pleasure, intellect, and conduct. Fie on this love of life of mine, which shares only in suffering!
"Fie upon my life, which is nothing but a vessel for suffering!
My sons, I shall not abandon you—my beloved ones obtained with such great difficulty.
Indeed, I am going to the forest; alas, Kṛṣṇā, why do you desert me?"
"In this world of transient phenomena, why indeed has the Creator acted out of negligence? No end was ordained for me, and therefore life does not desert me.
Alas, O Kṛṣṇa, dweller of Dvārakā, younger brother of Saṃkarṣaṇa, where are you?"
O Best of Men, why do you not protect me and these others from suffering—
those men who indeed meditate upon you, who are without beginning or end? How has this saying, "You shall protect them," come to be rendered meaningless?

"These followers of the greatness, fame, and valor of the True Dharma do not deserve to suffer calamity; surely compassion should be shown toward them. This [is the sentiment] directed toward Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others, who were experts in the meaning of political ethics (*nīti*).
While the lords of the lineage stand by, how has this calamity come upon us?
Alas, O Pāṇḍu! Alas, O Great King! Where are you? Why do you look on with indifference as your virtuous sons are being exiled, having been defeated at dice by their enemies?
"O Sahadeva, turn back; surely you are dear to me, even more so than my own body, O son of Mādrī! Do not abandon me like a wicked son.
Let these other brothers of yours go, provided they are true to their promise."
"Right here, may you obtain the merit born from protecting me.
Having thus consoled Kuntī as she lamented and having bowed down to her,
the Pāṇḍavas, devoid of joy, set out for the forest.

Vidura and the others, themselves deeply distressed, consoled the afflicted Kuntī with reasoned arguments and slowly led her into the house of the steward (Kṣattṛ). And those women of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s household perceived everything that had occurred in its entirety.
The departure and the dragging away of Kṛṣṇā at the gambling hall—
all of them wept piteously, severely censuring the Kurus,
and for a very long time they remained lost in thought, their lotus-like faces resting upon their hands.
Then, O Bhārata, a great sound arose from all the women of the inner apartments as they wept upon seeing Kuntī in such a state,
out of their affection for her sons and their pity for the Pāṇḍavas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Seeing all the Kuru women, they wept, overwhelmed by grief.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, leaving Kuntī behind, departed.
Having resolved to dwell in the forest, he set out together with his brothers.
Then, as Pārtha departed, stripped of both belongings and ornaments,
intense sorrow arose among all the people in the city.
Then, from behind Pārtha, as he departed deeply distressed while the men looked on, there arose a tumultuous cry of "Halahalā!
Then the women belonging to the Kuru lineage...
And whatever other sounds there were in Hastināpura,
they all broke out at that time when the high-souled Dharmarāja had set out for the forest.
The sound of those women weeping, O King, arose from their grief like the high-pitched cry of female ospreys; then,
[the tears] of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas fell down.
O King, when they departed, the entire multitude of citizens in Hastināpura became exceedingly distressed on account of the wives of the Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Just as sorrow arose in Ayodhyā when Rāghava departed for the forest in the past,
so too did sorrow arise in Hastināpura.
When Pārtha was departing for the forest, deprived of his kingdom,
all the people from every side—
women, the elderly, and children— [followed him].
Thus, as the King of Dharma was departing for the forest, the people,
afflicted by grief, took to the royal highway; they were then seen upon the palace rooftops, in the gate-towers, and on the ground.
A great clamor arose from both women and men;
then the Pāṇḍava king, overcome with grief, accompanied by his domestic priest,
proceeded along the royal road crowded with men and women.
With some difficulty, the wise one emerged together with Kṛṣṇā and his younger brothers;
having departed from Hastināpura by way of the Vardhamāna gate,
he turned back that great multitude of grieving people.
O King, just as that multitude of people, overwhelmed with grief, being dismissed by Pārtha, did not turn back from the city due to their affection for him, so too did it remain;
then the Dharmarāja spoke to that multitude filled with affection.
For you have shown affection for this people with voices choked by tears;
you are indeed our friends. Having circumambulated us, return toward home together with the old, the children, and the women.

"Having cast off my weariness with regard to this place and with my brothers and Kṛṣṇā, I shall dwell in the forest for thirteen years. I will return and see you again; you all ought to grant me your permission."
And having heard the compassionate words of the King of Dharma, O King, all the citizens and the women wept on every side,
covering their faces with their upper garments and their hands.
Tormented by grief for a moment like fathers and mothers, those people,
with hearts become empty due to the departure of the King of Dharma,
endured the suffering born of that exile; they became as if deprived of consciousness.
Having dispelled that distress born of separation from the King of Dharma,
they then spoke slowly to one another, saying, "We are ruined.
Then, O King, having dismissed them, the Pāṇḍavas departed.
Then, O King, all the twice-born and the citizens, together with their groups of women,
having reflected and lamented out of affection, went back toward Pārtha;
they cried out there in many ways, wailing again and again.
Indeed, evil among living beings was seen to be more powerful than righteousness;
even the sons of Pṛthā, though exceedingly virtuous, were deprived of their prosperity.
Such were the words of the people, filled with extreme compassion.
Then some lamented for the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira;
others lamented for Bhīmasena again and again;
and some indeed lamented for Pārtha, the best among those who bear arms.
Out of compassion, some [lamented] for Nakula, others likewise for Sahadeva,
and others for that princess Kṛṣṇā, who was constantly endowed with happiness and undeserving of forest exile; thus they wailed.
Having thus enumerated their virtues and lamented again and again,
O Great King, the people of the countryside spoke thus repeatedly. Hearing their lamentation, the Kurus along with their circles of friends [were deeply moved].
The women and men, overcome with grief, departed in shame. Then, O King, having beheld the sons of Pṛthā departing for the forest,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and Sañjaya likewise [followed].
Vidura, Vikarṇa, and other bulls among the Kurus,
as well as the brahmins and the citizens, O king of kings, went forth emaciated by grief;
yet no one spoke there at that time out of fear of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, some fearless Brahmins spoke to the sons of Pāṇḍu as they were grieving intensely:
"The king always perceives things unfairly, being perpetually shrouded in darkness."
The evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not perceive righteousness;
for the sinless Pāṇḍava will never take pleasure in wickedness,
nor will Bhīma, the best among the strong, nor Jiṣṇu, the foremost of chariot-warriors.
How much less could the two sons of Mādrī, who possess great wisdom, accomplish it?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot tolerate that kingdom obtained from his father;
otherwise, there would be total unrighteousness on the part of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others.
At that time, they were unable to prevent the gambling match there;
for when the Pāṇḍavas were being exiled to the forest by means of a fraudulent game,
King Śāṃtanava was formerly like a father to us.
The royal sage Vicitravīrya and the highly virtuous Pāṇḍu—
when that tiger among men had indeed departed for his exile,
these five wise Pāṇḍavas, who are devoted to righteousness, remain here together.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his sons, is indeed ever wicked and cannot endure this;
unable to tolerate it, let us all depart from this best of cities, leaving the Kurus behind and going wherever Yudhiṣṭhira goes.
To those Brahmins who were speaking thus, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma— himself emaciated by grief yet supremely delighted— spoke to them,
saying: "My father Dhṛtarāṣṭra is my supreme elder and the best of gurus."
"It is our vow that we must necessarily act so as to please him.
You are our friends; having circumambulated us clockwise, return home together with your sons, wives, and servants."
"I shall see you once again at the gathering of the thirteenth year," having said this,
Janamejaya,
the King of Dharma, then became silent and departed.
"How did those Pārthas depart from the city toward the forest?
O best of the twice-born, tell me that, for they were treated with deceit by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Vaiśampāyana said:
O great king, hear now of the conduct of the sons of Pṛthā as they departed,
just as Rāma in former times abandoned his city of Ayodhyā and went to the forest together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Sītā.
Just as [Rāma] was deprived of his kingdom by Kaikeyī, the hunchbacked woman, and King Daśaratha,
and having abandoned his royal fortune, went to the forest;
even so did the son of Pāṇḍu, Dharmarāja, the best of kings.
By the base and powerful Duryodhana, by Saubala,
and by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra— these three standing together in a fraudulent game of dice—
the king was deprived of his kingdom, even as he remained mindful of the dharma of the virtuous.
O Indra among kings, having abandoned the city called Nāgāhvaya as well as his most difficult-to-attain prosperity, Dharmarāja went forth together with his brothers and his wife Kṛṣṇā,
just as Rāma did, O great king.
And King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his mind overwhelmed with grief,
then brooding over the misconduct of his sons with an agitated heart, could find no peace.
Reflecting thus with a distracted mind,
he sent a messenger to the steward, saying, "Let him come quickly.
Thereupon Vidura went to the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Agitated, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, questioned him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the king [questioned] Vidura, the far-sighted one, who had arrived.
As if filled with apprehension, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, questioned him.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How does Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and King of Dharma, proceed?"
O Kṣattṛ, how did Bhīmasena, Savyasācin, both the sons of Mādrī,
Dhaumya, and the ascetic Draupadī [behave]?
I wish to hear all about their bodily gestures.
Vidura said:
"Kuntī’s son Yudhiṣṭhira goes with his face covered by a cloth,
while the Pāṇḍava Bhīma walks with his two arms outstretched."
Savyasācin, scattering sand, follows the king;
Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, goes along having smeared his face;
Nakula, with all his limbs covered in dust, is distraught in mind.
Most beautiful in the world, she follows the king;
the long-eyed Kṛṣṇā, covering her face with her hair,
follows the king weeping piteously as she looks most lovely.
"O lord of the people, Dhaumya goes along the paths singing the Sāmans dedicated to Yama and those dedicated to Rudra, carrying *kuśa* grass in his hand. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Vidura, tell me this: having assumed various forms here, the Pāṇḍavas are departing; why indeed do they travel in such a manner? Vidura said:

O Bhārata, although he has been treated with contempt by his sons and deprived of both his kingdom and his wealth, the mind of the wise Dharmarāja does not waver from righteousness— he who is that king, ever compassionate toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Tormented by anger because of that deceit, he does not open his eyes;
"I must not consume people with my terrible gaze.
Therefore, covering his face, the Pāṇḍava king proceeds.
Listen as I describe how Bhīma travels,
O bull of the Bharatas: thinking, "In the strength of my arms there is no one equal to me," Bhīma likewise proceeds with his two arms outstretched.
Displaying his arms, for he was proud of the strength of his limbs,
Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, then sought to perform deeds against his enemies befitting the power of his arms, while directing the falling showers of his arrows.
Savyasācin follows the king scattering sand;
O Bhārata, just as that sand falls without adhering to him now,
so too will he release showers of arrows against his enemies without them clinging to them.
"O Bhārata, so that no one may recognize my face today," said Sahadeva,
"he therefore goes along with his face smeared.
O Lord, he thinks, 'May I not captivate the hearts of women on the road.'"
With all his limbs covered in dust, Nakula went along;
then Draupadī spoke these words, weeping, clad in a single garment, her hair disheveled, and her wet clothes smeared with blood as she appeared in her menses.
On account of whom I have reached this state in the fourteenth year—
women whose husbands have been slain, whose sons have been killed, and whose kinsmen and loved ones have perished;
their limbs smeared with the blood of their kin, their hair disheveled, and in their menses.
"Having thus performed the water-libations, the women will enter Gajāhvaya.
But the steadfast family priest Dhaumya, having prepared the *darbha* grass for the Nairṛtas,
goes in front, O Bhārata, chanting the Sāman hymns dedicated to Yama."

"When the Bharatas have been slain in battle, the preceptors of the Kurus will sing these *sāmans*"; having said this, Dhaumya also departed. Having sent forth the best of the Pāṇḍavas, he said, "You shall remain without exception."
Thus Dhaumya, having made his resolve, sang the *Raudra-sāmans*.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra asked:
"What did the citizens say, and what indeed did the people of the countryside say?"
Vidura said:
"O Kṣattṛ, explain everything in its true nature and in its entirety—
those who speak, namely the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others."
"Listen to that, O Great King, which was spoken by me on your account:
'Alas, alas! Our protectors are departing; behold such a sight!
Oh, what a pity! The conduct of the elders of the Kurus is like that of children.'"
Those who, out of greed, exile the heirs of Pāṇḍu from their kingdoms—
we have all become protectorless, separated from the sons of Pāṇḍu;
what joy can we find in these ill-behaved and covetous Kauravas?
Thus the citizens, afflicted by great sorrow, cried out on all sides.
In this way, indicating their mental resolve through their outward appearance and gestures,
the high-minded sons of Kuntī departed for the forest.
As those foremost of men were thus departing from Hastināpura,
lightning flashed in a cloudless sky and the earth trembled;
O lord of the people, Rāhu swallowed the sun out of season.
A meteor, moreover, having circled the city in a counter-clockwise direction, shattered apart;
and flesh-eating creatures— vultures, jackals, and crows— screamed out from the temples of the gods, from the sacred shrines, and from the walls and watchtowers.
"Thus, O King, these great portents appear as the Pāṇḍava goes to the forest,
foreboding the destruction of the Bhāratas due to your evil counsel.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the wise Vidura were thus conversing there, O lord of the people,
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, O lord of the people, Vidura became silent;
and Nārada, standing in the midst of the assembly before the Kurus,
surrounded by great ṛṣis, spoke these terrible words.
"In fourteen years from now, the Kauravas shall perish here through the transgression of Duryodhana and by the power of Bhīma and Arjuna.
Having said this, he ascended to heaven and quickly vanished.
Bearing a vast and divine splendor, that best of celestial rishis [departed].
Then, after Pārtha had gone to the forest, those distressed citizens entered the city again like cows deprived of their calves.
The city of Hastināpura, along with its women, servants, and children, became as if joyless, silent, and devoid of celebration;
everyone was despondent, as if afflicted by a disease.
Men, constantly devoted to anxiety and grief regarding the sons of Pṛthā,
gathered here and there and conversed with one another;
and Kuntī, abandoned by all her sons, was deeply afflicted by sorrow.
Just as a cow deprived of her calf laments in great distress,
so did the Kuru elders, devoted to grief and sorrow, become intensely afflicted by anguish when the King of Dharma had departed for the forest.
Then all the citizens remained grieving for the lord of men,
while the Brahmins there engaged in conversations concerning the king.

How indeed does the righteous king dwell in the desolate forest? And how do his younger brothers, and Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Drupada— who though deserving of happiness, dwells in the forest afflicted by sorrow— endure it?
Thus, both the citizens and the Brahmins, together with their wives and sons,
all remembering the Pāṇḍavas, became exceedingly sorrowful;
as if pierced by a weapon, they did not rejoice in any way whatsoever.
Even when addressed, they did not offer any response;
whether by day or by night, without eating or sleeping,
their consciousness was struck by grief and they became as if deprived of their senses.
In the same state of distress that the city of Ayodhyā was formerly when Rāma had gone to the forest, leaving the kingdom behind with Lakṣmaṇa out of sorrow,
this city of Hastināpura has now become distressed in that very same condition.
02,071.031d@044_0026 Vaiśampāyana said: 02,071.031d@044_0026 When Pārtha had departed for the forest out of grief, along with his younger brothers and the kingdom, 02,071.031d@044_0027 [Dhṛtarāṣṭra],
having heard the words of Vidura as well as the speech of the citizens, remained silent.
Out of fear and grief, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his kinsmen, lost his senses.
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala,
regarded Droṇa as their island of refuge and offered him the kingdom.
Then Drona spoke to the impatient Duryodhana,
to Duḥśāsana, to Karṇa, and to all the Bharatas:
"The twice-born say that the Pāṇḍavas are incapable of being slain, for they are the sons of gods."
But as for me, acting according to my strength toward those who have come to me for refuge,
I cannot bring myself to utterly abandon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kings, for they are devoted to me with their whole soul; beyond this, everything has its root in destiny.
"By the very nature of things, the sons of Pāṇḍu, having been defeated, are indeed going to the forest;
those Kauravas shall dwell in the forest for twelve years. Having practiced the vow of celibacy, they will remain under the sway of anger and resentment."
"The Pāṇḍavas will bring back our enmity for my own suffering.
For it was I who, during a dispute between friends, deprived Drupada of his kingdom;
and out of anger, O Bhārata, he performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son to slay me."
Through the power of his sacrificial offerings and ascetic penance, he obtained from the Fire-god a son,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the slender-waisted Draupadī from the midst of the sacrificial altar. Thus,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna became a brother-in-law to the sons of Pṛthā, having entered into a relationship with them.
Because he was so dear to the Pāṇḍavas, fear entered me; [and] because Devadatta— though possessing the color of a flame, armed with a bow, clad in armor, and bearing arrows—
was subject to the nature of a mortal, fear entered me on that account.
For that son of Pṛṣata, that bull among men, has entered into the ranks of their partisans;
he who was the foremost youth Arjuna in the enumeration of Rathas and Atirathas has now surrendered his life. Therefore, I shall fight even more fiercely against your enemies.

O Kauravas, what other sorrow on earth could be more grievous or supreme than this? The word that Dhrishtadyumna is the death of Drona is widely proclaimed; indeed, it was heard for the sake of my own destruction and is exceedingly famous throughout the world.
Surely this turning of the wheel of time has come upon you because of your own actions.
Hasten to do what is beneficial; this matter is not settled by this much alone.
This pleasure lasts but a moment, like the shade of a palm tree in winter.
"Perform great sacrifices, enjoy pleasures, and give gifts;
for in the fourteenth year from now, you shall indeed suffer a great slaughter,
terrifying to the timid."
O mighty-armed Duryodhana!
O Duryodhana, having heard this, act as you desire;
or, if you so think fit, employ conciliation toward the sons of Pāṇḍu.
02,071.046 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Droṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke this:
"The preceptor has spoken rightly, O Kṣattṛ; bring back the Pāṇḍavas."
"Or if they do not turn back, let the Pāṇḍavas go with honor—
my sons, along with their weapons, chariots, and infantry, and possessing all enjoyments.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the sons of Pṛthā had gone to the forest after being defeated at dice,
O great king, anxiety then took possession of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
As King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat there lost in thought, [Vidura approached him].
"O lord of the earth, having obtained this land filled with wealth after banishing the Pāṇḍavas from their kingdom, O King, why do you grieve, sighing and distracted?"— thus said Saṃjaya.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"But how can there be anything not to be grieved for those who will have enmity with the Pāṇḍavas— those who are skilled in battle, possessed of allies, and great chariot-warriors?"
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, this great enmity of yours will result in the destruction of the entire world along with its dependents."
Though he was being restrained by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura,
your son Duryodhana sent word: "Bring Draupadī, the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas and a follower of dharma."
The dull-witted and shameless son of a charioteer, Prātikāmī,
was sent again and again for the sake of Draupadī with the command, "Bring her here.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When the gods ordain defeat for a man, they first withdraw his intelligence; thus he perceives things perversely. When the intellect has become clouded and destruction is at hand, [he acts wrongly].

This improper course, appearing as if it were proper, does not depart from his heart. At the end of his destruction, misfortunes arise in the form of benefits and benefits in the form of misfortunes; and that which is pleasing to him [is what he pursues].
Time does not raise a staff to sever anyone's head;
such is the power of Time that it causes one to perceive things in a distorted way.
This terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising calamity has now been encountered.
By those who dragged the ascetic Pāñcālī into the midst of the assembly—
she whose skin and nails were ruddy, who was dark-complexioned with a face like the full moon,
possessing a pure smile, the daughter of the son of Manu.

Who indeed, save for that wicked gambler, would drag into the midst of the assembly that illustrious Vibhāvarī— who was not born from a womb, who is beautiful, born of noble lineage, and a knower of all duties— only to treat her with contempt?
Seized by her hair, she was crying out like a kurarī bird; a woman of noble form, subject to her menses, drenched in blood,
clad in a single garment, the princess of Pañcāla looked toward the Pāṇḍavas.
Their wealth stolen, their minds shattered, their wives taken, and their prosperity lost; deprived of all their desires and fallen into the power of servitude,
they were bound by the fetters of dharma as if powerless to exert themselves.
To Kṛṣṇā, who was angry, indignant, and suffering in the assembly of the Kurus,
Duryodhana and Karṇa addressed harsh words:
"He would wish to sleep in comfort like a man who has drunk poison."
"O King, all this appears confused to me;
by her piteous eyes, even the earth might be consumed with fire.
O Sañjaya, will any remnant of my sons remain today?"
All the women of the Bharatas, gathered together with Gāndhārī,
let out a terrible cry there upon seeing Kṛṣṇā brought into the assembly hall. O bull of the Bharata race, a jackal howled there at that excellent woman.
Gathering together with their subjects, they constantly grieve for their most righteous and lawful wife, who was endowed with beauty and youth; there,
seeing the fierce jackal, he let out a terrifying cry.
In the evening, the *agnihotra* sacrifices were not performed anywhere;
the Brahmins were enraged by the dragging away of Draupadī,
and a terrible clamor arose along with a great atmospheric thunderclap.
Terrible celestial meteors fell, and Rāhu swallowed the sun out of season,
producing a most horrific fear among living beings;
likewise, fire burst forth within the chariot-sheds.
And the banners of the Bharatas fell to pieces for their misfortune;
at Duryodhana’s *agnihotra* sacrifice, jackals howled with terrifying cries,
and from every direction, donkeys brayed in response to them.
Then Bhīṣma set forth together with Droṇa, O Sañjaya,
as did Kṛpa, Somadatta, and the great car-warrior Bāhlīka.
Then, urged by Vidura, I spoke there.
"I shall grant a boon to Kṛṣṇā, whatever she desires. Thereupon, the princess of Pañcāla chose the Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess;
and I have granted permission for them to depart with their chariots and their bows.
Then the highly wise Vidura, who knew all dharmas, said:
"O Bharatas, this is your end, that Krishna was brought into the assembly hall. She is the daughter of the King of Pañcāla; she is unsurpassed prosperity."
This Pāñcālī approaches these Pāṇḍavas as if impelled by fate;
the sons of Pṛthā, being exceedingly intolerant, will not forgive her suffering,
nor will the Vṛṣṇis, those great archers, or the Pāñcālas of mighty energy.
Protected by Vāsudeva, who is devoted to truth,
Bībhatsu will arrive, well-guarded by the Pāñcālas;
in their midst is the great archer Bhīmasena, possessed of mighty strength.
He will come, brandishing his mace like the Staff of Death itself. Then,
upon hearing the roar of the wise Pārtha’s Gāṇḍīva bow and the force of Bhīma’s mace, the lords of men will not be able to endure it.
In this matter, it always pleases me not to have conflict with the sons of Pṛthā;
for I consider the Pāṇḍavas to be always more powerful than the Kurus.
For instance, King Jarāsaṃdha was mighty and possessed of great splendor.
Slain in battle by Bhīma with a mere blow of his arm,
let there be peace for you with the Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bharatas;
let that which is appropriate for both sides be done without hesitation.

"O Great King, by acting thus you shall attain the highest good. O Gāvalgaṇi, although the Steward (Vidura) spoke these words consistent with dharma and artha, they were not accepted by me out of my desire for the welfare of my son.
Beyond this, the third great section, the Āraṇyaka, should be known; this verse is proclaimed as its introductory link (pratisaṃdhi). [It concerns] Janamejaya.
O best of the twice-born, thus were the sons of Pṛthā defeated at dice and provoked to anger by the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their ministers through deceit;
this enumeration was told according to the truth in the Sabhā Parva by one of enlightened intellect.
The chapters here should be known to be seventy-two in number; likewise,
two thousand five hundred and ninety verses are proclaimed in this book.
And thus thirty-three episodes were narrated by the Great-Souled One;
all this, the Sabhā Parva, has been explained by the supreme Ṛṣi.
All this, the Sabhā Parva, has been recounted by me, O great Ṛṣis.
The chapters here should be known by number to be seventy-two;
and two thousand seven hundred and eleven verses are proclaimed in this section.
On this celebrated festival, the gift of juices should be performed;
there, fruits should be given according to one's means. The number of chapters to be known here is seventy-two.
Two thousand five hundred and eleven verses are proclaimed in this Parvan;
beyond this, the great Āraṇyaka, the third [book], is to be known.
O Indra among kings, during the Sabhā Parvan, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (haviṣya) provided with cakes (apūpa), fried cakes (pūpa), and sweetmeats (modaka);
then, having obtained roots and fruits, as well as milk-rice (pāyasa) with honey and clarified butter.
O King, during the Āstīka-parvan, one should feed the twice-born and give them rice with jaggery (*guḍodana*),
provided with cakes (*apūpa*), fried pastries (*pūpa*), and sweetmeats (*modaka*).
O Indra among kings, during the Sabhā-parvan, one should feed the twice-born sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
Whoever should constantly listen to this well-determined Sabhā-parvan,
for that person there shall never, anywhere, or at any time, arise any affliction.
Following the Sabhā-parvan, the Vanaparva is properly proclaimed.
The narrative of the eighteen Purāṇas is recounted therein in great detail;
by the mere hearing of which, human beings do not fall into delusion. Having crossed over suffering and attained steadfastness, a person shall reach his own true state.
Neither separation nor sorrow arises for me in any way whatsoever.
The beginning is the assembly hall; then the Virāṭa forest and the effort [of the cattle recovery].
Whether it is poorly composed or well-composed, no fault is found in me.
The Bhīṣma-parvan, the Guru-parvan, the Ravija-parvan, the Śalya-parvan,
the Sauptika-parvan, the Strī-parvan, the Śānti-parvan, the Anuśāsana-parvan, the Aśvamedha-parvan, the Vyāsāśrama-parvan, the Muśala-parvan, the Māhāprasthānika-parvan, and the Svargārohaṇa-parvan.
The virtuous ought to forgive the faults committed by the hand;
whatever may be missing in syllables or words, or lacking in prosodic measures,
I have written exactly as I saw it in the manuscript.
Whether it be unbound or well-bound, no fault of mine is found;
I go for refuge to that unborn and eternal Hari, by whose remembrance one becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness.
Whatever activity I perform constantly through deed, mind, or speech,
may it be directed straight toward the propitiation of Keśava, even throughout birth after birth.
